en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Second Fifty of the Middle Collection (Majjhimanikāya)
1. The Chapter on Devadaha.
1. The Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Devadaha Sutta. In that context, "Devadaha by name": kings are called "devas."
And there was a beautiful, well-guarded auspicious lotus pond belonging to the Śākya kings; because it was the lake of the gods (*deva*), it became known as "Devadaha.
Taking its name from that, the town itself came to be designated as Devadaha.
The Blessed One dwelt in the Lumbinī Grove depending on that town. All of this is due to causes made in the past.
"Due to conditions consisting of actions performed in the past. By this, he shows that they reject both karmic feeling and functional feeling, and accept only one:
resultant feeling. "These, monks, are the Nigaṇṭhas who speak thus"—by this, he shows that what was previously stated without specification is now being specified.
"‘Did we exist?’—the Blessed One asks this, knowing full well their state of ignorance, solely with the intention of bringing forward the teaching on the Kali age.
For how could those who do not even know ‘we existed’ understand whether an action was done or not done? The same principle applies to the subsequent questions as well."

2. “*Evaṃ sante*”: in the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta*, this refers to the statement of Mahānigaṇṭha being true; here, however, the meaning is that while such a state of affairs exists, it remains unknown to you.
“*Na kallaṃ*”: it is not fitting, it is not appropriate. 3. “*Gāḷhūpalepanena*”: by means of a thick coating, repeatedly smeared with lac, but not as if plastered with lime.
“*Esaniyā*”: by means of a probe, even down to a mere thread of cloth. “*Eseyya*”: [it would] penetrate deeply.
Or one might examine it while it is turned face up. "Agadaṅgāra" refers to the powder of *jhāma-harītakī* or *āmalaka*.
"Odaheyya" means one would throw [it] in. "Arogo" and so forth have already been stated in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
"Even so," in this context, the correlation with the simile is as follows: for one who has been pierced by an arrow, at the time of being pierced, there is pain.
The time when these [sufferings] become manifest may be like the time when one knows: "We existed in the past, or we did not; we performed evil karma, or we did not;
or we performed such-and-such evil. It is like the time when the sensation becomes manifest during the four stages of cutting open the wound's opening and so forth:
"So much of our suffering has been exhausted, or when so much has been exhausted..."
There may be a time of knowing: "All suffering indeed will be worn away; we shall be called those established in the pure end.
At a later stage, like the time of knowing well-being, there may be a time of knowing for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states in this very life.
Thus, in this context, three meanings are conveyed by a single simile.
A single meaning is illustrated by means of four similes.

Yet these people do not understand even one of them; like a man who has been struck by an arrow that has already passed through him, and who—without having been pierced at all—produces the perception "I have been pierced" merely on the authority of his enemy's words saying "You are pierced," and thus falls into suffering.
Merely believing all this on the authority of Mahānigaṇṭha’s word alone,
they were thus rebuked by the Blessed One with the simile of the thorn; being unable to offer a reply, they were like a weak dog that,
having roused a deer and turned it toward its master, retreats itself— so too did they leave the debate at Mahānigaṇṭha’s head.
As they were inserting [the words], they said, "Friend, the Nigaṇṭha," and so forth.
Then the Blessed One, rebuking them along with their teacher, said, "These five indeed... and so on.

In that context, "of the venerable ones" (*āyasmantānaṃ*) refers to those venerable ones regarding those five qualities. "Faith in the Teacher who teaches the past" (*atītaṃsa-satthari saddhā*) means faith in the one who propounds the past.
"Faith in the Teacher": What is this faith of yours, who believe in the doctrine of the past, regarding that Great Nigaṇṭha?
Is it based on what is real or what is unreal? Is it a result of what is real or a result of what is unreal? He asks this. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means with reason and cause. "A rebuttal of the doctrine" means a counter-argument.
To this extent, he demonstrates their so-called "doctrine of destroying faith," which says:

"Remove faith; it is the weakest of all. 6. "By ignorance" means by the lack of knowledge (*aññāṇa*) regarding ignorance (*avijjā*). "By delusion" means by confusion (*sammoha*). "Believe perversely" means believe erroneously, or grasp with a distorted perception (*vipallāsaggāha*); such is the meaning. 7.
"To be experienced in the present life" means yielding its result (*vipāka*) in this very selfhood (*attabhāva*). "By means" means by way of application (*payoga*).
"By exertion" means by energy (*vīriya*). "To be experienced in the future life" means that which yields its result in either the second or third personal existence.
"To be experienced as pleasant" refers to wholesome karma that yields a result consisting of desirable objects. The opposite is "to be experienced as painful.

"To be experienced when fully matured" means to be experienced in a personal existence that has already reached maturity and been produced; this is synonymous with "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
This is a designation. "To be experienced when the personal existence is not yet matured" means that which is to be experienced in an immature state of being;
this is a synonym for "to be experienced in a future life. Even so, there is this distinction here:

that which is performed in the first stage of life yields its result either in the first stage, the middle stage, or the final stage; and that which is performed in the middle stage [yields its result] in the middle stage... [or the final stage].

Or it gives its result in the final stage of life; or that which is performed in the final stage of life gives its result right there—that is called "to be experienced in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
However, that which gives its result within seven days is called "to be experienced upon ripening" (*paripakkavedanīya*);
that is both wholesome and unwholesome.
In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that a poor man named Puṇṇa lived in Rājagaha depending on the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi.
One day, when the city was proclaiming the festival of the constellations, the merchant said to him:
“If you will plow today, you shall receive two oxen and a plow. Why do you indulge in the festival? Will you plow?”
"What is the use of my star? I shall plow," he thought. "In that case, take whichever oxen you wish and plow," [the Buddha] said.
He went to plow. On that day, the Elder Sāriputta, having emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), reflected, "Whom shall I assist?
Seeing Puṇṇa, he took his bowl and robes and went to the place where he was plowing. Puṇṇa set aside his plow and—
Having given the elder a tooth-stick, she gave him water for rinsing the mouth.
The elder, having attended to his body, sat down not far from the workplace, waiting for the delivery of his meal.
Then, seeing his wife bringing the food, he revealed himself right on the path.
She took the food brought by her husband, placed it into the Elder’s bowl, and having returned home again, she prepared another meal and went out during the day.
After Puṇṇa had plowed once, he sat down. She too, taking the food, was coming along and said:
"Master, your meal was brought to you early this morning; however, on the way, I saw the Elder Sāriputta..."
“‘Having given that to him, while I was cooking and bringing another meal, the sun has set; do not be angry, Master. ‘It is well done by you, dear lady.
This morning I gave the Elder tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth; he has consumed our very alms-food.
Today we have become partakers of the merit of the ascetic’s duty performed by the Elder. Thus she thought.”
He bestowed his favor upon it. A single furrowed plot became pure gold.
Having finished his meal, he looked at the furrowed plot and, seeing it shining, stood up and struck it with a staff.
Recognizing its state as red gold, he thought, "It is not possible to enjoy this without telling the king," and went to inform the king. The king had all of it brought back by means of carts.
Having caused a heap [of gold] to be made in the king’s courtyard, he asked, “Who in this city possesses as much gold as this?
When it was said that no one had any, he granted him the status of a *seṭṭhi*. He became known by the name Puṇṇaseṭṭhi.
There is another story: in that same city of Rājagaha, there was a poor man named Kāḷaveḷiya. His wife—
She cooked a gruel of green leaves and sour gruel. The Elder Mahākassapa, having emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), reflected, "Whom shall I assist?
Seeing her, he went and stood at the door of her house. She took his bowl, placed everything inside it, and gave it to the Elder.
The Elder went to the monastery and presented it to the Teacher. The Teacher [ate] just enough for his own sustenance.
He took it, and the remainder was sufficient for the five hundred monks. Kāḷavaḷiya also arrived at that place and received a small portion.
Mahākassapa asked the Teacher about the karmic result for Kāḷavaḷiya. The Teacher said, "On the seventh day from now, he will receive the parasol of a guild-president.
Having heard this report, Kāḷavaḷiya went and informed his wife.
And at that time, as the king was wandering through the city, he saw a man sitting on a living stake outside the city.
When the man saw the king, he raised a loud cry, saying, “Your Majesty, send me some food to eat!
The king said, “I shall send it,” and when the evening meal had been brought, he remembered and said, “Find someone capable of carrying this.”
He said, "In the city, they circulated a proclamation for a thousand pieces of gold. On the third occasion, Kāḷavaḷiya’s wife seized it.
Then they presented her to the king; she assumed the guise of a man, equipped herself with the five weapons, took a bowl of food, and departed from the city.
Outside the city, a yakkha named Dīghatāla, who dwelt in a palm tree, [stood] at the foot of that tree."
Seeing her going along, he said, "Stop! Stop! You are my food! She replied, "I am not your food; I am a king’s messenger. "Where are you going? he asked.
"To the presence of the man sitting upon the spit," she said. "Will you be able to carry a message for me as well?
he asked. "Yes, I shall be able to," she replied. [She then spoke: "The wife of Dīghatāla, the daughter of King Sumanadeva..."
“Kālī has given birth to a son,” you should announce. “At the base of this *tāla* tree there are seven jars of treasure;
you may take them. She went along, proclaiming, “Kālī, the wife of Dīghatāla and daughter of King Sumanadeva, has given birth to a son.
Hearing this while seated in the assembly of *yakkhas*, Sumanadeva thought, “A certain person is bringing us news of our beloved.”
Having heard the command, “Summon him!,” the man became confident and said, “I give you the treasure jars located in the area where the circular shade of this tree extends.
The man sitting on the spit, after eating his meal, realized at the moment of wiping his mouth that it was a woman’s touch;
he bit her on the crest-lock. She cut off her own crest-lock with a sword and went straight to the presence of the king.
"She has gone. "How is it to be known that the king is eating his meal? Having said, "By the small sign," she explained it to the king and had that wealth brought forth.
The king thought, "Is there another who possesses such great wealth? "There is none, Your Majesty," they replied.
The king made her husband the foremost wealthy man in that city. The story of Queen Mallikā should also be told.
These, then, are the bases for wholesome karma.
However, the young man Nanda misconducted himself with the elder nun Uppalavaṇṇā;
as he rose from his bed and went out, the great earth split open and gave him way, and right there he entered the great hell. So too did Nanda.
A butcher, having practiced the work of slaughtering cattle for fifty years, once failed to obtain meat at mealtime.
On that day, he cut out the tongue of a living ox, roasted it over coals, and began to eat it.
Then, his own tongue was severed at the root and fell right into his bowl of rice; crying out in agony, he died and was reborn in hell.

The yakkha Nanda, while traveling through the air with another yakkha, saw the Elder Sāriputta sitting in the open air during the night with his hair recently shorn. Desiring to strike him on the head, he informed the other yakkha;
but even though he was restrained by him, he struck out, crying out "I am burning! I am burning! and fell to the ground right there.
"Having entered, one is reborn in the Great Hell"—these are the bases for unwholesome kamma.
Furthermore, whatever kamma—even if performed as close as the moment of death—yields its result in another existence, all that is called "to be experienced in the next life" (*samparāyavedanīya*).
Among these, that which will arise as the result of a meditative absorption (*jhāna*) not lost is...

Here, it is stated that this is the resultant [consciousness] produced in the present life. Its root-cause, the kamma, is neither to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) nor in a future life (*samparāyavedanīya*);

though this has not been specifically analyzed, it should nevertheless be understood as being exclusively to be experienced in a future life. That which is the resultant attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) in another existence for those who have attained the first path and so forth, is here—

It is simply called "the quality that has arisen. Although it is stated thus, it should nevertheless be understood that the work of the path is to be experienced after maturation (*paripakkavedanīya*).
For it is the volition of the path alone that yields fruit most swiftly, because its fruit is immediate (*anantaraphala*).

8. "To be experienced much" (*bahavedanīya*) refers to that which leads to the state of non-perception (*asaññabhava*). "To be experienced little" (*appavedanīya*) refers to that which leads to the state of non-perception. "To be experienced fully" (*savedanīya*)...
“Kamma with result” means kamma that has ripening. “Not to be experienced” means kamma without ripening.

“This being so” means when, despite the effort applied toward these types of kamma—such as those to be experienced in the present life—there is no obtaining of the cause for their becoming [kamma] to be experienced in future lives. “Fruitless” means without result, without purpose.
Having thus far shown the fruitlessness of the effort within a teaching that does not lead to liberation, [the author presents] the doctrine of the cutting off of striving.

It should be understood that this is what is meant by "named. "Discourses and reproaches from fellow-followers" means the discourses and reproaches of the Nigaṇṭhas which, being accompanied by reasons, arise through the reasons stated by others.
"They come to a ground of censure" means they come to a ground that is to be censured by the wise.
There is also a reading: "vādānuppattā gārayhaṭṭhānā," the meaning of which is: [grounds of censure] arising through the discourse stated by others.

Because they have approached the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas with its causal basis, they come to be criticized on ten grounds, such as "those who perform evil deeds," "those who cause that doctrine to wither and fade," and so forth. 9.

"Due to the cause of association" means due to the reason of fixed destiny (*niyati*). "Evil associates" refers to those whose destiny is evil. "Due to the cause of birth" refers to the sixfold cause of birth (*abhijāti*).

10. Having thus shown the fruitlessness of the Nigaṇṭhas’ exertion, he now spoke the words beginning with “And how, monks,” in order to show the fruitfulness of exertion and energy within the liberating teaching.
In that context, *anaddhabhūtaṃ* means “not overcome. The human state is called “not overcome by suffering”; one does not cause it to become overcome (*addhabhāveti*).
The meaning is "he does not overcome. Even one who incites others to various kinds of self-mortification is said to be "overwhelmed by suffering.
However, those who have gone forth in the Dispensation and become forest-dwellers, dwellers at the foot of trees, and so forth, are not overwhelmed by suffering.
For in the Dispensation that leads to liberation, energy is indeed called right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).

But the Elder said: "One who is reborn in a family of lords, having become seven years old, adorned and prepared, sitting on his father's lap while the Saṅgha of monks is seated after finishing their meal and is offering a blessing—such a person, by displaying the three kinds of success and proclaiming the Truths, attains Arahantship;
or else, when told by his parents, 'Will you go forth?'"
When addressed with "Father!", he replied, "Yes, I shall go forth. Having been bathed and adorned, he was led to the monastery;
there, after learning the Five Skins (*tacapañcaka*), he sat down and attained *arahantship* at the very moment his hair was being shaved off at the razor's edge.

Or else, as one newly ordained, having eaten on the following day the food and rice porridge sent by his parents, with his head still anointed with red arsenic oil (*manosilā-tela*), [he attained the goal].
One who attains *arahantship* while simply sitting in a monastery is said not to have "exalted himself through hardship.

This, however, is the highest form of honor. On the other hand, there is one born from the womb of a slave-girl, who—even after being adorned with a silver ring and having his body anointed with as much as a mere *goraka-piyaṅgu* [pigment], is led away on the very day of his shaving or the following day with the words, "Ordain him!"
Or he attains Arahatship; this too is called "not making oneself overwhelmed by suffering.
"Righteous happiness" (*dhammikaṃ sukhaṃ*) refers to the happiness arising from the four requisites through the Saṅgha or a group.
"Uninfatuated" (*anadhimucchito*) means not infatuated by the intoxication of craving. For one should not form an attachment there, thinking, "I will not give up righteous happiness."

For one who, having received from the Saṅgha either a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*) or a rainy-season residence gift (*vassāvāsika*), uses it within the midst of the Saṅgha among the monks after determining, "This is for this purpose," he grows through virtue, concentration, insight, the path, and the fruit—like a lotus in the middle of a bowl.
"Of this" means of the five present aggregates which have become its root. "Of the source of suffering" means...
[It is] because of craving; for that is the source of the suffering of the five aggregates. "Exerting effort" means making the energy associated [with the path].
"Dispassion arises" means dispassion arises through the Path. This is what is meant:
"By this exertion of effort, dispassion for this source of suffering arises for me"—thus he understands. By this, it is shown that the practice is pleasant and the direct knowledge is swift.
It has been explained. In the second section, the mode of neutrality of that associated energy is explained. Regarding the phrase "for whichever [person] indeed":
this is the summarized meaning—such a person, for whatever source of suffering there is, through the exertion regarding formations (*saṅkhāra-padhāna*), experiences fading away (*virāga*);
he exerts himself toward that formation, and he exerts himself through the exertion regarding the path (*magga-padhāna*). But for whatever source of suffering...
For one who looks on with equanimity and develops equanimity, there is fading away; he develops equanimity therein;
he develops it through the cultivation of the path. "Of him" means of that person.
"One whose mind is bound" means one whose mind is fettered by desire and lust. "Intense desire" means abundant desire. "Intense equanimity" means...
“Of intense longing. “Standing together” means standing on one side. “Laughing aloud” means laughing with a loud laugh.
“Chattering” means making a smile.
“In the same way, monks,” here this is the illustration of the simile: for just as a certain man [might act] toward a certain woman...
Being infatuated with her, he gave her food, clothing, garlands, ornaments, and so forth, and kept her in his house. She, having transgressed against him, served another man.
He thought, "Surely I am not showing her the honor she deserves," and so he increased her honors. Yet she continued to transgress even more excessively.
He thought, "Even while being honored, this woman continues to transgress; while living in my house, she is bringing me harm."
Having made her a person to be spoken to with sufficient authority in the midst of the assembly, saying, "I shall expel you," he dismissed her, telling her, "Do not enter the house again.
Being unable to establish an intimacy with him by any means, she wandered about with actors, dancers, and the like.
When that man saw her in such a state, no dejection arose in him; rather, joy arose.
In this context, the time when the man is infatuated with the woman is like the monk’s attachment to his own personal existence (attabhāva).
The time when, having provided food, clothing, and so forth, he causes her to dwell in the house is like the time of tending to that personal existence.

The time when she commits adultery is like the afflicted state of that very personal existence being tended to, due to the provocation of bile and other humors. “In accordance with oneself... [and so forth].
Having observed that "she transgresses when she receives no honor," one should regard it as a time for increasing honor;
having observed that "it becomes thus when one receives no medicine," it is a time for preparing medicine.

Just as there may be a further transgression even when honor has increased, so too, when medicine is prepared for one among the humors such as bile, there is again a state of illness due to the provocation of the remaining ones. In the midst of the assembly...

Having made it a matter of no further discussion—like being driven out from one's home—one reaches a state of indifference toward that [world], thinking: "Now I am neither your slave nor your laborer;
throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), I wandered about attending only to you; what use have I for you? Let it be cut or let it be broken!
Having thus made one's energy firm, one effects the eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*) by means of the Path. [This is not achieved] by means of dancing, acting, and so forth.

Just as that man, upon seeing her dancing and moving about, does not experience dejection but experiences only joy, even so, when this bhikkhu—who has attained arahantship—sees his own physical body afflicted by the disturbance of bile and other humors, he does not experience dejection;
rather, he thinks: "Ah, may I be released from the suffering of maintaining the aggregates!"
"Only joy arises. This simile, however, shows that by knowing "sorrow arises for one whose mind is bound, but not for one whose mind is unbound," one abandons desire and lust for a woman;
likewise, this bhikkhu abandons the source of suffering when he exerts himself toward formations or develops equanimity, and not otherwise.
It should be understood that [this passage] has come down to explain this meaning: "Having understood both of these, one who accomplishes them abandons the source of suffering.
12. "So that I may dwell in happiness" means: by whatever happiness I desire to dwell, [may there be] for me while dwelling [in that way].
"Exerting" means: of one who is striving. And herein, for one to whom a pleasant practice is unsuitable, even while wearing fine robes...
The mind of one dwelling in a pleasant lodging becomes distracted; for such a person, the practice is painful though suitable.

But for one who wears coarse robes that are torn and tattered, and who dwells in charnel grounds, at the foot of trees, and so forth, the mind becomes one-pointed. It is with reference to this that it was said.
"In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: for the yogi is like the fletcher, being afraid of birth, aging, and death.
It should be viewed as follows: crooked, bent, and warped mental states are like a crooked, bent, and warped reed; bodily and mental energy are like two firebrands;
faith is like the rice-gruel oil used by one straightening a reed; and the supramundane path is like the bending-stick.
Just as one who is making an effort straightens a crooked, bent, and warped reed by lubricating it with rice-gruel oil, heating it over firebrands, and [bending it] with a bending-stick...

Just as the straightening of an arrow— having softened its crooked, curved, and bent nature with heat and then heating it with physical and mental effort to straighten it by means of the supramundane path—
so too, for this practitioner, having straightened the mass of defilements with the mind thus straightened, there is the piercing of the enemy and the enjoyment of the attainment,
just as the fletcher pierces his target with the arrow thus straightened and experiences success.

Having pierced through [the obstacles], one should see the experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) for one who has reached the summit of cessation while staying in a delightful lodging.
Here, the Tathāgata has described the practices of a bhikkhu with a pleasant path and quick direct knowledge, as well as a bhikkhu with a painful path and sluggish direct knowledge;
he did not describe those of the other two. He began this teaching in order to explain them.

When these two [paths] have been explained, the other has also effectively been explained; however, the path leading to arrival (*āgamanīya-paṭipadā*) has not yet been told, and he began this teaching in order to explain it.

Alternatively, the path leading to arrival has indeed been explained along with [the other paths], but by showing one instance of a Buddha’s appearance that was not previously shown, he [concludes] the teaching on the renunciation of a son of good family through [the attainment of] Arahatship.
He began this teaching in order to show that he would turn [them] back. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the commentary on the Devadaha Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
2. Commentary on the *Pañcattaya-sutta* 21.
Thus have I heard: this is the *Pañcattaya-sutta*. Therein, "some" (*eke*) means certain ones. "Ascetics and brahmins" (*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*):

they are ascetics by virtue of having gone forth into homelessness, and brahmins by birth; or they are so designated as "ascetics" and "brahmins" by the world. [They speculate about] the future limit (*aparanta*).

They are "speculators about the future" (*aparantakappika*) because they grasp [theories] after having imagined and deliberated upon the future. Alternatively, they are "speculators about the future" because the speculation about the future belongs to them.
And here, "end" (*anta*)—as in such passages as, "Friends, identity (*sakkāya*) is one end"—intends a "portion" or "limit.
"Speculation" (*kappa*) refers to craving and views. For this has also been said: "In brief, there are two kinds of speculation..."

“Speculation based on craving and speculation based on views. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: they are called "speculators about the future" because they remain having speculated about the portion of the aggregates belonging to the future by way of craving and views.

Since their views follow after the future alone—by way of arising again and again for those who remain having thus speculated about the future—they are called "those whose views follow after the future" (aparantānudiṭṭhino).

Holding such views, and relying upon and depending on that [speculation about] the future limit (*aparanta*), they cause other people as well to fall into speculative views and assert various kinds of designative terms (*adhivuttipada*). "Various kinds" means of many sorts.
"Designative terms" means terms of designation. Alternatively, having overwhelmed a real fact, [they speak] contrary to its true nature.
Because they proceed by grasping [objects], views are called "adhivuttis"; "adhivuttipadāni" means words that express views—phrases that indicate views is the meaning.
"Saññī" means one possessing perception. "Arogo" means permanent. "Ittheke" means some [say] thus; the meaning is "some [say] in this way. By this...

Sixteen theories of perception (*saññīvāda*) have been stated; by the term "non-perceiving" (*asaññī*), eight theories of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*) are included; by the term "neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving" (*nevasaññīnāsaññī*), eight theories of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are included;
and by the phrase "or when a being exists" (*sato vā pana sattassa*), seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) are included.

In this context, "existing" (*sato*) means of one who is present. "Annihilation" (*uccheda*) means cutting off. "Destruction" (*vināsa*) means non-appearance. "Cessation of existence" (*vibhava*) means the disappearance of becoming.
All of these are merely synonyms for one another. By the phrase "nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*), the five theories of nibbāna in the present life are stated.
In this context, "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to a directly perceived phenomenon;

it is a designation for the individual existence (*attabhāva*) obtained here and there. Nibbāna in the present life means nibbāna within the present life—that is, the subsiding of suffering within this very individual existence.

Meaning: "Existing" (*santaṃ*) means existing in three ways, by way of [the triad] beginning with "one who perceives" (*saññī*). "There are three" means: one is the "existing self" (*santa-atta*) through the [formula] beginning with "one who perceives is the self" (*saññī attā*);
the other two are the remaining [formulas]. Thus, there are three. 22.

"Possessing form" (*rūpiṃ vā*) means possessing form either by way of the physical body (*karaja-rūpa*) or by way of the *kasiṇa*-form. Therein, one who has attained [the *kasiṇa*] takes the *kasiṇa*-form as "self."
The rationalist grasps both types of form as well. "Immaterial" refers either to the sign of the immaterial attainment or to the remaining immaterial phenomena excluding the aggregate of perception;
those who designate these as "self"—both those who have attained them and the rationalists—designate them in this way.
However, the third view proceeds by way of grasping a mixture [of the two], while the fourth proceeds solely by way of grasping through reasoning. In the second tetrad:
It should be understood that the first view is explained by way of one who has attained meditative absorption (jhāna); the second view, by way of one who has not attained absorption;
the third view, by way of the preliminary work for the kasiṇa using either a small measure of oil or a small measure of a saucer;
and the fourth view, by way of the extensive kasiṇa.
Alternatively, the phrase "those who have transcended" (*upātivattanta*) refers, in brief, to those who have gone beyond the "seven perceptions" mentioned by the word "perception" (*saññī*).
Others say there are eight. Both of these will be made clear later. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here:
for some are able to transcend these seven or eight perceptions, while others are not.

In that regard, only those who are able are included. Among them, for some who are able to transcend—that is, to go beyond—it is just as when, among people who have crossed the Ganges, one might stop after reaching a long irrigation channel, while another stops further on at a great village;
even so, some, having stated that the base of infinite consciousness is immeasurable and imperturbable, remain there.
Some [attain] the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). To first demonstrate the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) therein, it is said:
"Some [meditate on] the consciousness-kasina. Later, he will say: "Some [attain] the base of nothingness.

"This, indeed" means this very thing which is a course of view (*diṭṭhigata*), a condition for views, and an object of views. "The Tathāgata directly knows" means: by means of this condition, this [result] arises.
"Vision is grasped" means he knows by means of highly distinguished knowledge.
Now, explaining that very point in detail, he said, "Those which, venerable sirs," and so forth.
"Or whatever perceptions of these"—that is, whatever perceptions of these [perceptions] have been spoken of as "if there are perceptions of form. "Pure" means free from defilements.

"Supreme" means most excellent. "Foremost" means best. "It is declared as incomparable" means it is described as having no equal. By the phrase "if perceptions of form," the four perceptions of the fine-material sphere are spoken of.
By the phrase "if perceptions of the formless," the perceptions of the base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness are meant.

Furthermore, by the other two phrases, the section on those who have attained meditative absorption and the section on those who have not attained absorption are spoken of; thus these [perceptions] are [described].

From the perspective of their divisions, there are eight; however, from the perspective of their meaning, there are seven types of perception (*saññā*). For the section on those who have attained meditative absorption is already included within the preceding six. And this is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*);
all these categories of perception, together with the categories of views (*diṭṭhigata*), are conditioned, having been produced by the coming together of conditions.
It is "gross" (*oḷārika*) precisely because it is conditioned. Furthermore, there is indeed a cessation of conditioned formations (*saṅkhārānaṃ nirodho*).
Furthermore, there exists for these conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) which have been described as "conditioned," that which is called Nibbāna, characterized by cessation.
"Having known that 'this exists'" means having understood that this Nibbāna indeed exists.
"One who sees its escape" means one who sees the escape from those conditioned things, one who sees Nibbāna. "The Tathāgata has transcended that."
"Transcended that which is conditioned" means he has completely passed beyond it. 23.

"Therein" refers to those eight views concerning non-perception (*asaññīvāda*). "Possessing form" (*rūpī*) and so forth should be understood according to the same method explained under the views concerning perception (*saññīvāda*).
And because this is a view concerning non-perception, the second tetrad is not mentioned here. "They reject" means they oppose.

They refute [the following]. In the passage beginning with "perception is a disease," it is a "disease" (*roga*) in the sense of being an affliction, a "boil" (*gaṇḍa*) in the sense of being corrupt, and an "arrow" (*salla*) in the sense of having pierced [into the heart].

In the passage beginning with "coming or going," there is "coming" by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), "going" by way of death (*cuti*), "death" by way of passing away, "rebirth" by way of arising, and [growth] by way of arising again and again and increasing further and further.

[It leads to] growth, increase, and abundance. While it is true that in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*) consciousness can occur even without material form (*rūpa*), in the remaining [existences] it cannot occur without the other three aggregates (*khandha*).
However, this question was posed with reference to five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).
For in the five-aggregate existence, there is no occurrence of consciousness whatsoever without these many aggregates. Thus says the Vitanda-vadin.

Here, however, one might say: "Because of the statement 'except for form' and so forth, there is form even in the formless realm, and consciousness exists in the non-percipient realm, as well as for one who has attained the attainment of cessation. He should be told:

"If you interpret the meaning based on the mere shadow of the phrasing, then because of the statement 'or it goes to its destination' and so forth, that consciousness goes by flying up, like birds with two or four feet."
He would thus fall into the position that one travels even on foot, and that one grows like a cow's horn or a creeper.

Furthermore, regarding the three realms of existence (*bhava*) taught by the Blessed One in hundreds of suttas, because of the non-existence of the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), they would result in only two.
Therefore, do not speak thus; retain the meaning exactly as it was stated.

24. "Therein" (*tatra*) is the locative case used in reference to the eight views concerning neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*). Here too, the phrases beginning with "one who is material" (*rūpim vā*) should be understood according to the method already explained.
"Non-perception is delusion" (*asaññā sammoho*): this state of being without perception is indeed a ground for delusion.

For they say that one who knows nothing at all is "one without perception. "By means of the mere formations of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized" (*diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabba-saṅkhāramattena*): by means of the mere [objects] cognized through what is seen.

"By means of the mere cognizable through what is heard and the mere cognizable through what is sensed. And here, "cognizable" (*viññātabba*) means "that which one cognizes"; thus, the meaning here is:

"by means of the mere occurrence of perception through the five doors, [consisting of] the mere cognizable through what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. "By means of the mere formations" (*saṅkhāramattena*) means "by means of the occurrence of gross formations"—this is the meaning.
"Of this base" (*etassa āyatanassa*) refers to this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Attainment" (*upasampada*) means acquisition.
"Calamity is the cause" means that this is destruction; "emergence is the cause" is the meaning.
For one must enter that attainment after having made the occurrence of the five-door perceptions or the occurrence of gross formations non-occurrence.
He shows that emergence from it occurs through their occurrence. It is declared that what is to be attained is the attainment of formations, by means of the occurrence of gross formations.
"It is not declared that it is to be attained. "To be attained by the attainment with a residue of formations" means:
those formations which, through the process of development, have reached a state of extreme subtlety as the very residue of formations;

the meaning is that this [state] is to be attained through the occurrence of such formations. For when such formations are occurring, this is indeed called "to be attained. "That indeed" (tad idam) refers to that.
Although this is subtle, it is conditioned; and because it is conditioned, it is gross. 25.
"Therein" refers to the seven doctrines of annihilationism. "Above" means they remember what is above;
the meaning is that they remember the doctrine of future saṃsāra. "They assert attachment alone" means they speak only of clinging.
“Āsatta” is also a reading; the meaning is that it refers to craving itself. “Thus, having passed away, we shall become” means:
“Having passed away, we shall become. One should apply the method here as follows: “We shall become khattiyas,” “we shall become brahmins. “They appear to me like merchants” means:
they appear to me like merchants, resembling merchants, similar to merchants. “From the fear of self-identity” (sakkāyabhaya).
Out of fear of personal existence (*sakkāya*). For it has been said: "Great King, there are four who fear what is not to be feared.
Which four? Great King, the earth-worm does not eat the earth out of fear, thinking, 'Lest the earth be exhausted.
Great King, the crane stands on one leg, thinking, 'Lest the earth sink down. Great King, the *kikī* bird..."

"She lies on her back, thinking, 'May my mother not be wetted!'—Great King, one who lives the holy life according to the Dhamma of a Brahmin does not practice it thinking, 'May the world not be cut off.
These four fear what they have no reason to fear; thus they fear *sakkāya* (personality).
"Disgusted with *sakkāya*" means being thoroughly disgusted with that very *sakkāya* consisting of the three realms. "Like a dog tied by a leash."

A dog tied by inserting a rope through its nose: in this context, the "personality" (*sakkāya*), which consists of the phenomena of the three planes, should be seen as being like a sturdy pillar or a stake; the one possessed of wrong views is like the dog;
the view is like the leash; and craving is like the rope. [It is like] a dog bound with a leather thong and tethered to a pillar or a stake.

The "running around" of one who has been bound by the rope of craving—which has been inserted into the shaft of views—should be understood as being like the running around of one who, having cut [a bond] by his own nature, is unable to go away and remains tied to the body of self-identity (sakkāya). 26.
"These very five bases" means these very five causes. Thus, even by establishing the matrix (mātikā), there are only five.
They were set aside; five were concluded by the one who concluded them, but four were divided by the one who divided them. Where does "nirvana in the present life" (diṭṭhadhammanibbāna) enter?
It should be understood that it enters into two positions by way of unity and diversity. 27.
Having thus shown the forty-four [views] concerning the future limit (aparantakappika), now [he shows] the eighteen [views] concerning the past limit (pubbantakappika).
He spoke the words beginning with "There are, monks," in order to demonstrate this.

Therein, they are called *pubbantakappikā* (speculators about the past) because they construct (*kappetvā*), conceptualize (*vikappetvā*), and grasp a "past" (*pubbanta*) consisting of the category of the past. Alternatively, they are called *pubbantakappikā* because they possess such a construction of the past.
In the same way, the remaining [terms] mentioned previously should be understood according to the method already explained. "The self and the world are eternal... [and so forth].
Having grasped any one among form and the rest as both "self" and "the world," they assert that it is eternal, deathless, permanent, and stable.
As it is said in detail: "They proclaim a self and a world, [asserting] 'form is the self and the world, and it is eternal.

The same method applies to the views of non-eternality and so forth. And herein, by the first statement, the four types of eternalist views (sassatavāda) are expressed; by the second statement, the seven types of annihilationist views (ucchedavāda).
But surely, since these have already appeared below, why are they taken up again here?

They were included below for the purpose of showing that one who has died in this or that place is destroyed right there. Here, however, it is the holder of wrong views who possesses the knowledge of past lives;
he sees the past, but not the future, and it occurs to him: "The self that came from the beginningless past is destroyed right here."
These [terms] are taken for the purpose of showing the meaning: "From here on, he does not go.
By the third statement, the four types of partial-eternalists (ekaccasassatavāda) are stated; by the fourth statement, the four types of eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepika) are stated.
"Finite" (antava) means having a boundary, delimited, and circumscribed. Having grasped that kasiṇa—which has not been expanded—as both the self and the world...

It is thus. The second statement is spoken with reference to one who has expanded the kasiṇa; the third statement refers to one who, having expanded it across, has not expanded it upwards or downwards;
the fourth statement is spoken by way of reasoning (*takkī*). The subsequent tetrad is exactly according to the method explained below.
"Exclusively happy" means possessing uninterrupted happiness. This view arises by way of those who have attained [supernormal powers], those who remember past lives, and those who rely on reasoning.
For one who possesses the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), such a view arises when he recollects his own birth in exclusively happy states within families such as those of the Khattiyas.
Likewise, it arises for one who remembers his past selfhood as being exactly like that while experiencing present happiness as one who remembers his births (*jātissara*).
Furthermore, for a speculator (*takkī*) who is currently possessed of happiness here, [the thought occurs]: "In the past, I..."
"It was exactly so"—it arises through mere reasoning.
This view, "one is exclusively subject to suffering," does not arise in one who possesses [jhāna]. For he is indeed happy here by means of the bliss of jhāna.
However, it arises only in one who remembers past births (*jātissara*) and in one who relies on reasoning when touched by suffering in this life.
The third [feeling] arises here for all those who experience mixed pleasure and pain; likewise, so does the fourth view.

For one who is now a possessor of the fourth jhāna and thus experiences neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and for one who recollects the Brahma-world of the fourth jhāna from the past, as well as for one who possesses the knowledge of past births and is neutral toward the present while recollecting it—[for all these], the fourth [view arises].
This view arises in one who recollects only that which has been neutral, or in a speculator who is neutral toward the present,
or in one who grasps by speculating that "it will be thus" even regarding the past. Up to this point, there are four eternalists, four partial-eternalists,
four proponents of finite and infinite views, four eel-wrigglers, and two fortuitous-originists.
Thus, eighteen theorists regarding the past have been described.
Now, extracting the removal of views, he says, "In this regard, monks," and so forth.
Therein, "personal knowledge" (*paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ*) means direct knowledge. "Purified" (*parisuddhaṃ*) means free from defilements. "Brightly cleansed" (*pariyodātaṃ*) means radiant.

By all these terms, only insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is spoken of. For while the five qualities beginning with faith exist even in external systems, insight-knowledge exists only in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

In that context, "they purify only the portion consisting of knowledge" means that they apply themselves to that very section of knowledge, thinking, "We know this. "Grasping is declared" does not refer to that [external] knowledge.
This is indeed wrong view; therefore, the meaning is that even this is declared to be their clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).

Furthermore, although it is merely a portion of knowledge because its characteristic is mere knowing, nevertheless, because that seeing has not been transcended and because it is a condition for clinging, it is indeed clinging itself. "One who has transcended that" means one who has gone beyond that view.
To this extent, in the Brahmajāla [Sutta], there are four eternalists, four partial-eternalists, four proponents of the finite and infinite, four eel-wrigglers, two fortuitous-originationists,
sixteen proponents of percipient [existence after death], eight proponents of non-percipient [existence after death],
eight proponents of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient [existence after death], seven annihilationists, and five proponents of Nibbāna in the present life.
When this [Sakkapañha Sutta] has been recited, all sixty-two views are said to have been explained. However, when the *Brahmajāla* is recited, this sutta remains unrecited. Why?
Because here, the view of personality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is presented as exceeding that [of the *Brahmajāla*]. But when this [Sakkapañha Sutta] is recited, the *Brahmajāla* is indeed recited.
30. Now, these sixty-two views arise precisely with the view of personality as their head.
To show this, the Blessed One said here, "In this case, monks, a certain person," and so forth. Therein, "relinquishment" means by way of giving up.

"Non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire" is due to having emerged from craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure. "The rapture of seclusion" refers to the rapture of the two jhānas accompanied by rapture.
"It ceases" means it ceases through the cessation of the jhāna; however, for one who has emerged from attainment, it is said to have ceased.
It is so. For just as in the passage, “With the cessation of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises;

with the cessation of unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises,” the meaning here is not that one enters and dwells in the third jhāna through the cessation of the fourth jhāna. Rather, the meaning here is: having emerged from the fourth jhāna...
"He enters the third jhāna; having emerged from the third jhāna, he enters the fourth jhāna"—this should be understood as being of such a nature.
"Grief arises" refers to the grief that occurs at the exhaustion of the inferior jhānas.
However, the state of workability (*kammanīyatā*) of the mind that has emerged from attainment is what is being described.
"Rapture born of seclusion" refers to that very rapture of the first two jhānas. "The place where shade leaves" means the place from which shade departs.
What is meant? Where there is shade, there is no sunlight; where there is sunlight, there is no shade.
31. "Spiritual happiness" (nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ) refers to the happiness of the third jhāna.
32. "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (adukkhamasukhaṃ) refers to the feeling of the fourth jhāna. 33.
"I am one who is without clinging" (anupādānohamasmi) means "I am one who is free from grasping. "Conducive to Nibbāna" (nibbānasappāyaṃ) means suitable for Nibbāna.
It is beneficial. But surely, the vision of the path arises only when attachment has been dried up everywhere;
how then can this be called a "beneficial practice" for Nibbāna? It becomes a beneficial practice by way of non-clinging and non-grasping toward everything.
"He speaks abusively" means he reviles with overweening pride. "Views regarding the past" means...
The eighteenfold view concerning the past (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*). The forty-fourfold view concerning the future (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*).

It is called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because the grasping at "I am" (*ahamasmīti*) is included within the personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which is thus declared to be the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).

It is the "peaceful, supreme state" (*santivarapada*) because it is a state of supreme peace due to the subsiding of the defilements (*vūpasantakilesattā*). Of the six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*)...
By the Blessed One, in the passage: “Where the eye ceases and perception of forms ceases—that base (āyatana) should be known,” Nibbāna is shown by way of the negation of two bases.
[And it is said: “Where water, earth, fire, and air find no footing;”
“From this, the currents turn back; here the round does not proceed;
here name-and-form is ceased without remainder.
Here, however, Nibbāna is shown by the negation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
“Where do water and earth, fire and air find no footing?
Where do the long and the short, the subtle and the gross, the beautiful and the ugly cease?
Where do name-and-form come to an end without remainder?”
In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
"Consciousness is non-manifesting, infinite, and radiant on all sides.
Here, Nibbāna is shown by way of the negation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). But in this sutta, it is shown by way of the negation of the six sense bases (*cha-āyatana*).
Elsewhere, "liberation through non-clinging" (*anupādāvimokkha*) is shown to be Nibbāna itself; here, however, it refers to the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship.
The rest is clear in all instances.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Pañcattaya Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Kinti Sutta: 34.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Kinti Sutta. Therein, *pisinārāyaṃ* means in a district named so; *baliharaṇe* [means at a place for making offerings].
In that grove they bring an offering for the spirits; therefore it is called "the offering.
"For the sake of robes" means because of robes; the meaning is that he teaches the Dhamma while hoping for robes. "For the sake of such-and-such an existence" means:
thinking, "By depending on this basis for meritorious action consisting of teaching, I shall experience happiness in this or that state of existence," he teaches the Dhamma.
The meaning is: "Does it occur to you thus?

(35) The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*), are explained as being both mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those thirty-seven factors. "They might be" (*siyaṃsu*) means they would exist. "In the Abhidhamma" (*abhidhamme*) means in the distinguished [teaching].

"In the Dhamma" means "in these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). In that context, the word "also" (*ca*) likewise refers to the locative case regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "difference both in meaning and in phrasing": when it is said, "The body itself is the foundation of mindfulness;
feeling itself is the foundation of mindfulness," there is a difference in meaning; however, when it is said, "the foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*), there is a difference in phrasing.

"Knowledge" (nānaṃ) means "understanding. Regarding the phrase "you should know this even by this [reason]," having aligned both the meaning (attha) and the phrasing (byañjana), one must demonstrate how the meaning was grasped otherwise and how the phrasing was wrongly attributed.
In the expression "whatever is Dhamma, whatever is Vinaya," both the meaning and the phrasing are the very causes for making it known as Dhamma and Vinaya.
37. "In meaning, indeed, they coincide" means that mindfulness itself is taken as the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"In phrasing, they differ" means that you wrongly attribute the mere phrasing as either "the foundation of mindfulness" or "foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the expression "only a trifle," when it comes to a sutta, the phrasing is called a trifle; even if it is planted after being made slightly more emphatic (*dhanita*).
For it is indeed possible to attain Nibbāna.

Here is an illustration: A certain Elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), while residing at the Vijayārāma Monastery, was explaining a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) after reciting a discourse for two monks. He said: "Monks, 'the ocean, the ocean,' says the uninstructed worldling..."
“An ordinary person speaks thus,” he said, emphasizing the word. One bhikkhu replied, “Venerable sir, it is called ‘Samuddho’.
“Friend, whether one says ‘Samuddho’ or ‘Samuddo,’ we understand it to mean the salt ocean alone;
but you are seekers of the literal expression rather than seekers of the meaning. Go to the Mahāvihāra to [consult] those bhikkhus who are well-versed in the phrasing.”
He dismissed him, saying, "Have the phrasing corrected in my presence," and did not even explain the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to him.
Later, at the Mahāvihāra, he had the gong struck and, after discussing the questions on the four paths with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he attained final Nibbāna.
Thus, when one has mastered the Suttanta, the phrasing is indeed of minor importance.
But regarding the Vinaya, there is no such thing as "insignificant. For even the going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera) must be pure in both respects;

likewise, formal acts such as full ordination (upasampadā) are invalidated merely by the substitution of lax for firm, or soft for harsh, [pronunciations]. However, what is stated here refers to the phrasing of the Suttanta. 38. Now, why is there a dispute in the fourth section?

It is a dispute concerning perception (saññā). For their perception is: "I speak of mindfulness itself as the foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), whereas this one says 'the body is the foundation of mindfulness. The same principle applies to the phrasing (byañjana) as well.
39. "One should not rush to accuse" means that one should not act with haste for the purpose of accusing.

For some individuals, when told, "There is a pimple on your forehead no bigger than a mustard seed," will reply, "You see a pimple on my forehead no bigger than a mustard seed, yet you do not see the great tumor on your own forehead as big as a palm fruit. Therefore, a person must be examined.
"Of firm view" means one who does not grasp firmly, like one thrusting a crocodile into his heart; it is a view free from clinging.
"Affliction" refers to the arising of suffering, like that of a wound being rubbed by its own ferocity. "Easy to relinquish" means:
"What have I fallen into? When did I fall into it? or "You have fallen into it, your preceptor has fallen into it," or [one considers] another...
Even after saying it twice, he remembers, thinking, "Venerable sir, you have fallen into such-and-such an offense on such-and-such a day;
please recall it slowly," and he confesses it immediately. "Distress" refers to the physical and mental exhaustion of one who brings forward many points and reasons.
"I am able"—for when such a person has been granted the opportunity and told, "Venerable sir, you have fallen into an offense," [he is able to respond].
Having asked, "When? On what matter? and being told, "On such-and-such a day, on such-and-such a matter," he says, "I do not remember, friend.
Then, being urged with the words, "Please, venerable sir, reflect slowly," and having reflected after much prompting, he answers once he has remembered.
Therefore he said, "I am able. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
“Equanimity should not be despised” means that equanimity should not be transgressed; the sense is that it should be practiced and generated.
For if someone, even upon seeing such a person standing while urinating, says, “Friend, surely you ought to sit down,” he is said to despise equanimity.

40. *Vacīsaṃhāro* means the shifting of speech. The meaning is: one might convey what was said by these people into the presence of those others, saying, "These people said this and that," or one might convey what was said by those others into the presence of these people.

By the terms *diṭṭhipaḷāso* (pride of view) and so forth, the state of being unpleasing to the mind is described. "Knowing that, he would reproach" means that the Teacher, knowing that, would reproach him.
Being equal [to them], one might reproach him, saying, "He brings [this upon himself]. But this, friends, is a matter of quarreling and brawling;
that is, this very phenomenon. And "him" refers to the monk who made the conciliation. "Should answer thus" means:
instead of saying, "I have established these in the right view," he should answer thus, showing the very reason for which the conciliation was performed. That is the Dhamma.
Regarding the word "having heard" (*sutvā*): here, "Dhamma" is intended to mean the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (the qualities that lead to recollection). Regarding the phrases "nor himself," and so forth:
one indeed exalts oneself when saying, "This fire that has arisen is as vast as the Brahma-world;

who else but me is capable of extinguishing it? One also exalts oneself when saying, "So many people are wandering about; it is impossible to find space [for me]; not even a single person [could do it] to such an extent."
One who says, "There is no one capable of extinguishing it," is indeed disparaging another; he does neither of these two things.
Herein, the Dhamma is the proclamation of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Anudhamma is the act of conciliation toward those monks; he proclaims that very thing.
And there is no other person who is a fellow-practitioner (sahadhammika) or one who possesses a reason [to dispute].
There is no doctrine, whether it be one's own or that of another, which, when spoken, does not come to be subject to censure. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kinti Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
4. Commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta 41.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Sāmagāma Sutta. Therein, “at Sāmagāma” means in the village so named because of the abundance of *sāmāka* grass.
“Has recently passed away” means he has just died. “Divided into two” means having become dualistic, having split into two factions.

Regarding "quarreling" (*bhaṇḍana*) and so forth: quarreling is preliminary strife; that which has increased through the taking up of sticks and so forth, as well as by means of transgressing the formal rules (*paṇṇatti*), is strife (*kalaha*).
Contradictory speech such as "you do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya" is dispute (*vivāda*).
"Tearing apart" (*vitudanta*) means piercing. "My word is beneficial" (*sahitaṃ me*) means my speech is endowed with purpose. "Practiced excessively" (*adhiciṇṇaṃ*)...
They have turned back; that which was practiced by you for a long time and made proficient through repeated cultivation has been overturned upon encountering my argument.
"The burden of proof has been placed upon you" means that I have brought a charge of fault against you. "Go forth to release yourself from the debate" means:
take your bowl of almsfood and go about visiting various people, seeking further support in order to free yourself from the debate.
"Release yourself" means: now free yourself from the charge brought against you by me. "If you are able" means: if you can. "Only death" means: only dying.
"Among the followers of Nāṭaputta" means:
among the disciples of Nāṭaputta. "Averse to forms" means: having a nature that is weary [of them], [refraining] from salutations and so forth.

They do not act [upon it]. "Those whose nature is detached" means those from whom affection has departed. "Those whose nature is turned away" means those whose inherent disposition has turned back from performing services for them.
"Just as" means that just as one must become disenchanted, detached, and turned away from a Dhamma and Discipline that is ill-proclaimed and so forth, so too have they become;
this is the meaning. "Ill-proclaimed" means poorly expounded. "Ill-expounded" means poorly made known.
“Leading to non-quiescence” means being incapable of bringing about the quiescence of lust and the other defilements. “With its stupa destroyed” means with its foundation destroyed;
for here, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta alone was their stupa by virtue of being their foundation, and he has perished. Therefore it is said, “with its stupa destroyed.
“Without a refuge” means devoid of a refuge due to his very absence.
But surely this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was a resident of Nāḷandā; why then did he pass away at Pāvā?
It is said that when he heard the qualities of the Buddha being proclaimed in ten verses by the householder Upāli, who had realized the Truths, he vomited hot blood.
Taking him, who was thus unwell, they went to Pāvā, and there he passed away. Having passed away...
While acting thus, he thought: "My own doctrine is not conducive to liberation and is devoid of essence; we ourselves are already lost, but let the rest of the people not fill the states of misery.
However, if I were to say, 'My teaching is not conducive to liberation,' they would not believe me.
What if I were to have these two people learn it not by a single method, so that after my passing they will dispute with one another?"
“The Teacher will deliver a discourse on the Dhamma concerning this dispute, and through that you will come to understand the greatness of the Dispensation.
Then a certain pupil approached him and said, “Venerable sir, you are weak;
tell me the essence of this Dhamma, for the teacher is the authority. “Friend, after my passing away, you should hold [the view] that it is eternal.”

Another person approached him and had him grasp that doctrine of annihilationism. Thus, instead of making those two people hold the same view, he caused many others to learn various different doctrines and then passed away.

After they had performed the funeral rites for his body, they gathered together and asked one another, "Friends, what did our teacher declare to be the essential point? One stood up and said, "It was mine."
He asked, "What did he say? "That it is eternal," [another replied]. Another, having refuted him, said, "He told me the essence.
Thus, all of them increased their mutual dispute, saying, "He told me the essence; I am the eldest!
They reviled and abused one another, and engaged in striking with hands and feet and so forth. Traveling along the same path, they went in different directions.
Some departed, while others remained as householders.
Even during the Blessed One’s lifetime, no dispute arose within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

For as soon as a cause for dispute had arisen among them, the Teacher would either go there himself or summon those bhikkhus and, through patience, loving-kindness, and reflective discernment, resolve it.
Having stated non-violence as one of the principles conducive to harmony, he settled the dispute.
While living, he was thus a pillar of the Saṅgha; even while passing away, he passed into final Nibbāna by establishing the cause for the absence of dispute.
Indeed, the four great criteria (mahāpadesā) taught by the Blessed One in the Suttas remain a foundation for monks to this very day.
And [the Buddha was] a refuge. Likewise, the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*) taught in the *Khandhaka*, and the four ways of answering questions stated in the *Sutta*.
For this very reason, he said: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me—those shall be your teacher after my passing.
(42) Now, as for "Cunda the novice," this elder was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*). Regarding him...
The monks, having addressed Cunda as "novice" (*samaṇuddesa*) when he was not yet ordained, continued to address him in that same way even when he had become an elder.
Therefore it is said: "Cunda the novice. Why did he approach?
It is said that after Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had passed away, people throughout Jambudīpa were discussing the matter here and there: "Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta..."
"A single teacher was known; upon his passing away, such a dispute arose among his disciples.
But the ascetic Gotama is as well-known throughout Jambudīpa as the moon or the sun.
What kind of dispute will there be among the disciples when the ascetic Gotama has attained final nibbāna? Having heard this talk, the Elder reflected:
—“Having taken up this account, I will report it to the One of Ten Powers; and the Teacher, making this the occasion for a discourse, will deliver a teaching.
Having departed, he went to Sāmagāma, where the Venerable Ānanda was.
Instead of going directly to the presence of the Blessed One, he approached his preceptor, the Venerable Ānanda.
The meaning is as follows: It occurred to him thus: "My preceptor is of great wisdom;

he will report this matter to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will teach the Dhamma accordingly. "Kathāpābhataṃ" means the root of the discourse, for "root" (mūla) is called "pābhata. As it has been said:
“Even with a small load, the wise and discerning person raises themselves up, like a tiny fire when fanned. Regarding the word *dassanāya*:
it means for the purpose of seeing. But has the Blessed One not been seen before by this person? No, he has not been seen before.
For this venerable one goes for attendance exactly eighteen times in a single day—nine times by day and nine times by night.
Although he wishes to go a hundred or even a thousand times during the day, he does not go without a reason;
he goes only after taking up a specific question. On that particular day, wishing to go, he spoke as follows.
"For the harm and suffering of gods and humans": how does a dispute that arises within a single monastery in the midst of the Saṅgha lead to the harm and suffering of gods and humans?
For when two monks fall into a dispute—as in the case of the Kosalaka Chapter—their pupils also begin to quarrel within that monastery; and one who accepts their instruction...
The community of bhikkhunīs quarrels; consequently, their supporters quarrel;

then the protective deities of those people split into two factions. Therein, the protective deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma become speakers of the Dhamma, while those of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma become speakers contrary to the Dhamma.
Consequently, the earth-deities who were friends of those protective deities become divided.
In this way, by successive transmission up to the Brahma-world, with the exception of the noble disciples, all gods and humans fall into two factions.
Among them, those who speak according to the Dhamma are indeed fewer than those who speak against the Dhamma; therefore, they accept what is taken by the majority.
Rejecting the Dhamma, they accept what is more numerous—the non-Dhamma. Having fulfilled that which is non-Dhamma, they...

While dwelling [in such states], they are reborn in the lower realms. Thus, a dispute that arises within the midst of the Saṅgha during a single communal residence leads to the harm and suffering of many.

43. "Taught through direct knowledge" (abhiññā desitā) means it was proclaimed by one who had made it manifest while seated at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree. It is of a nature that inspires confidence.
“They dwell” means they dwell depending [upon him]. “After the passing away of the Blessed One”: at present, making the Blessed One their elder, they dwell with reverence;

they say that because of your venerable majesty and unassailability, they are unable to cause a dispute, but after the passing away of the Blessed One, they might cause a dispute. Wherever that dispute [might arise]...

Showing that [people] might [misunderstand], he said: "either regarding livelihood (ajjhājīva) or regarding the Pātimokkha (adhipātimokkha). Therein, "regarding livelihood" refers to the six training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed in the Parivāra by way of the method beginning with:
"If a bhikkhu claims a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)," which are for the sake of livelihood and on account of livelihood;
excluding those, all the remaining training rules constitute "regarding the Pātimokkha."

"Trifling, Ānanda. This dispute that has arisen concerning livelihood and the Pātimokkha is called "trifling" because it can be easily abandoned once one has observed it through the words of another or by one's own nature.
Therefore, it is said to be "trifling."

In this regard, the method is as follows: here someone, having reflected on such thoughts as, "Nothing can be gained without boasting of superhuman states," boasts of superhuman states for the sake of his livelihood, or engages in matchmaking;
or he practices indirect insinuation by saying, "The monk who dwells in that monastery is an Arahant," and so forth, while not being ill.
Or if one asks for exquisite foods for oneself and eats them, or if a bhikkhunī asks for them and incurs an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*);
or if anyone else commits any act involving a basis for wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), such as merely asking for curry and rice,
or if one lives while committing some transgression of the rules (*paṇṇatti-vītikkama*)— his fellow practitioners [should deal with him].

They perceive thus: "What is the use of this gain obtained by one who, having gone forth in the Dispensation, maintains his life through wrong livelihood and transgresses the rules? It occurs to him as well, by his own nature:
"Of what use is this gain to me, since I have gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya [only] to live by wrong livelihood?"
Having reflected, "I am making a living; I am transgressing the rules of training," one desists from it.
Thus, by reflecting both on the words of another and on one's own nature, one becomes easily relinquishing. Therefore the Blessed One said, "It is a mere trifle.
For, Ānanda, whether on the path or in the course of practice—that is, having attained the supramundane path—dispute is entirely stilled.
There is no dispute among those who have attained the Path. However, this was said with reference to the preliminary stage of the Path and the preliminary practice.
This is the method: when people perceive a bhikkhu as one accomplished in supramundane states, his co-residents and others come, pay homage, and stand before him;
he asks them, "Why have you come? in order for them to ask about the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that should be brought to mind.
“Venerable sir,” he said. “Sit down; I shall explain a meditation subject capable of bringing you to Arahantship in this very moment.
Having said this, he spoke: “Here, a bhikkhu enters his own dwelling and, sitting down, brings to mind the primary meditation subject.
As he brings it to mind, a light arises. This is called the ‘first path. He—”
"He produces the second knowledge of illumination; the second path is attained. Likewise for the third and the fourth.
At this point, he has both reached the path and reached the fruit. Then those bhikkhus come to the conclusion:
"One who is not yet free from the taints (asava) would not be able to explain the meditation subject in this way; surely this one is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)."
Then, at a later time, he passed away. People came from the surrounding villages where he had gone for alms and asked, "Venerable sir, was any question asked of the Elder by anyone?
The lay followers replied, "The Elder himself told us the answer beforehand.
They then prepared a pavilion of flowers and a gabled chamber of flowers, and fashioned eye-covers, face-covers, and so forth out of gold.
Having performed [the rites] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, having celebrated for seven days with great festivities, and having cremated him, they take the bones and construct a stupa.
Other visitors, arriving at the monastery, wash their feet and ask, "We shall see the Great Elder;
where is the Great Elder, friends? "He has attained final Nibbāna, venerable sirs. "It was difficult for the Elder to do, friends."

"Friend, you spoke thus because you were one who had realized the paths and fruits; you asked the question, 'Friend,' and when explaining the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to the monks, you explained it according to this method, saying, 'Venerable Sir. But this, friend, is not the Path;
this is merely a defilement of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*). You did not know that the Elder was an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), friend. As they were quarreling, they rose up.
“Neither the monks in the entire monastery nor the people in the alms-villages know [of your arrival]; you alone know.
By which path did you come? Did you not see the shrine at the monastery gate?
To those monks who speak thus—whether there be a hundred or a thousand—the heavenly realm and the Path are indeed blocked so long as they do not abandon that wrong view.
Another teacher, likewise explaining the meditation subject, speaks thus: "One should mentally place three pans on three hearths,
kindle a fire beneath them, and then, having mentally extracted one's own thirty-two bodily parts and placed them in the pans,
one should turn them over and over with a mental stick until they are roasted while burning."
It becomes ash, which must be winnowed away by the breath from the mouth. By this much alone he is called a "shaker-off of evil" (dhūtapāpa) ascetic.
The rest should be elaborated in the same manner as before.
Another speaks thus: "Having mentally set up a large vat and mixed in the grain-meal, [he imagines] himself..."
Having extracted the thirty-two parts [of the body], having placed them therein, and having poured in the cream, it should be churned. While being churned, it dissolves;
when dissolved, froth rises to the surface. That froth should be consumed. To this extent, you will have truly consumed the Deathless (*amata*).
Beyond this, the entire passage beginning with "Then those bhikkhus" and so forth should be expanded upon in the same manner as before.
44. Now, in order to show the root of whatever dispute might arise in this way, he said, "These six," and so forth.
Therein, "one who lacks reverence" (*agāravo*) means one devoid of respect. "One who lacks deference" (*appatisso*) means one without support, behaving without humility.
In this context, however, it refers to a monk who, while the Teacher is still living, does not attend upon him at the three times, nor when the Teacher is walking on a path without sandals.
He walks for exercise wearing his sandals; while others walk on a low walkway, he walks on a high one;
while others dwell below, he dwells above; at the place where the Teacher is to be seen, he covers both shoulders;
he carries a sunshade; he wears sandals; he voids excrement or urine at a bathing ford; or, after the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, he goes to worship at a stupa.
He does not go [to the monastery], yet at the place where the shrine is visible, or at the place where the Teacher is seen, he performs everything that has been prescribed;
and when other bhikkhus say to him, "Why do you act thus? This is not proper;
one ought to have shame before the Perfectly Enlightened One," he remains silent and says, "What, are you calling 'Buddha, Buddha'? This is what is called disrespect toward the Teacher.

But he who, when the proclamation of the Dhamma has been made, does not go with due care, does not listen to the Dhamma with due care, or sits dozing or chatting; or who does not grasp it with due care nor retain it;

or who, when asked, "Do you show disrespect toward the Dhamma?", remains silent and says, "You speak of 'Dhamma, Dhamma,' but what is this thing called 'Dhamma'? [is one who lacks respect for the Dhamma].
He speaks thus; this is what is called "lack of respect for the Dhamma.

Furthermore, he who teaches the Dhamma without being requested by an elder bhikkhu, sits down to discuss questions, walks while jostling elder bhikkhus, stands, sits, or folds his robe into a cushion or his hands into a lap-rest.
Or he acts [inappropriately]; he covers both shoulders in the midst of the Saṅgha; he uses a sunshade and sandals;
