even when it is said, "It is fitting for the Bhikkhu-saṅgha to feel shame," he remains silent; he says, "You speak of 'the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha,' but what is the Saṅgha?
Is it a herd of deer, a herd of goats? and so forth—this is called disrespect toward the Saṅgha. For if disrespect is shown even toward a single bhikkhu...
It occurs precisely within the Saṅgha. However, one who does not fulfill the three trainings is called "one who does not fulfill the training.
"Internally" means either within oneself or within one's own assembly. "Externally" means either toward another person or toward another's assembly.
46. Now, this dispute that has arisen based on these six grounds, as it increases, reaches various legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).

To show these, he said, "There are these four," and so forth. In this context, they are called *adhikaraṇas* because they are to be dealt with by means of the methods of settling (*samatha*) that proceed for the purpose of pacification.
A dispute itself is the *adhikaraṇa*; thus, it is a "dispute-adhikaraṇa" (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). The same method applies to the others as well.
Now, having reached these four *adhikaraṇas*, increasing [the discussion] further: that dispute, by which methods of settling...
It is pacified; and for the purpose of showing those [methods], he said, "There are, however, these seven," and so forth.

In that context, they are called *adhikaraṇasamatha* because they settle (*sameti*) and pacify (*vūpasamenti*) legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). "Of those that have arisen again and again" means of those that have arisen repeatedly.

"Of legal issues" refers to these four, beginning with the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). "For the sake of settling and pacifying" means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of pacifying.

The *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) is to be granted... [as before] ...up to the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass). These seven methods for settling disputes (*samatha*) are to be granted.

Herein, this is the exposition: first, regarding legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), the dispute among monks who are contending on eighteen grounds as to whether it is "Dhamma" or "not Dhamma" is called a *vivādādhikaraṇa* (dispute-legal-issue). Regarding failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*)...

The accusation and reproach, as well as the formal charge, of those who accuse others of failure in conduct, view, or livelihood—this is called a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
The seven classes of offenses—the five included in the *Mātikā* and the two in the *Vibhaṅga*—are called a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
Whatever constitutes the performance of the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the act of obtaining permission (*apalokana-kamma*), is [the legal issue arising from business].
What is called a legal issue concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)?

Among these, a legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means of settlement: by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
When it is being settled by resolution in the presence of the parties, it may be done either in the very monastery where it arose, or elsewhere.
For those going to settle [a dispute], whether on the way or at the place where it was submitted to the Saṅgha,
if the Saṅgha or the Gaṇa is unable to settle it there, it is settled right then by persons authorized by a committee (*ubbāhikā*).
While it is being settled in this manner, that which constitutes "presence before the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasammukhatā*) and "presence according to the Dhamma" (*dhammasammukhatā*)—
Face-to-face with the Vinaya, face-to-face with the person—this is called "decision in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*).
In this context, the presence of the Sangha of the performers by way of their concordance is "face-to-face with the Sangha.
The reality of the matter to be settled is "face-to-face with the Dhamma. Settling it exactly as it ought to be settled is "face-to-face with the Vinaya."
The presence of both parties—the one who disputes and the one with whom he disputes—being adversaries to one another, constitutes *puggalasammukhatā* (presence of persons).

However, in the case of settlement by a committee (*ubbāhikā*), *saṅghasammukhatā* (presence of the Saṅgha) is excluded here. Thus, it is settled by means of *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) alone.
But if even this does not settle it, then the monks appointed to the committee hand it back to the Saṅgha itself, saying, "We are not able to settle it.

Thereupon, the Saṅgha, having appointed a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of voting tickets (*salākaggāhaka*), [proceeds] by means of those three methods of distributing voting tickets:
the secret ballot (*guḷhakavivaṭaka*), the whispering into the ear (*sakaṇṇajappaka*), and [the open ballot].

Having had voting tickets distributed by means of a particular person, when the assembled assembly consists mostly of those who speak according to the Dhamma, the legal issue is settled in accordance with what those who speak according to the Dhamma say; thus it is settled by *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and by *yebhuyyasikā* (settlement by majority).
In this context, *sammukhāvinaya* is of the method already described. As for that which is [settled] by *yebhuyyasikā*...
The performance of the formal act—this is called a majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*). Thus, a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means of settlement.

A legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by four means of settlement: by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*), by resolution through recollection (*sativinaya*), by resolution for one who is no longer insane (*amūḷhavinaya*), and by the verdict of the worst offender (*tassapāpiyasikā*). When it is being settled by resolution in the presence of the parties alone, there is he who accuses and that which is accused.
Having heard their words, if there is no offense, both parties should be asked for forgiveness;

if there is an offense, the matter is settled once it has been adjudicated thus: "This is indeed the offense here. In this regard, the characteristic of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is exactly as described by the aforementioned method.
However, when a monk whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is accused of a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) on groundless charges, [the Teacher grants] *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection).

When the Saṅgha grants a verdict of past insanity (*sativinaya*) to one who requests it by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), then the matter is settled both by the verdict of presence (*sammukhāvinaya*) and the verdict of past insanity.
Once the verdict of past insanity has been granted, no further censure can take effect against that person.

When a monk who was insane commits unbecoming conduct inconsistent with the life of a recluse due to his insanity, [if another asks], "Does the venerable one remember having committed such an act?"...
When he is told by the monks, "It is an offense," even though he says, "Friends, this was done by me while I was insane;

I do not remember it," and being exhorted by the monks, he again requests *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer deluded) so that there may be no further exhortation, the Saṅgha grants him *amūḷhavinaya* by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). In that case, [the dispute is settled] both by *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and by *amūḷhavinaya*.
And it becomes pacified. But when the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) has been granted, no further reproach on account of that matter can take root against that person.

However, when a person who is evil—who, being accused of a *pārājika* offense or one bordering on a *pārājika*, evades the point with something else—thinks, "If this man is not cut off at the root, he might behave properly [in the future]," [then the *amūḷhavinaya* should be granted].
If the Saṅgha, thinking, "He will receive rehabilitation;

if his roots are severed, this itself will be his expulsion," performs a *tassapāpiyasika* (further-punishment) procedure against him by a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha kamma*), then it is settled both by the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and by the *tassapāpiyasika*.
In this way, a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by four means of settlement.

A legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by three means of settlement: by presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*), and by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). For this [issue], there is no resolution by means of presence alone.
However, when a monk confesses a light offense in the presence of a single monk, or in the midst of a group or the Saṅgha, then the legal issue concerning the offense [is settled].
It is settled by means of both *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been admitted).
In this regard, *sammukhā-vinaya* consists first in the presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom it is confessed; the rest is exactly as previously stated.
At the time of confession for an individual or a group, the presence of the Saṅgha is not required. As for that which is said here: "Venerable Sir, I..."

When one has been accused of having fallen into such-and-such an offense, and having admitted it by saying, "Yes, I see [it]," the act of making him undertake restraint for the future is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (the act of making an admission). In the case of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, the request for probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth is the admission;
the granting of the probation and so forth is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa*.
However, when monks who have become partisans and are quarrelsome, having committed much un-monkish misconduct, later develop a sense of shame,

they perceive the fault in making one another confess their offenses— thinking, "If we were to make each other confess these offenses, this legal dispute might lead to harshness"— and at that time, [they resort to] the act of covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
When they do so, that legal issue arising from an offense is settled both by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhā-vinaya*) and by the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
For in that case, as many as have come within arm’s reach do not reopen the matter—saying, "This was a wrongful act;

the formal act must be done again"—without having made a declaration of their view, saying, "I do not accept this"; rather, they even fall asleep, and thus all [the monks] remain [settled], setting aside...

All offenses, including those of grave transgression (*thullavajja*) and those connected with householders, are cleared. Thus, a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by three methods of settlement.
A legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is settled by one method of settlement, namely, by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*).
These four legal issues are settled by these seven methods of settlement as appropriate. Therefore it was said:
“For the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise, the resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) should be granted... [and so on] ...
up to the covering over with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). This is the method of determination here; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
Its determination is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

47. Furthermore, it should be understood that this detailed exposition stated in this sutta—beginning with “Here, Ānanda, the bhikkhus dispute”—is stated in brief according to this method. In that context, regarding the terms *dhamma* and so forth:

first, according to the method of the Suttanta, the ten courses of wholesome action (*kusalakammapatha*) are *dhamma*, and the courses of unwholesome action (*akusalakammapatha*) are *adhamma*. Likewise, [it is said]: “The four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*)...”
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment mentioned above— the three foundations of mindfulness, the three right endeavors, the three bases of psychic power,
the six faculties, the six powers, the eight factors of enlightenment, and the ninefold path—
as well as defiled phenomena such as the four types of clinging and the five hindrances, constitute what is called "non-dhamma."
In that regard, having taken up any portion whatsoever of what is non-Dhamma, they say, "We shall treat this non-Dhamma as Dhamma;
in this way our teacher’s lineage will become leading to liberation, and we too will become famous in the world.
Speaking thus, they dispute over it, saying, "This is Dhamma. It is precisely in this way regarding those portions of the Dhamma—
Having taken one side, those who say, "This is not the Dhamma," dispute that it is not the Dhamma.

However, according to the method of the Vinaya, an action performed after having accused and reminded [the person] by means of a factual basis and in accordance with what was admitted is called the Dhamma;
whereas an action performed without having accused or reminded [the person] by means of an unfactual basis and without [their] admission is not the Dhamma.
This is their name. Among them, those who say that what is not Dhamma is "this is Dhamma" dispute over it as Dhamma;
those who say that it is "not Dhamma" dispute over it as non-Dhamma.
But according to the method of the Suttas, the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, the removal of delusion, restraint, abandonment, and reflective discernment—these are the Dhamma.
This is called *vinaya*: the non-discipline, lack of restraint, non-abandonment, and lack of reflection regarding lust and so forth—this is called *avinaya*.

By way of the method of *vinaya*, the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthu*), the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*), the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvana*), the perfection of the boundary (*sīmā*), and the perfection of the assembly (*parisa*)—this is called *vinaya*;
the failure of the subject matter... [and so on] ...the failure of the assembly—this is called *avinaya*.
Among them, those who speak of whatever is non-discipline as "this is discipline" dispute it as being discipline; those who speak of discipline as "non-discipline" dispute it as being non-discipline.
"The guide of the Dhamma should be smoothed over" means the cord of the Dhamma should be smoothed over—it should be rubbed with wisdom and examined.
Furthermore, this "guide to the Dhamma" (dhammanetti) is stated as it appears in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta: "Thus, Vaccha, these ten things are unwholesome; these ten things are wholesome.
Let that be the case, or let it be whatever is here called both "Dhamma" and "Vinaya.
"In accordance with how it fits therein" means in accordance with how it fits with that guide to the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is indeed the Dhamma..."
"What is Dhamma is indeed Dhamma; what is non-Dhamma is indeed non-Dhamma; what is Vinaya is indeed Vinaya; what is non-Vinaya is indeed non-Vinaya.
Thus, in this manner, that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is to be settled. Regarding the phrase "of certain legal issues," here only the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) is indicated;
however, the settlement in the presence of those concerned (sammukhāvinaya) is not unavailable for any kind of legal issue whatsoever.

48. However, since this [dispute] is settled by two methods of settling—namely, by *saṃmukhāvinaya* and by *yebhuyyasikā*—therefore, although the turn for *sativinaya* has now arrived according to the sequence established in the preceding matrix (*mātikā*), that is not mentioned here.
Instead, showing the second method of settling for the *vivādādhikaraṇa* itself, he said: "And how, Ānanda, is it by *yebhuyyasikā*? and so forth.
In this context, "more numerous" means exceeding even two or three. The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained below.

49. Now, in order to explain in detail the remaining methods of settlement (*samatha*)—beginning with *sativinaya*, which was not expanded upon previously—the Buddha said, "And how, Ānanda, is there *sativinaya*?
and so forth. In that regard, "near to a *pārājika*" refers to two...
There are two types of "adjacent" (sāmanta): the adjacent of the categories (khandha-sāmanta) and the adjacent of the offenses (āpatti-sāmanta).

In this context, the category of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), the category of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), and the categories of offenses involving serious transgression (thullaccaya), confession (pācittiya), acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and frivolous speech (dubbhāsita)—thus, the subsequent category being adjacent to the preceding one is called "adjacent of the categories. Furthermore, prior to the first offense of defeat, there is wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"For the rest, it is a *thullaccaya*": this is what is called "bordering on an offense. In that context, among those bordering on the [major] aggregates (*khandha*), that which borders on a *pārājika* is called a "grave offense" (*garukāpatti*).
"May the Venerable One remember": may the Venerable One bear it in mind. "Of certain legal issues" (*adhikaraṇa*):
here, only the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is indicated.
50. *Bhāsitaparikkantaṃ* means that which was spoken by speech and subsequently executed by body; the sense is "having exerted effort, it was done.

Regarding *ekaccānaṃ*, here too, only the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is intended. In the section on "acting according to what has been admitted" (*paṭiññātakaraṇe*), the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is shown by the term "*ekaccānaṃ*."
52. *Davā* means impulsively. *Ravā* means that when one intends to say something else, something different is uttered.

"In this way, Ānanda, there is a *tassapāpiyasikā*"—this means that for such a person, the manifestation of their wickedness is the *pāpiyasikā*. By this, the basis for the legal act (*kamma*) is shown;
for it is against a person of such a kind that the legal act should be performed. Indeed, it is by means of the legal act that the settlement of the dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) occurs.

It is not because of the abundance of evil in the person. And here too, it should be understood that the *adhikaraṇa* (legal issue) is specifically the *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (issue arising from reproach).

53. As for the phrase "And how, Ānanda, is it like covering over with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*)?", this legal act is called "covering over with grass" because it is similar to covering over with grass.
For just as excrement or urine, when trodden upon, causes distress due to its foul odor, [but] by means of grass...
But when it has been spread over and well covered, that odor does not offend; even so, when a legal issue that,
if pursued from root to sub-root, would lead to harshness, ferocity, and schism,
is settled by this procedure, it becomes settled as if covered over with grass, like excrement.
This legal act (kamma) is called "covering over as with grass" because it is similar to covering over with grass.

Herein, Ānanda, by the statement beginning "when the bhikkhus have fallen into quarrels," only the mere form [of the procedure] is shown; however, the authoritative formal proclamation (kammavācā) is that which has come down in the Khandhaka itself.
With the exception of a grave offense (thullavajja) and with the exception of what is connected with householders—herein, however...

*Thullavajja* means a grave offense; that is, both a *pārājika* and a *saṅghādisesa*. *Connected with householders* refers to an offense incurred through the base acts of reviling, insulting, or making lawful demands against householders. Regarding *legal issues* (*adhikaraṇa*), here it should be understood as referring exclusively to the legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
Nothing is said here by way of the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). Although it is not mentioned, [it is implied].
However, it should be understood that its settlement occurs through the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties).
54. "Ānanda, these six things are conciliatory. Thus, while the discourse was commenced below concerning quarrels, the conciliatory qualities (*sāraṇīya-dhammā*) are presented above.
In this way, the teaching proceeds according to the proper sequence of connection. This concludes the section from the *Kosambiya-sutta* below.
However, while right view of the stream-entry path was spoken of [previously], it should be understood that in this sutta, right view of the fruit of stream-entry is stated.
"Minor" means slightly blameworthy; "grave" means greatly blameworthy. The rest here is self-evident.
[This concludes] the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sunakkhatta Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Sunakkhatta Sutta. Therein, "known" means Arahantship. "Declared" means by such statements as "birth is exhausted," and so forth.

It is explained by four terms. "By overestimation" means that, having perceived themselves as having attained what they had not attained and having perceived themselves as having achieved what they had not achieved, they declared, "We have attained it," out of pride. 56.
"If, Sunakkhatta, the Tathāgata thinks thus in this case" means, Sunakkhatta, in this matter regarding these bhikkhus...
In answering questions: "This point is obscure and dark to them; therefore, these people perceive what has not been attained as attained.
Come now, having cleared it up and made it plain, I shall teach the Dhamma to them"—such is the thought that arises in the Tathāgata.
And yet, here some... [as before] ...there is a change in him too—thus the Blessed One [teaches] the Dhamma to those who have entered upon the path.
He teaches. However, where there are certain foolish persons who persist in their own wayward conduct, the Blessed One perceives:

"Having learned this question, these people will wander about among villages, market towns, and so forth, pretending to know what they do not know, and imagining they have attained what they have not attained;
that will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Thus he considers this.

For those established in conduct according to their own desires, even for the sake of those practicing the path, there is a change in the state of the mind that has arisen with the thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma.
It is with reference to this that it was said. 58.

"Devoted to worldly gain" means being intent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure, which constitute the worldly gain of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭāmisa*), the worldly gain of sensual desire (*kāmāmisa*), and worldly gain in general.
Inclined toward that, weighted by that, leaning toward that. "Resembling that" means having a nature similar to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

"Connected with the imperturbable" means connected with the attainment of the imperturbable (*āneñjasamāpatti*). "He would converse" means he would speak. "Indeed, he is dissociated from the fetter of the imperturbable" means he is detached from the fetter of the attainment of the imperturbable.
"Intent upon worldly bait" refers to one such as this who wears coarse robes.
Taking his clay bowl, he goes to a border district together with a few companions who resemble himself.
When he enters a village for alms, people, seeing him, think, "The Mahāpaṃsukulika has arrived," and having prepared rice gruel, food, and so forth, they give their offerings with great respect.
When the meal is finished and he has delivered the blessing, [they think]: "Tomorrow too..."
“Venerable sir, please enter right here for alms,” they say. “Enough, lay followers; you have already given much today.
“In that case, venerable sir, please stay here during the rains retreat. Having consented, they ask the way to the monastery and go there.
Having taken up a lodging there, they put away their bowls and robes. In the evening, one of the resident monks—
He asked those bhikkhus, "Where did you go for alms? "To such-and-such a village. "Were you successful in obtaining alms? "Yes;
indeed, such is the faith of those people. "Are they only like this today, or are they always like this? "Those people are always like this;
it is by depending on them alone that this monastery prospers. Then those wearers of rag-robes...
They speak of their virtues again and again; having spoken for the remainder of the day, they speak even through the night.
At this point, for one who persists in such conduct, the head has emerged and the belly is split open. Thus should one understand the person who is intent upon worldly bait.
Now, showing the conceited person who has attained the immovable attainments (*āneñjasamāpatti*), he says: "But it is possible," and so forth.

"Of one intent upon the imperturbable" means: of one who is intent upon, inclined toward, devoted to, and leaning toward the six lower attainments which are free from the sprinkling of defilements. "That has been declared" means: that has been stated.
For to one who is conceited and has attained the six attainments, the bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure appears like a fallen withered leaf. Therefore this was said.

60. Now, in order to show the destruction of one who is conceited (adhimānika) despite having attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), he said, "But there is this possibility," and so forth.
In that context, "split in two" means split in the middle.
"Without reconnection" (appaṭisandhika) means small, like pebbles the size of a fist, which could be joined together by means of lacquer or glue; [but] a large...
However, this was said with reference to the size of a gabled house (*kuṭāgāra*). "That is broken" means it is shattered.

For one who has attained a higher meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the lower absorption becomes like a mountain split in two; thus, the thought "I shall attain that" does not arise. Therefore, this was said. 61.

Now, in order to show the friction between one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) and one who is conceited (*adhimānika*), [the Buddha spoke of] the occasion...
He said, "But as for him," and so forth. In that context, "that which has been vomited" (*se vantaṃ*) means that which has been vomited out.

For one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), the lower attainments appear like vomit; the thought "I shall enter them again" does not arise. Therefore, this was said. 62.
Now, showing the state of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), he said, "But as for his standing," and so forth. In that context, "with its root cut off" (*ucchinnamūla*)...
Thus it is "cut off at the root. For one who has attained the higher attainments, the lower attainment appears like a palm tree whose roots have been severed;
the thought "I shall enter that attainment" does not arise. Therefore this was said. 63.
"But as for the possibility... is a separate connection. For previously, even in the case of one who has attained [the lower stages] but is overweening in his pride...

The "grinding" (nighaṃsa) has been described for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), but it has not been described for either the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) or the one who is conceited (adhimānika), even if their taints are destroyed.
He began this teaching in order to demonstrate the grinding for both of those two types. However, that [position] is rejected;
for if the grinding were described for the conceited person who attains meditative absorption (samāpatti-lābhin), then [it would also apply] to the conceited dry-insight practitioner.

It is as if it were spoken for one who has attained meditative absorption; and when it is spoken for an arahant who has attained absorption, it is as if it were spoken for an arahant who is a dry-insight practitioner.
It was with the purpose of explaining what is suitable and what is unsuitable for these two types of bhikkhus that he began this teaching.
In this regard, it might be asked: "Granted that the object is unsuitable for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), how can it be unsuitable for an arahant who has destroyed the taints?"
To whatever extent something is unsuitable for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), to that same extent it is indeed unsuitable for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

Poison is simply poison, whether it is eaten knowingly or eaten unknowingly. For even one whose taints are destroyed should not remain unrestrained with the thought, "I am one whose taints are destroyed.
Even one whose taints are destroyed must remain properly and diligently engaged.
64. In this context, "by the ascetic" means by the Buddha-ascetic. "By lust, passion, and ill will":
that poison of ignorance, known as the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhāra*), is corrupted and agitated by lust, passion, and ill will. "Unsuitable" refers to objects that do not lead to growth.
"He would wither away" means he would cause it to dry up or wither. "With a residue remaining" means with a remainder still to be grasped; that which is to be taken up or seized.
"Here it is said: 'clinging' (upādī). "And it is not capable of being an obstacle for you" means it is incapable of causing an obstacle to your life.
"Dust and awns" refers to dust and the awns of rice and so forth. "And that poisonous corruption" refers to that poisonous corruption.
"By both of these" means by both that unwholesome action and that poisonous corruption. "Puthutta" means magnitude.

"In the same way" (*evameva kho*): here, the uneliminated poison of ignorance (*avijjā-visadosa*) should be understood as being like the extraction of a poisoned arrow while still accompanied by grasping (*saupādāna*).
The state of remaining engaged in unwholesome actions is like the time when the six sense-doors (*cha-dvāra*) are unrestrained.

By both of these, the falling away from the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattanā*)—which is like death when the wound has become suppurated—is like the suffering that is tantamount to death. Regarding "one or another": [it refers to]...

The commissioning of a grave and defiled offense is to be understood [as the first simile]. In the bright side (the wholesome sequence) as well, the application of the similes should be understood by this same method.

65. “This is a designation for mindfulness”: here, mindfulness follows the course of wisdom (*paññā*). It is mundane when it is mundane wisdom, and supramundane when it is supramundane. “By means of noble wisdom” refers to the completely purified wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).

Now, demonstrating the power of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), he said, "He indeed," and so forth. Therein, "one who acts with restraint" means one who acts with closed doors [of the senses].

"Having known thus, free from acquisitions" (*nirupadhi*) means that having understood in this way, one becomes free from acquisitions through the abandoning of the acquisitions that are the defilements;
the meaning is "free from clinging" (*nirupādāna*). "Liberated in the destruction of acquisitions" means liberated by way of the object in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of acquisitions.
“Attachment to the acquisitions” means attachment to the acquisition of sensual pleasures. “He will apply his body” means he will cause the body to adhere [to them]. This is what is meant:

it is impossible that one whose taints are destroyed, being liberated from the object through the destruction of craving in Nibbāna, would either indulge in the five strands of sensual pleasure or apply his body or arouse his mind toward them. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Sunakkhatta Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 6.
Commentary on the Āneñjasappāya Sutta.
66. Thus have I heard: this is the Āneñjasappāya Sutta. In this context, "impermanent" means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been.

"Sensual pleasures" (kāmā) refers both to sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*) and to defilements (*kilesakāmā*). "Empty" (*tucchā*) means void because they are devoid of permanence, solidity, stability, and a self;
however, it should not be understood as meaning that they do not exist at all. For when one says "an empty fist," it does not mean that the fist itself does not exist.
This has been said. Furthermore, that which has nothing within it is called "empty" (*tuccha*). "False" (*musā*) means subject to destruction.

"Of a nature to perish" (*mosadhamma*) means having the inherent quality of perishing; like a field, a site, or gold and silver, they were not perceived, for in just a few days they vanished and were no longer seen, as if seen only in a dream. Therefore it was said.

“Deceptive by nature” means that this is something produced by illusion (*māyā*). Just as water might be shown by means of an illusion as being a gem, or a jujube leaf shown as being a coin, or some other such thing appears exactly so to one standing within the range of vision, yet from the moment that range is exceeded, it appears as it truly is;
in the same way, sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) also [are deceptive] in the sense of presenting a transient appearance.

They are called "made by illusion" (*māyākata*). And just as a magician deceives by showing water and so forth through the power of gems and such, even so, sensual pleasures deceive by showing impermanent things and the like as having the nature of being permanent and so forth; thus they are called "made by illusion" in the sense of being deceptive.
They are called "the deluder of fools" because of such thoughts as: "This is my son," "This is my daughter," "This is my silver," "This is my gold."
Thus, it is "enticing the foolish" because it entices fools. "Sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life" refers to the five strands of human sensual pleasure.

"Those pertaining to the future life" refers to all others besides those. "Perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to the present life" is the perception that arises with reference to human sensual pleasures.
"Both of these are the realm of Māra": both these—sensual pleasures and the perception of sensual pleasure—are the realm of Māra.
Since both of these have been grasped, Māra holds sway over them; it is with reference to this that it is said, "Both of these are the domain of Māra.

In such expressions as "this is the domain of Māra," just as the domain of Coḷa is called the "Coḷa-domain" (coḷavisaya) and the domain of Paṇḍa is called the "Paṇḍa-domain" (paṇḍavisaya), [so too is this usage].
The "domain of the restraints" (*saṃvaravisaya*) refers to the sphere of activity, which is called the "domain" because it is the place where they operate;
thus, Māra exercises his power over those by whom these sensual pleasures have been grasped. With reference to this, it is said that "this is the domain of Māra.
Furthermore, Māra goes about scattering the five strands of sensual pleasure like baited seed. But as for those by whom they have been grasped—
Māra exercises his power over them; with reference to this, it is said, "this is Māra’s snare.

And just as that place where elephants and other animals exercise their power is called an elephant-haunt, a horse-haunt, or a goat-haunt, so too, Māra exercises his power over those by whom these sensual pleasures have been grasped. With reference to this, it is said, "this is Māra’s domain."
“In these” means in these sensual pleasures (*kāma*). “Mental” means born of the mind. Here it might be asked:

“Granted that covetousness, characterized by longing for the two kinds of sensual pleasures, and hostility, characterized by the desire to excel others, may arise; but how does ill-will (*byāpāda*) arise?
[The answer is: They grieve when an object cherished as "mine" has been taken away, and they grieve even while it is being taken away.
"Even those who have severed their attachments grieve"—thus arises that which is called "an affliction of the mind.

"Those very [afflictions] for the noble disciple" means: for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). The particle *va* serves merely as a grammatical conjunction (*āgama-sandhi-matta*). "Training here in the human way" means:
for one training in this teaching (*sāsana*), those three defilements (*kilesa*) become obstacles. "Having overcome the world" means: having overcome the world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*).
"Having resolved with the mind" means having resolved by means of a consciousness that takes the jhāna as its object.

"Not limited" (*aparitta*): sense-sphere consciousness is called "limited" (*paritta*); by way of its opposite, the exalted is called "not limited. "Measured" (*pamāṇa*) refers likewise only to the sense-sphere;
the fine-material and immaterial spheres are "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*). Furthermore, "well-developed" (*subhāvita*) is a term for the sense-sphere and the others.

It does not exist; this is a name for the supramundane alone. Therefore, by virtue of this, everything described as "not limited," "immeasurable," and "well-developed" applies only to the supramundane.
"Dwelling much therein" means dwelling having made that very path predominant by warding off sensual desire.
"The mind becomes confident in the sphere" means the mind becomes confident in the cause. What, then, is the cause here?
It is either Arahantship, or insight leading to Arahantship, or the fourth jhāna, or the access concentration (upacāra) of the fourth jhāna.
Regarding the phrase "when there is confidence," there are two kinds of confidence here: confidence as resolution (adhimokkha-sampasāda) and confidence as attainment (paṭilābha-sampasāda).
Furthermore, for one who dwells having established insight into Arahantship, when the great elements and so forth appear, [he reflects]:
"In what manner do these great elements appear? How do derived matter, name-and-form, and conditions appear in every way?
How does insight with its specific characteristics as its object appear? Today itself I shall attain Arahantship."
The expectation that has not yet been attained becomes established, and one gains resolution. Or, taking the third jhāna as a basis,
for one who performs the preliminary work with the kasiṇa for the sake of the fourth jhāna and contemplates the suppression of the hindrances and so forth—
observing by what method these hindrances are suppressed, the defilements settle down, mindfulness becomes established, and the conditioned process...
Or, having become manifest and clear, it appears to one with the divine eye like the world beyond;

the arising of consciousness becomes concentrated through access concentration as if clinging to a lump of clay; the hope "I shall produce the fourth jhāna this very day," though not yet attained, becomes firmly established, and one gains resolution.
This is called "confidence born of resolution" (*adhimokkha-sampasāda*). In that confidence...
[This] exists. However, for one who attains either Arahatship or the fourth jhāna, their mind indeed becomes serene.

Here, however, because of the statement "the mind becomes confident in the sphere," it should be understood that the attainment of both the insight of Arahatship and the access to the fourth jhāna constitutes "confidence through attainment. For insight—
The cause for resolving through wisdom is the preliminary stage for the attainment of imperturbability (*āneñja-samāpatti*).
One either enters the attainment of imperturbability now, or resolves through wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "or resolves through wisdom," the meaning should be understood by reversing the order of the words as follows: "one either resolves through wisdom now, or enters the attainment of imperturbability."
This is what is meant: when that confidence exists, one either resolves with wisdom now, which means one realizes Arahantship;

or, failing to achieve that, one enters the imperturbable (āneñja) attainment; or else, one resolves with wisdom, meaning one develops the path to Arahantship; or, failing to achieve even that, one enters the imperturbable attainment.
Being unable to develop the path to arahantship, he now realizes the Four Truths;
failing to achieve that, he enters the imperturbable state (*āneñja*).
Herein is the method: here a bhikkhu, having made the third jhāna the basis, performs the preparatory work for the kasiṇa of the fourth jhāna.
He practices. His hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness becomes established, and his mind enters into concentration by way of access.
He examines both the material and the immaterial, he examines the conditions, and he defines insight that has the specific characteristics as its object.
It occurs to him: "May my jhāna become distinguished by way of access; let alone being distinguished."
Thinking, "I shall make this [concentration] partaking of penetration," he develops insight and realizes Arahantship.
By this much, his task is said to be accomplished. However, one who is unable to realize Arahantship does not stop midway with a mind that has retreated from there;
rather, he enters the fourth jhāna itself. How is this? Just as a man [aiming at] a wild forest elephant...
Thinking, “I shall kill him,” he takes up a spear and pursues him;

if he succeeds in killing him, he will satisfy all the inhabitants of the village, but if he fails, he continues on his way after killing small animals such as hares and iguanas along the path and filling his carrying-pole with them.
In this context, the third jhāna of this bhikkhu is like that man’s pursuit of a forest buffalo after taking up a spear.
Taking the fourth jhāna as a basis, the performance of its preliminary work is like the killing of a wild buffalo in the forest.
Thinking, "For one who contemplates the suppression of the hindrances and so forth, this might lead to distinction;
let alone distinction, I shall make it conducive to penetration," one develops insight and realizes arahantship, just as one kills the buffalo.
Just as one who is unable [to reach his destination] might kill small animals such as hares and iguanas along the way, fill his carrying-pole with their meat, and continue on his journey,
so too should the attainment of the fourth jhāna be understood for one who is unable to realize arahantship and consequently regresses from it.
This same principle applies to the development of the path and its connection to the realization of the Four Noble Truths.
Now, showing the place where one who is unable to realize *arahatta* (liberation) will be reborn, he said, "With the breakup of the body," and so forth.
Therein, "that" (*yaṃ*) means that for which reason—that cause by which that consciousness conducive to rebirth becomes one that goes to the imperturbable (*āneñja*)—that cause exists;
such is the meaning. And here, "conducive to that" (*tassaṃvattanikaṃ*) means conducive to that [state] for that bhikkhu. By which...
That bhikkhu proceeds and is reborn by means of resultant consciousness; that is the consciousness.

"Attained to the imperturbable" (*āneñjūpaga*) means it would have attained the state of wholesome imperturbability (*kusalāneñjasabhāva*); the meaning is that it would be of such a nature. Some say this refers to wholesome consciousness.
That wholesome consciousness which is conducive to his rebirth—the cause for his arising—would be "attained to the imperturbable," even at the time of its fruition.

The meaning is that it would have that very name. Furthermore, this meaning is to be understood by way of the following method: “If one performs a meritorious volitional formation, consciousness proceeds toward merit;
if one performs a demeritorious volitional formation, consciousness proceeds toward demerit;
if one performs an imperturbable volitional formation, consciousness proceeds toward the imperturbable.”
“Favorable to the imperturbable” means favorable to the fourth jhāna, which is the imperturbable.

And it should be understood that this is not only favorable to the imperturbable itself, but is also indeed favorable and beneficial even for the higher state of Arahantship. Thus, in this first kind of imperturbability, falling back is explained by way of concentration.
67. "He reflects thus": having attained the fourth jhāna, he reflects in this way.
For this bhikkhu is wiser than the previous bhikkhu; combining the meditation subjects of both himself and that bhikkhu, he comprehends them together.
"Dwelling much therein" means that by warding off form, he dwells frequently in that very same path of practice.
For one who dwells having performed [this], "he enters the imperturbable" means he enters the imperturbable of the base of infinite space.
The rest is exactly as before. And just as it is here, so it is everywhere; we shall, however, state only the specific differences.
Thus, in this second imperturbable, falling back by way of insight has been explained through the path of insight, namely, "whatever form... and so forth.
The meaning is: "spoken by one who has seen.
"Thus he reflects" means that having reached the base of infinite space, he reflects in this way.
For he was more wise than the two bhikkhus below; thus, he [considered] the meditation subject for all three, namely, those two bhikkhus and himself.

Having brought them together, one contemplates them. Regarding the phrase "both of these are impermanent," the eight individual sections are here condensed by way of the present life and the future life, and thus called "both.
"Not fit to be delighted in" means it is not proper to delight in them by way of craving or views.
The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. "Dwelling frequently therein" refers to the warding off of sense-desires and the warding off of fine-material form.
And for one who dwells having frequently practiced that very same path, "he attains the imperturbable" means he attains the imperturbable of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
In this third imperturbable, falling back (*osakkanā*) is explained by way of insight (*vipassanā*). 68.
"Thus he reflects" means that having reached the base of infinite consciousness, he reflects in this way. For this [state] below—
Being more wise than those three bhikkhus, he combines the meditation subject of those bhikkhus and his own—making four in total—and contemplates them together.
"Where these cease without remainder" refers to that base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), having reached which all the aforementioned perceptions cease.
"This is peaceful, this is sublime" is said because of the peace inherent in that factor.
It is "peaceful" because of the continuity of its object, and "sublime" in the sense of being non-afflictive.
"Dwelling frequently therein" means dwelling having made that very path frequent by warding off those [other] perceptions.
In this first base of nothingness, falling back is described by way of concentration.
"He reflects thus" means that having reached the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), he reflects in this way.
For he is more wise than the four monks below him; and having combined the meditation subject of those four monks with his own—making five—he comprehends them together.
"Empty of self or of what belongs to self" means empty and void of that which can be grasped as "I" or "mine."
It is empty. Thus, here the emptiness with two aspects is shown.
"Dwelling frequently therein" means dwelling by making frequent practice of both the method of practice mentioned above and this method of emptiness.
In this second base of nothingness, falling back is described by way of insight.
70. "He reflects thus" means that having reached the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), he reflects in this way.
For he is more wise than the five monks below;
he comprehends by taking together the meditation subjects of those five monks and his own—six in total. "I am not anywhere in anything belonging to anyone, nor is there anything belonging to me."
Regarding the statement "in some place, in something, there is nothing," emptiness (*suññatā*) is here explained by way of four alternatives (*catukoṭika*).
How so? For herein, "I am not anywhere" means that he does not perceive a self anywhere;

"in anything belonging to anyone" means that he does not perceive his own self as being capable of being brought into the state of being a possession for anyone else; [and] "a brother in the place of a brother."

The meaning is that, having approached with the conceit of thinking "this is a companion" in the place of a companion, or "this is a requisite" in the place of a requisite, one does not perceive what should be brought near. Regarding the phrase "and nowhere mine":

setting aside the word "mine" for a moment, the meaning is that one does not perceive anything anywhere as belonging to another, nor does one perceive a self anywhere. Now, bringing back the word "mine":
Thinking, "I have nothing whatsoever belonging to anyone," he does not see the self of another as having the state of being something belonging to him.

He does not bring the self of another into the state of being something belonging to himself by way of this sense of ownership— whether in the place of a brother, in the place of a friend, or in the place of a possession— in any such situation.

The meaning is "he sees. Thus, because he does not see a self anywhere, nor does he see anything belonging to another as something to be brought into the state of being his own, nor does he see another's self, nor does he see another's self as something to be brought into the state of being his own property—therefore, this emptiness should be understood as having four aspects. One who dwells frequently in that [emptiness]...

For one who dwells having frequently practiced this fourfold emptiness and the method of practice described below, falling back is said to occur even from this third base of nothingness by means of insight alone.
Thus he reflects: having reached the base of nothingness, he reflects in this way. For this [method] below—
Being more wise than those six bhikkhus, he combines the meditation subject of those six bhikkhus with his own—thus, for all seven of them—and contemplates it.
"Where these cease without remainder": having reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), it is here that all the perceptions mentioned below cease.
"Dwelling much therein" means dwelling frequently in those perceptions.

By means of repelling, for one who dwells having made that very same practice abundant, the falling back from this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is described by way of concentration. 71.
"May there be nothing, and may nothing be mine": if, in the past, the fivefold cycle of kamma had not been accumulated by me...
"May it not be for me"—the meaning is: "may this fivefold wheel of result that I currently have not exist, may it not proceed.
"It will not be" means: if the fivefold wheel of karma that has been accumulated now were not to exist. "It will not be for me" means:
when that [karma] is absent, the fivefold wheel of result will not be for me in the future.
"Whatever exists, whatever has come to be, that I abandon"—meaning, whatever exists and has come to be, namely the present five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*), that I abandon.
"In this way he attains equanimity" means that the monk thus attains insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*).
"Would that monk, venerable sir, attain final Nibbāna, or would he not attain final Nibbāna?"—he asks this in order to inquire what [the answer] is.
For one who stands having made the third jhāna the basis, both falling back (osakkanā) and the path (paṭipadā), as well as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), have been explained;

likewise for those standing having made the fourth jhāna and so forth the basis. However, nothing has been said regarding one who stands having made the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) the basis. "I ask about that," he asks. "Api ettha" means "also here."
Herein, "he delights in that equanimity" means he delights in that insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) through delighting by way of craving and views.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "Consciousness is dependent upon that" means consciousness is dependent upon insight.
"That is its clinging" means that which is the consciousness of attachment is called its clinging—that is, its grasping.
"With acquisition" means with grasping. "Does not attain final Nibbāna" means that a bhikkhu who has a longing for insight does not attain final Nibbāna in my teaching.
However, he shows that there is nothing at all to be said regarding one who has a longing for the monastery, the courtyard, the attendants, and so forth.
But where [does he go]? That is to say, in what place? "Taking up, he takes up" means taking up rebirth.
"He grasps. "He grasps the best of acquisitions, venerable sir," means: venerable sir, that bhikkhu indeed grasps for rebirth the most excellent and supreme state among all things to be grasped;
the meaning is that he takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the best of existences.
By this, the rebirth-linking of that bhikkhu has been explained. Now, in order to explain his attainment of Arahantship, [the Blessed One] said: "In this case, Ānanda," and so forth.
"Depending on this or that" means depending on this or that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). "The crossing of the flood has been declared" means the crossing of the flood has been explained;

it is said that the crossing of the flood is declared for a bhikkhu who stands having made the third jhāna his basis... [and so on] ...up to the crossing of the flood being declared for a bhikkhu who stands having made the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) his basis.
"But what, venerable sir, is the noble liberation?"—what is being asked here?

First, taking meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) as the proximate cause and increasing insight (*vipassanā*), the bhikkhu who attains Arahantship does not become weary, just like one crossing a great flood by means of a boat or a raft and reaching the further shore. However, the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*) [takes] miscellaneous formations...
One who, having practiced right reflection, attains arahantship, fatigues himself like one crossing to the far shore by cutting through the current with the strength of his arms.
Thus, thinking "I ask this dry-insight practitioner about arahantship," he asks.
"A noble disciple" (ariyasāvaka) refers to the dry-insight practitioner who is a noble disciple. For he is wiser than the eight monks mentioned below, and compared to those monks, he—
Thus, having combined all nine meditation subjects together, he comprehends them. He reflects:
"This is identity (sakkāya), as far as identity extends"—that is, whatever is called identity, consisting of the round of existence in the three planes, all that is this very identity;
there is no identity beyond this. Thus he contemplates.
"This is the Deathless, namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging"—he reflects thus:
"This which is called the liberation of the mind through non-clinging is the Deathless, this is the Peaceful, this is the Sublime.
Elsewhere, "the liberation of the mind through non-clinging" is said to refer to Nibbāna; however, in this sutta, it refers to the Arahantship of a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*).
This has been explained. The remainder is clear everywhere.
However, it should be understood that in this sutta, falling back (osakkanā) is mentioned in seven instances, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in eight instances, and Arahantship in nine instances.
How so? First, the third jhāna serves as the basis (pādaka).
For the bhikkhu who remained having made [the base of infinite consciousness] his footing, falling back was mentioned, rebirth-linking was mentioned, and Arahantship was mentioned;
likewise for the fourth jhāna, and likewise for the base of infinite space.
However, for the three bhikkhus who remained having made the base of infinite consciousness their footing, falling back was mentioned, rebirth-linking was mentioned, and Arahantship [was mentioned].
Thus it has been explained. Likewise, for a bhikkhu who stands having made the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) his foundation, there is falling back (osakkanā).

However, for one who stands having made the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) his foundation, there is no falling back; rather, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and even Arahantship have been explained [as possible].
For the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka), only Arahantship has been explained. Thus, falling back has been explained in seven instances.
It should be understood that rebirth-linking is taught in eight places and Arahantship in nine places.
Furthermore, by combining this discussion of retrogression in seven places with the teaching on rebirth-linking in eight and Arahantship in nine,
this *Āneñjasappāya Sutta* is considered well-expounded.
The commentary on the Āneñjasappāya Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta.

74. Thus have I heard: this is the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta. Therein, the phrase "as far as the lowest step" means that it is not possible to construct a seven-storied palace in a single day, even up to the first step-sill;
rather, there is a gradual process here, beginning from the clearing of the site and the raising of the pillars, up until the execution of the painting.
He shows that it "is manifested. By the phrase "in recitation," he shows that even regarding the three Vedas, it is not possible to master them in a single day;
rather, it is only through gradual practice that their mastery is manifested. Regarding "archery," even in the science of weaponry, it is not possible to become a "hair-piercer" in a single day;
rather, [it is achieved] through such means as taking the proper stance and forming the correct grip.
This shows that even here a gradual process is discernible. "In calculation" means in counting.
Therein, showing the gradual process himself, he said, "One should count thus," and so forth. 75.
"Just as if, brahmin," [the Blessed One said this] because in the external systems, however they learn a craft, [he was referring to that].
In such and such a way they become like jackals; therefore, without comparing his own teaching to an external system, he said "just as," beginning with the words "just as a noble thoroughbred horse.
For a noble thoroughbred horse does not transgress the reason for which it has been trained, even for the sake of its life.
In the very same way, a clansman who practices rightly in the Teaching does not transgress the boundary of virtue.
“Mukhādhāne” means “in placing at the mouth.

(76) “And for the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension” means for the purpose of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. For there are two types of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*):

those who dwell constantly and those who do not dwell constantly. Among them, the one who dwells constantly, even after performing any kind of activity, [attains] the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
He is able to attain [the fruition attainment], but one who dwells constantly, being occupied with even a slight task, is unable to enter the fruition attainment. Here is an illustration:
it is said that a certain elder whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), taking along a novice whose taints were also destroyed, went to live in the forest.
When they arrived there, the dwelling was assigned to the Elder; it did not fall to the novice.

While reflecting on this, the Elder was unable to enter the attainment of fruition even for a single day. However, after spending the three months enjoying the bliss of the attainment of fruition, the novice asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, has the forest life become suitable? The Elder replied, "It has not, friend."

He said: By saying "and through mindfulness and clear comprehension," he shows that one who is such as this—one whose taints are exhausted—will be able to enter these states after having adverted to them from the very beginning. 78.

Regarding the phrase "These, Master Gotama": it is said that while the Tathāgata was speaking in this manner, the method by which the brahmin discerned, "These persons do not please [him], these do please him," arose; showing this, he began to speak thus.

"Among the doctrines of today" (*ajjadhammesu*): the "doctrines of today" are the teachings of the six teachers; among them, the doctrine of Gotama alone is "supreme," meaning most excellent. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Gaṇakamoggallāna-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
8. Commentary on the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta. 79.

"Thus have I heard" refers to the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta. Therein, "not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna" means when the Blessed One had recently attained final Nibbāna, at the time when [the monks], having divided the relics, came to Rājagaha to perform the recitation of the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgīti).
"Apprehensive of King Pajjota" means that this king named Caṇḍapajjota was a friend of the great king Bimbisāra;
however, from the time he sent Jīvaka to have medical treatment performed, they became firm friends.
Having heard that "Ajātasattu, having accepted Devadatta’s words, has killed his father," he thought, "Having caused the death of my dear friend, this man..."
He spoke these words in the assembly: "I shall rule the kingdom," and "I shall let my companion know that he has need of companions.
Upon hearing this, a suspicion arose in him; therefore it is said, "fearing King Pajjota.
"The work-site" refers to a place of labor outside the city for the purpose of repairing the city.

"He approached" means he approached thinking, "We shall convene a council for the Dhamma and Vinaya," and further thinking, "If this person of great influence, who is a favorite of the king, is won over, he will provide protection for the Veḷuvana.
"By those qualities" means by those qualities of omniscient knowledge. "In every way, all" means in every manner, all. "In every respect, all" means...
"In every respect, it is all. Why does he ask, "What do I ask?
There were six teachers who, having gone forth from families unknown, passed away while the Tathāgata was still living; their disciples also went forth from families unknown.
After their passing, they engaged in great disputes. But the ascetic Gotama went forth from a great family.
After his passing away, the talk arose that there would be a great schism among the disciples; this report spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
While the Perfectly Enlightened One was still living, no dispute occurred among the bhikkhus, and even when one did arise, it was settled right then and there.
But at the time of his Parinibbāna—[regarding] Sineru, which is six hundred and eighty thousand yojanas in height—
"Before a wind capable of sweeping away even an old leaf, how could it stand?
When the Teacher has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience, of whom would the shameless King of Death feel any shame?
Having thus generated a great sense of spiritual urgency, the monks became even more united and exceedingly tranquil; what indeed...
"Etanti" means "this," as in "I ask this. "Anusaññāyamāno" means "forming perceptions," which has the sense of "discerning what has been done and what has not been done," or "wandering about.
(80) "Atthi nu kho" (Is there, indeed?)—this too asks the same question as the previous one. "Appaṭisaraṇe" means "in the absence of a refuge."
"In the Dhamma and Vinaya. "What is the cause for concord? means: what is the cause, what is the condition, for your state of concord?
"The Dhamma is our resort" (*dhammappaṭisaraṇā*) indicates that the Dhamma is our resort, the Dhamma is our refuge.
81. "It occurs" means it comes forth as something familiar. "An offense is a transgression"—both of these belong to the Buddha.
It is simply the transgression of a command. "Let them act according to the Dhamma and according to the instruction" means:
let them act in such a way that the Dhamma and the instruction remain established; this is the meaning.

Regarding the two phrases, "Indeed, it is not the venerable ones who cause [this] to be done, but the Dhamma causes it to be done," the word *no* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). This being so, the meaning here is: "Indeed, it is not the venerable ones who cause it to be done, but the Dhamma alone causes it to be done."
83. *Taggha* is a particle used for emphasis. But does he not know that the Venerable Ānanda resides at Veḷuvana?
He does know. However, because the protection of Veḷuvana has been entrusted to him, he asks this desiring to exalt himself.
Why, then, was the protection there entrusted to him? It is said that one day, the Elder Mahākaccāyana...
Seeing him descending from Vulture Peak, he said, "This one is like a monkey. When the Blessed One heard those words, he said, "If he asks for forgiveness, that will be well;
if he does not ask for forgiveness, he will become a Gonaṅgala monkey in this Veḷuvana grove.
Having heard those words, [the other] thought, "The speech of the ascetic Gotama is of two kinds..."

[Thinking,] "There is no [other] name; later, when I have become a monkey, this will be my feeding ground," he planted various kinds of trees in the Bamboo Grove and provided protection for them. At a later time, having passed away, he was reborn as a monkey.
When the words "Vassakāra" were spoken, he came and stood nearby. *Taggha* is an indeclinable particle used in all instances as a term of emphatic affirmation. *Taggha*,...
“O Ānanda!”—having thus perceived his own state of being extolled by the Elder in the midst of the assembly, he spoke these words, thinking, “I too shall extol the Elder.
“But not so, O Brahmin,” [said the Elder]. It is said that the Elder thought: “There is indeed jhāna praised by the Perfectly Enlightened One;”
“There is indeed criticism of jhāna, yet this brahmin praises it all; thus he deceives the question.
However, it is not possible to look him in the face nor to protect one’s alms-food; therefore, I shall answer the question straightforwardly.
Having begun to say this, [he said]: “Having made an interval,” meaning having created a space within. Such as this...
“O Brahmin, that Blessed One praised *jhāna*”—here, what is called *jhāna* is explained as the *jhāna* that encompasses all [levels].
As for the phrase “this which we have,” it is said that this Brahmin was envious of the Brahmin Vassakāra;
thus, while hoping that the question he had asked would not be answered, he learned that it had been answered and [asked] again and again about the question posed by Vassakāra.

He was displeased because, while reciting that person’s name, he spoke at length, yet when it came to the question asked by me, he spoke only a single portion as if pressing down with the tip of a stick;
therefore, he spoke thus. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta: 85.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta. Therein, *tadahū* means “on that day,” that is, on that particular day.

The meaning [of *uposatha*] is as follows: it is called *uposatha* because they dwell (*upavasanti*) therein. "They dwell" means that they dwell having become endowed with either virtue (*sīla*) or fasting (*anāsana*).
Now, here is the analysis of the meanings: in such passages as, "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the *uposatha*," the *uposatha* refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
However, in such passages as, "The *uposatha*, O Visākhā, when observed, is endowed with eight factors," [it refers to the observance day].
*Śīla* (virtue). In such passages as, “For the pure one, indeed, there is always Phaggu; for the pure one, there is always the *uposatha*,” it refers to the observance day (*upavāsa*).

In such passages as, “The *uposatha* is the name of a king of nāgas,” it refers to a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as, “Monks, on that very *uposatha* day, [one should not depart] from a residence where monks are present,” it refers to the day on which one should observe the fast.
Here too, that same meaning is intended. Furthermore, this [day] is divided into the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth.
It is threefold. Therefore, in order to exclude the remaining two [types], it is stated as "the fifteenth.

By this it is said: "That wherein they observe the fast (upavasanti) is the Uposatha. Because of the fullness of the month, it is full; because it is completely full, it is *puṇṇā*. The word *mā* refers to the moon;
since that [moon] is full (*puṇṇa*) here, it is the *puṇṇamā* (full-moon day). Thus, the meaning of these two terms, *puṇṇāya* and *puṇṇamāya*, should be understood.
He understood the reason. "In that case, monk, sit down on your own seat and ask," the Blessed One said;
why did he not speak while the monk was standing, but instead had him sit? It is said that this monk was the senior elder (*saṅghatthera*) of about sixty monks who were striving in meditation;
taking those sixty monks with him, he lived in the forest, and they received their meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from him.

Having grasped them, they practice and strive. They discern the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived forms (*upādārūpa*); they discern insight (*vipassanā*) that takes as its object the characteristics of the conditions for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Then, when they have come to attend upon the teacher and sat down after paying homage, the Elder asks them about the discernment of the great primary elements and so forth.
They explain everything, but when asked about the questions concerning the Path and the Fruits (*maggaphala*), they are unable to explain them.
Then the Elder thought: "There is no decline in their receiving instruction from me, and they dwell with energy aroused.
There is not even a moment's negligence on their part, such as the time it takes for a cock to drink water.
Even so, they are unable to realize the paths and fruits. I do not know their underlying disposition; they are to be converted by a Buddha."

"These men will become [monks]; having taken them, I shall go into the presence of the Teacher, and then the Teacher will teach the Dhamma to them according to their individual dispositions. Having taken those monks, he came into the presence of the Teacher.

At the time of evening, the Teacher took the water brought by the Elder Ānanda, warmed his body, and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the courtyard of Migāra’s Mother’s palace; the community of monks also sat down, surrounding him.
At that time, the sun was setting and the moon was rising, and the Blessed One was seated in the center.
There was no radiance from the moon, nor was there any radiance from the sun;
having eclipsed the light of both the moon and the sun, the six-colored twin Buddha-rays shone forth, forming mass upon mass as they spread through the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Everything should be expanded upon according to the method explained below. This is called the "ground for praise," and herein the strength and measure belong solely to the preacher of the Dhamma;
however much he is able to do, that much should be spoken. It should not be said that it was poorly delivered.
When the assembly was thus seated, the Elder rose and requested the Teacher to grant him the opportunity to ask a question. Then—
The Blessed One said: “If, while I am standing, the other monks stand up thinking, ‘Our teacher has risen,’ then disrespect will have been shown toward the Tathāgata.

On the other hand, if they ask while remaining seated, disrespect will have been shown toward the teacher, and they will not be able to receive the teaching of the Dhamma with one-pointed attention. Toward the teacher...”
"But when they are seated, they too will sit; then, being one-pointed, they will be able to receive the teaching of the Dhamma.
For this reason, the Blessed One did not speak while [the Elder] was standing, but had him sit.
"Venerable sir, are these..."—this was stated as if it were a question arising from doubt. However, the Elder [was reflecting on] the arising and passing away of the five aggregates.
Having reflected, he attained Arahatship and became one whose great taints were destroyed; he has no doubt.
However, it is appropriate to ask as if one did not know, even though one knows.
For if one asks as if knowing, thinking "he knows," and then answers each question, one speaks only partially. But when one asks as if not knowing, then while speaking...
He speaks by bringing forward reasons from here and there, making the matter clear. Yet someone, though not knowing, asks as if they did know.
One should understand that such a person—though actually knowing—asks as if they were ignorant, thinking, "What will the Elder do with such words?"
"Rooted in lust" means rooted in craving (*taṇhā*). "May I be such-and-such" means: if one desires to be white, one aspires, "May I be green like a palmyra leaf or the color of realgar";
if one desires to be black, one aspires, "May I be the color of a blue lotus, or the color of collyrium, or the color of an *atasī* flower.
"Such-feeling" means having wholesome feeling or pleasant feeling.

...or they may wish for them. The same method applies to perception and the other [aggregates]. However, because there is no such thing as a "wish" regarding the past, and even one who wishes cannot obtain it;

nor does it exist in the present—for instance, by wishing for a white person to become black in the present, one does not become black, nor does a black person become white; nor does a tall person become short, nor a short person tall.
Furthermore, for one who has given a gift or undertaken moral discipline and makes the aspiration, "In the future, may I be a khattiya or a brahmin," that aspiration is fulfilled.
Therefore, only the future is taken [as the object].
He asks: by what means does the designation of the aggregates (khandha-adhivacana) occur? That is, by how much is there a designation of the aggregates?

The great elements (*mahābhūta*) are called "causes" (*hetu*) in such passages as "the three wholesome causes," where "cause" refers to a causal factor (*hetu-hetu*). Ignorance (*avijjā*) is a common cause because it is shared by meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the rest.
Wholesome and unwholesome states are the primary causes for the giving of their respective results. Here, however, "cause" is intended in the sense of a condition (*paccaya-hetu*).
In this context, the earth element (*pathavī-dhātu*) is a great element (*mahābhūta*) with respect to the other three elements and derived matter (*upādārūpa*).
And it is both the cause and the condition for the manifestation and the seeing [of that]. In this way, the application should be understood for the remaining [aggregates] as well.
Regarding "contact": from the statement, "Bhikkhus, one who is touched feels; one who is touched perceives;
one who is touched intends," contact is both the cause and the condition for the manifestation of the three aggregates. Regarding "of the consciousness aggregate": here...

First, together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), thirty material phenomena arise within the upper boundary of those in the womb, as well as the three associated aggregates (*khandha*). That name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is both the cause and the condition for the manifestation of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
At the eye-door, the sensitivity of the eye and the visible object are material phenomena, along with the [associated] mental factors.
The three aggregates are "name. That name-and-form is both the cause and the condition for the manifestation of eye-consciousness.
The same method applies to the remaining consciousnesses.

"But how, venerable sir?"—this was said by one asking about the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) with the question, "To what extent indeed [does it exist]? "There is no personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)"—this was said by one asking about the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*).
88. By the phrase "This is the gratification in form," both the penetration of full understanding and the truth of suffering are stated.
By the phrase "This is the danger in form," both the penetration of abandonment and the truth of the origin are stated.
By the phrase "This is the escape from form," both the penetration of realization and the truth of cessation are stated. Those factors beginning with right view that exist in these three instances...
These phenomena (*dhammā*)—this penetration through development (*bhāvanāpaṭivedha*) is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

89. "External" (*bahiddhā*) refers to another's body possessed of consciousness (*saviññāṇaka-kāya*). By the phrase "all signs" (*sabbanimittesu*), however, one includes even that which is not bound to the faculties (*anindriyabaddha*).
Alternatively, by the expression "body possessed of consciousness," both one's own body and another's body are indeed included.
And by grasping all external signs, he grasps that which is not bound to the sense faculties.
"Made by one who is non-self" means made by one standing in what is non-self.
"Whom will they touch?"—asking in what kind of self they will show their result while falling into the view of eternalism, he speaks thus. "By the predominance of craving."
"By craving as the chief. "In this and that" means among those various phenomena.

"About sixty" means these monks, having abandoned their regular meditation subjects and contemplating another new meditation subject, attained Arahantship on that very seat without breaking their cross-legged posture.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 10.
The commentary on the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta.
91. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ*: thus [ends] the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta. Therein, "silent, silent" means that whichever direction he looked toward, in each of those places they were indeed silent.
