"Having looked around" means having opened his eyes adorned with the fivefold grace and gazed here and there, even to the extent of observing the absence of any fidgeting of hands or feet.

"Having seen. "An *asappurisa*" means a wicked person. "'No hetaṃ, bhante' (Not so, venerable sir)"—they said this because, like one blind man [failing to see] another blind man, he is unable to know him;
the meaning should be understood in this same manner for the subsequent sections as well.
"*Assaddhasamannāgato*" means endowed with wicked qualities. "*Asappurisabhattī*" means devotion to wicked persons.

One who thinks like an untrue person (*asappurisacintī*) is one who contemplates with the thoughts of an untrue person. One who counsels like an untrue person (*asappurisamantī*) is one who deliberates on the counsel of an untrue person.

One who speaks like an untrue person (*asappurisavācī*) is one who utters the speech of an untrue person. One whose actions are those of an untrue person (*asappurisakammanto*) is one who performs the deeds of an untrue person.

One who holds the views of an untrue person (*asappurisadiṭṭhī*) is one endowed with the views of an untrue person. One who gives to an untrue person (*asappurisadānaṃ*) is [one who gives] to untruly persons.
A gift should be given. "They are his friends" means they are his friends. "He intends for his own affliction" means he thinks thus for the sake of his own suffering:
"I shall kill a living being, I shall take what is not given, I shall engage in sexual misconduct; having undertaken the ten unwholesome courses of action, I shall abide by them.
"For the affliction of others" means, for example, [thinking], "Such-and-such a person kills such-and-such a living being."
"He takes what is not given belonging to such-and-such a person; he undertakes and dwells in the ten unwholesome courses of action;
thinking, 'I will command him thus,' he thinks in this way for the sake of another's suffering. "For the affliction of both" means:
"Having taken such-and-such and such-and-such [persons], I will undertake and dwell in the ten unwholesome courses of action"—thus he thinks in this way for the sake of the suffering of both.
In such passages as "one plots for one's own harm," plotting with the thought, "I will undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action," is called plotting for one's own harm.
Plotting with the thought, "I will incite someone else to undertake the ten unwholesome courses of action," is called plotting for the harm of others.
Plotting together with another, thinking, "Let us both, acting in concert..."
Thinking, “We shall undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action,” one is said to counsel for the harm of both [self and others].
One gives a gift without respect means that one honors neither the object to be given nor the person.
To not honor the object to be given means that one gives food possessed of defects such as coarse rice and so forth, rather than making it pleasing. To not honor the person...
Without sweeping the place where the seat is to be placed, having seated [the recipient] anywhere at all, and having set down any kind of footstool whatsoever, one gives a gift.
"Not with one's own hand" means one does not give with one's own hand, but causes it to be given by slaves, laborers, and so forth.
"Without respect" means one gives without showing honor toward either the object to be given or the person receiving it, according to the method explained below.
He gives as if throwing away, like one who wishes to discard and instead thrusts a snake into an anthill.
"One with the view of non-return" means he gives without expecting a result.
Regarding that, "he is reborn there": having given a gift, he is not reborn in hell. However, by that [gift], through his acquisition of evil views...
Wrong view is grasped; through that wrong view, one is reborn in hell. The "white side" (the wholesome path) is to be understood by way of the method opposite to what has been stated.
"Greatness among the gods" refers to the six classes of sense-sphere deities. "Greatness among humans" refers to the prosperity of the three [noble] families.
The rest is clear everywhere. However, this sutta is taught solely by way of the pure cycle [of existence].
The commentary on the Cūḷapuṇṇamasutta in the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Section on the Unarisen (Anupada-vagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unarisen (Anupada-sutta). 93.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Discourse on the Unarisen. Therein, "he said this" refers to the sequence beginning with "He is wise," and so forth.

He spoke of the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. Why? Because among the remaining elders, the virtue of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was well known as being a master of psychic power (*iddhimā*);
that of Mahākassapa as being a proponent of the ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*); that of the Elder Anuruddha as being possessed of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*);
that of the Elder Upāli as being a master of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*); and that of the Elder Revata as being a meditator who delights in jhāna (*jhāyī jhānābhirata*). [As for] the Elder Ānanda...
"Learned. Thus, while those various qualities were well-known to this or that elder, they were not known to the Elder Sāriputta.

Why? For it is impossible to know the qualities of one possessed of wisdom without them being told. Therefore, thinking, "I shall speak of Sāriputta’s qualities," the Blessed One waited for the assembly of like-minded people to gather. Indeed, [he would not do so] in the presence of persons who are dissimilar.
It was not appropriate to speak in praise [of him], for when his praises were spoken, they would only speak of his faults.
On this day, however, an assembly of like-minded followers gathered around the Elder; seeing that they had assembled, the Teacher began this teaching while speaking in praise of him.

In this context, "wise" (*paṇḍita*) means wise by virtue of these four reasons: skill in the elements (*dhātu-kusalatā*), skill in the sense bases (*āyatana-kusalatā*), skill in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kusalatā*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna-kusalatā*).

Regarding the terms "of great wisdom" (*mahāpañña*) and so forth, the meaning is "endowed with great wisdom" and the rest. Herein, this is the distinction between "great wisdom" and the others: therein, what is great wisdom?

It is called "great wisdom" because it grasps the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), the great aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), the great aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*), and the great aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*).
She grasps the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; thus she is one of great wisdom. Great are the [distinctions between] the possible and the impossible;
great are the dwellings and attainments; great are the Noble Truths; great are the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power;
great are the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment; great is the Noble Path; great are the fruits of recluseship.
She is called "of great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*) because she grasps the great direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the great ultimate goal, Nibbāna.
What is "vast wisdom" (*puthupaññā*)? It is called vast wisdom because knowledge proceeds extensively across various aggregates (*khandha*).

[It proceeds] extensively across various elements (*dhātu*), extensively across various bases (*āyatana*), extensively across various meanings (*attha*), extensively across various dependent originations (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and extensively across various emptinesses and non-apprehensions (*suññatamanupalambha*).
In various and diverse meanings, phenomena, etymologies, and inspired insights; in various and diverse aggregates of virtue;
in various and diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; in various and diverse points and non-points;
in various and diverse abidings and attainments; in various and diverse noble truths; and in various and diverse foundations of mindfulness and right efforts.

Wisdom that transcends the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the various individual noble paths, the fruits of recluseship, and the higher knowledges, and which proceeds toward Nibbāna—the ultimate truth—after having transcended the various phenomena common to ordinary people, is called "wide wisdom" (puthupaññā).
What is "joyful wisdom" (hāsapaññā)? Here, someone is full of laughter, full of rapture, full of contentment, and full of gladness, [and] virtue...

It fulfills [the faculties]; it fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; it fulfills moderation in eating, application to wakefulness, the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is "wisdom accompanied by joy.
One who abounds in joy and abounds in gladness penetrates what is possible and what is impossible; one who abounds in joy [attains] the meditative dwellings and attainments.
It fulfills [the path]—this is "laughter-wisdom" (*hāsapaññā*); one who is abundant in laughter penetrates the Noble Truths.
One develops the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path—this is "laughter-wisdom";

one who is abundant in laughter realizes the fruits of recluseship and penetrates the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). This is "laughter-wisdom"; one who is abundant in laughter is abundant in joy, satisfaction, and gladness.
Wisdom of laughter (*hāsapaññā*) is that which realizes the ultimate truth, Nibbāna.
What is wisdom of speed (*javanapaññā*)? Whatever form—past, future, or present... [as before] ...whether far or near—all form it quickly speeds over as impermanent;
thus it is wisdom of speed. It quickly [speeds over it] as suffering; it quickly [speeds over it] as non-self.
It is called "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*) because it speeds along. Whatever feeling there is... [and so on] ...whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present...
all consciousness it swiftly speeds along as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; thus it is swift wisdom. The eye...
[and so on] ...aging-and-death, past, future, or present—it swiftly speeds along as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; thus it is swift wisdom.

Having weighed, scrutinized, and analyzed form—past, future, and present—as impermanent in the sense of being subject to destruction, as suffering in the sense of being fearful, and as non-self in the sense of being coreless, and having made it manifest, one swiftly courses toward the cessation of form, which is Nibbāna; thus it is "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*).
[The same applies to] feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness, the eye... [and so on] ...up to aging-and-death, past, future, and present.
It is impermanent in the sense of destruction... [and so on] ...having made it manifest, it swiftly speeds toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death;
thus it is "speeding wisdom" (javanapaññā). Form—past, future, and present... [and so on] ...consciousness. The eye...

[and so on] ...aging and death, past, future, and present, are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Having weighed, having scrutinized, having analyzed, and having made it manifest, one swiftly speeds toward the cessation of aging and death, which is Nibbāna;
thus it is "speeding wisdom" (javanapaññā).
What is "sharp wisdom" (tikkhapaññā)? It is sharp wisdom because it swiftly cuts off defilements. [It cuts off] a sensual thought that has arisen...
He does not tolerate a thought of ill will that has arisen, a thought of cruelty that has arisen,
various evil and unwholesome states as they arise, or lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity,
contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, and vanity that have arisen.

She does not tolerate, but abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and renders non-existent negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations, and all kamma leading to existence; thus she is one of sharp wisdom.
In a single sitting, she attains the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges, and the six...
The superknowledges have been attained, realized, and seen with wisdom—this is "sharp wisdom. What is "penetrative wisdom"?
Here, a certain person is full of agitation regarding all conditioned phenomena, full of terror, full of weariness, full of dissatisfaction, and full of lack of delight;
he does not find pleasure in conditioned phenomena, as his mind is turned outward.
It is "penetrative wisdom" (nibbedhikapaññā) because it penetrates and shatters the mass of greed (lobhakkhandha) never before penetrated or shattered;
it is penetrative wisdom because it penetrates and shatters the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, enmity...
[and so on] ...all kamma leading to existence, which have never before been penetrated or shattered.

"Insight into phenomena according to their sequence" means that one contemplates insight into phenomena in successive order, either by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or by way of the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*).

Contemplating in this manner, [the Venerable Sāriputta] attained Arahantship within half a month, whereas the Elder Mahāmoggallāna did so in seven days. Nevertheless, the Elder Sāriputta possessed greater great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*) than the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
For while striving for seven days by contemplating only a single portion of the disciples' method of contemplation—as if pressing down with the tip of a staff—he attained Arahatship.

The Elder Sāriputta, however, setting aside the methods of contemplation of the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, contemplated the disciples' method of contemplation in its entirety. Contemplating in this way for half a month, [he attained Arahatship].

I am going. And it is said that having attained Arahantship, he realized: "Except for Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, there will be no other disciple capable of attaining what I have attained through wisdom.
For just as a man who intends to take a bamboo pole, upon seeing a bamboo with a great tangle of knots, finds delay in cutting through those knots; so too was there delay for me.
Thinking, "It will be there," one might thrust one's hand inside and, taking a bamboo pole that has already grown, cut it at both the base and the tip and depart;
although he goes first, he does not obtain a bamboo pole that is either solid or straight.
And another, seeing such a bamboo pole, [thinks]: "If I take a bamboo pole that has already grown..."

"Whether I obtain heartwood or straight [bamboo]," he thought; and having bound his waist-cloth, he cut through the bamboo thicket with a large knife, selected and took away both heartwood and straight poles, and departed.
Although this man goes behind, he nevertheless obtains both heartwood and straight poles. In the same way, this should be understood regarding these [five bhikkhus].
The striving of the two elders. Thus,
after striving for half a month, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma,
while the discourse on the Comprehension of Feelings was being taught at the entrance of the Sūkarakata Cave to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, [beheld] the One of Ten Powers.
Standing as if fanning [his insight], he directed his knowledge according to the sequence of the teaching;

on the fifteenth day from the day of his going forth, having reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), he penetrated sixty-seven knowledges and attained sixteenfold wisdom.
In this regard, monks, this is Sāriputta’s "insight into phenomena one by one" (*anupadadhammavipassanā*), which is that very insight into phenomena one by one.
"Vipassati" refers to "insight into phenomena one by one" (*anupadadhammavipassanā*). Regarding that insight into phenomena one by one, this [passage] belongs to Sāriputta.
What follows now is stated with reference to each respective stage of insight.
94. "In the first jhāna": those phenomena which exist within the attainment of the first jhāna. "Tyāssa" means "those would be his. They are "determined one by one" (*anupadavavatthitā*).
"They exist" means they are established in their proper sequence, delimited, known, and understood.

How so? For as the elder surveys those mental states, he knows: "Applied thought (vitakka) functions with the characteristic of directing onto; likewise, sustained thought (vicāra) with the characteristic of examining;
rapture (pīti) with the characteristic of pervading; pleasure (sukha) with the characteristic of gratification; and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) with the characteristic of non-distraction."
Contact has the characteristic of touching; feeling has the characteristic of being felt; perception has the characteristic of perceiving; volition has the characteristic of intending;
consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing; desire has the characteristic of wishing to act;
resolve has the characteristic of conviction; energy has the characteristic of exertion; mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; equanimity has the characteristic of neutrality.
He knows that attention characterized by inclination is occurring. Knowing thus, he defines thought (vitakka) by way of its intrinsic nature as the act of directing onto [the object];
… pe … he defines attention (manasikāra) by way of its intrinsic nature as the act of inclining toward [the object].
Therefore it was said: "Those states have been defined by him one after another."
"Known as they arise" means that while arising, they arise known—that is, they arise having become manifest.
"Known as they persist" means that while persisting, they persist known—that is, they persist having become manifest.

"Known as they pass away" means that while ceasing, they cease known—that is, they cease having become manifest. Herein, however, one must resolve both the state of knowing that [single] state and the multiplicity of knowings.

For just as it is impossible for that very fingertip to touch itself, even so it is impossible for that very consciousness to know the arising, the presence, or the dissolution of that same consciousness. Thus, first of all, its state of being known by itself must be relinquished.
Furthermore, if two consciousnesses were to arise simultaneously, then by one consciousness the arising of the other...
Either its persistence or its dissolution could be known. However, there are no two contacts, feelings, perceptions, volitions, or consciousnesses that arise simultaneously;
rather, each arises one at a time. Thus, one must be liberated by means of the multiplicity of knowledge.
This being so, how [is it]? Within the meditative attainment, sixteen factors were discerned by the Great Elder.
"They become manifest" means: because the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*) have been discerned. For the Elder has discerned both the basis and the object;
therefore, when he adverts to the arising of those phenomena, their arising becomes manifest;
when he adverts to their presence, their presence becomes manifest; when he adverts to their dissolution, their dissolution becomes manifest. Hence it was said:
“Known they arise, known they persist, known they pass away. By the phrase “having not been, they come to be,” one sees arising (*udaya*).
By the phrase “having been, they vanish,” one sees passing away (*vaya*).
“Without approach” means not approaching by way of lust (*rāga*). “Without departure” means not departing by way of aversion (*paṭigha*). “Independent” means...
Not dependent on craving and views; unattached means not bound by desire and lust;
fully released means released from sensual lust; dissociated means dissociated from the four yokes or from all defilements;
with a mind made free from boundaries means with a mind that has transcended limitations; he dwells with such a mind.
In this context, there are two boundaries: the boundary of defilement (*kilesamariyādā*) and the boundary of the object (*ārammaṇamariyādā*).
For if, while he is engaged within the attainment, lust and other defilements were to arise with respect to the sixteen states, then the boundary of defilement would have been established by him;
however, since not even one of them has arisen, there is no boundary of defilement. But if, while he is engaged within the attainment...
When one adverts to the sixteen states in their occurrence, some might not come into the range of his perception;

thus there would be a limit to the object for him. But when he adverts to those sixteen states, there is no state whatsoever that does not come into the range of his perception, and thus there is no limit to the object.
There are two other kinds of boundaries: the boundary of suppression and the boundary of eradication.
Of these, the boundary of eradication will be discussed later; however, in this context, the boundary of suppression is intended.
Because its opposites have been suppressed, he dwells with a mind that has transcended boundaries.
“An escape beyond” means an escape further than this. In other suttas, “an escape beyond” is stated to be Nibbāna;
however, here it should be understood that the immediately preceding distinction is intended.
“By making much of that” means by the frequent cultivation of that understanding. “There is indeed its existence” means that for that elder, there truly exists [this state].
It becomes more firm. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining sections as well.
However, in the second section, it is "tranquillity" (*sampasāda*) in the sense of being serene; one defines it according to its intrinsic nature.
In the fourth section, "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers specifically to the equanimity of feeling in the place of pleasure; because of the serenity of the mind, there is non-exertion.
That which is the mental application (ābhoga) thinking, "Whatever there is pleasant therein"—by this it is declared to be coarse;

thus, due to the mind being tranquilized, non-application (anābhoga) is spoken of, meaning the absence of that [coarse application]. "Purity of mindfulness" (satipārisuddhi) is simply purified mindfulness.
Equanimity (upekkhā) is also equanimity as purity (pārisuddhi-upekkhā).
95. "He emerges mindfully" means that he emerges possessing mindfulness, being possessed of knowledge and clear comprehension.

"He contemplates those phenomena" is said thus because, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is only insight into phenomena as they arise (anupadadhammavipassanā) for Buddhas and not for disciples;
therefore, he speaks in this way while demonstrating insight into the aggregates (kalāpavipassanā).
"Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed": having seen the four truths with the wisdom of the path, the four taints are exhausted.
There is also the occasion when the Elder Sāriputta attained Arahantship by bringing forth serenity and insight in union, as well as the occasion when he entered the attainment of cessation;
it is the occasion of attaining Arahantship that is taken here.
They say that one who has attained mastery over cessation will enter it again and again.
In this regard, at whatever time the attainment of cessation is the head [of his practice], when the turn for cessation arrives, the attainment of fruition remains hidden.
At whatever time the attainment of fruition is the head, when the turn for fruition arrives, [the attainment of cessation remains hidden].
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is profound. However, the elders dwelling in Jambudīpa say:
"The Elder Sāriputta, having brought forth serenity and insight in union, realized the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and entered the attainment of cessation;
emerging from cessation, he attained Arahantship. "Those phenomena" refers to the material phenomena produced by the three causes that occur during the internal state of the attainment.

Or [it refers to] the phenomena occurring in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) below. For these too are indeed the phenomena to be insighted (vipassitabba) in this section;
therefore, it should be understood that this was said in order to show that "he insighted those.
97. *Vasippatto* means one who has attained mastery (*ciṇṇavasi*). *Pāramippatto* means one who has reached perfection (*nipphatti*). Regarding *oraso* and so forth:
The Elder is to be understood as "born from the breast" (*orasa*) because he was born having heard the sound produced on the Blessed One’s chest;

as "born from the mouth" (*mukhato jāto*) because he was born having heard the sound uttered by the mouth; as "born of the Dhamma" (*dhammajo*) and "fashioned by the Dhamma" (*dhammanimmito*) because he was born and fashioned through the Dhamma;

as "an heir to the Dhamma" (*dhammadāyādo*) because he received the inheritance of the Dhamma; and as "not an heir to material things" (*no āmisadāyādo*) because he did not receive an inheritance of material goods.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
Thus ends the commentary on the Anupada Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
2. Commentary on the Chabbisodhana Sutta. 98.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Chabbisodhana Sutta. Therein, in such passages as "Birth is destroyed," final knowledge (*aññā*) is declared even by a single phrase, or even by two.
Here, however, the declaration of final knowledge is presented through four phrases. [Regarding] "seen" (*diṭṭhe*):
Regarding the phrases beginning with "one who speaks of what was seen" (*diṭṭhavāditā*): that volition by which one says of what was seen, "I have seen it," is called "speaking of what was seen.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "This is the natural law" (*anudhammo*) means this is the inherent nature.
"It should be rejoiced in": not only should it be rejoiced in, but for one who has attained final nibbāna, all honor should be rendered to that one whose taints are destroyed.
"Furthermore, a question" means: it shows that if you were not satisfied with his answer, this further question should also be asked.
This same method applies to the three subsequent sections as well.
99. "Weak" means feeble. "Subject to fading away" means having the nature of passing away. "Without consolation" means devoid of comfort.
"Approach and grasping" (*upāyūpādāna*) is a designation for craving and views. For craving and views "approach" (*upenti*) the phenomena of the three planes;

thus they are "approaches" (*upāyā*). They "grasp" (*upādiyanti*); thus they are "graspings" (*upādānā*). Furthermore, "the mind's stationing, adherence, and underlying tendency" is also a name for those very same things.

For the mind "stands" (*tiṭṭhati*) and "adheres" (*adhitiṭṭhati*) to the phenomena of self-identity (*sakkāya*) by means of craving and views; thus, craving and views are [the mind's]... [stationing].

They are foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*); because one adheres to that [object] by means of them, they are called "adherences" (*abhinivesa*); because it is by means of those very same things that it underlies [the mind], they are called "underlying tendencies" (*anusaya*).
In such phrases as "through destruction, through dispassion," the meaning is "by means of destruction, by means of dispassion.

All of these are indeed synonyms for one another. 100. The earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) is the element of support. The water element (*āpodhātu*) is the element of cohesion. The fire element (*tejodhātu*) is the element of maturation.
The air element (*vāyodhātu*) is the element of distension. The space element (*ākāsadhātu*) is the element of non-obstruction. The consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*) is the element of cognizing.
"I did not approach them as non-self" means that I did not approach them by way of the portion of self, thinking "I am the self.

"Nor do they depend on the earth element" refers to the remaining elements dependent on the earth element, as well as derived form (*upādārūpa*) and the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandhā*). For these too [depend] on the physical bases of the supported [mental states].
Because it is dependent upon the earth element, in one sense it is indeed dependent upon the earth element.
Therefore, by saying "and not dependent upon the earth element," he states that one does not regard even the remaining material and immaterial phenomena as self.

However, regarding the phrase "dependent upon the space element," all primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādārūpa) are called "dependent upon the space element" in the sense of being inseparable; likewise, those [phenomena] which have as their basis the matter dependent upon that [space element].
The immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandhā*). Thus, here too, both the material and the immaterial are indeed included.

However, in the phrase "dependent on the consciousness element" (*viññāṇadhātunissita*), the three co-nascent aggregates (*sahajātā khandhā*) and mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ*) are "dependent on the consciousness element"; thus, both the material and the immaterial are indeed included.
101. Regarding the passage: "In the case of material form, eye-consciousness, and those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness," herein, that which [occurred] in the past at the eye-door...
That which has ceased after having come into the range [of the senses], and that which will cease after coming into the range in the future,
and that which has ceased after coming into the range right now— all that is called "form" (rūpa). However, that which has ceased without having come into the range even in the past,

which will cease without having come into the range in the future, and which has ceased without having come into the range even right now— that, among the phenomena to be cognized by eye-consciousness, is as follows:
When it was said, "It is included," the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "In this place you should divide it into two;
as for what you will do in the subsequent section on prosody (chandovāra), this is not possible.

Therefore, all that form—whether it has entered the range of the senses during the three times or has not—is indeed just form (rūpa); however, the three aggregates associated with eye-consciousness are phenomena to be cognized by eye-consciousness.
These are to be understood. Herein, the meaning is: "among those phenomena to be cognized together with eye-consciousness. *Chanda* is the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*).
*Rāga* is that same [desire] as passion (*rāga*) by way of being impassioned. *Nandī* is that same [desire] as delight (*nandī*) by way of rejoicing.
*Taṇhā* is that same [desire] as craving (*taṇhā*) by way of craving. This same method applies to the remaining doors as well.

102. Regarding "the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) consisting of the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ (*ahaṅkāra-mamaṅkāra*): here, “conceit” (*ahaṅkāra*) is pride (*māna*), and “the notion of ‘mine’” (*mamaṅkāra*) is craving (*taṇhā*), which is itself the underlying tendency to conceit.
Why was this stated without mentioning past lives (*pubbenivāsa*) and the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) [as in the previous case]?
Monks do not ask about mundane phenomena (*lokīya-dhamma*), but only about the supramundane (*lokuttara*). Therefore, he speaks only on the question that was asked.
Thus he spoke. This is called the *Ekavissajjita-sutta*, and it is also named the *Chabbisodhana*.

For herein, these six sections—the four conventional expressions, the five aggregates, the six elements, the six internal and external bases, one’s own conscious body, and the conscious bodies of others—are purified; therefore, it is called the "Sixfold Purification."
The elders dwelling beyond the sea, however, treat one's own and another’s aggregate of consciousness as a single unit and speak of six factors, including the four kinds of nutriment.
These six factors are: "What have you attained? How have you attained it? When did you attain it? Where..."

"Which defilements have been abandoned by you? Of which states are you a possessor?"—in this way they should be examined by means of the method of instruction through guidance. For here, "What has been attained by you? is a question regarding attainment;
that is, among the meditations, liberations, and so forth, or among the stream-entry path and so forth, what has been attained by you?
"How has it been attained by you? is a question regarding the means. For this is the intended meaning here: what...
Was it by making the characteristic of impermanence the primary focus that this was attained, or one of the other two characteristics—suffering or non-self?
Or was it by way of concentration (*samādhi*) that one focused upon it, or rather by way of insight (*vipassanā*)?
Likewise, did one focus upon the form realm (*rūpa*), or the formless realm (*arūpa*); or did one focus internally, or externally? When was it attained?
"Regarding 'at what time': this is a question concerning time, meaning it is asked at which time—such as morning, midday, or others—it was stated. Regarding 'where was it attained':
this is a question concerning place, meaning it is asked in what location—in the night-quarters, the day-quarters, at the foot of a tree, in a pavilion, or in which monastery—it was stated.
Regarding 'which defilements were abandoned': [this refers to] the defilements that have been abandoned."
"He asks" means it is said: "Which of your defilements, belonging to which path, have been abandoned?
"Of which states are you a possessor? is a question regarding attained states; it is said: "Of which states among the first path and the others are you a possessor?
Therefore, even if some bhikkhu were now to declare the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), he would not [be a true arahant] on that account alone.
He should be honored. Furthermore, for the sake of purification regarding these six points, he should be asked: "What have you attained?
Is it a *jhāna*, or one of the liberations (*vimokkha*), and so forth? For whatever Dhamma has been attained by someone becomes manifest to him.
If he says, "I have attained this," then he should be asked, "How was it attained by you?"
Regarding the characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*), what should be made the primary focus?

Or, among the thirty-eight objects or among phenomena classified as material, immaterial, internal, external, and so forth, by which approach should one apply one’s attention? For whatever one’s application of attention is directed toward, that becomes clear to them.
However, if one says, "This is my application of attention; this is how it was realized by me," then [one should ask]: "When did you..."
He should be asked, "When was it attained?"—"Was it in the morning, or at one of the other times such as midday?
For the time when all [monks] have attained [insight] is evident to themselves.
If he says, "I attained it at such-and-such a time," then he should be asked, "Where was it attained by you?"—"Was it in a daytime resting place, or in a nighttime resting place, and so forth?"
“In a certain place”? For the place where one has attained realization is evident to oneself.

If he says, “I attained it in such-and-such a place,” then he should be asked, “Which defilements have you abandoned?”—“Are they those to be abandoned by the first path, or rather those to be abandoned by the second and subsequent paths? For all [who have attained] by means of the path they themselves have realized...
The abandoned defilements become manifest.

If he says, "These specific defilements have been abandoned by me," then he should be asked, "Of which states are you a possessor?"—is it of the stream-entry path, or of one among the once-returner path and so forth? For [the abandonment] of all [defilements]...
The Dhamma realized by himself becomes manifest. Even if he says, "I am a possessor of these qualities," his word should not yet be trusted on that account alone.
For monks who are learned and skilled in inquiry can verify these six points. The path by which this bhikkhu has arrived must be verified.

If his way of arrival is not purified, he should be excluded [from the Saṅgha] on the grounds that "by this way of practice, the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhammā) are not obtained. However, if his way of arrival is purified,
and it is recognized that "for a long time he has been diligent in the three trainings,
devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like open space," then regarding that bhikkhu:
The exposition accords with and conforms to the practice. It is just as it has been said:

"Just as the waters of the Ganges accord with and conform to the waters of the Yamunā, even so the practice leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples accords with and conforms both to Nibbāna and to the practice. Thus it is.

Moreover, honor should not even be accorded to this extent. Why? Because even some worldlings may possess a practice similar to that of one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, that bhikkhu must be intimidated by various means.
For one whose taints are destroyed, there is no fear, trepidation, or horripilation even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon his head.
Or it does not exist [in an Arahant], yet for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it occurs even due to a slight [cause].

In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that the Elder Abhaya, a reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, being unable to take charge of a certain alms-collector (*piṇḍapātika*), gave him a signal. While he was bathing, [the alms-collector] submerged at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River.
He seized him by the foot. The alms-collector, thinking he was a *kumbhīla* (crocodile), let out a great cry; at that time, they perceived him as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*).

However, during the reign of King Candamukhatissa, there was a senior elder (*saṅghatthera*) in the Mahāvihāra who was an arahant with exhausted taints (*khīṇāsava*), yet he remained in the monastery itself due to weak eyesight.
When the monks had gone out for alms, the king, thinking, "I will attend upon the elder," went quietly.
Having approached, he seized his feet like a snake. The Elder, remaining as motionless as a stone pillar, asked:
"Who is here? "I am Tissa, venerable sir. "Do you smell a fragrance, Tissa? "Indeed, for one whose taints are exhausted, there is no such thing as fear.
However, even some worldlings may be exceedingly brave and fearless; such a person should be tested with an object that is provocative of passion.
King Vāsava, too, while attending upon a single elder, had him seated in his palace and sat beside him crushing jujube leaves.
The elder’s saliva began to flow, and from that, his state as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) was revealed.
For one whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted, craving for flavors has indeed been thoroughly abandoned; even toward divine tastes, there is no attachment whatsoever.
Therefore, having supported him with these means, if fear, trepidation, horripilation, or craving for flavors should arise in him,
he should be removed with the words, "You are not an arahant. But if, being fearless, undaunted, and unafraid,
he sits like a lion and does not conceive attachment even toward divine objects, this bhikkhu is one who possesses the full explanation.
"He is worthy of the honor sent from all sides by kings, royal ministers, and others.
The commentary on the *Chabbisodhana Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*,
the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is hereby concluded.
3. Commentary on the Sappurisadhamma Sutta (The Discourse on the Dhamma of the True Person) 105.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Sappurisadhamma Sutta. Therein, "the Dhamma of the true person" (*sappurisadhamma*) means the Dhamma of those who are true persons.
"The Dhamma of the untrue person" (*asappurisadhamma*) means the Dhamma of evil persons. Having thus established the matrix (*mātikā*), [the Buddha] further—
Just as a man skilled in the paths, having released the left hand, takes hold of the right;
and just as he speaks first of that which must be released, so too, while teaching first the state to be abandoned, the Blessed One said: "And what, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person?
and so forth. In this context, "noble families" refers to either the khattiya clans or the brāhmaṇa clans. For it is these two types of clans alone that are called "noble families."
It is said: "He is worthy of honor there" means that the bhikkhu is deserving of honor among those bhikkhus. "Having placed between" means having made an interval.
"Noble families" refers to khattiya families, brahmin families, or vessa families; for it is these three types of families that are called "noble families.
"Families of great wealth" refers to families endowed with vast riches. "Families of magnificent wealth" refers to [families endowed with] magnificent riches.
"Families endowed with excellent wealth. Within these two phrases, all four types of families are included.
For one born into any family whatsoever may indeed become possessed of great wealth or magnificent wealth through the power of merit.

106. "Renowned" means endowed with a large retinue. "Unknown" means they are not recognized within the midst of the Saṅgha and so forth, like arrows shot in the night. "Of little influence" means having a small retinue.
107. "A forest-dweller" (*āraññika*) is one who has undertaken the forest-dwelling ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). The same method applies to the remaining ascetic practices as well.
In this sutta, only nine ascetic practices are mentioned in the text; however, in detail, there are thirteen.
Whatever needs to be said regarding them has all been stated in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅganiddesa*).

108. *Atammayatā*: "Being-attached-to-that" (*tammayatā*) is said to be craving; thus, the meaning is "being free from craving. "Making non-attachment itself the internal" means making freedom from craving itself the cause, or making it internal—that is, generating it within the mind.

In the section on cessation (*nirodha*), since only those who are Non-returners with taints exhausted enter that attainment, and it does not exist for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the section on the "unworthy person" (*asappurisa*) is omitted.
"He does not conceive anything" means [he does not conceive] any person by means of the three types of conceiving.
"He does not conceive. "He does not conceive about anything" means he does not conceive regarding any location.
"He does not conceive by means of anything" means he does not conceive that person even by means of any basis (*vatthu*). The rest is entirely clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Sappurisadhammasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Sevitabbāsevitabbasutta*. 109.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Sevitabbāsevitabbasutta*. Therein, [the phrase] "that mutual bodily conduct... [is explained].

"I say that one bodily conduct is to be cultivated and another is not to be cultivated; I do not say that what is to be cultivated is, by some method, not to be cultivated, nor that what is not to be cultivated is to be cultivated"—this is the meaning.
The same method applies to verbal conduct and the rest. Thus, the Blessed One established a matrix with seven terms without yet analyzing them in detail.
He brought the teaching to its conclusion. Why? For the sake of making way for the Elder Sāriputta.
(113) Regarding mental conduct, wrong view and right view are not included as separate factors because they exist by way of the acquisition of views.
(114) In the arising of the mind, covetousness and the rest, when they have reached the level of courses of action, are to be understood [as such].

115. In the section on the acquisition of perception (*saññāpaṭilābhavāra*), the phrases beginning with "perception accompanied by covetousness" (*abhijjhāsahagatāya saññāya*) are stated for the purpose of showing the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) and so forth.

117. "With affliction" (*sabyābajjha*) means accompanied by suffering (*sadukkha*). "For the sake of the non-termination of existence" (*apariniṭṭhitabhāvāya*) means for the sake of the non-termination of the various states of existence (*bhava*).
And here, there are four types of states characterized by affliction. For even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who, by that very individuality (*attabhāva*)...

If one is unable to bring existence to its conclusion, unwholesome states increase from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, wholesome states decline, and one is said to produce a personal existence accompanied by suffering.
This is likewise the case for stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. Let alone ordinary worldlings and the rest; how could even a non-returner [produce such a state]?
He produces a personal existence; and how is it that unwholesome states increase for him while wholesome states decline?
For even a non-returner reborn in the Pure Abodes, upon beholding the pleasure groves, celestial palaces, and wish-fulfilling trees, utters this exclamation:
"Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! Yet for such a non-returner, greed for existence and craving for existence have not been abandoned.

Because craving has not been abandoned, unwholesome states increase for him, wholesome states decline, he produces a personal existence accompanied by suffering, and his existence remains unfulfilled; this is how it should be understood.
"Harmless" means free from suffering. This too should be understood by way of four types of persons. For even one who is a worldling (*puthujjana*)...
By means of that individual existence (attabhāva), he is able to bring existence to its final conclusion; he does not take rebirth again.
From the moment of taking rebirth onwards, his unwholesome states (akusala) diminish and only wholesome states (kusala) increase;

he produces an individual existence that is entirely free from suffering, and is thus said to be one whose existence is finalized. The same applies to the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the once-returner (sakadāgāmin), and the non-returner (anāgāmin).

Let it be granted for now that stream-enterers and the others [attain such states]; but how does an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) produce a state of existence free from affliction (*abyābajjha-attabhāva*), and how do his qualities such as the diminution of unwholesome states come about?
Even an ordinary person who is in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) is capable of bringing that state of existence to its conclusion.
For example, even in the case of Aṅgulimāla, who was killing one short of a thousand people, [he was capable of doing so].
One’s personal existence (*attabhāva*) is indeed called "unafflicted," and one indeed brings existence (*bhava*) to its final conclusion.
Only the unwholesome (*akusala*) diminishes, and insight (*vipassanā*) indeed causes [the wholesome] to take conception. 119.
Regarding the phrases "cognizable by the eye" and so forth, because for some person, lust and other defilements arise toward that very same form (*rūpa*),...
One delights in them and relishes them; delighting and relishing them, one comes to ruin and disaster. For some, however, these states do not arise;
they become disenchanted and dispassionate, and through disenchantment and dispassion, they reach Nibbāna. Therefore, it is not said that "they are mutually related.
This same method applies everywhere.
Regarding the phrase "Thus they should understand the meaning in detail": here, who among them understand the meaning of this speech of the Blessed One, and who do not?

First, those who have mastered both the text (*pāḷi*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) of this sutta, yet do not practice it—that is, they do not undertake the path of conformity (*anuloma-paṭipadā*) as it has been described—they are said not to understand. However, those who...
They are doers; they practice the path of conformity as it has been described, and thus they are said to "understand.
Even so, while this may lead to long-term welfare and happiness for those who undergo rebirth, one might ask: what happens to those who do not?
Those who do not undergo rebirth, being without clinging, attain final Nibbāna like a fire that has gone out, even after hundreds of thousands of eons.
After that lapse, there is no further suffering for them; thus, it is unilaterally for their own long-term welfare and happiness.
The rest is clear everywhere.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Bahudhātuka Sutta* 124.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the *Bahudhātuka Sutta*. Regarding the terms "fears" (*bhayāni*) and so forth therein: "fear" (*bhaya*) is the agitation of the mind.
“Calamity” (*upaddava*) is the state of distractedness. “Affliction” (*upasagga*) is the state of being beset, the state of clinging here and there.

Their distinction should be understood in this way: robbers dwelling in uneven terrain such as mountains send word to those living in the countryside, saying, “On such-and-such a day we shall attack your village. From the moment that news is heard...
They fall into fear and terror; this is what is called mental panic (*cittutrāsa*).

Thinking, "Here, angry thieves might bring us harm," they take their valuables and enter the forest together with their bipeds and quadrupeds, lying down here and there on the ground, entering the thickets while being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, [and avoiding] stumps and thorns.
They crush [the crops]. As they wander about in this manner, their state of being distracted is called the aspect of lack of one-pointedness (*anekaggatā*).

Then, when the thieves do not return on the aforementioned day, [the farmers] think, "That must have been a false report; we shall enter the village," and they enter the village with their belongings.
Thereupon, having learned that they have entered, [the thieves] surround the village and [station themselves] at the gates.
Having set fire [to the village] and killed people, the thieves plunder all the wealth and depart.

Among them, those who have survived the slaughter extinguish the fire and, clinging here and there to the shadows of storehouses, the shadows of walls, and so forth, sit down lamenting what has been lost.
This is the mode of being "assailed," which is called the mode of "clinging."
"Reed-houses" (*naḷāgāra*) are houses covered with reeds; however, the other structural materials therein are made of wood.
The same principle applies to grass-houses as well. "They arise from a fool" means they arise depending solely upon a fool;
for a foolish person who desires sovereignty, the rank of a viceroy, or some other great position, [employs] a few [servants] similar to himself...
Having seized the widow’s son and the great rogue, saying, "Come, I will make you lords," he struck them from village to village in the remote areas near mountain thickets and the like;
having made his nature as a bandit known, he gradually struck out even into market towns and the countryside.
Abandoning their homes, people departed, longing for a place of safety; depending on those [robbers], they [the robbers]...
In the springtime, both the monks and the nuns depart, abandoning their respective dwelling places.
In whatever place they go, almsfood and lodgings become difficult to obtain. Thus, fear indeed comes upon the four assemblies.
Even among those who have gone forth, two foolish monks, having initiated a dispute with one another, begin to accuse each other.
Thus, as in the case of the residents of Kosambī, a great quarrel arises; indeed, fear comes upon the four assemblies.
In this way, whatever fears arise, all of them should be understood to arise from the fool. "He said this":
the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma was concluded without having reached its ultimate conclusion. "What if I were to [inform] the One of Ten Powers..."
Thinking, "Having asked this, he will bring the teaching to its completion through his own omniscient knowledge," he spoke these words beginning with, "To what extent, venerable sir? (125).
Among the eighteen elements, eight and a half elements constitute the discernment of form, while seven and a half elements constitute the discernment of the formless.
Only the grasping of the material and immaterial has been explained. All [phenomena], by way of the aggregates, constitute the five aggregates.
The five aggregates are the truth of suffering; the craving that originates them is the truth of the origin; the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation;
and the practice that leads to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path. Such is the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths for a single bhikkhu.
The conclusion has been stated by bringing it to its ultimate point. This is the summary here;
however, these elements have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "He knows and sees" refers to the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
The earth element and the others were mentioned to show that the conscious body is empty and devoid of a self-entity. Those [latter elements] also [are to be understood] through the former ones...
It is to be filled with eighteen elements. While filling it, one should fill it by extracting from the consciousness element.
This consciousness element is sixfold, according to eye-consciousness and so forth.
Therein, when the eye-consciousness element is discerned, its two bases—the eye element as its physical basis and the form element as its object—are necessarily discerned as well.

This method applies everywhere. However, when the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is discerned, two elements are necessarily discerned by way of its preceding and succeeding moments as the mind-element (manodhātu), and by way of its object as the mental-object element (dhammadhātu).
Thus, among these eighteen elements, ten and a half elements constitute the discernment of form; according to the previous method, this too belongs to one person.
The discourse has been explained by bringing the bhikkhu’s departure to its conclusion.
Regarding the terms "the element of pleasure" (*sukhadhātu*) and so forth: it is both pleasure and an element in the sense of being empty of a sentient being, thus it is the "element of pleasure.
This same method applies everywhere. And herein, the first four elements are taken by way of their opposites, while the last two are not.
By way of similarity: for the equanimity element is similar to the ignorance element by virtue of its unmanifested nature.
And here, when the elements of pleasure and pain have been discerned, the body-consciousness element has necessarily been discerned;
when the remaining [four] have been discerned, the mind-consciousness element has necessarily been discerned. These six elements should also be completed in the same manner as the eighteen below.

While filling [the body], it should be filled by drawing [the air] out from the equanimity element (*upekkhā-dhātu*). Thus, among these eighteen elements, nine and a half elements constitute the discernment of form;
this too has been explained as bringing a single bhikkhu’s mastery to its ultimate conclusion according to the previous method.

The meaning of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth should be understood in the same manner as was stated for sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and the rest under the "Two-fold Thoughts" (*dvedhāvitakka*). This is also the case in the Abhidhamma.

The detailed exposition of these [elements] has already been given in that very manner, beginning with: “In this context, what is the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*)? It is reasoning and applied thought associated with the sense-spheres,” and so forth.
These six elements must also be filled out using the same eighteenfold scheme as mentioned below.
When filling them out, they should be extracted from the sense-sphere element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, there are ten and a half elements.
"Comprehension of form" (rūpapariggaha) has also been explained by bringing this [topic] to its conclusion for a single bhikkhu, according to the same method as before.

Among the sense-sphere elements and so forth, the five aggregates of the sense sphere are called the "sense-sphere element" (kāmadhātu); the five aggregates of the fine-material sphere are called the "fine-material element" (rūpadhātu);
and the four aggregates of the immaterial sphere are called the "immaterial element" (arūpadhātu). However, in the Abhidhamma it says: "Therein..."
The detailed exposition of these [elements] has already been given in the manner beginning with, "What is the sense-sphere element? Taking the Avīci hell as its lower limit," and so forth.
These three elements must also be filled out from below, exactly as the eighteen [elements].
When filling them out, they should be filled by taking them out from the sense-sphere element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, there are ten and a half elements.
“Comprehension of form” is explained here as having brought this [teaching] to its conclusion for a single bhikkhu, in the same manner as before.
“Conditioned” means made by the coming together of conditions; this is a designation for the five aggregates. “Unconditioned” (asaṅkhata) means not conditioned;
this is a designation for Nibbāna. These two elements also must be completed with eighteen [instances] each, just as below.

By filling [the elements], one must fill them after having extracted them from the conditioned elements (*saṅkhatadhātu*). Thus, among these eighteen elements, ten and a half elements constitute the discernment of form;
this has been explained by the same method as before, bringing the conclusion for a single bhikkhu to its ultimate point.

126. "Internal and external" means both internal and external. For here, the six beginning with the eye are internal, and the six beginning with visible forms are external. Here too, the path together with insight (*vipassanā*) is described by the words "he knows" and "he sees."
The passage beginning with "When this exists, that comes to be" has already been explained in detail in the *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta*.
(127) "Impossible" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause; "no occasion" (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition. By both terms, he negates the cause itself.
For a cause is called the "standing place" (*ṭhāna*) and the "occasion" (*avakāsa*) of its own fruit, because the existence of that fruit is dependent upon it.
And it is said: “Yan” means by which reason. “One endowed with right view” (diṭṭhisampanno) refers to a noble disciple who has entered the stream and is endowed with the vision of the Path.
“Any conditioned phenomenon whatsoever” (kañci saṅkhāraṃ) means even a single conditioned formation among the conditioned phenomena belonging to the four planes of existence.
“Should regard as permanent” (niccato upagaccheyya) means he would grasp it as being eternal. “This is not possible” (netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati) means that such a cause does not exist.
It is not found. "That which is called an 'ordinary person' (puthujjana)" refers to the reason why one is an ordinary person. "This possibility exists" means that this reason is present.
For, by way of the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi), he might grasp some conditioned formation among the conditioned formations belonging to the three planes as permanent;
this is the meaning. However, because the formations of the fourth plane are characterized by an abundance of heat, they are like a day heated [by the sun].
Like a red-hot iron ball, they do not become an object for flies or for other unwholesome states.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood regarding any conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) when it is said to be "pleasurable" and so forth.
"One might approach [it] as pleasurable" means by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), thinking: "The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death."

This was said with reference to grasping [something] as pleasant. However, when overcome by feverish distress, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) approaches some formation (saṅkhāra) as pleasant—like one terrified of a rutting elephant in order to quell that distress, or like a clean brahmin approaching excrement—with a consciousness dissociated from views.
In the section on the self (attavāra), it is called "a formation" for the purpose of including the designations (paṇṇatti) such as the kasiṇas.

It is said, "without grasping at any phenomenon. Here too, this should be understood in terms of the four planes for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), and in terms of the three planes for the worldling (*puthujjana*).

In all instances, the delimitation for the noble disciple is appropriate solely in terms of the three planes. For whatever the worldling grasps, from that very thing the noble disciple undoes his grasping. The worldling...
For whatever is permanent, pleasant, or self that one grasps as such, the noble disciple—grasping it instead as impermanent, suffering, and non-self—undoes that grasping.
128. Regarding the terms "mother" and so forth:
she who gives birth is the mother; he who begets is the father; and one who is a human being, whose taints are destroyed, is an arahant.
This is what is intended. But could a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) deprive another of life? That too is impossible.
For even if someone were to say to a noble disciple who has passed into another existence—even one unaware of his own noble status:
"Having deprived this ant of life, you shall exercise the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) throughout the entire interior of the universe," [the noble disciple would never do so].
He would not deprive him of life. Even if one were to say to him, "If you do not have him killed, I will cut off your head," he might even cut off his own head, but he would not kill him.

This was said for the purpose of showing the great blameworthiness of the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and for the purpose of demonstrating the power of the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). This, then, is the point here.

The underlying intention is this: the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*) is blameworthy, for it is possible that a worldling might even commit immediate transgressions (*ānantariya*) such as matricide.
Furthermore, the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) possesses great power, in that he does not perform such deeds.
"With a corrupt mind" means with a mind defiled by murderous intent. "He should shed blood" means [blood] from a living body.
He might cause even as much blood as would be drunk by a small gnat to flow.

"He should split the Saṅgha" means he should split the Saṅgha—those who share the same communion and reside within the same boundary—by means of five causes. For it has been said: "In five ways, Upāli, the Saṅgha is split:
by a formal act (kamma), by a recitation (uddesa), by a proclamation (voharanta), by a motion (anussāvana), and by the distribution of voting tickets (salākaggāha)."
In that context, "by means of a formal act" (*kammena*) refers to by means of one of the four formal acts, such as the *apalokana* (informal resolution) and so forth.
"By means of a recitation" (*uddesena*) refers to by means of one of the five recitations of the *Pātimokkha*. "Speaking" (*voharanto*) means conversing;

that is, pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as declaring what is non-Dhamma to be Dhamma, and so forth, through various specific instances. "By means of a proclamation" (*anussāvanena*) [refers to] "Is it not you... [and so on].
"You know my noble birth, my state as one who has gone forth, and my great learning;
it is not fitting for you even to conceive the thought that one such as I would embrace a teaching contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, subverting the Teacher’s instruction.
Is Avīci cool to me like a grove of blue lotuses? Do I not fear the states of misery?"—in this manner [he spoke] into his ear.

"By making a verbal declaration and by means of a proclamation. "By the taking of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*)" means: having thus proclaimed, having steadied their minds, and having made them of a nature not to turn back, [the monk says] "Take this voting ticket," and [this is done] by the taking of voting tickets.
And here, the formal act (*kamma*) itself, or the recitation (*uddesa*), is the criterion; however, the preliminary speech, the proclamation, and the taking of voting tickets are the prior stages.

For when one who is proclaiming by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds makes an announcement there for the sake of generating consent and even distributes voting tickets (*salākā*), the Saṅgha remains undivided.

But when four or more have thus distributed the voting tickets and perform a separate formal act (*kamma*) or recitation (*uddesa*), then the Saṅgha is said to be "divided. Thus, one endowed with right view...

That an individual could split the Saṅgha—this is impossible. Up to this point, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) have been shown, which an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) commits but not a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). To clarify them:
"By way of the deed, by way of the door, and likewise by way of duration for an eon;"
The detailed exposition should be understood through the *Pākasādhāraṇa* and other such works.

Regarding that, first, from the perspective of the deed (*kamma*): here, for one who is already a human being, the act of depriving of life a mother or a father who is also a human being—even if their gender has been changed—constitutes an immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), and its result...
Even one who thinks, "I shall ward it off," and fills the entire world-system with golden stupas the size of the Great Cetiya,

and even after giving a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks seated throughout the entire world-system, and even after wandering about without letting go of a corner of the Blessed Buddha’s outer robe,
is reborn in hell alone upon the dissolution of the body. But he who, being himself a human being...

If one deprives of life a mother or father who has become an animal, or if one is oneself a human being and deprives of life one who has become an animal, or if an animal itself deprives of life another who has become an animal, that action does not constitute an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense;
however, it is still grave, and it remains as an *ānantariya* by way of its impact. This question, moreover, was stated with reference to those of human birth.
In this regard, the "fourfold sheep" case, the "fourfold battle" case, and the "fourfold thief" case must be explained.
For even with the intention, "I am killing a sheep," if one kills a human being—whether mother or father—who stands in the place of that sheep, one incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
However, [if one kills] a sheep with the intention of a sheep, or with the intention of mother or father...

One who kills [them] does not incur an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. However, one who kills one's own mother or father with the specific intention (*abhisandhi*) directed toward them as mother and father certainly incurs it.
This same method applies to the other two tetrads as well. And just as it is with respect to mother and father, so too should these tetrads be understood regarding an *arahant*.
One incurs an *ānantariya* only by killing a human *arahant*, not one who is a *yakkha* or a spirit. Nevertheless, the kamma is still grave.

It is exactly like an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). If a person who was an *arhat* at the time of being an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) is struck with a weapon or given poison while still an ordinary worldling, and he dies after having attained *arahatta*, it is indeed the killing of an *arhat*.
However, if he consumes a gift given while he was an ordinary worldling after having attained *arahatta*, it is considered as if it were given to an ordinary worldling.

It exists. For one who kills the remaining noble persons (ariyapuggala), there is no immediate retribution (ānantariya); however, the kamma is grave and is indeed equivalent to an immediate retribution.
Regarding the shedding of blood: because the Tathāgata possesses an indestructible body, there is no such thing as the flowing of blood from a wound inflicted by another’s assault;
rather, the blood collects internally within the body at a single spot. By Devadatta...
A splinter from a discarded stone broke off and struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot;
his foot became filled with blood as if it had been struck by an axe. For one who acts in such a way, an *ānantariya* offense occurs.
However, Jīvaka, with the Tathāgata’s consent, cut the skin with a blade and removed the foul blood from that place.
He made it comfortable; for one acting in such a way, there is only meritorious karma.
Now, what happens to those who destroy a shrine (*cetiya*) after the Tathāgata has attained *parinibbāna*, or who cut down the Bodhi tree, or who take action against the relics?
Their karma is grave, similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). However, [if they act against] a stupa containing relics...
Or it is permissible to cut down a branch of the Bodhi tree that is damaging a clay image.

Even if birds perched there void their excrement upon the shrine (cetiya), it is still permissible to cut it down; for the bodily relic-shrine (sarīracetiya) is more important than a shrine used for enjoyment (paribhogacetiya).
If someone is going away after breaking up the site of a shrine, it is permissible to cut down even the root of the Bodhi tree and carry it off.
However, if a branch of the Bodhi tree obstructs the Bodhi house, it may not be cut down for the sake of protecting the house;
for the house is for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same principle applies to the Seat House (āsana-ghara).
But in a Seat House where a relic (dhātu) has been deposited, it is permissible to cut down a Bodhi branch for the purpose of protecting that [relic]. For the purpose of tending the Bodhi tree—
It is indeed permissible to cut off a branch that withers vitality or a place that is putrid; merit is even gained in such acts, just as in the tending of the Blessed One’s body.

When a schism in the Saṅgha occurs while the Saṅgha within the boundary has not assembled, if one forms a separate assembly and performs an act—whether by making a formal declaration, by proclaiming a resolution, or by taking a vote—there is both a schism and an act of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*). This applies even if one acts with the perception that the assembly is united.
However, it is permissible [to speak against him]; for one who causes a schism in this way, it is merely a formal act (*kamma*), not an immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*).
Likewise, it is so when there is an assembly of fewer than nine members. At the very least, for one who divides the Saṅgha with a group of nine persons, there is an immediate retribution.
For those followers who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma, it is a highly blameworthy act; however, those who speak according to the Dhamma are blameless.
In that regard, this sutta concerns precisely nine persons in a schism of the Saṅgha: “On one side, Upāli, there are four;
on the other side, there are four; the ninth proclaims: ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction;
take this, approve of this. In this way, Upāli, there is both a fracture of the Saṅgha and a schism of the Saṅgha.”
“Upāli, when there are nine or more than nine [monks], it is both a fracture in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha.
Among these five, the schism in the Saṅgha is verbal action; the rest are bodily actions. Thus should the analysis be understood by way of action. By way of door:
all of these arise from both the bodily door and the verbal door. However, among these, the former...
The four [offenses] arising from the door of speech by way of the application of the *āṇattika-vijjāmaya* (the magic of commanding) fulfill the door of the body alone;
whereas schism in the Saṅgha, for one who effects a split by means of hand gestures (*hatthamuddā*), arises from the door of the body but fulfills the door of speech alone.
Thus is the analysis to be understood here also by way of the doors.
Regarding "lasting for an eon" (*kappaṭṭhitiya*): here, it is the schism of the Saṅgha itself that lasts for an eon.
For if one causes a schism in the Saṅgha either during an eon (*kappe*) or in the interval between eons (*kappavemajjhe*), one is liberated only upon the destruction of the eon.

Even if one causes a schism today with the thought, "This very same eon will perish tomorrow," one is liberated on that very day; one suffers in hell for only a single day. Such is the act of causing [the schism].
But there is none [of that]. The remaining four types of karma are indeed *ānantariya* (immediate) and do not persist for the duration of an eon (*kappa-ṭṭhitiya*).
Thus, the analysis here should be understood even in terms of persistence for an eon.
As for "manifest" (*pākata*): for one who has committed these five types of karma, it is the schism of the Saṅgha itself that functions as the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
It ripens; the remaining [offenses] fall under such categories as "kamma that has been" (*ahosikamma*) or "there was no ripening of kamma" (*nāhosi kammavipāka*).
In the absence of a schism in the Sangha, the shedding of blood [from a Buddha’s person] ripens; in its absence, the murder of an arahant;
and in the absence of that, if the father is virtuous while the mother is immoral—or if she is not likewise virtuous—then patricide ripens by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

If there is the killing of mother and father—when both are equal in terms of either virtue or lack of virtue—it is the killing of the mother alone that ripens by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For the mother is one who has performed difficult tasks and is of great benefit to her children; thus should the analysis (*vinicchaya*) here be understood even from common knowledge.
Regarding "common [offenses] and so forth": the first four are common to all, whether householders or those gone forth. Schism in the Saṅgha...
However, because of the statement: "Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not split the Saṅgha; a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā does not split the Saṅgha;

rather, Upāli, it is a bhikkhu who, being of normal status (pakatatta), belonging to the same community (samānasamvāsaka), and standing within the same boundary (samānasīmā), splits the Saṅgha," it belongs only to a bhikkhu of the kind described.

It does not belong to another; therefore, it is unique. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it should be understood that all those [states] are accompanied by painful feeling and associated with hatred and delusion;
thus, the analysis here is to be known through the categories of commonality and so forth.

"Another teacher" means: even in another existence, one might think, "This teacher of mine is unable to perform the duties of a teacher," and thus take up another sectarian founder as "this is my teacher"—but such a thing is impossible. This is the meaning.

129. "In one world-system" means in a ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*). For there are three kinds of fields: the field of birth (*jātikhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakhetta*).
Among these, the "field of birth" refers to the ten-thousandfold world-system.

This is because at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, his birth, his attainment of enlightenment, his turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and his relinquishing of the life-faculty...
And at the time of the Parinibbāna, it trembles. However, the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*) is a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

For within this, the authority of the *Āṭānāṭiya*, *Moraparitta*, *Dhajaggaparitta*, *Ratanaparitta*, and so forth, prevails. But there is no limit to the measure of the field of the domain (*visayakhettassa*).
For the Buddhas, "as far as their knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends their knowledge; the knowable is coextensive with knowledge."
Because of the statement, "knowledge has a limit that must be understood," there is nothing that is not an object [of knowledge].
However, regarding these three fields, there is no Sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this Cakkavāḷa;
yet there is one stating that they do not so arise. The Three Piṭakas are the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Suttanta Piṭaka... [and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka].
The Abhidhamma Piṭaka consists of the three councils: the council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the council of the Elder Yasa, and the council of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.

Regarding these three councils, within the word of the Buddha as established in the Tipiṭaka, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere apart from this Cakkavāḷa; however, there is [sutta] stating that they do not so arise.
"Neither before nor after" means not earlier and not later. It is said that they do not arise simultaneously, but rather arise either before or after.

In this context, "before" should not be understood as the period from the time he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree with the resolve, "I shall not rise until I have attained enlightenment," up until his taking of rebirth-linking in the mother's womb. [This applies] to the Bodhisatta...

Indeed, by the very act of taking rebirth and by the shaking of the ten thousandfold world-system, the demarcation of his field was established, and the arising of another Buddha was thereby prevented.

It should not be understood that this [prevention] occurs only after the relics remain for as long as they do—from the time of the final *parinibbāna* until the relics persist even in the size of a mustard seed. For as long as the relics remain, the Buddhas remain. Therefore...
Within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is indeed precluded. However, once the Parinibbāna of the relics has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is not precluded.
For there are three kinds of disappearances: the disappearance of the scriptures (pariyatti), the disappearance of realization (paṭivedha), and the disappearance of practice (paṭipatti).
