In this context, "learning" (*pariyatti*) refers to the three baskets (*piṭaka*). "Realization" (*paṭivedha*) refers to the realization of the truths.
"Practice" (*paṭipatti*) refers to the path. Among these, both realization and practice may exist or may not exist.
For at one time there were many monks who possessed realization, such that one had to point a finger and say, "This monk is an ordinary person" (*puthujjana*). Even in this very [time]...
At one time in the island of Dīpa, there was not a single bhikkhu who was still a worldling (*puthujjana*). Those who fulfill the practice (*paṭipatti*) are sometimes many and sometimes few.
Thus, both realization (*paṭivedha*) and practice may exist or may not exist; however, for the endurance of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) is the measure.
For a wise person, having heard the Three Piṭakas, fulfills both as well—just as our Bodhisatta did in the presence of Āḷāra.
Having produced the five supernormal powers and the seven meditative attainments, he asked about the preliminary exercise for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

[the other] said, "I do not know. Then, having gone to Udaka and compared the distinction he had attained, he asked about the preliminary exercise for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he explained it, and immediately upon his words—
The Great Being accomplished that; in the same way, a wise bhikkhu, having heard the scriptures (*pariyatti*), fulfills both.
Therefore, when the scriptures remain, the Dispensation (*sāsana*) remains.
But when they disappear, first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is lost. Among those, the *Paṭṭhāna*...
First of all, the Abhidhamma-piṭaka disappears; subsequently, the Dhamma-saṅgaṇī disappears.
When that has disappeared and the other two Piṭakas remain, the Dispensation still persists.

Therein, as the Sutta-piṭaka is disappearing, first the Aṅguttara-nikāya disappears, starting from the Elevenfold (Ekādasaka) down to the Singlefold (Ekaka). Immediately after that, [the Saṃyutta-nikāya disappears].
The Saṃyutta Nikāya disappears starting from the Cakka-peyyāla up to the Oghataraṇa;
immediately after that, the Majjhima Nikāya disappears starting from the Indriyabhāvanā up to the Mūlapariyāya;
and immediately after that, the Dīgha Nikāya disappears starting from the Dasuttara up to the Brahmajāla. This applies to one, or even two [collections].
The questioning of verses (*gāthānaṃ pucchā*) passes the course of time; it is unable to sustain the Dispensation, as in the case of the questions of Sabhiya and Āḷavaka.
It is said that these [questions] belonging to the era of Kassapa Buddha were unable to sustain the Dispensation in the interim.
However, even when two of the Piṭakas have disappeared, the Dispensation persists as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, including the Parivāra and the Khandhakas.

When both Vibhaṅgas have disappeared, the Sāsana remains as long as the *Ṭhitavastu* (the Section on Discipline) remains. When both Vibhaṅgas have disappeared, the Sāsana remains even as long as the *Mātikā* (the Schedule) remains.

When the *Mātikā* has disappeared, the Sāsana remains as long as the *Pātimokkha*, the going forth (*pabbajjā*), and full ordination (*upasampadā*) remain. The outward signs (*liṅga*) last for a long duration;
however, the lineage of white-robed recluses (*setavattha-samaṇa-vaṃsa*) dates back from the time of the Buddha Kassapa.

From that point on, he was unable to uphold the Dispensation. However, from the time of the last penetration of the Truths and from the time of the last breach of morality, the Dispensation is said to have declined. From that point onward, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.
There are three kinds of *parinibbāna*, namely: *parinibbāna* of the defilements (*kilesa*), *parinibbāna* of the aggregates (*khandha*), and *parinibbāna* of the relics (*dhātu*).
Among these, the *parinibbāna* of the defilements occurred at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*); the *parinibbāna* of the aggregates occurred at Kusinārā;
and the *parinibbāna* of the relics will take place in the future. It is said that when the Dispensation (*sāsana*) declines, the relics in this island of Tambapaṇṇi will assemble together.
They will go to the Mahācetiya; from the Mahācetiya they will go to the Rājāyatana-cetiya on Nāgadīpa, and from there they will go to the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Even from the abode of the Nāgas, from the world of the gods, and from the Brahma-world, the relics will go specifically to the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Not even a relic the size of a mustard seed will be lost along the way. All the relics [will arrive] at the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Having become a single mass like a solid bar of gold, they will emit six-colored rays that will pervade the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*).
Then, the deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*) will assemble and say: "Today the Teacher attains final *parinibbāna*; today..."
Thinking, "The Dispensation is declining; this is now our final sight," they will feel even greater compassion than on the day the One of Ten Powers passed away into Parinibbāna.
With the exception of those non-returners whose taints are destroyed, the rest will not be able to maintain their composure.
From among the relics, the fire-element will arise and ascend as far as the Brahma-world; even a portion the size of a mustard seed—
As long as the relics remain, there will be a single continuity; once the relics have reached their end, it will be severed.
When the relics have thus vanished after displaying such great majesty, the Dispensation is said to have vanished.
As long as it has not thus vanished, it is said to be "not last. In this way, they may arise neither before nor after one another.
This situation is not possible.
But why do they not arise simultaneously? Because it would not be marvelous. For Buddhas are marvelous persons. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, one person, arising in the world, arises as a marvelous person. Who is he? [And so forth.]
“There is one person, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For if two, four, eight, or sixteen were to arise together, they would not be marvelous;
for even in a single monastery, there is no great gain or honor for two shrines, nor is it so when there is a multitude of monks.
If they were not marvelous when born, then Buddhas would be like that [ordinary beings] as well; therefore, they do not arise [frequently].

Furthermore, it is because there is no distinction in their teaching. For whatever Dhamma—one such as the divisions of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)—one [Buddha] teaches, that same Dhamma would have to be taught by another who had arisen [subsequently].
Consequently, it would not be marvelous; however, while one [Buddha] is teaching the Dhamma...
The teaching is also marvelous because it is free from dispute.
For if many Buddhas were to arise, many teachers and their disciples would quarrel,
saying, "Our Buddha is handsome," or "Our Buddha has a sweet voice, is successful, and is meritorious."
Therefore, they do not arise in this way either. Furthermore, this reason has already been explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda. For it was said:
"In this regard, venerable Nāgasena, this was spoken by the Blessed One: 'It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that...'"
‘That two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and without precedence or succession in a single world-system—such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, venerable Nāgasena, all Tathāgatas teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
when speaking, they speak of the Four Noble Truths; and when training [disciples], they train them in these very things.”
And they train them in the three trainings, and while instructing them, they instruct them in the practice of heedfulness.

If, venerable Nāgasena, the teaching of all Tathāgatas is one, their discourse is one, their training is one, and their instruction is one, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise at the same moment? By the arising of even a single Buddha, this—
"The world has become filled with radiance. If there were a second Buddha, this world would become even more intensely filled with radiance through the light of both.
Furthermore, two Tathāgatas teaching would teach with ease, and two Tathāgatas instructing would instruct with ease.
Tell me the reason for this, so that I may be free from doubt."
"Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the single domain of one Buddha; it sustains the qualities of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain them;
it would shake, tremble, quake, incline, lean, bend, scatter, dissolve, and be utterly destroyed, and it would not remain in its place."
“Just as, great king, there might be a boat capable of carrying only one person. When that one person has boarded, the boat would be level with the water.

Then a second person were to come along, similar in lifespan, complexion, age, stature, and in every limb and member—whether thin or stout—and were to board that same boat. Would that boat, great king, [sink]?”
"Could it support both? "No, venerable sir; it would move, shake, waver, incline, lean, scatter, be blown away, and be destroyed;
it would not remain stable, but would sink into the water.
"In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the support for only one Buddha—for only one Tathāgata."
It sustains this quality: if a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him;
it would shake... [and so on] ...it would not remain stable.
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to eat food to his full satisfaction, filling his throat until he is completely satiated.
Suppose, O Great King, that this person—his elements nourished, fulfilled, and made continuous, his body made supple and his limbs no longer bent—were to eat that same amount of food once again;
would that man, O Great King, be happy? "Certainly not, Venerable Sir; having eaten it once, he would surely die.
"In the very same way, O Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the single domain of one Buddha."
…pe… “It would not find a place [to stand],” he said.
“Venerable Nāgasena, does the earth tremble because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma?
“In this case, Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to their very rims. Having taken a jewel from one cart,” he said.
“Suppose they were to pour [the jewels] into a single cart; would that cart, O Great King, be able to bear the weight of the jewels from both carts?
“No, venerable sir. Its nave would burst, its spokes would break, its rim would give way, and its axle would snap.
“What do you think, Great King? Is it because of the excessive weight of the jewels?”
“Does a cart break? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, Great King, the earth shakes because of the excessive burden of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, Great King, this reason has been set forth to illustrate the power of the Buddha;
now hear another fitting reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously. If, Great King...”
If two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, a dispute would arise among their assemblies:

"The Buddha belongs to you; the Buddha belongs to us," and they would become divided into two factions. Great King, it is just as when a dispute arises between the retinues of two powerful ministers: "Your minister is ours; our minister is yours," and they become divided into two factions.

In the same way, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same moment, a dispute would arise within their assemblies, saying, "The Buddha belongs to you; the Buddha belongs to us," and they would become divided into two factions.
This, Great King, is one reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same moment.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
If, Great King, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at one and the same moment, then the statement that "the Buddha is the foremost" would be false;
the statement that "the Buddha is the eldest" would be false.

If the statement that "the Buddha is the best," "the Buddha is distinguished," "the Buddha is supreme," "the Buddha is excellent," "the Buddha is peerless," "the Buddha is equal to the unequaled," "the Buddha is without equal," "the Buddha is without counterpart," and "the Buddha is without rival" were false, then you,
Great King, should accept this reason according to its meaning.
For this reason, two perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously.
Moreover, Great King, it is the natural disposition of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world at a time.
For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha. Furthermore, Great King—
Whatever is great in the world, that is but one. The earth, Great King, is great, yet it is but one. The ocean is great, yet it is but one.
Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, yet it is but one. Space is great, yet it is but one.
Sakka is great, yet he is but one. Māra is great, yet he is but one. Brahmā is great, yet he is but one.
“The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is great; he alone appears in the world.
Wherever they arise, there is no room for another. Therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises all alone in the world.
“It is well explained, Bhante Nāgasena, by means of similes and reasons.”
"In one world-system" means in one *cakkavāḷa*. By this very phrase, ten thousand *cakkavāḷas* below are included;
these too must be delimited by way of a single *cakkavāḷa*. For when Buddhas arise, they arise only in this very *cakkavāḷa*;
however, once the place of arising has been restricted [to this one], [they do not arise] in other *cakkavāḷas* than this.
Or rather, it is already excluded by the statement "they do not arise.

Regarding the phrase "neither before nor after": here, "before" refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*), and "after" refers to the period following its disappearance.
In that regard, the disappearance of the Wheel-Treasure occurs in two ways: either through the death of the Universal Monarch (*cakkavatti*)...
Or [it may disappear] through going forth into homelessness. Furthermore, as it disappears, it vanishes either upon death or upon going forth on the seventh day;
beyond that, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is not obstructed.
But why do two wheel-turning monarchs not arise in a single world-system (cakkavāḷa)? Because it would put an end to disputes and because of their marvelous nature.
And it is because of the great majesty of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*). For if two were to arise, a dispute would arise, [each side saying], "Our king is great! Our king is great!
Furthermore, it would not be extraordinary for there to be a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) on one continent and another Wheel-turning Monarch on another continent.
And as for this Wheel-Treasure, among the four [continents] surrounded by two thousand islands...
One of great power, capable of bestowing sovereignty over the great islands, would thus decline.

Therefore, because of the cessation of dispute, because of the marvelous nature [of the phenomenon], and because of the great power of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*), two do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

130. As for the statement, "Could a woman be an *arhat*, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*)?"—let alone the state of Buddhahood, which is capable of delivering the world after having produced the qualities of omniscience, even the mere aspiration of a woman does not succeed.
Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause [of merit], meeting with a Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
For these are the causes for the fulfillment of one’s aspiration. Thus, since a woman is incapable of fulfilling even an aspiration, how could she attain Buddhahood? Therefore it was said:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
Furthermore, a mass of merit fulfilled in every aspect produces a personal existence (attabhāva) that is likewise fulfilled in every aspect.
Only a man can be an Arahant or a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).

This is because, even in cases such as "if a woman were to be a Wheel-turning Monarch," the marks do not reach fulfillment due to the absence in a woman of such features as the male organ concealed in a sheath;
furthermore, by the absence of the Woman-Treasure (itthiratana), the possession of the seven treasures cannot be achieved.
Furthermore, there is no personal existence (attabhāva) superior to that of all men; therefore it is said:

"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should be a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavattī). And because the three positions of Sakka and so forth are supreme, while the female gender is inferior, the status of Sakka and the others is likewise prohibited for her.
But surely, just as the female characteristic does not exist in the Brahma-world, so too the male characteristic does not exist there? Therefore, one should not even say:
"It is possible that a man might become a Brahmā. It is not the case that this should not be said.
Why? Because a man is reborn there. For by "Brahmā-hood," the state of being a Mahābrahmā is intended.
A woman here, having developed jhāna and passed away, is reborn into the company of the Brahma-parisajja devas, but not among the Mahābrahmās;
however, it cannot be said that a man does not arise there.
Even though both are equally devoid of gender marks in this regard, the Brahmās have the form of males and not the form of females; therefore, this is well-stated.

131. Regarding the passage beginning with "Of bodily misconduct," etc.: just as the seeds of the nimba tree, the kosātaki creeper, and so forth do not produce sweet fruit, but rather produce that which is unpalatable and not sweet, even so, bodily misconduct and the like do not produce a sweet result, but rather produce a result that is not sweet.
And just as the seeds of sugarcane, rice, and so forth [produce] what is sweet and of excellent flavor...
They produce a sweet fruit, not one that is unpleasant or bitter; likewise, bodily good conduct and so forth produce only a sweet result, not one that is not sweet. And this has been said:
"As is the seed that is sown, such is the fruit that is reaped."
“The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil.
Therefore it was said: “It is impossible, it cannot happen that [one who has committed] bodily misconduct... and so forth.
In the phrases “one possessed of bodily misconduct,” etc., “possessed” (samaṅgī) refers to fivefold possession: possession as accumulation, possession as volition...
Possession of kamma, possession of result, and possession of presence. In this context, at the moment of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, it is called "possession of accumulation.

Likewise, there is "possession of volition. Furthermore, as long as they have not reached Arahantship, all beings are said to be "possessors of kamma" with reference to the kamma accumulated in the past that is capable of yielding a result.
These are called the possession of kamma. The possession of result (vipāka-samaṅgitā) should be understood as occurring only at the moment of fruition.

As long as beings have not reached Arahantship, for them—whether they pass away from here or there and are reborn in hell, appearing there in the forms of masses of flames, cauldrons of molten iron, and so forth, or whether they enter the womb and attain the state of lying in a mother’s womb—the hellish state persists.
For those being reborn among the devas, the "devaloka" appears as a sign of rebirth through such modes of manifestation as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) and celestial palaces (*vimāna*);
thus, their state of possessing the appearance [of that world] consists in their not being free from this manifestation of the sign of rebirth.
That [appearance] wavers, while the others are immovable. For even when hell appears, the devaloka may also appear; and in the devaloka...

When hell appears, the human world also appears; when the human world appears, the animal realm also appears; and even when the animal realm appears, the human world likewise appears. Here is an illustration of this:
it is said that at the foot of Soṇagiri, in the Acela monastery, there was a certain Dhamma-preacher named the Elder Soṇa.
His father was a dog-keeper. Although the Elder tried to dissuade him, he was unable to establish him in self-restraint;
thinking, "Lest this old man perish," he reluctantly ordained him when he had grown old.
As he lay on his sickbed, hell appeared before him, and from the foot of Soṇagiri, large dogs came one after another as if desiring to devour him.
They surrounded him. Terrified by that great fear, he cried out, "Save me, dear Soṇa!
Save me, dear Soṇa! "What is it, Great Elder? "Do you not see, dear one? he said, and explained what was happening.
The Elder Soṇa thought, "How indeed could my father, such as I am, be reborn in hell? I shall be his support. Then, with the novices, [he gathered] various flowers.
Having had [the ground] brought, he had the offering of floor-coverings and the offering of seats performed on the terrace of the shrine and the terrace of the Bodhi tree;
then, having brought his father to the shrine terrace on a couch and having seated him upon the couch, he said: “This offering to the Great Elder has been made for your sake;
saying, ‘This is my gift of thanks to the Blessed One,’ pay homage to the Blessed One and gladden your heart.”
He said: When that great elder saw the offering and performed it in such a manner, his heart was filled with serene confidence;

at that very moment, the celestial realm appeared before him, and the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove, along with their celestial palaces and dancing nymphs, seemed as if they were standing there surrounding him.
He cried out, "Go away, go away, you jackals! "What is this, Elder? they asked.
"These mothers of yours, dear one, are coming. The Elder thought, "The great Elder’s heaven has appeared.

Thus, it should be understood that the possession of the state of being a *upatthāna-samaṅgin* (one who possesses attendance) is subject to fluctuation. Among these various types of possession (*samaṅgitā*), here, by way of the possession of the kamma consisting of volition of accumulation, the terms "one who possesses bodily misconduct," and so forth, are stated.

132. When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda thought: “Now that the Blessed One has spoken this discourse in this way, the Elder has listened to the entire sutta from beginning to end and has thus rendered it beautiful;
yet the Blessed One has not taken a name for the discourse he has taught. Let me cause a name to be given to it. Having reflected thus, he addressed the Blessed One as follows.
Therefore, in the passage beginning with "Therefore, in this case, you," the construction of the meaning is as follows:

Ānanda, because in this discourse on the Dhamma the many elements have been analyzed thus—"Ānanda, these eighteen elements; Ānanda, these six elements"—therefore, in this case, you [should master] this discourse on the Dhamma.

Remember it also as the *Bahudhātuka* (Many Elements). Furthermore, because four cycles (*parivaṭṭa*) are explained here by way of the elements, the bases, dependent origination, and the foundations of mindfulness, remember it also as the *Catuparivaṭṭa* (Four Cycles).

And because, just as the reflection of a face becomes manifest to one looking into a mirror, these meanings—the elements and so forth—become clear to one who contemplates this discourse on the Dhamma.
Therefore, you should remember him as "the Mirror of Dhamma. And because,
just as warriors who crush the enemy host seize victory for themselves by grasping the battle-drum, entering the enemy ranks, and crushing their foes,
even so do the yogis who crush the army of defilements grasp the victory of their own Arahantship here by grasping insight (vipassanā) according to what has been stated.
They seize it; therefore, remember it as "the drum of the Deathless.

And because, just as warriors in battle take up the five weapons, destroy the enemy army, and secure victory, so too do practitioners here take up the weapon of insight (vipassanā) as described, destroy the army of defilements, and secure the victory of Arahantship—therefore, remember it as "the unsurpassed victory in battle."
The commentary on the Bahudhātuka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 6.
Commentary on the Isigili Sutta.
133. Thus have I heard: this is the Isigili Sutta. Regarding the phrase "there was another designation":
at the time when the mountain Isigili acquired the designation "Isigili," Vebhāra was not known as "Vebhāra"; it had simply another designation.
"Another description" is a synonym for the preceding term. The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well.
At that time, it seems, the Blessed One, having emerged from meditative attainment in the evening and come out from the Fragrant Chamber,
sat down surrounded by the community of monks in a place where five mountains were visible,
and there he described these five mountains in their proper order. However, the Blessed One had no need for the mountains.
Now, as these mountains are being described in succession, the reason for Isigili’s name "Isigili" must be told.

While that is being told, the names of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Padumavatī, as well as Padumavatī’s own aspiration, will have to be related; thus the Blessed One explained this sequence of five mountains.

"They are seen entering, but once entered they are not seen" means that after walking for alms in a suitable place and finishing their meal, they returned and, as if opening the twin great doors of the shrine-chamber, split that mountain in two and entered within.
Having prepared night-quarters and day-quarters there, they dwelt therein; therefore he spoke thus: "These seers."
These were the requisites of the Paccekabuddhas.

But when did they dwell there? It is said that in the past, before a Tathāgata had appeared, a daughter of a noble family living in a certain village near Bārāṇasī, while guarding a field, [offered] five hundred parched grains of rice to a Paccekabuddha.
Having offered a single lotus flower together with her, she made a wish for five hundred sons.
At that very moment, five hundred deer-hunters, having offered sweet meat, also made a wish, saying, "May we become her sons.
Having lived out her full lifespan, she was reborn in the world of the devas; passing away from there, she was reborn within the calyx of a lotus in a lake.
A certain ascetic saw her and took care of her; as she walked about, lotuses rose up from the ground at every step.
A forest-dweller saw her and informed the King of Bārāṇasī.
The king had her brought and made her his chief queen, and she conceived. Prince Mahāpaduma dwelt in his mother’s womb, while the others...

They were born free from the impurities of the womb. When they reached maturity, while sporting in a lotus pond in a pleasure grove, they each sat upon a lotus flower and, having established the contemplation of decay and fall, they realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
This was the verse of their prophecy: “The lake-born lotus, with its petals and calyx, is in full bloom and frequented by swarms of bees;”
"Having understood that all things are subject to impermanence, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
At that time they lived there, and then the mountain acquired the name Isigili.
135. Those who were the essence of beings were Ariṭṭha, Upāriṭṭha, Tagarasikhī, Yasassī, Sudassana, Piyadassī, and Gandhāra.

Having stated the names of the thirteen Paccekabuddhas—Piṇḍola, Upāsabha, Nīta, Tatha, and Sutavā Bhāvitatta—he now declares the names of these and others in verse form, beginning with "Those who are the essence of beings" (sattasārā).
Therein, "essence of beings" (sattasārā) means they have become the core of sentient beings. "Untroubled" (anīghā) means free from suffering. "Desireless" (nirāsā) means free from craving.
"Two Jālis" refers to two named Jālis: Cūḷajāli and Mahājāli. "Santacitta" (Tranquil-Minded) is also the name of one [of them].
Regarding the phrase "Passi abandoned the substrate, the root of suffering": here, *Passi* is the name of that Paccekabuddha;
however, "he abandoned the substrate (*upadhi*), the root of suffering," is his praise. *Aparājita* is also the name of one [of them].
The Teacher, Pavattā, Sarabhaṅga, Lomahaṃsa, and Uccaṅgamāya—these are five persons. Asita, Anāsava, and Manomaya—these are also three persons.
Mānacchida and Bandhumā; Bandhumā is one person, who is called "Mānacchida" (the cutter of pride) because his pride has been severed.
"Tadādhimutta" is likewise merely a name.
Ketumbharāga, Mātaṅga, and Ariya—these are three persons. Athaccuta means "then, having passed away. Accutagāma and Byāmaṅka—these are two persons.
Khemābhirata and Sorata—these are exactly two. Sayha is the name of that Buddha; however, because of his extraordinary exertion (*anoma-vīriya*), he is called Anomanikkama.
Ānanda, Nanda, and Upananda—twelve [each] makes four Ānandas, four Nandas, and four Upanandas.
Thus there are twelve. "Bhāradvāja, bearer of his final body" refers to the Buddha named Bhāradvāja;
"bearer of his final body" is a praise. "Cutter of craving" is a praise of Sikhī. "Free from passion" is a praise of Maṅgala. "The Bull who cut the net, the root of suffering":
the meaning is that the Buddha named Usabha cut the net which is the root of suffering. "The Peaceful One..."
"He has attained the state, he is led" (*upanīta*): he is called "led" because that Buddha has attained the state of peace.
"One who is free from passion" (*vītarāga*) is merely the name of one [Buddha]. "One whose mind is well-liberated" (*suvimuttacitta*): this is a praise of Kaṇha. "These and others":
these who have appeared in the Canon and others who have not appeared in the Canon are all of the same name as these.
For among these five hundred Paccekabuddhas, two, three, ten, or even twelve had the same names as Ānanda and others.

Thus, since the names of all of them are stated by means of the very names appearing in the Pāḷi, he said "these and others" without mentioning each one individually hereafter. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Isigili Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 7.
The commentary on the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta.
136. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahācattārīsakasutta. In this context, "noble" (ariya) means faultless and supramundane;
for that which is faultless is called "noble. "Right concentration" (sammāsamādhi) refers to the concentration of the Path. "With its proximate cause" (saupanisa) means with its condition.
"With its requisites" (saparikkhāra) means with its equipment.
"Encompassed" means surrounded. "Right view is forerunner" means that right view is forerunner in two ways:

it is both the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*) and the right view of the path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*). The right view of insight investigates the conditioned phenomena of the three planes as impermanent and so forth;
however, the right view of the path [arises] at the conclusion of that investigation.
Arising as it eradicates and pacifies the cycle of existence attained on the stages, it is like pouring a thousand jars of cool water over one's head.
For just as a farmer preparing a field first cuts down the trees in the forest and afterwards applies fire, and that fire completely burns up the trees already cut down, even so—
Insight-right-view first investigates formations by way of impermanence and so forth;
path-right-view arises subsequently, uprooting those same formations by way of their non-occurrence for the purpose of that investigation.
Both of these two kinds are intended here.
"He understands wrong view" means that he understands wrong view from the perspective of its object through the penetration of its characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
he understands right view from the perspective of its function through non-delusion.
"That becomes his right view" means that such understanding becomes what is called his right view.

“I speak of a dyad” means I speak of a dyad; the meaning is that I speak of a twofold division. “Conducive to merit” means they have become a portion of merit. “Resulting in acquisitions” means they bestow the fruition known as acquisitions (*upadhi*).
In such passages as “wisdom is the faculty of wisdom,” it is called wisdom (*paññā*) because it defines and demonstrates the door to the Deathless after having analyzed [the matter] again and again.

It is called the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indatta*) over that meaning. It is called the power of wisdom (*paññābala*) because it does not waver due to ignorance. When it has reached the stage of a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*),...
The factor of enlightenment called investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) is so called because, having offered [the mind] into the Dhamma of the Four Truths, one investigates it.
Right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is a beautiful view that is praised due to the perfection of the Path. A "path-factor" (*maggaṅga*) is a limb of the Noble Path. "He" refers to that bhikkhu.

"For the sake of abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing. "For the sake of attaining" means for the purpose of acquisition. Right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) is wholesome effort that leads to liberation.

"Being possessed of mindfulness" means being endowed with mindfulness. "They run along and revolve around" means that, having arisen simultaneously (*sahajāta*) and having arisen prior (*purejāta*), they surround it.

For here, right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) and right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) surround supramundane right view (*lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi*) simultaneously, like the sword-bearer and the parasol-bearer standing in a single chariot with a king. [This refers to] insight-right-view (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*).
However, having arisen prior [to the mind], they surround it like infantrymen and others positioned in front of a chariot.
From the second chapter onwards, it should be understood that the triad beginning with right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) are indeed conascent attendants. 137.
"He understands 'wrong intention'": this means he understands wrong intention through the penetration of its characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

One understands right intention by way of its object; one understands it by way of its function and by way of non-delusion. The same method of application should be understood for the remaining factors, right speech and so forth.
"Intention regarding sensual pleasures" and the rest have already been explained in the *Dvedhāvitakka Sutta*. Regarding the terms "reasoning" (*takka*) and so on:
it is called "reasoning" (*takka*) in the sense of the act of reasoning. That very same term, with the prefix added to extend the word-form, is called "applied thought" (*vitakka*).
It is itself "intention" (saṅkappa) by virtue of its nature as intending. Because it, having become one-pointed, applies itself to the object, it is called "absorption" (appanā).
By prefixing the word with a preposition, it is stated as "application" (byappanā). "Directing of the mind" means the directing of consciousness.

For when there is initial application (vitakka), that initial application directs the consciousness toward the object; but in the absence of initial application, [the mind directs itself] of its own accord.
It is the natural law that the mind ascends to its object, just as a man of noble birth and high reputation enters the royal palace.
For one who is unknown, there is need for an usher or a doorkeeper;
but one who is well-known and of noble birth, all the kings and great ministers recognize him, and thus he goes out and enters by his own natural power.
It should be understood in this way. That which constructs speech is the verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*).
And here, it is mundane thought (*vitakka*) that constructs speech, not the supramundane. Even though it does not construct [speech], it nevertheless receives the name "verbal formation.
They run around following right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) means they surround the supramundane right intention.
And here, while all three— renunciation-intention and the others— are found in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*),

at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*), however, a single right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) arises, fulfilling the path-factor (*maggaṅga*) by effecting the cutting off and eradication of all three—
sensual intention and the rest— and receives three names according to its aspects as renunciation-intention and so forth. Hereafter...
The same method applies to right speech and the others as well.
138. In such expressions as "abstention from false speech" (*musāvādā veramaṇī*), both *virati* (abstinence) and *cetanā* (volition) are applicable.

In such terms as *ārati*, it is called *ārati* because one delights in being far removed (*ārakā*) from verbal misconduct. It is called *virati* because one delights in being free from those [misconducts]. Having turned away from this and that, by means of those...

"Abstaining" (*paṭivirati*) means to delight in being apart from [the unwholesome]. Alternatively, the word is expanded by means of a prefix; all of this is a synonym for the state of refraining (*oramanabhāva*).
"Veramana" means that which crushes or destroys enmity (*vera*); this too is a synonym for refraining.
Regarding such terms as "abstaining from the destruction of life" (*pāṇātipātā veramaṇī*), both "volition" (*cetanā*) and "abstinence" (*virati*) are equally appropriate.

140. Regarding "guile" (*kuhana*) and the following terms: they are called "guile" (*kuhanā*) because by means of this, people practice guile—that is, they deceive and mislead the world—through the three bases of guile.

They are called "flattery" (*lapanā*) because those who seek gain and honor speak with it. They are called "hinters" (*nemittika*) because hinting is their habit; the state of being such is "hinting" (*nemittikatā*).
They are called "sycophants" (*nippesika*) because backbiting is their habit; the state of being such is "sycophancy" (*nippesikatā*).
"Seeking to win gain by means of gain, they pursue and search for it; thus, it is 'seeking to win gain by means of gain' (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā*).
The state of those [who do so] is 'the seeking to win gain by means of gain' (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā*). This is the summary here;

however, in detail, these practices such as hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and so forth have been explained by citing both the canonical texts and the commentaries in the "Description of Virtue" (*Sīlaniddesa*) section of the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*):

Regarding the term "for the abandoning": here, wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) includes not only that which is explicitly mentioned in the Canon, but also the volitions (*cetanā*) of the seven courses of action, such as killing living beings, when they are undertaken for the sake of livelihood.

The abstinence (*virati*) that arises, fulfilling the factor of the Path (*maggaṅga*), by effecting the cutting off and eradication of those very same seven volitions, is called right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).
141. "Of one with right view" means of a person established in the right view of the path (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*). "Right intention arises" means the right intention of the path arises;
for one who possesses the right view of the fruit (*phalasammādiṭṭhi*), the right intention of the fruit also arises—the meaning should be understood in this way for all instances.
Regarding "right knowledge and right liberation," here [it refers to] the right concentration of the path (*maggasammāsamādhi*).
For one established in the path, right knowledge of reviewing the path arises; for one established in the fruition and right concentration, right knowledge of reviewing the fruition arises.
And for one established in the right knowledge of reviewing the path, right liberation of the path arises;
for one established in the right knowledge of reviewing the fruition, right liberation of the fruition arises—this is the meaning. And here, setting aside...
It is said that after reviewing the eight factors of fruition with right knowledge, it is appropriate to realize right liberation as the fruit.
Regarding such passages as, "Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is worn away," the teachers of the remaining Nikāyas state that the fruit is being described;
however, the Majjhima-bhāṇakas maintain that this refers to the context where the ten bases for wearing away are mentioned.
They say that the path has been explained. In this context, right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) should be understood in the sense of seeing;
right knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) in the sense of making known; and right liberation (sammā-vimutti) in the sense of being intent upon that.
The twenty factors on the side of the wholesome consist of the ten beginning with right view, and the many wholesome states conditioned by right view.

The ten [factors] stated by way of the method beginning with “phenomena” (*dhammā*)—thus there are twenty factors on the side of the wholesome (*kusalapakkha*). Regarding the twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome (*akusalapakkha*):

the ten beginning with wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), stated by way of the method beginning with “wrong view is worn away,” and the ten stated by way of the method beginning with “and the many evil states conditioned by wrong view”—thus the twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome are to be understood. This is the Great Forty.

It is called the "Great Forty" because it elucidates forty states—both those belonging to the side of the wholesome and those belonging to the side of the unwholesome—by way of yielding great results.
Furthermore, in this sutta, five kinds of right view are taught: right view as insight (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi) and right view regarding the ownership of one's actions (kammassakatā-sammādiṭṭhi).
Right view of the path, right view of the fruit, and right view of reviewing.
Among these, that which is described by the method beginning with, “One understands wrong view as wrong view,” is called right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*).

That which is described by the method beginning with, “There is what is given,” is called right view of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatā-sammādiṭṭhi*). [As it is said: “Bhikkhus, for one of right view, there is right intention...”
In the phrase “right view arises,” both right view of the path and right view of the fruit are spoken of.
In the phrase “right knowledge arises,” it should be understood that right view of reviewing is spoken of.
(143) Even one who says, “If you, sir, criticize right view, then this so-called wrong view is beautiful,” [is still criticizing] right view.
Even one who says, "This name is not beautiful," is said to be censuring right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). The *Okkalas* are the inhabitants of the country of Okkala.
The *Vassabhaññas* are two individuals, namely Vassa and Bhañña. The *Ahetuvādins* are those who hold such views as, "There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings.
The *Akiriyavādins* are those who hold such views as, "For one who acts, no evil is committed."

They were proponents of the denial of action (kiriyapaṭikkhepavādino). As for the nihilists (natthikavādino), they were those who held views such as "there is no giving" and so forth. They had entered the fixed course (niyāma) in these three views. But how does the fixed course come about in these?
For one who, having adopted such a doctrine, sits in a night-station or a day-station, recites, and investigates it, [the thought occurs to him]: "There is no cause, there is no..."

“Evil is not done by one who acts; there is no gift; with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated”—thus, wrong mindfulness settles upon that object, the mind becomes one-pointed, and impulsion-moments (javana) proceed. In the first impulsion, it is curable;
likewise in the second and so on. In the seventh, even for Buddhas, it is incurable, irreversible, and resembles the thorn of Ariṭṭha.
In that regard, one person falls into one wrong view, another into two, and another even into all three;
he becomes one whose wrong view is fixed, having reached both an obstruction to the path to heaven and an obstruction to the path to liberation.

Such a being is incapable of going to heaven in the very next existence, let alone to liberation; indeed, this being is called a "stump in the cycle of existence" (vaṭṭakhāṇu), a guardian of the earth.
For the most part, there is no emergence from such a state of existence. Even the Vassa and Bhañña brothers were like this.
"Fear of blame, reproach, and attack" means: fear of being blamed by oneself, fear of being provoked, and fear of being censured. The rest is clear everywhere.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdani*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahācattārīsakasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Ānāpānassatisutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Ānāpānassatisutta. Therein, the phrase "and by others" means excluding those who have appeared in the text.
The ten elders together with many other well-known disciples. At that time, it is said, the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus was beyond counting.
"They exhort and instruct" means that they have gathered them in by means of two kinds of gathering: the gathering through material gifts and the gathering through the Dhamma.

They exhort and instruct by means of instructions on meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) and counsels. The word “ca” (and) in the phrase “te ca” (they and) is merely for the purpose of connecting the preceding grammatical element.

“Knowing the sublime distinction between what precedes and what follows” means that they know the subsequent distinction—such as the preliminary work for the kasiṇas—which is more sublime than the previous distinction, such as the fulfillment of virtue (sīla).
145. *Āraddha* means joyful. *Appattassa pattiyā* means for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, namely, Arahantship.
The same meaning applies to the other two phrases as well. *Komudiṃ cātumāsinim* refers to the full-moon day of the last month of Kattika, the fourth month of the rainy season.
It is called *komudī* because of the presence of water-lilies (*kumuda*), and it is called *cātumāsinī* because it marks the conclusion of four months of the rains.
It is said: "I will wait" means "I will look forward to her"; the meaning is: "Having performed the *pavāraṇā* today, until she arrives, I shall not go anywhere but remain right here.
Thus he spoke while authorizing the inclusion of the monks' *pavāraṇā*. Regarding the so-called "inclusion of the *pavāraṇā*":
it is granted by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). To whom, then, is it granted, and to whom is it not?
"It is given. First of all, it is not given to the foolish worldling who is not a practitioner; likewise, it is not given to the noble disciple who has already begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
However, it is given to one whose serenity (*samatha*) or insight is still in its tender stage.
At that time, the Blessed One, examining the mental conduct of the monks, [perceived] the tender state of their serenity and insight.
He understood: "Today, when I am inviting [the Sangha], monks who have spent the rains retreat in various directions will arrive here.
Consequently, these monks will not be able to achieve spiritual distinction once their lodgings have been taken by senior monks.
Even if I were to set out on a journey, it would be difficult for them to find a place to stay. However, if I..."
"If the monks who are being sent away do not descend upon Sāvatthī, and I too do not set out on tour,
then the dwelling places of these monks will remain unobstructed.
Living at ease in their respective residences, they will be able to develop strength in serenity and insight and thereby achieve distinction."
Thinking, "I shall postpone this day and perform the *pavāraṇā* on the full moon of Kattika," he authorized the monks' *pavāraṇā-saṅgaha* (postponement of the invitation ceremony).
For when the *pavāraṇā-saṅgaha* is obtained, even for one who is undergoing formal dependence (*nissaya*), if his teacher (*ācariya*) or preceptor (*upajjhāya*) departs, he may think:
"If a suitable provider of dependence comes, I will receive dependence from him."
One may stay until the last month of the summer. Even if sixty-year-old bhikkhus arrive, they do not obtain his lodging.
Furthermore, this invitation-extension (*pavāraṇasaṅgaha*), though granted to one person, is as if granted to all.
"They descend upon Sāvatthī" means that, having heard that the Blessed One had granted the invitation-extension, they went directly to the place where it was heard.
This was said with reference to those returning after having dwelt for one month and observed the Uposatha on the full moon of Kattika.

Regarding the phrase "the former is not like the latter": here, having performed the work of both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) while they were still young, they brought serenity and insight to a state of firm strength;
this is what is called the "former distinction. Then, with a concentrated mind, some, having reflected upon mental formations (*saṅkhāra*), [attained the fruit].
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry... [and so on] ...some realized arhatship. This is another sublime distinction.
146. *Alam* means "fitting" or "proper. Regarding "yojana-calculations": one *yojana* is simply a *yojana*, ten *yojanas* are simply *yojanas*, and beyond that they are called "yojana-calculations.
However, in this context, even a hundred *yojanas* or a thousand *yojanas* are intended.
“Even with a bundle on his shoulder”: a “bundle” (puṭosa) is said to be provisions for a journey. The meaning is that even taking those provisions, it is indeed appropriate to approach [the Teacher].
There is also a reading, “puṭaṃsenā,” the meaning of which is as follows: one who has a bundle on his shoulder is a “bundle-shoulder” (puṭaṃsa);
by means of that “bundle-shoulder”—it is said, “even by one carrying a bundle of provisions on his shoulder.”
147. Now, in order to show that there are monks here who are endowed with such qualities, he said, "There are, O monks," and so forth.
In that context, the phrases beginning with "of the four foundations of mindfulness" are spoken for the purpose of showing the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) in which those monks are established.
Therein, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), both mundane and supramundane, are explained. For therein—
For those bhikkhus who, at that moment, are developing the path, [the perception] is supramundane;

for those practicing insight (vipassanā), it is mundane. Regarding the phrase "devotion to the development of the perception of impermanence," here insight is spoken of by way of the term "perception" (saññā).
However, since many bhikkhus are intent upon this very meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna), the remaining meditation subjects are therefore mentioned in brief.
Having thus spoken, while explaining the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*) in detail, he said: "Mindfulness of breathing, monks," and so forth.
This meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing has been explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, its textual meaning and the method of development should be understood according to the system set forth therein.
149. "One or other of the bodies" means one or other among the four bodies, beginning with the earth-body; the meaning is that I speak of the air-body (*vāyokāya*).
Alternatively, the twenty-five components of form—beginning from the base of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) up to physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*)—are called the "body of form" (*rūpakāya*).

Among these, because mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) is included within the base of tangible objects (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*), it is "one or other of the bodies"; for this reason as well, he spoke thus.

"Therefore, in this way" means: because one contemplates either one of the four bodies—the body of air—or one of the twenty-five components of the material body, namely inhalation and exhalation, therefore the meaning is "contemplating the body in the body. The meaning should be understood in this same way in all instances.
"One of the feelings" refers to one among the three types of feeling; this was said with reference to pleasant feeling.
"Attentive application" (*sādhukaṃ manasikāra*) refers to the beautiful mental application that has arisen by way of experiencing rapture (*pīti*), and so forth.
But is mental application itself a pleasant feeling? It is not; rather, this is merely the heading of the teaching.

For just as in the passage "devoted to the practice of the cultivation of the perception of impermanence" (*aniccasaññābhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā*), wisdom (*paññā*) is spoken of under the name of "perception," so too here it should be understood that feeling (*vedanā*) is spoken of under the name of "mental application."
In this tetrad, in the first phrase, feeling is stated under the heading of "rapture" (*pīti*); in the second phrase, it is stated by its own specific form as "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Regarding the two phrases on "mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhāra*), because of the statement: "Perception and feeling are mental factors;

these phenomena, being bound to the mind, are mental formations," [it follows that] all phenomena associated with the mind, excluding applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), [are included].
Because of the statement, "They are included within the mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra)," feeling (vedanā) is spoken of by the name "mental formation.
Having subsumed all of that under the name "attention" (manasikāra), it is here called "careful attention.
Even so, since this feeling is not itself the object [of contemplation], the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) would not be appropriate.
This is not tenable; for even in the commentary on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), it is stated:

"It is feeling alone that experiences by taking as its object the respective basis for pleasure and so forth; however, based upon the occurrence of that feeling, there is the mere conventional expression, 'I experience.
Furthermore, the resolution of this point has already been stated in the commentary on the meaning of the phrases "experiencing rapture" (*pītipaṭisaṃvedī*) and so on.
For this has been said in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"Rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of its object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture experienced by way of its object?
One enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of that attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna..."
Rapture is experienced by way of its object because the object is experienced. How is it experienced by way of non-delusion?
Having entered and emerged from two jhānas accompanied by rapture, one contemplates the rapture associated with those jhānas in terms of its exhaustion and vanishing;
at the moment of insight, through the penetration of the characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self], it is experienced by way of non-delusion.
"Rapture is clearly experienced. And this has been said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:

'For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction by means of long inhalation, mindfulness is established; through that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is clearly experienced.
In this same manner, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning."

Thus, just as through the attainment of jhāna the mental formations of rapture, pleasure, and consciousness are clearly experienced according to their object, so too, through this attainment of attention—which is termed feeling and is associated with jhāna—feeling is clearly experienced according to its object.
Therefore, it is well said: "At that time, he is one who contemplates feelings in feelings."
“A bhikkhu dwells [thus], monks.

Regarding the phrase “not unmindful and not clearly comprehending,” this is the intended meaning: because a bhikkhu who proceeds in the manner of “I shall breathe in experiencing the mind,” etc., although he has the sign of the breath—inhalation and exhalation—as his object, [is nevertheless mindful].
However, because he proceeds by establishing mindfulness (*sati*) and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) regarding the object of that mind, he is indeed one who contemplates the mind in the mind.
For there is no development of mindfulness of breathing for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension.
Therefore, at that time, by way of the recognition of the mind through its object and so forth, he is one who contemplates the mind in the mind.

"A bhikkhu dwells": regarding the phrase "having seen with wisdom that which is the abandoning of covetousness and dejection, he dwells having thoroughly looked on with equanimity," here the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is shown by way of covetousness, and the hindrance of ill-will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) by way of dejection.
For this tetrad is stated specifically by way of insight (*vipassanā*), and it is the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) by way of the section on the hindrances and so forth.
It is sixfold; of that, the section on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is the beginning, and of that too, these two hindrances are the beginning.
Thus, in order to show the beginning of the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*), he said: "Of covetousness and dejection.

"Abandoning" refers to the intended knowledge that performs abandoning, such as when one abandons the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence. "Having seen that with wisdom" means having seen that which is comprised of the knowledge of impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment.
The knowledge of abandoning is [contemplated] by a subsequent insight-wisdom, and that too by a subsequent one; in this way, he shows the succession of insights (*vipassanā-paramparā*).
"He is one who looks on with equanimity" means that he looks on with equanimity in two ways: toward one who has entered into calm (*samatha*), and toward the single-pointed presence [of mindfulness];
thus it is called "looking on with equanimity. In that context, there is also looking on with equanimity toward those things that are co-nascent.
There is equanimity regarding the object as well; here, "equanimity regarding the object" is intended.

Therefore, monks, because one has seen with wisdom and looked upon with equanimity not only the states such as the hindrances, but also the knowledge of abandoning the states described under the heading of covetousness and dejection—by way of the method beginning with "I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence"—[this is so].
Therefore, it should be understood that "on that occasion the bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
(150) "He investigates" means he investigates by way of impermanence and so forth. The other two phrases are synonyms for this very term.
"Unworldly" means free from defilements. "It subsides" means that through the subsiding of physical and mental distress, both body and...
The mind also becomes tranquil. It is "concentrated" (samādhiyati) in the sense that it is correctly established; it becomes as if it has reached absorption (appanā).
He "becomes one who looks on with equanimity" (ajjhupekkhitā hoti) in the sense that he looks on with the co-nascent equanimity (sahajāta-ajjhupekkhanā).
Thus, for a bhikkhu who comprehends the body in these fourteen ways, there is the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) in regard to that body.
Knowledge associated with mindfulness is the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor; bodily and mental energy associated with that same [mindfulness] is the energy enlightenment factor;
rapture, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind are the concentration enlightenment factor;
and the mode of neutrality consisting in the avoidance of both deficiency and excess regarding these six enlightenment factors is the equanimity enlightenment factor.

For just as when horses are proceeding evenly, there is no prodding by the charioteer thinking "this one is lagging" nor any pulling back thinking "this one is over-speeding," but rather there is only the posture of one who observes thus; even so,
the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga) is the state of neutrality consisting in the non-deficiency and non-excess of these six factors of enlightenment.

This is the name [of the factors]. What has been stated up to this point? It has been stated that the factors of enlightenment consisting of insight (vipassanā-sambojjhaṅga) are momentary, occurring within a single thought-moment, and characterized by various flavors.
152. The phrases beginning with "dependent on seclusion" have already had their meaning explained. Here, however, the mindfulness that grasps inhalation and exhalation (ānāpāna) is mundane;
mundane inhalation and exhalation fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and the mundane foundations of mindfulness [fulfill] the supramundane factors of enlightenment.
They fulfill [the factors]; the supramundane factors of enlightenment fulfill the fruit of knowledge and liberation, which is Nibbāna.
Thus, where the mundane occurs, the mundane is spoken of; where the supramundane occurs, the supramundane is spoken of.
But the Elder said: "It is so elsewhere; however, in this sutta, the supramundane comes later, while the mundane [refers to] the breaths."
They fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness; the mundane foundations of mindfulness fulfill the mundane factors of enlightenment;
the mundane factors of enlightenment fulfill the supramundane Nibbāna, which is the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.
For by the term "true knowledge and liberation," it is here the Nibbāna that is the fruit of true knowledge and liberation which is intended.
The commentary on the Ānāpānassati Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya-Ṭīkā, the Papañcasūdanī, is completed. 9.
The commentary on the Kāyagatāsati Sutta.
153–4. Thus have I heard: this is the *Kāyagatāsati-sutta*. Therein, "worldly" (*gehasita*) means dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. "With running thoughts" (*sarasaṅkappā*):
for "running thoughts" (*sara*) are so called because they run; the meaning is that they run. "Internally only" (*ajjhattameva*) means precisely within the internal range of the field of experience.
"Mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*) refers to mindfulness that both encompasses the body and has the body as its object. "Encompassing the body" (*kāyapariggāhika*)...

When "calm" is mentioned, serenity (samatha) is spoken of; when "body as an object" is mentioned, insight (vipassanā) is spoken of. By both, serenity and insight are spoken of. Furthermore... [as before] ...
"In this way too, monks, a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body"—thus, in the *Satipaṭṭhāna*, the fourteenfold contemplation of the body is explained.
156. "Included within": they are indeed included within that monk’s development. "Conducive to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*): [they lead to the penetration of the four truths].

In this context, they are called "factors conducive to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*) because they partake in true knowledge by way of association. Alternatively, they are called "factors conducive to true knowledge" because they occur within the sphere of true knowledge, that is, within the division of true knowledge.
In this regard, there are eight types of true knowledge: insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
According to the former sense, the phenomena associated with these are also "factors conducive to true knowledge. According to the latter sense, any one of them [is so called].

"Knowledge is knowledge; the rest are factors conducive to knowledge. Thus, it should be understood that not only is knowledge itself associated with knowledge, but the states associated with it are likewise factors conducive to knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "pervaded by the mind," there are two kinds of pervasion: pervasion by water and pervasion by the divine eye.
Therein, pervasion by water after having attained the water-kasiṇa attainment is called "pervasion by water. Even when the great ocean is thus pervaded...

All small rivers that flow toward the ocean are already included within it; however, by extending one's light and seeing the entire ocean with the divine eye, this is called the "pervasion of the divine eye.
Even when pervading in this way, all small rivers flowing toward the great ocean remain included within the great ocean itself.

They enter through an opening or a crack. "An object" (*ārammaṇa*) means a condition for the arising of defilements. "They would find entry" (*labhetha otāraṃ*) means they would obtain an entrance; the meaning is that they would pierce through and go right to the end. "A place of deposit" (*nikkhepana*) means a place where something is laid down. 157.

Having thus illustrated a person who has not developed mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) by way of such similes as a heap of wet clay, he now says "Just as if," etc., in order to illustrate a person who has developed mindfulness directed to the body by way of such similes as a plank of heartwood. Therein, "a door-panel" (*aggaḷaphalaka*) means a door-leaf.
158. "Drinkable by a crow" means that it can be drunk by a crow sitting on the rim of the mouth without having to stretch its neck.

"To be realized through direct knowledge" (abhiññāsacchikaraṇīya) means that which is to be realized by means of direct knowledge. "He reaches the state of being capable of witnessing" means he reaches the state of personal verification.
"Whenever there is a basis" (sati sati āyatane) means whenever there is a cause. But what is the cause here? Direct knowledge itself is the cause. "Bound by embankments" means bounded by a boundary.
"Made into a vehicle" means made like a properly yoked chariot. "Made into a foundation" means made into a support.
"Established" means set in motion. "Cultivated" means made familiar through practice. "Well undertaken" means well commenced and well exerted.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished. 10.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta*.

160. Thus have I heard: this is the *Saṅkhārupapatti-sutta*. Therein, "rebirth through formations" (*saṅkhārupapatti*) means the rebirth of formations themselves, not of a being (*satta*), nor of a person (*puggala*); it is the rebirth of the aggregates that lead to becoming by means of the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
161. "Endowed with faith": the five qualities beginning with faith are mundane and belong to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"Burns" (*dahati*) means he establishes. "Resolves" (*adhiṭṭhāti*) means he settles. "Formations and abidings" (*saṅkhārā ca vihārā ca*) refers to those same five qualities beginning with faith, together with aspiration (*patthanā*).

Dhammas. "For rebirth there" means for the purpose of being born in that place. These five factors, together with aspiration—namely, "this is the path" and "this is the practice"—constitute the five dhammas.
For one who possesses the five dhammas but lacks aspiration, their destination is unbound.
For one who possesses aspiration but lacks the five dhammas, their destination is likewise unbound. For those who possess both...

There is a fixed destination for them. For just as there is no certainty that a stick thrown into the air will fall with its tip, its middle, or its base [downward], so too the taking of rebirth-linking by sentient beings is undetermined.
Therefore, it is appropriate to make a wish for a particular place after having performed wholesome kamma.

165. *Āmaṇḍa* means the *āmalaka* fruit. Just as it is entirely manifest to a person with pure vision, so too is the thousandfold world-system (*sahassī lokadhātu*) to that Brahmā, together with the beings born there.

This same method applies everywhere. 167. *Subha* means beautiful. *Jātimā* means endowed with a source [of excellence]. *Suparikammakata* means well-prepared through washing and other such processes. *Paṇḍukambale nikkhitto* means placed upon a red blanket.
168. *Satasahassa* means a Brahmā who pervades a hundred thousand world-systems with light.
*Nikkha* refers to an ornament made of *nikkha*; a *nikkha* is [an ornament] made of five parts of gold. For an ornament made of less than a *nikkha* is not capable of enduring rubbing and polishing;
one made of more than that can endure rubbing and polishing, yet it does not possess a beautiful luster, as its material is coarse.
It shines. The polishing and rubbing performed with gold is both appropriate and beautiful.
"Jambūnada" means produced in the Jambu River. For each branch of the great Jambu tree extends fifty yojanas;
from them flow great rivers, and on both banks of those rivers grow wild Jambu fruits.
At the place where it falls, golden sprouts arise; carried along by the river water, they gradually enter the great ocean.

It is with reference to this that it is called "jambūnada. "Well-forged in the mouth of a skilled smith’s forge" means well-forged after being heated in the mouth of the forge by a clever and highly skilled son of a smith. "In the mouth of the forge" means on the hearth.
"Sampahaṭṭhaṃ" means washed, scrubbed, and rinsed. In the *Vatthūpama Sutta* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, the cleansing of a raw material is described;
in this sutta, the cleansing of a finished product is described.
As for what is said in all sections—"having pervaded and resolved upon"—therein, pervasion is fivefold.
The pervasion of the mind, the pervasion of the kasiṇa, the pervasion of the divine eye, the pervasion of light, and the pervasion of the body.

Therein, "pervasion of the mind" means knowing the minds of beings throughout a thousand world-systems. "Pervasion of the kasiṇa" means the extension of the kasiṇa throughout a thousand world-systems.
"Pervasion of the divine eye" means seeing a thousand world-systems by increasing the light with the divine eye.
The pervasion of light is also this very same thing. "Pervasion of the body" means the spreading of the radiance of the body throughout a thousand world-systems.
In all cases, these five kinds of pervasion should be described without omitting any of them.
However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "Just as in the simile of the gem there is the pervasion of the kasiṇa, so too in the simile of the jewel there is the pervasion of the body."

"It appears as if [it were]. Having rejected the claim that there is no such thing as a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) corresponding to his doctrine, it is stated that the pervading of the body is not constant at all times;
rather, it should be explained without losing these four modes of pervasion.
The term *adhimuccati* is a synonym for the term *pharaṇa*; alternatively, "to pervade" (*pharati*) means to spread out. "To resolve upon" (*adhimuccati*) means to know.

169. Regarding the "Ābhā" and other terms: there are no separate deities named Ābhā and so forth. The three classes of deities beginning with the Parittābhā are called "Ābhā"; likewise those beginning with the Parittasubhā. Those beginning with the Subhakiṇhā are called "Subha.
The sections on the Vehapphala and others are self-evident. Having developed these five qualities, one may be reborn among the sense-sphere realms (kāmāvacara).
But how does one who is reborn in the Brahma-world reach the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya)? These five qualities constitute virtue (sīla); established in this virtue, [one proceeds].

Having performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and developed those respective attainments, one is reborn in the fine-material Brahma-world; having produced the immaterial jhānas, one is reborn in the immaterial Brahma-world;

and by increasing insight, which has the attainments as its proximate cause, one realizes the fruit of non-returning and is reborn in the five Pure Abodes. By developing the higher path, one attains the destruction of the taints.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*,
the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is completed.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is completed.
3. The Chapter on Emptiness (Suññatavagga) 1. Commentary on the Cūḷasuññata Sutta (The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness) 176.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷasuññata Sutta. Regarding the phrase "one [time]," it is said that the Elder [Ānanda] was performing his duty toward the Blessed One.
Having made his own daytime resting place, he went there, set a time limit, and sat down having entered the fruition attainment of emptiness (*suññatā-phala-samāpatti*) with Nibbāna as its object.
When he emerged at the appointed time, mental formations appeared to him as empty.
He then became desirous of hearing a discourse on emptiness. Then this thought occurred to him: "But it is not possible to take up one burden by means of another burden."
As if striking out, he went and said to the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, please teach me the discourse on emptiness.
Thinking, “Well then, let me remind the Blessed One of that one discourse which he gave while staying near the town of Nagaraka;
thus will the Blessed One teach me the discourse on emptiness,” he spoke the words beginning with “One thing... while reminding the One of Ten Powers.

In this context, *idam* is merely a particle. [The Elder] thought: "The Elder [Ānanda], who is capable of learning and retaining sixty thousand words while standing on a single word—would he not be able to retain even a single word such as 'dwelling in emptiness' (*suññatāvihārena*)?
However, it is not proper for one who knows [the answer] to ask as if desiring to hear; rather, [the question is asked] so that it may be made clear and explained in detail."
Desiring to hear the discourse on emptiness (*suññatākatha*), he spoke thus as if he were ignorant. One person, though ignorant, may appear as if they know;

what kind of hypocrisy could an Elder like this possibly practice? Even in a matter that he himself already knew, he spoke the words beginning with "I hope it is so" (*kaccimetan*) in order to demonstrate his reverence for the Blessed One.
“In the past” means even during the time he was dwelling near that small town during the First Enlightenment.
“Even now” means at this present time. Having spoken thus, he thought: “Ānanda desires to hear a discourse on emptiness;
yet one person is able to hear but not to master it, another is able to both hear and master it but not to explain it, while Ānanda is indeed able to both hear and master it.”
"To learn and to speak—the discourse on emptiness. Speaking thus, he said, "Just as if," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the phrase "empty of elephants, cattle, horses, and mules":

there are elephants and so on made by means of wooden figures, cloth figures, and painted figures; and furthermore, there are those made by means of painting in places where Vessavaṇa, Mandhātā, and others reside.
Furthermore, there is gold and silver present in the form of window frames, door bolts, beds, chairs, and so forth, which have been fashioned with jewels;

there is also gold and silver set aside for the purpose of repairing what is worn out. There are also men and women who come for the sake of hearing the Dhamma, asking questions, and the like, appearing in the form of wooden figures and so on.
Therefore, it is not empty of these things. As for those bound by the sense-faculties who possess consciousness—
This was said with reference to the absence of elephants and the like, of gold and silver that may be used at any desired moment, and of men and women living in permanent residence.
"In dependence upon the community of bhikkhus" means that even when the bhikkhus have entered for alms, those who accept meals provided at the monastery...
It was not empty because of the monks themselves, and also because of those monks who were attending to the sick, assigning duties, engaged in robe-making, and so forth;
thus he spoke in this way because of the constant presence of monks. "Aloneness" (*ekatta*) means the state of being one, the sense that there is a single non-emptiness;
what is meant is that there exists a single state of non-emptiness. "Without paying attention" means without taking it to heart.
Without having adverted to it and without having reflected upon it. "Village-perception" means the perception of a village that has arisen either by way of its occurrence or by way of defilement.
The same method applies to the perception of people as well. "He attends to unity dependent on forest-perception" means:
[he attends] thus, "This is the forest, this is the tree, this is the mountain, this is the green-gleaming grove."
He attends to the perception of the forest depending solely on the forest itself. "Enters" means he descends into it.

"Resolves" means he resolves, thinking, "It is so. Whatever disturbances there might be—whether disturbances of active existence or disturbances of the defilements—that would arise depending on the perception of a village, those do not exist here through the perception of the forest.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. There exists...
They are agitated; however, there is this mere agitation occurring that arises dependent upon a single perception of forest.

As for what is not present there: just as elephants and so forth are absent from Migāra’s Mother’s Palace, so too, in this perception of forest, the agitation, defilement-agitation, and the mass of agitation arising by way of the perception of village and the perception of people do not exist.
"But what remains there" means that, just as in the Migāramātupāsāda, only the mere movement of the mind's activity proceeding with the perception of forest remains;
