"he understands that which exists as 'this exists'" means he understands that very thing which is present as "this is"; "descent into emptiness" means the arising of emptiness.
177. "Without attending to the perception of people": here, one does not take up the perception of a village. Why? It is said that he thought thus:

"Having set aside the perception of a village by means of the perception of people; having set aside the perception of people by means of the perception of forest; having set aside the perception of forest by means of the perception of earth;

having set aside the perception of earth by means of the perception of the base of infinite space... [and so on] ...having set aside the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception..."

“Having removed the perception of the base of nothingness by means of insight, and having turned back insight by means of the Path, I shall gradually demonstrate what is called absolute emptiness. It was for this reason that he began the teaching in this way.
In that context, as to why he abandons the perception of the forest and attends to the perception of earth: it is because of the perception of the forest...
Because of not attaining distinction. For example, when a man sees a delightful field site and thinks, "Rice and other crops grown here will turn out very well;
I shall obtain a great profit," yet the rice and other crops do not succeed at all even though he gazes at that field site seven times over;
however, if that place has its stumps and thorns cleared away...
Just as one who ploughs and sows reaps only when these conditions are met,
so too, even if one attends to the perception of the forest seven times— thinking, "This is the forest, this is the tree, this is the mountain, this is the green-gleaming woodland"—
one will reach neither access concentration nor absorption. However, for one whose meditation subject is the constant cultivation of the perception of earth, it is otherwise.

Having performed the preliminary work on the earth-kasiṇa, having generated the jhānas, and having further developed insight (vipassanā) which has the jhānas as its proximate cause, it is possible to attain Arahantship.
Therefore, abandoning the perception of forest, one attends to the perception of earth.
"Dependent" (paṭicca) means arisen dependent [on conditions].
Now, in order to provide an illustration for that earth-kasiṇa in which one perceives earth, he said “Just as if,” and so forth.
Therein, “āsabhaṃ” means “of a bull” (usabha). However, other cattle have both swellings and wounds;
for when their hide is stretched, it does not become free of blemishes, whereas due to the bull’s possession of the [auspicious] marks, those defects do not exist.
Therefore, its hide was taken. "With a hundred pegs" means with a hundred wooden stakes. "Well-stretched" means having been stretched out and thoroughly beaten.
For if it were beaten with fewer than a hundred stakes, it would not be free of wrinkles; but when beaten with a hundred stakes, like the surface of a drum, it becomes free of wrinkles.
That is why he spoke thus. "High and low" refers to the elevated places and the sunken places.
"Difficult terrain by rivers" refers both to rivers and to places that are difficult to traverse.
"He attends to the unity dependent on the perception of earth" means he attends to a single perception produced in dependence upon the earth-kasiṇa itself. "Merely a disturbance":
from this point onward, in all instances, it should be understood as "merely a disturbance" in accordance with the disturbance occurring in each case.
182. “The signless concentration of mind” means the concentration of the mind associated with insight (*vipassanā*).
For that is called “signless” because it is devoid of the signs of permanence and so forth. “This very body” indicates the basis for insight.
Therein, “this very” refers to this very body composed of the four great elements. “Consisting of the six sense bases” means connected with the six sense bases. “With life as condition” means...
It is said that as long as the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) continues to function, there exists merely the agitation (daratha) occurring with the life-faculty as its condition.
Furthermore, the phrase "signless" (animitta) is stated in order to show the counter-insight (paṭivipassanā) regarding insight (vipassanā).

Regarding the phrase "dependent on the taint of sensual desire" (kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca): here, the agitations arising and occurring dependent on the taint of sensual desire do not exist, because [this occurs] in the Noble Path and the Noble Fruit.
And it is said, "there is not even this. "This very body" is stated for the purpose of showing the distress remaining in the substrate of clinging (*upādisesa*).

Thus, having set aside the perception of a village by means of the perception of a human being... [and so on] ...having set aside insight by means of the path, that which is called ultimate emptiness (*accantasuññatā*) is demonstrated in due order.
184. "Pure" means free from defilements. "Unsurpassed" means devoid of anything higher, the most excellent of all.
"Emptiness" refers to the attainment of the fruit of emptiness (*suññataphalasamāpatti*). Therefore:

because in the past, as well as in the future and even now, there have been ascetics and brahmins—namely those known as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—who [have realized] this very...
They entered and dwelt in the utterly pure, supreme, unsurpassed voidness; they will so dwell, and they do so dwell.
Therefore [this is said]. The rest is clear throughout.
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷasuññata Sutta is finished.
2. The commentary on the Mahāsuññata Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāsuññata Sutta. Therein, "of Kāḷakhemaka": he was black by the color of his skin.

Its name was Khemakūṭa. "Monastery" (*vihāra*) refers to a dwelling constructed in a certain area of that very Nigrodha Monastery, enclosed by a wall, provided with a gateway tower, and furnished with lodgings such as the Haṃsavaṭṭaka and so forth, as well as a circular pavilion (*maṇḍalamāḷa*), a dining hall, and other facilities.
"Many lodgings" (*sambahulāni senāsanāni*) refers to beds, chairs, mattresses, and bolsters.
Mats, leather pads, straw mats, leaf mats, and hay mats were prepared; they were placed so that mat met mat...
and so on, up to hay mat meeting hay mat, such that it resembled a dwelling place for a community of monks.
"Is it not many?"—since all defilements were eradicated right on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), there is no such thing as doubt for the Blessed One;
rather, this is a question preceded by reflection (*vitakkapubbabhāgā pucchā*), and in the context of being preceded by reflection, the particle *nu* is merely an expletive (*nipātamatta*).
When one proceeds to the very pinnacle of the path, there is nothing that remains undecided. It is said that prior to this, ten or twelve [questions] had been asked by the Blessed One.
The monks living in that one place had never been seen before.
Then this thought occurred to him: "This so-called 'living in a group' is practiced and habitual within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), like water that has flowed down a river;
it exists even in the realms of hell, the animal womb, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras, as well as in the world of humans, the world of gods, and the Brahma-world."
It is customary [to say this]. For the hell that extends ten thousand yojanas is filled with beings without any gaps, like a tube filled with sesame husks;
there is no measure or limit to the number of beings subjected to the fivefold tortures and punishments, nor likewise in the places where they are flayed with axes and so forth;
thus they are cooked as a mere multitude. In the animal realm, in one...
In an anthill, there is no measure or limit for the number of female ants; likewise, there is no limit for the number of termites and other such creatures in each individual hole.
Even among the animal realm, there is communal living. The cities of the *petas* (hungry ghosts) are filled with *petas*, measuring a quarter-league (*gāvuta*) or even half a league (*yojana*).
Thus, in the sphere of *peta*-existence as well, there is only communal living. The abode of the *asuras* is ten thousand leagues, like a needle inserted into the ear.
It is like an ear-hole; thus, even among the hosts of asuras, there is only communal living.
In the human world, in Sāvatthī, seven million five hundred thousand families lived together, and in Rājagaha, both inside and outside the city, eighteen koṭis of people resided.
Likewise in other places as well—thus, even in the human world, there is only communal living. This is true starting from the earth-deities up through the celestial worlds and the Brahma-worlds.
It was like living in a crowd. For each son of the gods has two and a half crores of celestial nymphs, some even have nine crores;
ten thousand Brahmās also dwell in one place.
Then he thought: "For four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons more, I have lived in this way for the sake of destroying the life of crowds."
“The ten perfections have been fulfilled; yet these bhikkhus, from this very moment, have formed a group and, delighting in groups, are acting in a manner unbecoming.
Having thus aroused a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*), he thought again:
“If it were possible to lay down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) stating that ‘two bhikkhus must not dwell in one place,’ then a training rule [should be established].”
I might establish it, yet this is not possible.
Well then, I shall teach the discourse named *Mahāsuññatāpaṭipatti*, which will serve for clansmen who desire training as a formulation of training rules and like a mirror placed at the city gate.
Then, just as when [clansmen] such as kṣatriyas see their own blemishes in a single mirror...

"By abandoning that, they become blameless; even so, after I have attained final nibbāna, for five thousand years, noble sons who—having reflected upon this discourse and having abandoned the company of the crowd—delight in solitude, will make an end to the suffering of saṃsāra.
And as if fulfilling the Blessed One’s own wish, having reflected upon this discourse and having abandoned the company of the crowd, [they shall put an end to] the suffering of saṃsāra.
Having exhausted [the taints], these sons of noble family have attained final nibbāna, transcending the path of calculation.

Indeed, at the Vālikapiṭṭhi Monastery, during the time of the rains-retreat, the Elder Ābhidhammika-Abhaya, together with many bhikkhus, having recited this sutta, said: "The Fully Enlightened One acts in this way;
what shall we do? During that very rains-retreat, they all dissolved their groups and took delight in solitude.
They attained arahantship. This sutta is called "The Breaking of the Assembly.
186. "Ghaṭāya" refers to a Sakka of that name. Regarding the "vihāra":

it should be understood that this vihāra was also built as a part of the Nigrodhārāma itself, just like the Kāḷakhemaka-vihāra. "Cīvarakamma" refers to [the work] such as providing patches for worn and soiled robes, washing them, and so forth.
Even a prepared border is permissible, as is the arrangement of cloth acquired for the sake of robes that has not yet been processed through sorting, sewing, and so forth;
however, what is intended here is an arrangement that has not yet been processed. For people gave robe-cloth to the Elder Ānanda;
therefore, the Elder, taking several monks with him, performed the work on the robes there. Those monks also...
From the time they were appointed as needle-cases early in the morning, they sat until the time for their appointment had passed;
when it was no longer the time for their appointment, they rose. Thinking, "We shall assign the lodgings once the needlework is finished," they did not assign them.
The Elder thought, "It is indeed the robe-making season; surely these monks have not assigned the lodgings, as the Blessed One..."

"And they will be seen [in such a state]. Thus, being displeased and wishing to thoroughly restrain them, [the Teacher thought], 'I shall be a support for these bhikkhus,' and therefore he spoke thus. This, however, is the underlying intention here:
'Venerable sir, it is not that these bhikkhus are merely fond of work; rather, they are living in this way because of their duties regarding robes.'"

“Indeed not, Ānanda,” [the Blessed One said]. “Ānanda, whether it be a time for work or a time not for work, whether it be a time for making robes or a time not for making robes, a bhikkhu who delights in company does not shine at all.
Do not be one who provides support where there is no need for support. In this context, “company” means the gathering together of one’s own retinue.

A "group" (*gaṇa*) is a gathering of various people. Thus, whether one delights in company or delights in a group, a bhikkhu who in every way takes pleasure in the abundance of a group and is bound by the fetters of a group does not shine.

However, after the meal, having swept the daytime resting place and washed his hands and feet well, a bhikkhu who has taken up his primary meditation subject and is devoted to delighting in solitude shines within the Buddha’s dispensation.
It shines. "The bliss of renunciation" is the bliss of one who has emerged from sensual desire. The "bliss of seclusion" is likewise the bliss of seclusion from sensual desire.

It is called the "bliss of tranquility" because it leads to the subsiding of lust and the other defilements. It is called the "bliss of enlightenment" because it leads to the attainment of the path and full awakening.
"One who gains at will" means one who gains according to their wish; "one who gains without difficulty" means one who gains without hardship.
"Of easy acquisition" means obtained extensively.
"Temporary" means liberated from defilements at the very moment it is applied. "Pleasant" means agreeable.
"Liberation of mind" refers to the liberation of mind pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. For this has been said: "The four jhānas and the four immaterial attainments..."
“This is a temporary liberation. “Non-temporary” means that it is not liberated from the defilements by way of time;

rather, it is said to be the supramundane, which is absolutely liberated. For this has been said: “The four noble paths and the four fruits of recluseship—this is the non-temporary liberation. “Unshakable” means it cannot be shaken by the defilements.
What has been stated by this much? A monk who delights in company and is bound by the ties of a group is unable to produce either mundane or supramundane qualities;
however, having dispelled the group, one who delights in solitude is able to do so.
For instance, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, though surrounded by eighty-four thousand renunciants, for seven years...

While wandering about, he was unable to realize the quality of omniscience; however, after dismissing his retinue, delighting in solitude for seven days, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and realized the quality of omniscience.
Our Bodhisatta, while wandering with the group of five for six years, was unable to realize the quality of omniscience; once they had departed, he delighted in solitude.
Having ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he produced the quality of omniscience.
Having thus shown that one who delights in company lacks the attainment of virtues, he now spoke the passage beginning with "I am not, Ānanda," in order to show the arising of faults.
In this context, "form" (rūpa) refers to the body. "In which one is delighted" means by way of lust for that form.
"Of one who is lustful. "I do not perceive any form in which, for one who is lustful, [defilements] would not arise"—
this is stated by way of the change of state (aññathābhāva) known as Sāriputta and Moggallāna’s attainment of discipleship under the One of Ten Powers,
just as in the case of Sañcaya, or by way of the change of state of the householder Upāli, just as in the Piya-jātaka-sutta.
And they arise just as they do for the merchant and others. 187.
Now, regarding the phrase "But this, Ānanda," what is the connection? For if some person of dull wit who has newly gone forth were to say:
"The Perfectly Enlightened One is leading us away from the group, like cows that have entered a field, toward solitude..."

[Thinking,] "He encourages others [to practice], yet he himself dwells surrounded by kings, royal ministers, and so forth," the Blessed One began this teaching in order to cut off the basis for such speech—to show that "even when seated in the midst of an assembly as vast as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), the Tathāgata is all alone.
In this context, "all signs" (*sabbanimittānaṃ*) refers to the conceptual signs (*saṅkha-nimitta*) of form and the other sense objects. "Internally" (*ajjhattaṃ*)...

*Visayajjhattaṃ*: "The sphere of the object. *Suññataṃ*: "Emptiness," meaning the attainment of the fruit of emptiness (*suññataphalasamāpatti*). In that context, *tatra* is used in the locative sense; it means "in that [attainment].
Again, *tatra* refers to one standing in the midst of that assembly. *Vivekaninnenā*: "Inclined toward seclusion," meaning inclined toward Nibbāna. *Byantībhūtenā*:

"Brought to an end," meaning one who has become free from, emerged from, and dissociated from those states of phenomena that are the basis for the taints (*āsava*). *Uyyojanikapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ*: "Connected with sending forth."
"Go, you yourselves"—this is connected with such words of dismissal.
At what time, however, does the Blessed One speak thus? At the time for the duties after the meal, or at the time for the duties during the first watch of the night.
For the Blessed One, having finished his meal, enters the lion’s posture in the Fragrant Chamber, and rising from that, he enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Having sat down after lighting [the lamp], at that time the assembly gathers for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.

Then the Blessed One, having discerned the proper time, emerges from the Gandhakuṭī and, having ascended the excellent Buddha-throne and taught the Dhamma, dismisses the assembly without letting the time pass, with a mind inclined toward seclusion, as if taking up a medicinal oil decoction. During the first watch of the night as well...
“Vāseṭṭhas, the night has passed; now you may consider it time to depart. Thus he dismisses them.
For from the moment the Buddhas attain enlightenment, even their two sets of fivefold sensory consciousness are inclined toward Nibbāna.
Therefore [the Buddha says], “Therefore, Ānanda,” because the dwelling in emptiness is peaceful and sublime.
188. "Internally" means internally with respect to the range of experience (*gocara*). "Internal emptiness" here refers to one's own internal state;

the meaning is that it is dependent upon one's own five aggregates. "Possessing full awareness" means being fully aware through knowing the state of non-attainment regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Externally" means in the five aggregates of another. "Internally and externally" means internally at times...
At the appropriate time, externally. "Imperturbable" means he brings to mind the immovable formless attainment, thinking, "I shall become one liberated in both ways.
"In that very same prior [state]" is said with reference to the foundational jhāna;

for when one has emerged from a foundational jhāna that is not yet fully mastered and brings to mind emptiness internally, the mind does not leap into it. Then, [he directs it] toward the continuum of another...
Thinking, "How indeed [is it]? he directs his attention externally; yet even there, he does not leap forward.
Then, thinking, "At one time within my own continuum, and at another time within the continuum of another—how indeed [is it]? he directs his attention both internally and externally;
yet even there, he does not leap forward. Then, desiring to be liberated in both ways, he thinks: "In the formless attainment..."

"How so? He attends to the imperturbable (*āneñja*), yet even there he does not leap forward. Now—thinking "my mind does not leap forward"—one should not follow behind the attendants and others with slackened energy; rather, one must carefully and repeatedly bring to mind that very foundational jhāna.
Thus, it is like a man cutting a tree whose axe becomes blunt; he must sharpen it again.

He said, "In that very [object]," etc., in order to show that for one who has had it made thus, mental attention flows toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) like an axe when it is being whetted.
Now, showing that for one who has practiced in this way, mental attention succeeds in whatever he attends to, he said, "it leaps forward."
189. "By this abiding" means by this abiding in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

"Thus being fully aware therein" means that even while walking, because one is accomplishing that meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), one is fully aware through the knowledge: "My meditation subject is succeeding.
"He lies down" means he reclines. Having walked for some time here—now, for so much...
Knowing, "I will be able to walk at the proper time," one should remain without abandoning the postures. This same method applies to all instances.
Regarding the phrase "I will not speak": by knowing, "In this way I will not speak there," one acts with full awareness (*sampajañña*) therein.

Furthermore, in the second instance, by knowing, "I will speak such talk," one acts with full awareness; for this bhikkhu’s serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are still tender, and it is for the sake of protecting them—
“Dwelling, pasture, speech, person, and then food;
climate and posture—these are the seven suitable things that should be cultivated.

These seven suitable things are to be sought after. This was said for the purpose of showing them. Through the knowledge of both non-thinking and thinking in the sections on thought, clear comprehension is to be understood.

190. Having thus explained two paths by means of the abandoning of applied thought (*vitakka*), he now spoke the passage beginning with "Ānanda, these five strands of sensual pleasure... while explaining the insight (*vipassanā*) for the third path.
"In the sense-sphere" (*āyatane*) refers to any among those very strands of sensual pleasure that serves as a cause for the arising of defilements.
"Occurrence" (*samudācāro*) refers to the active manifestation [of defilement] by one whose defilements have not been abandoned. "Being thus" (*evaṃ sante*) means in this way...
"Existing" means it is actually present. "Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*) means clearly comprehending by knowing the non-attainment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
In the second instance, "evam santam etam" means "this being so, this [is the case]. "Clearly comprehending" means clearly comprehending by knowing the attainment of the meditation subject.
For he, while reviewing, "Has my desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned or not?", perceives their unabandoned state.
Having understood this and exerted energy, one eradicates it by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). Immediately after that path comes the fruit;
emerging from the fruit and reviewing it, one knows its state of being abandoned. By virtue of that knowledge, it is said: "He is clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*). 191.
Now, explaining the insight (*vipassanā*) of the path to Arahatship, he said: "Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging... and so forth.
"In that regard, it is abandoned" means that the conceit "I am" regarding form, the desire "I am," and the underlying tendency "I am" are abandoned.
Likewise, the state of clear comprehension regarding feeling and the other aggregates should be understood according to the method already stated.
"These, Ānanda, are those states" refers to the states of serenity, insight, the path, and the fruit mentioned previously.
"Wholesome with a wholesome outcome" means they have come from the wholesome. For the wholesome states are both wholesome and wholesome with a wholesome outcome;
for example, the first jhāna is wholesome, and the second jhāna is both wholesome and wholesome with a wholesome outcome...

[and so on] ...the base of nothingness is wholesome, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is both wholesome and wholesome with a wholesome outcome. The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
The stream-entry path is wholesome and has a wholesome result; ... [and so on] ... the non-returning path is wholesome, and the arahant path is both wholesome and has a wholesome result.
Likewise, the first jhāna is wholesome, and the states associated with it are both wholesome and have a wholesome result;
... [and so on] ... the arahant path is wholesome, and the states associated with it are wholesome.
And they are both wholesome and leading to the future.
"Noble" (ariya) means free from defilements and purified. "Supramundane" (lokuttara) means superior and distinguished above the world.

"Unassailed by the Evil One" (anavakkantā pāpimatā) means not overcome by Māra, the Evil One. For one who has sat down after entering the eight attainments that serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā-pādaka):
For Māra does not see the mind of a bhikkhu; he is unable to know, "It is turning out by depending on such-and-such an object.
Therefore it is said, "unassailed.
Why did he say, "What do you think of this"? He said this to show that there is also a benefit in the company [of others]. "To follow" means to go after or to attend upon.
Regarding the phrase "Not so, Ānanda," although the Blessed One has here—by saying, "Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who is a listener abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he maintains himself in purity"—likened the learned one to a warrior endowed with the five weapons, nevertheless, because that [learning] consists of the acquired scriptures...
"Even if one has mastered it, if one does not practice the corresponding conformable way of training, that weapon does not belong to him;
it belongs only to one who practices it. Therefore, showing that it is not fit to pursue this for its own sake, he said:
'Not so, Ānanda.'"
Now, in order to show for what purpose [the discourse] should be followed up, he said, "And whatever... and so forth.
Thus, in this sutta, ten topics of discussion (*kathāvatthu*) appear in three places: they appear by way of suitability and unsuitability in the thought, "I shall speak such talk as this";
they appear by way of the study of the scriptures (*sutapariyatti*) in the phrase, "namely, the Sutta and Geyya"; and in this present place—
They have come down by way of fulfillment. Therefore, one who speaks on the ten bases of discourse should speak while standing upon this point in this sutta.
Now, since for some person even dwelling alone the goal is not accomplished, with reference to such a person:
Showing the danger in becoming one, he said, "But this being so, Ānanda," and so forth. Therein, "this being so" means this being so in the state of oneness. 193.
"Teacher" refers to an external teacher, a founder of a sect (*titthakara*). "They follow after" means they turn toward him and approach him.
"He desires fainting" means he yearns for the craving of fainting; the sense is that he brings it about. "By the calamity of the teacher."
The teacher’s own affliction arises from the calamity of the defilements that has arisen within him. The same principle applies to the other types of affliction as well.
*Avadhiṃsu* means they struck or killed him; by this, "death through virtue" (*guṇamaraṇa*) is expressed.
*Vinipātāya* means for the sake of falling down thoroughly. But why is the affliction of one living the holy life (*brahmacāri*) said to have a more painful ripening?
And it has been said: “Furthermore, it results in a bitter ripening and leads to a state of ruin. For the external renunciation yields little gain;
there is no great quality to be realized therein, for it consists merely of the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers.
Thus, just as one who falls from the back of a donkey experiences no great suffering, but only the mere smearing of his body with dust.
In this way, in the external system, one declines from merely mundane qualities; therefore, the first two calamities were not described in that manner.
However, in the Dispensation, going forth is a great gain; therein, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna are the great qualities to be attained.
Thus, just as a well-born noble youth, mounted upon the back of a preeminent elephant, [proceeds].

Just as one wandering through a city might fall from the back of an elephant and undergo great suffering, so too one who declines from the Dispensation (sāsana) falls away from the nine supramundane qualities (lokuttaraguṇa).
Therefore, this "calamity for the practitioner of the holy life" (brahmacārupaddava) is spoken of in this way.
196. "Therefore" means because the calamity for the practitioner of the holy life has a more painful result than the other calamities, or because it constitutes the conduct of an enemy.
Transgressing [this duty] leads to harm and suffering for a long time, whereas the practice of friendship leads to welfare;
therefore, it should be applied in this way both to the subsequent and the preceding meanings. "By means of friendship" means by the practice of friendship.
"By means of enmity" means by the practice of hostility.
"And transgressing the Teacher’s instruction" means that one who intentionally oversteps even a minor offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*) is said to be "transgressing.
One who does not overstep that very same thing is said to be "not transgressing. "I will not strive for you in such a way, Ānanda" means:
"I will not practice toward you in that manner. "Unbaked" means: not yet fired. "In an unbaked [but] not too dry vessel" means: for a potter [uses] an unbaked [vessel] that is not too dry.
He grasps the uncooked [clay] gently with both hands, thinking, "May it not break.
Thus, I will not deal with you in the same way that a potter deals with his clay there. "Repeatedly restraining, repeatedly restraining" means:
I will not remain silent after advising you once; having restrained you again and again, I will advise and instruct you repeatedly.

"Having winnowed, having winnowed" means having sifted out faults again and again. Just as a potter, from among vessels that have been baked, sets aside those that are broken, cracked, or worn out, and taking only those that are well-baked, strikes them repeatedly with a mallet before collecting them;
even so, I too, having sifted you out again and again, shall exhort and instruct you repeatedly. "That which is the essence shall remain"—thus it has been said by me to you.
Of those being exhorted, that which is the essence of the path and its fruit shall endure. Furthermore, even mundane qualities are intended here by the term "essence.
The rest is self-evident throughout.
[Thus ends the portion from] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahāsuññata Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta. In that context, the phrase "yatra hi nāma" (that it should be so) is used in the sense of something wonderful (*acchariya*).
"Nipāto" means "one who is called a Tathāgata. Regarding "chinnapapañca": here, "papañcas" refers to these three defilements—craving, conceit, and views.
Regarding "chinnavaṭuma": here, "vaṭuma" denotes the cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
"Pariyādinnavaṭṭa" is a synonym for that same term. "Sabbadukkhavītivatta" means one who has transcended all suffering, which is to say, the entire cycle of resultant existence (*vipākavaṭṭa*).
"Having transcended suffering. Regarding the phrase "he will recollect," this is a future tense expression used by way of a particle (*nipāta*), yet its meaning here should be understood as past.
For the Blessed One did recollect those Buddhas; he does not recollect them now. "Of such birth":
Vipassī and the others were of kṣatriya birth; Kakusandha and the others were of brahmin birth. "Of such clan": [and so forth].
Vipassī and the others were of the Koṇḍañña clan; Kakusandha and the others were of the Kassapa clan. "Of such virtue" means they possessed such virtue by way of both mundane and supramundane virtue.
"Of such Dhamma": here, the factors belonging to the side of concentration are intended; the meaning is that they possessed such concentration by way of both mundane and supramundane concentration.
"Of such wisdom" means they possessed such wisdom by way of both mundane and supramundane wisdom. "Dwelling thus" means...
But here, since the factors belonging to the side of concentration were already included below, one might ask: "Why is that which was already included being taken up again?
It is not that this is merely what was already included; rather, this is for the purpose of illustrating the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Therefore, the meaning here is: "one who dwells in such an attainment of cessation."

"Thus liberated": herein, there are five kinds of liberation—liberation by suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), liberation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vimutti*), liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), liberation by tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and liberation by escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).

Among these, the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are designated as "liberation by suppression" because they are liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth that have been suppressed. The contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth...

The seven contemplations (anupassanā) receive the designation "liberation by factor" (tadaṅgavimutti) because they are liberated from the perceptions of permanence and so forth, which have been abandoned by way of their respective opposing factors.

The four noble paths (ariyamagga) receive the designation "liberation by eradication" (samucchedavimutti) because they are liberated from the defilements that have been utterly cut off. The four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala)...
Because they arise when the defilements have been calmed by the power of the Path, they are designated as "liberation through subsiding.
Because it has escaped from, departed from, and stands far away from all defilements, Nibbāna is designated as "liberation as escape.
Thus, by way of these five kinds of liberation, the meaning here should be understood as "liberated in this way."
199. "Therefore, indeed" means: since you say, "The Tathāgatas are wonderful," therefore let the wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata occur to you even more abundantly.
Regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending," there are two kinds of clear comprehension:
that pertaining to the world of humans and that pertaining to the world of devas. In this regard, in the *Vessantara Jātaka*, after giving away his two sons to the brahmin, on the following day—
Having given the goddess to Sakka and having gained Sakka’s favor, he chose eight boons, saying:
“When released from here, may I go to heaven and attain distinction;
may I never return from there—this is the eighth boon I choose.”
Thus he took a boon, saying, "May my rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) be in the Tusita heaven";

from that point on, he knew, "I shall arise in the Tusita heaven"—this is clear comprehension (sampajañña) regarding the human world. Furthermore, having passed away from the Vessantara existence, he was reborn again in the Tusita heaven and recognized, "I have been reborn"—this is clear comprehension regarding the deva world.

But do the other deities not know this? It is not that they do not know; however, having looked upon their pleasure gardens, celestial palaces, and wish-fulfilling trees, and being awakened by the sound of musical instruments played by divine nymphs, they are reminded and know: "O noble one, this is the world of the gods; you have been reborn here.
The Bodhisatta does not know during the first cognitive moment (javana), but from the second moment onward, he knows.
Thus, he possesses a knowledge that is not shared with others. Regarding the phrase "stood there":
although other deities standing there also know, "We have stood here," they are nevertheless overwhelmed by powerful, desirable objects at the six sense doors;
consequently, having abandoned mindfulness, they do not even remember their own state of eating and drinking.
Being unaware, they pass away through the cutting off of their nutriment. Does the Bodhisatta not have such an object of focus?
Indeed, he does not lack it. For he surpasses the other devas in ten respects;
yet, he does not allow himself to be overwhelmed by that object, but remains having mastered it. Therefore it was said: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda..."
“The Bodhisatta remained in the Tusita realm. [Question:
“As long as his lifespan lasts”—in the remaining existences, does he not remain for the full duration of that lifespan? [Answer: Yes, he does not remain.
For at other times, having been reborn in a heaven of long life, he closes his eyes, thinking, “It is not possible to fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) there.”
Having performed what is called the "ornamentation of his final resolve," he was reborn in the human world. This kind of passing away does not occur for others;

however, at that time, there was no such thing as "giving what has not been given" nor "unprotected virtue," and because all the perfections (pāramīs) were fulfilled, he remained for the full span of his lifespan.

“Mindful and clearly comprehending, he passes away from the Tusita realm and descends into a mother’s womb”—thus, having fulfilled all the perfections, the Bodhisatta remained there for the duration of his lifespan. However, for the devas, five portents appeared, indicating:
“In seven days from now, according to human reckoning, his passing will occur”: [first,] the garlands...
The flowers wither, the garments become soiled, sweat breaks forth from the armpits, ugliness descends upon the body, and the deva cannot remain steady in his celestial throne.
In this context, "garlands" refers to the garlands worn on the day of conception. It is said that there were more than six million of them.
Without withering for fifty-seven koṭis of years, they then wither. The same principle applies to their clothing as well.
During that time, there is neither cold nor heat for the devas; at that time, sweat is released from their bodies drop by drop.
And during that time, no discoloration occurs in their bodies by way of mottling, graying, or other such changes.
The daughters of the gods appear as if sixteen years of age, and the sons of the gods appear as if twenty years of age.
However, at the time of death, their physical forms become exhausted. During all that time in the world of the gods, they experience no weariness;
yet at the time of death, they sigh and stretch, finding no delight in their own seats.

Furthermore, these preliminary signs—just as in the world signs such as the falling of meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses appear only for those of great merit, such as kings, royal ministers, and the like, and not for everyone; even so, they appear only to powerful deities and not to all.
And just as among humans, those who read the stars and the like alone recognize these preliminary signs, and not others...
In this very way, all those gods do not know; only the wise know.
Among them, those sons of the gods who have been reborn through weak wholesome karma fear when they arise there, thinking: "Now who knows? Where shall we be reborn?
But those of great merit [think]: "The gift given by us has been protected."
They do not fear, thinking, "By relying on the cultivation of virtue, we shall experience prosperity in the higher heavenly worlds.
The Bodhisatta too, seeing those preliminary signs, did not fear, thinking, "Now, in my very next existence, I shall become a Buddha.
Then, when those signs had appeared, the deities of ten thousand world-systems assembled before him.
“O worthy one, while you were fulfilling the ten perfections, you did not do so aspiring for the attainment of Sakka, nor for the attainment of Māra, Brahmā, or a Wheel-turning Monarch;
rather, you fulfilled them aspiring for Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world.
Now, O worthy one, is the time for your Buddhahood; O worthy one, this is the moment for your Buddhahood,” they entreated him.

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his promise to the deities, performed what is known as the five great observations (*pañcamahāvilokana*) regarding the time, the continent, the country, the clan, the mother, and the limit of the lifespan.
Therein, he first observed the time, considering: "Is it the right time, or is it not the right time?
In this regard, a period when the lifespan has increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why is that?
For at that time, birth, aging, and death are not perceived among beings; and the teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas is never apart from the three characteristics.
When they speak of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, people do not even think to listen or have faith, wondering, "What is it they are saying?
Consequently, there is no realization (abhisamaya); and in its absence, the Dispensation is not conducive to liberation.
Therefore, that is not the right time. Even a period when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is not called the right time.
Why? Because at such a time, beings have defilements in abundance; and advice given to those with abundant defilements does not remain in its proper place.
It vanishes quickly, like a line drawn with a stick upon water. Therefore, that too is not the right time. However, from a lifespan of one hundred thousand years onwards...
The period of life from one hundred years below upwards is called "the time. At that moment, it was the time of a hundred-year lifespan.
Then the Great Being, perceiving that "the time for rebirth has come," looked toward the continents;
having surveyed the four continents along with their surroundings, he perceived the continent, seeing that "Buddhas are not born on three continents, but are born only in Jambudīpa."
Then, observing the region while wondering, "Jambudīpa is indeed vast, measuring ten thousand yojanas;
in which part, then, do Buddhas take birth? he beheld the Middle Country (*majjhima-desa*). As for the Middle Country, it is described in the Vinaya by way of such passages as:
"In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala," and so forth. Furthermore, that [Middle Country] is three [yojanas] in length...
It is one hundred *yojanas* in length, two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in width, and nine hundred *yojanas* in circumference.
For it is in this place that Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen *asaṅkhyeyya*s and a hundred thousand aeons;
or [in the case of Paccekabuddhas] after fulfilling the perfections for two *asaṅkhyeyya*s and a hundred thousand aeons.
Paccekabuddhas arise; after fulfilling the perfections for one incalculable aeon and a hundred thousand aeons, the great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna arise;
and Cakkavatti kings who exercise sovereignty and lordship over the four great continents and two thousand minor islands arise, as do others of great influence.
“Kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and great landowners will arise. And herein, this city named Kapilavatthu shall be the place where I must be reborn”—thus he reached his conclusion.

Then, surveying the family, he saw: “Buddhas are born into families esteemed by the world; at present, the kṣatriya family is esteemed by the world, so I shall be born there, and King Suddhodana shall be my father. Thus he perceived the family.
Then, looking for a mother, he reflected: “The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful or a drunkard;
she is one who has fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and has maintained the five precepts unbroken from birth onwards. This queen named Mahāmāyā is indeed such as this.
She shall be my mother. But how long is her lifespan? As he reflected thus, he perceived: “Beyond ten months...”
He saw that it would be "seven days.
Having thus performed these five great observations, he thought, "The time has come for me, friends, to attain Buddhahood.
Granting his promise while gathering the deities together, he dismissed those deities with the words, "Go, you," and [remained] with the Tusita deities.
Surrounded [by these beings], he entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita heaven. For indeed, the Nandana Grove exists in all the worlds of the devas.

There, the devatas wander about, reminding him of the sphere of wholesome kamma performed in the past, saying: "When you pass away from here, go to a happy destination; when you pass away from here, go to a happy destination.
Thus, while wandering there surrounded by devatas who were reminding him of his wholesome deeds, he passed away.
Thus he understands, "I am falling away; I am falling away," yet he does not know the death-consciousness. Even after having taken rebirth-linking, he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness;
rather, he knows, "Rebirth-linking has been taken by me in this place.
However, some elders say, "It is necessary to obtain the method of adverting; he will know it only at the second or third moment of consciousness."
But the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "The rebirth-linking of Great Beings is not like the rebirth-linking of others;

their mindfulness and clear comprehension reach the ultimate limit. However, because it is impossible for that very same consciousness to know that same consciousness, the death-consciousness is not known.
Even at the moment of death, one understands, 'I am dying,' and even after having taken rebirth-linking..."
"One does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness itself, but one understands: 'Rebirth has been taken in such-and-such a place.

At that time, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembles. Thus, for one who descends into the mother's womb mindful and clearly comprehending, among the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousnesses, it is the wholesome, non-reactive (asaṅkhārika) consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and preceded by loving-kindness (mettā).
He took rebirth with a consciousness of great fruition accompanied by equanimity. However, the Elder Mahāsīva stated that it was "accompanied by equanimity.
Furthermore, when taking rebirth, he did so on the full moon of Āsāḷhī under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā.

It is said that at that time, starting from the seventh day before the full moon in the city of Kapilavatthu, Queen Mahāmāyā had abstained from drinking intoxicants and was adorned with garlands, perfumes, and ornaments.

While enjoying the festival of the constellations, she rose early on the seventh day, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all her ornaments, and after eating excellent food, undertook the observances of the Uposatha.
Having entered the inner chamber and reclined upon her royal couch, as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: "The four Great Kings, it seems, [are carrying her] right from her bed..."
Having lifted them up together and led them to Lake Anotatta, they stood to one side.
Then their goddesses came, bathed them to remove human impurities, clothed them in divine garments, anointed them with perfumes, and adorned them with celestial flowers.
Not far from there was a silver mountain; within it was a golden palace, and therein, toward the east—
They laid him down with his head facing north. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered upon a certain golden mountain not far from there;

descending from that, he ascended a silver mountain, came from the northern direction, entered a golden palace, circumambulated his mother keeping her to his right, and appeared as if he had entered her womb by splitting open her right side.
Then, having awakened, the queen reported that dream to the king. When the night had turned to dawn, the king summoned sixty-four leading brahmins.
On ground smeared with green cow dung and adorned with auspicious ceremonies such as parched grain, he prepared costly seats;
and for the brahmins seated there, he [prepared] a mixture of ghee, honey, and sugar...
Having filled bowls of gold and silver with excellent milk-rice, he gave them to them, covering each bowl with another bowl of gold and silver respectively;
and he satisfied them with other gifts such as unwashed garments and brindled cows.
Then, after they had been satisfied with every desire, he had them report their dream and asked, "What will come of it? The brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King."
“O Queen, an embryo has taken root in your womb; moreover, it is a male embryo, not a female one. You will have a son.
If he dwells at home, he will become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
If he goes forth from the home into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world, a remover of the veil. Thus, being mindful and clearly comprehending—
The Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Tusita realm, descends into his mother’s womb.
By the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending," this shows that he enters via the fourth mode of descent into the womb. For there are four modes of descent into the womb:
"There are these four, venerable sir, modes of descent into the womb. Here, venerable sir, a certain person descends into his mother’s womb without clear comprehension... [and so forth].
One enters the mother’s womb without full awareness, stays in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness;
this is the first descent into the womb.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, stays in the mother’s womb without full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness; this is the second descent into the womb.

"Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness, but emerges from the mother’s womb without full awareness; this is the third descent into the womb.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone enters the mother’s womb with full awareness, remains in the mother’s womb with full awareness, and emerges from the mother’s womb with full awareness; this is the fourth descent into the womb."
Among these, the first belongs to worldly humans; the second, to the eighty great disciples; and the third, to the two chief disciples and the paccekabodhisattvas.

It is said that by the winds born of karma, they are turned head-downwards and feet-upwards, as if in a precipice hundreds of fathoms deep, and pass through the birth canal—which is exceedingly narrow like the opening of a palm-leaf—like an elephant.
As they emerge, they encounter infinite suffering; therefore, they lack the clear comprehension that "we are emerging.
The fourth case concerns the omniscient Bodhisattvas. For even while taking rebirth in the mother’s womb, they know it;
while dwelling there, they know it; and at the time of emergence, their kamma-born winds turn them upside down.
They are unable to throw him out even by placing him head-downwards; rather, with both hands extended and eyes wide open, he emerges while remaining exactly as he stood.
Regarding the phrase "he descends into the mother’s womb," the meaning here is that he has already descended into the mother’s womb;

for it is when he has *descended* that this occurs, not while he is *descending*. "Immeasurable" means immeasurable by the standards of a Buddha; the meaning is "vast. "Sublime" refers to that very same thing.
This is a synonym. "By the power of the devas" means that here this is the power of the devas:
the radiance of the garment they wear pervades twelve *yojanas*, as does that of their body, their ornaments, and their celestial mansion (*vimāna*); the meaning is "having surpassed that.

"The intermediate spaces between worlds" (*lokantarika*) refers to the fact that between every three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there is one intermediate space between worlds, like the space between three cart-wheels.
It is like the space in the middle of iron plates placed touching one another.
Furthermore, that Lokantarika Niraya is eight thousand yojanas in extent. "Agha" means always open. "Asaṃvuta" means having no foundation even below.
"Andhakāra" means consisting of darkness. "Andhakāratimisa" refers to the blinding gloom that prevents the arising of visual consciousness and thus causes blindness.
Endowed [with these qualities]. It is said that there, visual consciousness does not arise.
"Possessing such great power" means that the moon and sun appear simultaneously across the three continents; thus they possess such great power.
Having dispelled darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction, they provide light; thus they possess such great majesty. "They do not outshine by their radiance" means their own...
They do not reach with their light. It is said that they move through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and having passed beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain, there is the Lokantarika hell;
therefore, they do not reach it with their light there.
"The beings who are there" refers to those beings who have been reborn in that great Lokantara hell. But what is the karma?
Having committed heavy and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous recluses and brahmins,
as well as other acts of violence such as the killing of living beings day after day, they are reborn there— just like the Abhaya-cora, Nāga-cora,
and others in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their individual bodies (attabhāva) measure thirty gavutas in height, like those of the Vaggulī spirits.
They have long nails like those of a *dīghanakha* (long-nail) demon. Like bats clinging to trees, they cling to the base of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) with their nails.

But when, crawling about, they come within arm’s reach of one another, then thinking, "We have found food," they become preoccupied there, turn over, and fall into the water that sustains the world. When the wind strikes them...
Like honeycomb fruits, they are cut off and fall into the water. As soon as they have fallen, they dissolve like a lump of dough in extremely alkaline water.

On that day, they see other beings as well, thinking: "Just as we experience this great suffering, so too, it seems, other beings have been reborn here experiencing this same suffering. This, however—
The radiance does not remain even for the duration of a single spoonful of rice-soup; it lasts only as long as it takes one to perceive the object after waking from sleep.

However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say: "Like a flash of lightning, it issues forth for only the duration of a finger-snap and vanishes even as people are saying, 'What is this? It "trembles" (saṅkampati) on all sides.
It trembles. The other two [terms] are synonyms for the preceding one. Again, the passage beginning with "and immeasurable" is stated for the purpose of a conclusion. 202.
Regarding the statement, "Four sons of gods approach for protection in the four directions":
here, "four" is said by way of the four Great Kings; however, if one counts four for each of the ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there would be forty thousand.
Thus it was. Therein, the Great Kings of this world-system, arriving with swords in hand, approached for the purpose of guarding the Bodhisatta and entered the chamber of glory (*sirīgabbha*).
The others, having driven back the hosts of *pisācas*, *yakkhas*, and other obstructive spirits from the very threshold of the chamber, took up their guard as far as the edge of the world-system.

But for what purpose has this protection come? Indeed, at the moment of rebirth-linking, from the time of the *kalala* stage onwards, even if hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras were to lift up hundreds of thousands of millions of Sinerus and come to create an obstacle for the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother, they would all vanish midway. And this has also been said:

Regarding the occasion of the shedding of blood, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of another's assault.
Bhikkhus, Tathāgatas attain final nibbāna without being subject to such assault. Go, bhikkhus, each to your own dwelling; bhikkhus, Tathāgatas are not to be guarded. Thus it is. Not...
There was a threat to their lives from the attacks of others. Furthermore, there were non-human beings who were deformed, hideous, and birds of terrifying appearance;
seeing their forms or hearing their cries, fear or terror might have arisen in the Bodhisatta’s mother.
To ward them off, they took up protective measures. Moreover, for the sake of the Bodhisatta—
Filled with reverence born from the power of his merit, and impelled by their own sense of respect, they acted in this way.
But did the four Great Kings, standing within the inner chamber, reveal themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not?
They did not reveal themselves at times when she was performing bodily functions such as bathing, adorning herself, or eating; however, [they appeared] in the glorious chamber...
But they appear when she has entered and is reclining on her excellent couch.

Although seeing non-human beings is indeed a source of fear for ordinary people, the Bodhisatta’s mother, through the power of the merit of both herself and her son, does not fear them upon seeing them;
rather, her mind toward them arises as it would toward the ordinary guards of the inner palace.

203. "By nature virtuous" means endowed with virtue by her very essence. It is said that before the Buddha appeared, people would receive the precepts after paying homage to ascetics and wanderers and sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture;
the mother of the Bodhisatta likewise received them from the seer Kāḷadevila. However, once the Bodhisatta had entered her womb, she did not [receive them] at the feet of anyone else.
It was not possible for him to sit down; even having sat upon a seat, his taking up of the precepts would have been merely an act of contempt.
Therefore, it is said that he took up the precepts himself.
Regarding "among men": this refers to certain people, beginning with the Bodhisatta’s father, toward whom he conceived a mind of malevolence.
It does not arise. And that is due to reverence for the Bodhisatta, not because of the abandonment of defilements.
Furthermore, even highly skilled artisans cannot replicate the form of the Bodhisatta’s mother in works such as paintings;
yet, one cannot say that lust does not arise in a man upon seeing it. However, if he approaches her with a mind full of passion, [lust arises].
Their feet do not carry them forward; they are bound as if by divine chains. Therefore, it is said: "unpassable," and so forth.

Regarding the "five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañca kāmaguṇā*): previously, in the phrase "connected with the strands of sensual pleasure," the prohibition of the physical object was stated from the perspective of human intention;
here, however, the acquisition of the object is shown. At that time, it is said: "Such a son as this was in the womb of the queen..."
Having heard that [the Bodhisatta] had been born, kings from all directions sent forth gifts consisting of costly ornaments, musical instruments, and so forth—
objects serving as the sensory bases for the five doors; and because of the abundance of the merit performed by the Bodhisatta and his mother,
there was no limit whatsoever to the honor and offerings they received.
204. "With an untiring body" means that, unlike other women who become exhausted by the burden of pregnancy and whose hands and feet become swollen and so forth, she experienced no such fatigue.
"Having gone beyond the belly" means having entered within the belly.
Having passed through the stages of the *kalala* and so on, she sees [the child] as one whose limbs and members have fully developed and who has reached the state of having complete sense faculties.
For what purpose does she look? For the sake of dwelling in comfort.

Just as a mother sitting or lying down with her child looks at the child for the sake of dwelling in comfort—thinking, "I shall lift up and straighten his hand or foot if it is hanging down"—so too the Bodhisatta’s mother [looks] during the times of the mother’s rising, walking, turning over, sitting, and so forth, and during the times of swallowing food that is hot, cold, salty, sour, bitter, or pungent.
And while suffering arises for the embryo, she wonders, "Does my son have this [suffering] as well? For the sake of his comfortable dwelling, she gazes upon the Bodhisatta;

she sees the Bodhisatta sitting with his legs crossed in the *pallaṅka* posture, whereas other beings within the womb cover the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), lift up the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*), place the abdominal membrane behind them, and [lean against] the spinal column.
Relying on their knees, with their chins resting upon two clenched fists, they sit like monkeys in tree hollows when it rains;

the Bodhisatta does not do so. Instead, the Bodhisatta sits facing east, having placed his spine behind him and crossed his legs in the full lotus posture (pallaṅka) like a preacher at a Dhamma seat. Previously...
However, her past karma purifies the physical basis; when that basis is purified, the characteristic of fine skin is produced.
Then, being within the womb, the skin is unable to conceal it, and as she looks [at him], he appears as if standing outside.
Explaining this matter by means of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. But the Bodhisatta, having entered within the womb—
He does not see his mother; for visual consciousness does not arise within the womb.
He dies not because of the condition of having been born, but solely through the exhaustion of his lifespan.
For the place where a Bodhisatta has dwelt is like a shrine-chamber, not to be used by others, and it is not possible to remove the Bodhisatta’s mother from there.
To appoint another in the position of chief consort, the lifespan of the Bodhisatta’s mother is exactly that much;
therefore, she passes away at that time. At what stage of life, then, does she pass away? In middle age.
For in early youth, beings’ desire and lust for their own personal existence (*attabhāva*) are powerful; thus, a woman who has conceived a fetus at that time—
If they are unable to protect [the womb], the pregnancy becomes fraught with many afflictions.
However, when two-thirds of middle age have passed and one enters the third stage, the physical basis (*vatthu*) becomes clear; children born when the physical basis is clear are free from disease.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s mother, having experienced the splendors of early life, [gave birth] during the third stage of middle age.
Having been born, he dies.
Regarding the phrase "nine or ten," it should be understood that by the word "or" (*vā*), there is an inclusion of other alternatives such as "seven or eight, or eleven or twelve," and so forth.
Among these, one born after seven months may live, yet is not yet capable of enduring cold and heat.
There is none. One born after eight months does not survive; the others survive.
"Remaining as she was" means having remained exactly as she was. Queen Mahāmāyā also announced to the King, "I am about to give birth; I shall go to my kinsmen's home.
The King had the road from Kapilavatthu to the city of Devadaha decorated, and [placed] the Queen in a golden palanquin.
He had her seated. All the inhabitants of the city, being Śākyas, surrounded her and, honoring the Queen with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, escorted her away.
Upon seeing the Lumbinī grove garden not far from the city of Devadaha, she conceived the desire to wander through the park and signaled her wish to the King.
The King had the garden prepared and established a guard over it.
As soon as the Queen had entered the garden, she experienced physical weakness.

Then, having prepared a couch of honor at the foot of the auspicious sal tree, they surrounded it with a curtain. Having entered inside the curtain, she stood holding a branch of the sal tree with her hand;
at that very moment, her delivery took place.
"The deities receive him first" means that the *Suddhāvāsa* Brahmās, whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted, receive him. How so?
Some say it is by assuming the guise of a midwife; however, having rejected that, this is what is stated:
at that time, the Bodhisatta’s mother, having put on a garment inlaid with gold, and having wrapped herself in a *dukūla* cloth resembling a fish-eye down to her feet—
She stood there. Then her delivery was very easy, like water flowing out from a water-pot.
Then those deities, approaching in their natural brahma-forms, first received him with a golden net.
From their hands, human beings received him with a soft *dukūla* cloth. Thus it is said: "The deities received him first..."
"Later, people receive them.

(206) "The four sons of the gods" refers to the four Great Kings (*mahārāja*). "Having received them" means having received them upon a deerskin rug. "Of great authority" means possessing great majesty, great fame, and being endowed with the [auspicious] marks (*lakkhaṇa*).
"He emerges quite unhindered" means that unlike other beings who emerge stuck and mangled along the path of birth, he does not suffer such distress.
"He does not depart in this way; rather, he departs without clinging"—this is the meaning. "By water" means by means of fluid.

"By no impurity whatsoever" means that unlike other beings who, driven by the winds of karma, enter the birth canal with feet upturned and head down, as if falling into the precipice of the Sataporisa hell, being dragged out through a palm-wood opening like elephants experiencing great suffering and smeared with various kinds of filth; [he departs] without such impurity.
They emerge [in such a way], but the Bodhisatta does not. For the kamma-born winds are unable to place the Bodhisatta with his feet upward and his head downward.

Descending from the Dhamma-seat like a preacher of the Dhamma, or like a man descending from a ladder, he remains standing with both hands and feet extended, by means of some [quality] born of his mother’s womb.
He emerges unsmeared by impurity.
"Streams of water" refers to columns of water; among them, the cold falls into golden basins and the hot falls into silver basins.
And this water on the surface of the earth is unmixed with any impurity, being both drinking water and water for washing.
This was said in order to show the sporting water that is not shared by others.

However, there is no such limitation for the water being brought by golden and silver jars, nor for the water contained in lotus ponds such as those frequented by swans and ducks. 207. “Just born” means having been born for a mere moment;
however, in the Pāḷi, he is depicted as if he had only just emerged from his mother’s womb.
But it should not be viewed in this way. For as soon as he had emerged, the Brahmās first received him with a golden net;
from their hands, the Four Great Kings [received him] on a deerskin rug that was considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch;
from their hands, humans [received him] on a cushion of fine linen; and when released from the hands of humans, he stood firm upon the earth.
"While a white sunshade is being held over him" means while a divine white silk sunshade is being held over him.

And here, the five royal insignia, such as the sword and so forth, which are the attendants of the sunshade, are also indeed included. However, in the canonical text (pāḷi), regarding the king’s procession, only the sunshade is mentioned, just as with the king himself.

Among those [five insignia], only the sunshade is visible, not the bearers of the sunshade. Likewise, only the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather whisk, the yak-tail whisk, and the turban are mentioned.
They appeared, yet there were no perceivers of them. It is said that all of those were taken up by deities whose forms were invisible.
And this has been said: “The Maruts held in the sky a parasol with many branches and a thousand circles.”
"Golden-handled yak-tail whisks fall down,
yet those who hold the whisks and the parasol are not seen.
As for the phrase "all directions," this refers to the surveying of all quarters as if standing upon the seven steps after the Great Stride.

But it should not be viewed in that way. For when the Great Being had escaped from the hands of men, he looked toward the eastern direction, and thousands of world-systems became a single open space. There, gods and humans, worshipping him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said:
"Great Being, there is no one here equal to you; how much less anyone superior?"

Thus, having surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—and seeing no one equal to himself, he proceeded with the stride of seven steps, thinking, "This is the northern direction. This is how the meaning here should be understood.
*Āsabhiṃ* means supreme. *Aggo* means the very first in terms of qualities. The other two words are synonyms for this same term.
With the two phrases, "This is the last birth; now there is no further becoming," he prophesied the attainment of Arahantship to be reached in this very life.
Furthermore, in this context, standing with feet level upon the earth was the omen for the acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*);
facing the north was the omen for proceeding while overwhelming and surpassing the great multitude.
The walking seven paces is the omen of obtaining the treasure of the seven factors of enlightenment; the holding of the divine white parasol is the omen of obtaining the parasol of liberation;
the five regalia of a king are the omen of being liberated by the five kinds of liberation;
and the surveying of the quarters is the omen of obtaining unobstructed knowledge.
The utterance of a bull-like voice is the precursor to the irreversible turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The lion’s roar, “This is my final birth,” should be understood as the precursor to the final *parinibbāna* in the element of *nibbāna* without residue.
These sections have been handed down in the Canon; however, the section concerning many [disciples] has also been handed down and should be illustrated by being cited here.
On the day of the Great Being’s birth, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
Deities from throughout the ten-thousandfold world system assembled in a single world-system. First the gods received him, and afterwards humans.
Stringed lutes and leather-bound drums, though played by no one, sounded of their own accord; and the fetters and bonds of humans...
They broke into pieces. All diseases vanished like tarnish washed from copper with sour gruel.
Those blind from birth saw forms; those deaf from birth heard sounds; the cripples became endowed with speed;
mindfulness was established even in those who were mentally dull and mute from birth; ships sailing abroad reached safe harbors; and treasures dwelling in the sky and on the earth appeared.
All things were illuminated by his own splendor; enemies conceived thoughts of loving-kindness; the fires in the Avīci hell were extinguished.
A light arose in the intervals between worlds; water ceased to flow in the rivers; the waters in the great oceans became as sweet as honey; the wind did not blow;
and the birds dwelling in the sky, the mountains, and the trees fell silent and descended to the earth.
The moon shone brightly; the sun was neither hot nor cold, being stainless and endowed with perfect seasons.
Devas stood at the doors of their respective celestial mansions and engaged in great festivities with hand-clapping, shouting, and the waving of garments.

A great cloud rained over the four continents, and the great multitude of people were neither oppressed by hunger nor by thirst. Door-leaves and gates opened of their own accord, and [trees] bearing flowers and fruits [blossomed].
The trees took up flowers and fruits, and the ten-thousandfold world-system became adorned with a single banner.
Therein, this earthquake of the ten-thousandfold world-system was a premonitory sign of the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*);
and the gathering of the deities in a single world-system was for the purpose of receiving the Dhamma all at once when the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion.
The first acceptance by the deities is a foretoken of the attainment of the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
Subsequently, the acceptance by human beings is a foretoken of the attainment of the four immaterial-sphere jhānas.
The spontaneous sounding of stringed lutes is a foretoken of the attainment of the successive meditative abidings (*anupubbavihāra*).
The sounding of leather-bound drums is a precursor to the proclamation of the great Dharma drum;
the severing of fetters and the like is a precursor to the eradication of the conceit "I am"; the disappearance of all diseases is a precursor to the disappearance of all defilements;
and the sight of forms by those born blind is a precursor to the attainment of the divine eye. [Likewise for] those born deaf...
Hearing sounds is the precursor to the acquisition of the divine ear-element; the attainment of speed by those who are cripple is the precursor to the realization of the four bases of psychic power;
mindfulness established in the dull-witted is the precursor to the acquisition of the four foundations of mindfulness;
and the reaching of a well-established port by ships sailing to foreign lands is the precursor to the realization of the four analytical knowledges.
The first sign is that the jewels are illuminated by their own radiance; this is the first sign of that light of the Dhamma which will be shown to the world.
The acquisition of a mind of loving-kindness toward enemies is the first sign of the acquisition of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). In the Avīci hell...

The extinguishing of fire is a precursor to the eleven kinds of the extinguishing of fire; the light between worlds is a precursor to the manifestation of the light of knowledge after dispersing the darkness of ignorance;
the sweetness of the great ocean is a precursor to the state of having a single flavor with the taste of Nibbāna;
the non-blowing of the wind is a precursor to the shattering of the sixty-two types of views; [the silence] of the birds...
The earth’s shaking was a premonitory sign that the great multitude would go for refuge with their very lives upon hearing the instruction;

the moon’s excessive brilliance was a premonitory sign of its being beloved by many people; and the sun’s freedom from heat and cold, resulting in pleasant seasons, was a premonitory sign of the arising of physical and mental happiness.
Furthermore, the gods’ [actions] at the doors of their celestial mansions, such as clapping their hands...
The play [of the Bodhisatta] was the precursor to attaining the state of Buddhahood;

the raining of the great cloud over the four continents was the precursor to the raining of the great cloud of Dhamma; the absence of affliction by hunger was the precursor to obtaining the nectar of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati);
and the absence of affliction by thirst was the precursor to being made happy by the bliss of liberation.
The doors and gates opening of their own accord is a precursor to the opening of the door of the Eightfold Path;
the trees taking up flowers and fruits is a precursor to being blossomed with the flowers of liberation and being laden with the burden of the fruits of recluseship;
and the ten-thousandfold world system becoming a single garland of banners is a precursor to being adorned with the garlands of the noble ones' banners.
This should be understood as a "foretoken. This is called the section on the many.

Here they ask a question: "When the Great Man, having stood upon the earth, walked facing north and uttered a lion's roar, did he go by way of the earth or through the air? Did he go while being visible..."

"Did he go while visible, or was he invisible? Did he go as a naked ascetic, or was he fully adorned? Did he go as a youth, or as an old man? And later on, did he remain the same, or did he become a young child again?

This question, however, was already answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya during an assembly of the Saṅgha at the Lohapāsāda. It is said that the Elder spoke thus on this matter: [The Elder replied: "He went while visible, not while invisible; he went as a naked ascetic, not as one fully adorned; he went as a youth, not as an old man; and later on, he remained the same, and did not become a young child again. Thus it was answered. The Elder, it is said, [spoke] here...

Having spoken at great length on various matters according to the doctrines of destiny (*niyati*), past deeds (*pubbekata-kamma*), and the creation of a supreme lord (*issaranimmāna*), he finally declared:
"The Great Man has gone upon the earth, yet to the multitude it was as if he were going through the sky;
he went while being seen, yet to the multitude it was as if he were unseen; he went naked, yet to the multitude he appeared as if fully adorned and prepared."
He attended upon him. Although he had gone away while still young, to the great multitude he appeared as if sixteen years old;
but later he became like a mere child, not such as he was before. When this was said, the assembly was delighted, saying, “The Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself!
The section on the intermediate space between worlds is to be understood according to the method already stated.

"Known" means having become manifest. For while disciples are unable to comprehend past formations that have passed away and reached no location—such as those occurring at times of bathing, washing the face, eating, or drinking—and instead comprehend only those that have reached a specific location, the Buddhas are not like this.
For the Buddhas, within seven days, comprehend from the very beginning the formations that have already been determined.
They answer only after having applied the three characteristics; for them, there is no such thing as a dhamma that has not been seen through insight (vipassanā).
Therefore, he said, "known. The rest is clear everywhere.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Acchariyabbhuta-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Bākula-sutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Bākula-sutta*. In this context, "Bākula" is [a name] just as [the names] "twenty-two," "thirty-two," and so forth [are used].
