Just as one would say "twenty-two" or "thirty-two" when such numbers ought to be stated, so too, when it should have been said "two clans" (*dvikula*), it was stated as "Bākulā.
For that elder had two families. It is said that after passing away from the world of the gods, he was reborn in the great merchant family of the city named Kosambī;
on his fifth day, they bathed his head and took him for a festival on the banks of the Ganges.

While a nurse was playing with the boy by repeatedly submerging him in and lifting him out of the water, a fish saw the boy and, thinking, "This is my prey," opened its mouth and approached him. The nurse abandoned the boy and fled;
the fish swallowed him. Yet, because he was a meritorious being, he did not experience suffering; instead, he entered his mother’s womb and lay there.

It was as if [the fish] were being scorched. By the power of the boy, the fish swallowed the hot frying pan and, as if burning, traveled thirty *yojanas* with great speed until it entered the net of a fisherman living in the city of Bārāṇasī.
It is said that large fish die when caught in a net and struck. However, this one died the very moment it was pulled out of the net by the power of the boy. The fishermen—
Having caught a large fish and split it open, they used to sell it. But because of the power of the boy, they could not split it;
instead, carrying the entire fish on a carrying-pole, they wandered through the city saying, "We will give this for a thousand pieces. No one would take it.
Now, in that city, there was a merchant family worth eighty crores who had no son; [they went] to the threshold of their house.
Having arrived, when asked, "What have you brought? Give it here," they replied, "A kahāpaṇa coin. He took it from them after they had given the kahāpaṇa.
On other days the merchant’s wife did not even look at the fish, but on that day she placed the fish on a wooden board and cut it herself.
Fish are usually cut by those who are loathsome, but she cut it from behind.
Seeing a golden-colored boy within the belly of a fish, she cried out, "I have found a son in the belly of a fish!

and taking the boy with her, she went into the presence of her husband. The merchant immediately had a drum beaten and, taking the boy, went into the presence of the king, saying, "Your Majesty, I have found a boy in the belly of a fish; what [shall I do]?"
"I shall do so," he said. "This is a man of merit, who dwelt healthy within the belly of a fish," they said, and began to praise him.
The other family heard the news: "It is said that a certain merchant's family in Bārāṇasī has obtained a boy from the belly of a fish.
They went there. Then his mother, having adorned the boy, saw him being played with.
Thinking, “How delightful this boy is!”, she went and announced the news. The other said, “He is my son,” and so forth. [The first asked: “Where did you get him?
“From the belly of a fish. “He is not your son; he is my son. [The second asked: “Where did you get him?
“I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then, while we were playing in the river, a fish swallowed him. [The first replied: “He is yours...”
"The boy must have been swallowed by another fish, yet this one was found by me inside the belly of a fish.
Thinking thus, both went to the royal palace. The king said, "Since she carried him in her womb for ten months, it is impossible not to regard her as his mother;
furthermore, among those who catch fish, there are none who do not catch them having removed the scales, bones, and so forth from the outside. Therefore, [he must be inside] the belly of a fish."
"Since he has been obtained, it is not possible for me alone to raise him; let the boy be the heir to both families, and let both of us look after him.
So they both looked after him.
When he reached the age of discretion, they had palaces built for him in both cities and provided him with theatrical performances. In each [palace]...
He dwells in one city for four months; having stayed in one city for four months, they have a pavilion constructed with a canopy for him and place him there together with the dancers.
While experiencing such prosperity, he goes to another city. The inhabitants of that city go halfway on the road with the dancers; they go out to meet him.
Surrounding him, they lead him to his own palace. The other theatrical troupes, however, turn back and go to their own city.
Having stayed there for four months, he returns again to the other city by that same routine.
As he thus enjoys his prosperity, eighty years are fulfilled.
Then the Blessed One, wandering on his alms tour, arrived at Bārāṇasī. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he gained faith and went forth.
Having gone forth, he remained an ordinary worldling for only seven days;
however, on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus he had two families, and therefore he became known as Bākula.
"Former householder companion" means a companion from his previous time as a householder. He too was long-lived;

having gone to see the Elder who had gone forth, he had reached eighty years of age. "The practice of sexual intercourse"—the foolish naked ascetic asks a foolish question, not a word of the Dispensation;
now, standing by the method given by the Elder, he asked these [questions] with them.
210. The phrases beginning with "In whomsoever, venerable sir," and so forth, were established by the Elders of the Dhamma-Saṅgaha after determining them for all the sections.

In that context, perception (*saññā*) is merely the arising [of the thought], while applied thought (*vitakka*) is what constitutes the breach of the path of action (*kammapatha*). However, the Elder said: "Why do you separate these?
Both of these are indeed what constitute the breach of the path of action."
“Householder’s robe-cloth” means robe-cloth for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*). “With a knife” means with a small knife (*pipphalaka*).

“With a needle” means that he does not recall having sewn by taking up a needle; this is the meaning. “Robe-cloth for the *kathina* ceremony” means *kathina*-robe-cloth; for even *kathina*-robe-cloth falls under the category of robe-cloth for the rainy-season residence.
Therefore, in that case, he said, “I do not recall having sewn it.”
"But for how long, while not accepting a householder’s robe and not performing the cutting, sewing, and so forth, could a robe arise for him? "From two cities. For the Elder was of great renown;
his sons, daughters, grandsons, and great-grandsons had robes made from fine cloth, dyed them, placed them in boxes, and sent them [to him].
At the time of bathing, they place those robes in the bathing shed for the Elder.

The Elder puts them on as an inner garment and a cloak, and gives his old robes to those who have recently gone forth. Having put them on as an inner garment and a cloak, the Elder does not perform any new work;
there is no laborious task for him at all. He simply sits down, repeatedly entering into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
When four months had passed, [the robes] became soiled with body hair; then they sent them back again and gave him others by that same method.
They even say that he changed them every half-month.
And this is no wonder for the Elder, who possessed great merit and great supernormal powers, and who had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons.
The Elder Nigrodha, who was a family attendant of King Aśoka-dhamma, changed his robes three times a day.

For he would have his triple robe placed upon the neck of an elephant and brought to him every morning, along with five hundred boxes of perfumes and five hundred boxes of garlands; likewise at midday and in the evening. It is said that the king...
Twice a day, while changing his garments, he would ask, "Has the elder’s robe been brought? and upon hearing, "Yes, it has been brought," he would change his clothes.
The elder, for his part, did not tie the bundle up and set it aside; rather, he gave it to the fellow-celibates who arrived.
At that time, it is said, the robes belonging to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in Jambudīpa were, for the most part, the property of Nigrodha alone.
"Ah, would that someone were to invite me!"—but what is more difficult: the non-arising of a thought, or the abandoning of one that has already arisen?
The mind is indeed quick to change; therefore, the non-arising [of unwholesome thoughts] is difficult, and the abandoning of those that have arisen is likewise difficult.
"In the midst of houses" refers to the interior of a house, starting from the threshold, as described in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta.
Here, "place" refers to the spot where the nimba-water falls. But from where did his alms arise?
The Elder was well-known in two cities; as soon as he arrived at a house door, they would take his bowl, fill it with food of various flavors, and give it to him.
He would return from wherever he received [alms], but the place where he performed his meal-duty was fixed.
It happened thus. Regarding "the minor details": it is said that the Elder had never before looked upon a woman after having grasped the sign in a form [of meditation].
"The Dhamma for a woman" means that it is permissible to teach the Dhamma to a woman using five or six sentences;
even if asked a question, it is likewise permissible to speak a thousand verses. Yet the Elder did not do what was allowable; for the most part...
For this is the duty of the resident monks (*kulūpaka-theras*). "Bhikkhunupassaya" means a nunnery.
It is permissible to go there as one who inquires after the sick, yet the Elder did not do what was appropriate.

This same principle applies everywhere. "With powder" means with *kosamba* powder and so forth. "In the application of ointment" refers to the act of massaging the body. "Vicāritā" means employed or directed.
"Gaddūhanamattaṃ" means even for the duration of time it takes to milk a single drop of milk from a cow by holding her teat.

For what reason, then, was the Elder free from affliction? It is said that when the Blessed One Padumuttara, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, was wandering on tour, the *visarukkha* trees blossomed in the Himālaya. And yet, the hundred thousand bhikkhus suffered from a disease caused by grass and flowers.

[The disease] arose. At that time, the elder was a powerful ascetic; traveling through the air, he saw the community of monks, descended, inquired about the illness, and brought medicinal herbs from the Himalayas to give them.
By the mere act of smelling them, the illness was pacified. Even during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, on the first day of sowing, having set aside the seed for the community of monks...
Having had a refectory and a restroom constructed for his own use, he established a regular supply of medicinal requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
through this deed, he became free from illness. Furthermore, because he was one who used superior medicines and lived in the remote forest, he said:
"I do not recall ever having used a bolster," and so forth.
"Saraṇa" means one who possesses defilements. "Full knowledge arose" (aññā udapādi): it is not permitted for one who is not ordained to declare full knowledge.
Why did the Elder declare it? The Elder did not say, "I am an Arahant"; rather, he said, "Full knowledge arose. Furthermore, the Elder was well-known as an Arahant;
therefore, he spoke in this way.
212. As for going forth, the Elder himself neither went forth nor conferred full ordination; rather, he had other bhikkhus do so. "Taking his key" means having taken the lock.

"He attained final nibbāna while still seated": thinking, "While I am living, I was not a burden to any other bhikkhu, and even after I have passed away, let my body not be a hindrance to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," he entered the fire-element and attained final nibbāna.
Flames rose from the body; the skin, flesh, and blood were consumed and exhausted as if being boiled like clarified butter (*sappi*), until only the relics remained, resembling jasmine buds.
The rest is clear everywhere. This discourse, however, was recited in the Second Council.
The commentary on the Bākula Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 5.
The commentary on the Dantabhūmi Sutta.

213. Thus have I heard: this is the Dantabhūmi Sutta. Therein, "in a forest hut" refers to a dwelling constructed for the sake of monks engaged in strenuous effort in a secluded spot within that very Veḷuvana grove.
"The prince" refers to the legitimate son of Bimbisāra.
"Should touch" means he should obtain. "One-pointedness": he says, "I have heard that one who practices in this way obtains what is called attainment (samāpatti) and what is called jhāna.
"Fatigue" means bodily fatigue. "Distress" is just another term for that same fatigue.
"You should remain in your own place" means you should remain in the very spot where you do not know [the path].

214. "He taught" means he explained the preliminary work for a single kasiṇa after having brought it to the stages of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā), saying, "One obtains one-pointedness of mind in this way; one produces meditative attainment in this way. "Having proclaimed" means having made manifest.

"To be known by renunciation" means to be known by the quality of having emerged from sensual desire. This was said with the intention that a person established in the quality of having emerged from sensual desire must know what is called one-pointedness. The remaining terms are synonyms for that very same thing.
"Enjoying sensual pleasures" means enjoying both kinds of sensual pleasure. 215.
Regarding the phrase "whether elephant-tamers, horse-tamers, or ox-tamers": here, persons devoid of one-pointedness of mind should be understood as being like untamed elephants and the rest;
those endowed with one-pointedness of mind are like tamed elephants and the rest. Just as untamed elephants and the rest...
Just as those who do not construct a roof-peak and do not abandon their burden are unable to proceed by means of their tusks or reach the ground that must be reached by tusks,
even so, those devoid of one-pointedness of mind are unable to produce the qualities produced by those endowed with one-pointedness of mind or to reach the stage that has been attained by them.
216. *Hatthavilaṅghakena* means by taking hand in hand.
*Daṭṭheyyaṃ* means what is fit to be seen. *Āvutaṃ* means covered. *Nivutaṃ* means obstructed. *Ophuṭaṃ* means enveloped. 217. *Nāgavanikaṃ*:
In the *Hatthipadopama-sutta*, a man who wanders in the elephant forest is called a "forest-keeper of elephants" (*nāgavanika*); here [the term is used in the same sense].
One skilled in the training of elephants is capable of capturing an elephant. *Atipassitvā* means having seen.
*Etthagedhā* means those whose greed is directed toward this [object]. *Sarasaṅkappānaṃ* means of those with the intention to run away. Regarding the phrase *samādapanāya manussakantesu sīlesu*:
here, when the elephant is being coaxed by men, women, boys, and girls who have taken hold of its trunk and other parts...
When he does not react with agitation and remains at ease, then it is said that he has undertaken the virtues (*sīla*) beloved by humans.
"Pleasing" means, dear one, such talk as: "The King is pleased with you;

he will station you in the very place of the auspicious state elephant, and you will receive food and other requisites worthy of a king"—this is the kind of speech that is to be cherished even by elephants. "Desirous of hearing" means wishing to hear that pleasing talk.
"Grass, fodder, and water": this means both grass for fodder and water; "grass for fodder" (*tiṇaghāsa*) refers to grass that is to be grazed upon, meaning it is to be eaten.

"A drum" (*paṇava*) is a *ḍiṇḍima* drum. "With all crooked faults removed and impurities eliminated": this means having both all crooked faults removed and impurities (*kasāva*) taken away. "It comes to be reckoned as a mere part": it becomes equal to a part. (219) "Of those whose virtue is based on the household life":
of those whose virtue depends on the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Of the method": of the Eightfold Path.
222. “The death of the untamed” (*adantamaraṇa*): the king’s elephant, Mahallaka, has passed away; the king’s elephant Mahallaka has died an untamed death, having met his end.
The meaning here is that what is called “the death of the untamed” is being brought about as the passing away [of one who was not tamed].
This same method applies everywhere. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Dantabhūmi Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 6.
The commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta.
223. Thus have I heard: this is the Bhūmija Sutta. Therein, "Bhūmija" refers to this elder, who was the maternal uncle of Prince Jayasena.
"Hope and hopelessness" means at one time hope and at another time hopelessness.
"With his own *thālipāka*" means he served him with food even from his own finished meal, rather than with the ordinary alms-food. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta.
230. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Anuruddha Sutta. In that context, "they spoke thus" means that there was a time when that lay follower was unwell;
having approached him then, they spoke as follows. "Incontrovertible" (*apaṇṇaka*) means unerring.

"In one thing" (*ekattha*)—referring either to the immeasurable or the sublime—he spoke thus with reference to the fact that it is precisely the jhāna, or indeed one-pointedness of mind, that is so described.

231. “As far as he dwells having pervaded and resolved upon one tree-root as exalted” means that he dwells having covered an area the size of one tree-root with the kasiṇa-sign, and having pervaded and resolved upon exalted jhāna within that kasiṇa-sign.
However, there is no mental preoccupation (*ābhoga*) for him regarding it as "exalted"; it is solely by way of the occurrence of exalted jhāna.
This has been said. This method applies everywhere. "By this means, householder" means by this reason.
For herein, the sign of the immeasurables—the Brahma-vihāras—does not increase; the breakthrough does not arise;
those jhānas do not become the basis for the direct knowledges (abhiññā) or for cessation (nirodha); nor do they become the basis for insight (vipassanā).
Furthermore, they serve as the basis for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and as the means for ascending to higher realms (*bhavokkamana*).

However, for those "exalted" (*mahaggata*) kasiṇa-jhānas that have been mentioned, the sign (*nimitta*) expands, the removal of the physical base (*ugghāṭana*) occurs, there is transcendence (*samatikkama*), and they serve as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), the basis for cessation (*nirodha*), the basis for the cycle of existence, and the means for ascending to higher realms.
Thus, these states have different meanings; they are immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) and exalted (*mahaggata*).
And thus it has various expressions.

Now, having drawn out [the discussion] from the exalted attainments (*mahaggata-samāpatti*), in order to show the cause for rebirth in existence (*bhavūpapatti*), he said, "These four indeed," and so forth.
For one who knows by pervading [them] as "limited light" (*parittābhā*), there is this mental application (*ābhoga*); however, among those of limited light...
He is described thus because he is developing jhāna as the cause for rebirth among the gods. This same method applies everywhere.
Among the Parittābhā (Limited-Light) gods, some have defiled light and some have purified light; among the Appamāṇābhā (Immeasurable-Light) gods, some have defiled light and some have purified light.
How so? By performing the preliminary work of the kasiṇa on the scale of a spoonful or a bowlful, one enters into attainment.
Having attained mastery through five modes, yet because the opposing states have not been thoroughly purified, he employs only a weak attainment;
remaining in a jhāna of limited proficiency, he passes away and is reborn among the Parittābhā devas.
However, his complexion is both limited and defiled. But one who has mastered [the practice] through five modes...

Because he has thoroughly purified the opposing states, having enjoyed a well-purified attainment and remaining firm in a mastery-jhāna, he passes away and is reborn among the Parittābha devas. His radiance is both limited and pure.
Thus, while the Parittābhas may have defiled radiance, they may also have pure radiance. However, regarding the kasiṇa, there is extensive preliminary work.
Having attained and produced the meditative absorption (samāpatti), it should be understood that everything up to "having mastery through five modes" is exactly the same as before.
Thus, while the measureless radiance may be defiled or pure, there is no diversity in its light.

"Diversity of color" refers to the diversity of the body's complexion. "But no diversity in the radiance" means that no diversity is perceived in the light itself. "Diversity of flame" refers to the diversity of the flame by way of being long, short, small, or large.
"Wherever" (yattha yattha) means in whatever place—whether in gardens, celestial palaces (*vimāna*), wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*), riverbanks, or lotus ponds.
"They settle down" (*abhinivisanti*) means they dwell there. "They delight" (*abhiramanti*) means they take pleasure and do not feel weary.

"With a carrying-pole" (*kājena*) means with any kind of carrying-pole used for carrying rice-gruel, boiled rice, oil, molasses, fish, or meat. There is also a reading "with a jar" (*kācena*), which has the same meaning. "With a basket" (*piṭakena*) means with a small wicker tray. In that regard:
"In that very place" means that they do not give rise to thoughts such as,
"Our former dwelling place was comfortable; there we lived happily," or "Here, salt irritates us,

or the smell of rotten fish causes headaches," but rather they take delight right there, having been led from a place where ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth are easily obtained to a place where salt, rotten fish, and the like abound.

234. “She shines, endowed with radiance. “By that factor” means by a factor of that rebirth in existence; the meaning is, by the cause for rebirth in existence. Now, asking about that cause, he said, “Who indeed, venerable sir?
and so forth. “Bodily corruption” means the state of physical sloth. “Jhāyanto” means burning. 235. “For a long time, indeed, it was mine,” [said the Elder].
It is said that while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), the Elder had gone forth as an ascetic (isi) and attained meditative absorption (samāpatti).
Having been reborn continuously for three hundred existences in the Brahma-world, he said this with reference to that.
And it is also said:
“Unmixed for three hundred lives, I went forth in the ascetic’s going-forth.”
“Seeking the unconditioned, I have previously wandered through [many] births.
The remainder is entirely clear throughout.
[Thus ends the portion] from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Anuruddhasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Upakkilesasutta: 236.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Upakkilesasutta. Therein, “he said this” was not with the intention of causing a schism, nor...
Out of a desire for their welfare, he then thought: "These monks will not desist even if they accept my word;

however, the Buddhas are indeed compassionate for the benefit of others. Surely the Blessed One will explain a certain reason to them, and having heard it, they will desist, whereby they will dwell in comfort.
Therefore, he spoke these words beginning with, "In this case, venerable sir."
In the passage beginning with "Mā bhaṇḍanaṃ," the meaning should be understood by supplying the word "akattha" (you have quarreled), thus:
"Do not quarrel. As for "a certain one": it is said that this bhikkhu was desirous of the Blessed One’s welfare; his intention was as follows:
"These bhikkhus, overcome by anger, do not accept the Teacher’s word; let not the Blessed One instruct them..."
"I am weary," he said; therefore, he spoke thus.
"He entered for alms" means that he did not merely enter, but also resolved: "Let even those people who have not seen me see me.
For what purpose did he resolve this? To subdue those monks. For at that time, the Blessed One had returned from his almsround.
Having spoken the verse beginning with “A multitude is a common crowd,” he went from Kosambī to the village of Bālakaloṇakāraka.
From there he went to the Pācīnavaṃsa grove, and thence to the Pālileyyaka forest thicket, where he dwelt for three months being attended upon by the elephant-king Pālileyya.
The city-dwellers also thought, “The Teacher has gone to the monastery; let us go to hear the Dhamma.”
Carrying perfumes and flowers in their hands, they went to the monastery and asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Teacher?

"Where will you see the Teacher? The Teacher came thinking, 'I shall bring these monks into harmony,' but being unable to bring them into harmony, he departed and has gone away. "We would give even a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold] to bring the Teacher back."

“We are able [to refuse]. He has come here of his own accord, uninvited. Because of these monks, we were not able to hear a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. These men have gone forth under the Teacher;
yet even while he was acting with harmony, they did not become harmonious themselves. Whose word will they follow now? Enough! Alms should not be given to these monks.”
They imposed a fine upon the entire city. On the following day, having wandered for alms throughout the whole city and not receiving even a single spoonful of food, they returned to the monastery.
The lay devotees spoke to them again: "As long as you do not ask the Teacher for forgiveness, this same punishment shall remain for you.
Thinking, "We shall ask the Teacher for forgiveness," they [approached] the Blessed One.
When [the Buddha] had arrived at Sāvatthī, they went there. The Teacher taught them the eighteen bases for schism;
this is the narrative not found in the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka-kathā*).

237. Now, regarding the verses beginning with "A loud sound" (*puthusaddo*): it is called "loud-sounding" (*puthusaddo*) because it possesses a great, widespread sound (*puthu mahāsaddo*). "Common people" (*samajano*) means equal people (*samāno*).
"Like a single person": it is said that this entire multitude of people who engage in quarreling is alike in that they emit sound from all sides and are thus characterized by a great clamor.
"No one thinks he is a fool": therein, not even a single person thinks, "I am a fool";
rather, everyone considers themselves wise. "They did not think anything more than that": not even a single person [thought], "I..."

"A fool" means he does not even conceive [such a thought]; furthermore, when the Saṅgha is being split, he does not conceive even this other reason, namely, "The Saṅgha is splitting because of me"—this is the meaning.
"Forgetful" means those whose mindfulness is lost. "Speaking with speech as their range": the long vowel *rā* has been replaced by a short vowel; thus it means "those whose range is merely speech."

They do not have the foundations of mindfulness as their domain, yet they are speakers. How are they speakers? As far as they wish to open their mouths, as far as they wish to stretch their faces, so far they stretch them and speak;

the meaning is that not even one person would refrain from contracting their face out of respect for the Saṅgha. "By which they were led" means by which quarrel they were led to this state of shamelessness. "The wise do not know that"—they do not recognize it.
They do not know that "this has such a disadvantage.
And those who harbor resentment (*upanayhanti*) refers to those who harbor resentment in such ways as "He abused me," and so forth. "Sanantano" means ancient.
"Others" (*pare*) means those other than the wise—those who engage in quarrels are called "others. They, in this context, [are present] in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Engaging in quarrels, they do not realize: "We are being restrained, we are being bound, we are perishing; we are constantly and continuously going into the presence of Death.
And those who understand therein are those wise ones who understand: "We are going into the vicinity of Death.
Thus, knowing this, they settle their disputes through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
Having generated [this], they proceed toward the pacification of disputes and quarrels.
The verse beginning with "Aṭṭhicchinnā" (those whose bones are broken) is found in the Jātaka; it was spoken concerning Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu.
This is the meaning here: even for those who have thus engaged in enmity, there comes a meeting; why then, for you?
"It does not exist for those by whom neither the bones of their parents have been cut, nor living beings taken away, nor cattle, horses, and wealth seized.
The verse beginning with "If one should obtain... was spoken for the purpose of illustrating the praise and blame of a companion who is wise and a companion who is foolish.
"Having overcome all dangers" refers to both manifest dangers and concealed dangers.
"Having overcome [them], one should dwell with a contented mind and mindfulness together with that [virtue].

"Like a king over a conquered kingdom" means that just as the Great King Mahājanaka and the Great King Arindama wandered alone after abandoning their conquered kingdoms, so too should one wander. "Like an elephant in the Mātaṅga forest": *Mātaṅga*...
"Like an elephant in the forest. "Mātaṅga" refers to an elephant; "nāga" is a designation for something great.

Just as the Mātaṅga-nāga, who supported his mother, wandered alone in the forest and committed no evil deeds, and just as Pālileyyaka did, so too one should wander alone and commit no evil deeds—this is what is meant.
238. *Bālakaloṇakāragāma* was the village belonging to the householder Upāli. Why did he approach him?
It is said that having seen the danger in living in a group, a desire arose in him to see a monk living alone;
therefore, like one oppressed by cold and so forth who longs for heat and so forth, he approached him. "With a discourse on the Dhamma" means with a discourse connected to the benefits of solitude.
Why did he go there to Pācīnavaṃsadāya? It is said that because he had seen the danger in those who cause quarrels, a desire arose in him to see monks living in harmony;
therefore, like one oppressed by cold and the like who longs for heat and the like, he went there.
The passage beginning with "And the Venerable Anuruddha" is exactly as previously explained.

241. "But does it exist?"—with this final question, he might ask about supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*). However, since that is not within the scope of the elders, it is not appropriate to ask about it; therefore, he asks about the preliminary radiance (*parikamma-obhāsa*).
"And we perceive the radiance" means we perceive the preliminary radiance. "And the seeing of forms" means we perceive the seeing of forms with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).
"We do not penetrate that sign" means we do not know that cause by which our radiance and the vision of forms disappear.
"But you, Anuruddha, must penetrate that sign" means you must know that cause.
"I too, Anuruddha, am very well"—why would they not drag me along with you? I too [am subject] to these eleven defilements.
He began this teaching in order to show that he had previously been agitated.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Doubt indeed arose in me," after the Great Being had increased his light and seen various kinds of forms with the divine eye, doubt arose as to what these things were.
"Concentration lapsed" means that the preliminary concentration lapsed. "The illumination" means that even the preliminary illumination vanished.
He did not see forms even with the divine eye. Regarding "non-attention": as he was looking at forms, doubt arose;
thinking, "Now I will attend to nothing at all," non-attention arose.
Regarding "sloth and torpor": as he was attending to nothing at all, sloth and torpor arose.
“Trembling” (*chambhitatta*): Having extended his vision toward the Himalayas, he saw dānavas, rakkhasas, pythons, and so forth; then trembling arose within him. “Agitated” (*uppila*):

Thinking, “The fear I have seen does not exist when looking at things in their natural state; what indeed is this fear regarding what has not been seen? agitation arose within him. “All at once” (*sakideva*): By a single stroke, he might even see five pots of treasure.

"Coarseness": "I exerted energy too strongly; because of that, agitation arose in me," so he relaxed his energy. Thereupon, bodily distress, bodily coarseness, and bodily sloth arose. "Excessive energy":
while relaxing my energy because agitation had arisen, and then again exerting energy, excessive energy arose. "He might fall away": he might die. "Over-lax energy":
while exerting my energy because [agitation] had thus arisen, and then again relaxing my energy, over-lax energy arose.
"Longing" (*abhijappā*) means that craving arose as he looked upon the host of devas after extending his vision toward the world of the devas.
"Perception of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*) means that while he was attending to my form as being of a single kind, the longing arose;
then, thinking, "I shall attend to forms of various kinds," he at times extended [his vision] toward the world of the devas and at times toward the world of humans.
As I was attending to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose.
Regarding "because of over-contemplation": as I was attending to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose;
thinking, "I shall attend only to what is of a single kind, whether desirable or undesirable," as I attended in that way, there arose in me an over-contemplation of forms.
243. "I attend to the sign of light" means I attend only to the preliminary-stage light.
"And I do not see forms" means I do not see forms with the divine eye. "I attend to the sign of form" means I attend only to the objective form with the divine eye.
“Limited radiance” means radiance in a limited place. “And limited forms” means forms in a limited place.
The second section should be understood by way of the opposite. “Limited concentration” refers to the limited preparatory radiance;
for it is with reference to the limitation of the radiance that the preparatory concentration here is called “limited. “Limited for me...”
"At that time" means that at that moment even the divine eye is limited (*parittaka*). The same method applies to the section on the immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). 245.

"Without applied thought, with sustained thought only" refers to the concentration of the second jhāna in the fivefold system. "Without applied thought and without sustained thought" refers to the concentration of the three jhānas in both the fourfold and fivefold systems.
"With rapture" refers to the concentration of the two or three jhānas.
"Free from rapture" refers to the concentration of the second jhāna. "Accompanied by pleasure" refers to the concentration of the third and fourth jhānas.
"Accompanied by equanimity" refers to the concentration of the fourth jhāna in the fourfold system, and the concentration of the fifth jhāna in the fivefold system.
But when does the Blessed One develop this threefold concentration? While seated at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree during the last watch of the night.
For the Blessed One’s first path was associated with the first jhāna, while the second and subsequent paths were associated with the second, third, and fourth jhānas respectively.
Since there is no path associated with the fifth jhāna in the fivefold system, that [fifth path] was mundane;
thus, this statement was made with reference to a mixture of mundane and supramundane paths. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Upakkilesa Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*.
246. Thus have I heard: this is the *Bālapaṇḍita-sutta*. In that context, "characteristics of a fool" (*bālalakkhaṇāni*) means those by which a fool is characterized or known;
they are the "marks of a fool" (*bālanimittāni*) because they are the causes for identifying him as such.
"Deeds of a fool" (*bālāpadānāni*) refers to the actions of a fool. "One who thinks ill-thought thoughts" means one who, while thinking, does so by way of covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.
He thinks only what is ill-conceived. One who speaks ill-spoken words means that even while speaking, he speaks only what is ill-spoken, such as the various forms of lying and so forth.
One who performs ill-done deeds means that even while acting, he performs only ill-done deeds by way of killing living beings and so forth.
And "therein" means in whatever assembly he is seated; "appropriate to that, suitable for that" means of that same nature and fitting for it.
The intention is that [this discourse] is connected with the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) of the five kinds of enmity pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
"Therein" (*tatra*) means while that discourse was being delivered. "A fool" (*bāla*), and so forth, are accusative cases used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmivat*). 248.
"Hanging down" (*olambanti*) means they appear. The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that very term, [describing it] by way of the manner of hanging down and so forth.
For those [signs] appear; therefore it was said thus. "Hanging down upon the earth" means they spread out upon the surface of the earth.
The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that very same thing, for this is simply the manner of spreading out.
In that regard, monks, "for the fool" means that when that mode of appearance has come into range, such a thought occurs to the fool.
249. “It is possible, Bhante,” the monk, skilled in connecting the discourse, said this after reflecting: “The Blessed One does not say that it is impossible to provide a simile for hell;
rather, he says it is ‘not easy. It is not easy, yet it is possible to do so. Come now, I shall have the One of Ten Powers provide a simile.
“They would kill” means they would pierce [them] through.
By way of their movement, they would strike him as if two blows were falling upon one spot; thus he would have two hundred wound openings.
The same principle applies to what follows. 250.
"The size of a hand" means the amount that can be placed within a closed fist. "Does not even approach a count" means it does not even reach the measure of being calculable.
It does not go [near it]. It does not even come within a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousandth part;
indeed, it does not even admit of comparison. "Even as a mere deposit" means it does not even admit of being placed alongside for comparison;
there is not even so much as a glance from one who looks on. "A red-hot iron pillar" refers to a body three *gāvutas* in length, set ablaze.
Having made him lie flat on his back upon the iron ground, they drive an iron spike the size of a palm tree into his right hand, and likewise into his left hand and other limbs.

And just as they have him lie on his back, so too do they inflict that same torture upon him while he lies on his chest, his right side, and his left side. "Having laid him down" means upon the blazing [iron ground].
Having caused his own body to lie down upon the iron ground for three *gāvutas*, they plane it with axes—axes as large as the roofing of one side of a house.
Blood flows forth like a river, and flames rising from the iron ground seize the spot being planed.
Great suffering arises; yet the planers, treating it as if it were wood, continue their work even through eight watches of the night.
They even perform the sixfold [torture]. With axes means with axes as large as great mortars.
While planing with them, they plane slowly from the skin down to the bones; each part that has been planed becomes restored to its original state.
Having yoked them to chariots means having yoked them to chariots that are blazing all over, together with their yokes, straps, axles, wheels, and poles.
"Large" means the size of a great gabled hall (*kūṭāgāra*). "They cause to ascend" means they cause it to ascend by striking it with glowing iron hammers.
"It rises up even once" means it moves upward, downward, and across, like rice grains placed in a well-boiled cauldron.
"Divided by portions" means distributed, having been set aside portion by portion. "Encircled" means surrounded. "Covered above with iron plates" means it is roofed over with iron sheets from above.

"It stands pervading a hundred leagues on all sides" means it stands having spread out in this way, such that for one standing and looking at it from a place a hundred leagues away on every side, the eyes seem as if they were popping out like twin marbles.

"It is not easy to reach [the end] by means of description" means that even if one were to speak for a hundred years or a thousand years, saying "Niraya is suffering in this way, it is suffering in that way," it would not be easy to describe it to its ultimate limit.
251. *Dantullehakaṃ*: having licked with the teeth; what is meant is, having torn it off. *Rasādō*:
the taste enjoyed through greed for flavor. 252. *Aññamaññakhādikā*: mutual devouring.
"Ugly" means ill-formed. "Repulsive to look at" means difficult to behold, like a yakṣa fashioned for the purpose of frightening children.
"Hunchbacked" means a dwarf with a sunken neck and a protruding belly. "One-eyed" means blind in one eye or blind in both eyes.
"Lame" means lame in one hand or lame in both hands. "Palsy-stricken" means a cripple who moves on a wooden board. "By that body"—so it is said.
This has been undertaken for the purpose of showing the continuity of his suffering.
"By a lucky throw" means by defeat. "He would incur imprisonment" means that since he has lost much, even his entire property is not enough;
therefore, he himself would incur imprisonment. "The whole, complete plane of the fool" refers to the fool as threefold.

Having fulfilled the wrong modes of conduct, one is reborn in hell; remaining there until the karmic residue is exhausted, when one returns to the human state, one is reborn in one of the five low-born families;
then, having again fulfilled the three wrong modes of conduct, one is reborn in hell—this is the entire, complete plane of the fool.

253. "The characteristics of a wise man" and so forth should be understood according to what has already been stated. Herein, "one who thinks well-thought thoughts" and so on should be applied by way of mental good conduct and the rest.
256. Commentary on the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*):
"Of one whose head is washed" means of one who has bathed with scented water together with the head. "Of one observing the Uposatha" means of one who has undertaken the factors of the Uposatha.

"Of one who has gone to the excellent upper palace" means: having eaten a fine meal and gone to the great terrace above the excellent palace, he enters the chamber of glory (*sirīgabbha*) and recollects the precepts (*sīla*).
At that time, it is said, the king had already given a great almsgiving by distributing a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at dawn;
furthermore, having bathed his head with sixteen jars of scented water and having finished his morning meal, he was there.

Having adjusted his pure upper robe over one shoulder and sitting cross-legged on the royal couch atop the palace, he sits reflecting upon the accumulation of merit consisting of his own acts of giving; this is the natural law for all wheel-turning monarchs.
While they are thus reflecting, conditioned by that aforementioned meritorious deed, there arises—produced by the seasonal elements—a canopy resembling a mass of blue jewels.
The divine Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) appears, as if cleaving the surface of the waters of the eastern ocean and as if adorning the sky.
It is called "divine" (dibba) because it is endowed with divine power (anubhāva). It is "thousand-spoked" (sahassāra) because it has a thousand spokes (ara).

It is "with felloe and with nave" (sanemika sanābhika) because it possesses both a rim (nemī) and a hub (nābhī). It is "perfect in all its aspects" (sabbākāraparipūra) because it is complete in every respect.
In this context, it is a wheel (*cakra*) and, in the sense of producing delight, it is a jewel (*ratana*); thus it is the "Wheel-Jewel" (*cakkaratana*).
Furthermore, the nave (*nābhi*) by which it is described as "having a nave" (*sanābhika*) is made of sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*).
In its center, however, is a silver tube through which a row of pure, lustrous teeth shines as if smiling. It appears like the orb of the moon with a hole in its center.
Both outer rims are encircled by a silver band.
Furthermore, at the points where its navel-tube joins the encircling bands, the demarcation lines appear perfectly well-proportioned.
Such, then, is the complete perfection of all its aspects regarding the navel.
Furthermore, those spokes which are called "thousand-spoked" are made of the seven precious gems and are endowed with radiance like the rays of the sun.
Even on them, the divisions, rims, and lines of the pot-shaped jewel are clearly and well-proportioned.
This is the perfection of all aspects regarding its spokes.

Furthermore, that which is described as "with a rim" (*sanemika*) because it possesses such a rim is made of coral, intensely red, pure, and lustrous, as if mocking the splendor of the mass of rays from the morning sun.

At its joints, bands of Jāmbunada gold—resplendent with the color of the twilight—are visible, and its circular divisions and lines are well-proportioned. This is the perfection of its rim in every respect.

On the back of its rim, however, between each set of ten spokes, there is a coral handle that is hollow inside like a bamboo reed, with a circular pattern of perforations and capable of catching the wind;
when struck by the wind, it produces a sound as sweet, enchanting, and lovely as that of a five-piece musical ensemble played with great skill. Of that, moreover—
Above the coral staff was a white parasol, and on both sides were rows of garlands of gathered flowers;
thus, with two hundred such rows of gathered flower-garlands surrounding it, it was beautifully adorned by a hundred coral-staffed holders of the white parasol.
Within the two central shafts of the nave of the wheel, whose rim was encircled by a hundred such [staffs], there were two lion-mouths.
From these two clusters of pearls, as large as palm trunks, radiant as a mass of full-moon rays,
and bordered by crimson woolen tassels like the young sun, hang down as if surpassing the beauty of the Ganges’ course through the sky;
and when they revolve together with the Wheel-treasure in the air, the three wheels appear as if they were turning in unison.
This is its complete fulfillment in every aspect.
Now, when this meal, thus fulfilled in every aspect,
is being eaten as the evening meal by people who have sat down on seats prepared at their respective doorways and are engaged in conversation and discussion in the streets, crossroads, and so forth—
While children were playing, it seemed to beautify the tips of the tree branches with a canopy of sky that was neither too high nor too low,
situated close above the forest grove; with its sweet voice heard from as far as twelve leagues away,
it captivated the ears of sentient beings, and from a distance of one league, it shone with a complexion radiant with a multitude of diverse lusters.
It came toward the capital city, drawing the eyes [of all] and as if proclaiming the power of the merit of the Wheel-turning Monarch.
Then, upon merely hearing the sound of that Wheel-treasure, those people—whose hearts were inclined with the thought, "Whence indeed is this?
To whom does this sound belong?"—looking toward the eastern direction, one among them [said to] another:
He spoke thus: "Behold, sir, this marvel! Formerly this full moon rose alone;
but today it has risen with a companion. Indeed, like a pair of royal swans, this pair of full moons is traversing the vault of the sky, one after the other.
Another said to him: "What are you saying, friend? Where indeed have you seen two..."
“Have you not seen the full moon rising alone? Is it not this sun, bearing rays of molten gold and possessing a mass of feathers-like beams, that has risen?
Another, having smiled, said to him: “Are you mad? Has the sun not just now set?
How could it rise again following after this full moon? Surely...”
“This must be the celestial mansion of some meritorious person, resplendent with the radiance of many jewels.
But all of them, expressing their disbelief, said to others: “Why do you prattle so much? This is neither the full moon, nor the sun, nor a celestial mansion.
For these possess no such glorious splendor; this must surely be the Wheel-Treasure (cakraratana).”
While that people was thus engaged in conversation, the moon’s orb vanished and the Wheel-Treasure appeared facing them.
Then, when they asked, "For whom has this arisen?", there arose those who said, "It is not for anyone else;
surely our king has fulfilled the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti); it has arisen for him. Then he—
The great multitude and whoever else sees it all follow after the Wheel-Treasure alone. That Wheel-Treasure,
as if desiring to make known its arrival for the sake of the king, circles the city seven times along the very top of the rampart,
circumambulates the royal inner palace, and comes to rest near the northern lion-window of the inner palace.
In that place, just as it is possible to worship easily with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, it remains as if struck by a thunderbolt.
When it stands thus, the king— having seen the mass of radiance entering through the openings of the windows and other apertures,
illuminating the interior of the palace with the brilliant luster of jewels of various colors— becomes filled with longing to behold it.
The attendants, having approached him with pleasant words, reported that matter to him.
Then the king, his body suffused with powerful joy and gladness, released his cross-legged posture, rose from his seat, and went near the lion-window;
seeing the Wheel-Treasure, he reflected upon the thought beginning with, "I have indeed heard this," and so forth. Therefore it was said: "Having seen [it], the Khattiya king... and so on.
"Would I indeed be a Wheel-turning Monarch? In this context, how does one become a Wheel-turning Monarch?
It is when the Wheel-treasure, having risen even by the measure of a single finger or two fingers, proceeds through the air.
Now, in order to show what must be done for its setting in motion, the Blessed One said: "Then, monks," and so forth.
Therein, "having risen from his seat" means having stood up from where he was sitting and approached the vicinity of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*).
"Taking the water-pot" means lifting up a golden water-pot with a spout like an elephant's trunk, taking water in his left hand, and saying:
"May your majesty’s Wheel-Treasure roll forth; may your majesty’s Wheel-Treasure conquer! Immediately thereafter—

"The Wheel-turning King together with his fourfold army"—for indeed, after all wheel-turning kings have been consecrated with water, at the very moment the words "May your lordship, O Wheel-treasure, conquer!
are spoken, the Wheel-treasure rises up into the air and sets in motion;
and at the same time as it sets in motion, that king becomes known as a Wheel-turning King.
Furthermore, while following that Wheel-Treasure as it rolls along, the Cakkavatti king mounts his excellent vehicle and ascends into the air,
followed by his retinue with parasols, fly-whisks, and other items in their hands, as well as the inhabitants of the inner palace. Then,

[he proceeds] accompanied by an army adorned with various types of armor such as tunics and breastplates, resplendent with the radiance of diverse ornaments, and decorated with raised banners and flags.
The royal viceroy and many others, together with their respective armies, rose into the air and surrounded the king.
Furthermore, the king’s officials, for the purpose of winning over the people, caused drums to be beaten in the city streets, proclaiming:
"Sirs, the Wheel-Treasure has appeared for our king; therefore, adorn yourselves according to your respective means and wealth."
"assemble! Now, the great multitude had already abandoned all their affairs and assembled, taking perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, simply at the sound of the Wheel-Treasure;
they too all rose up into the air and surrounded the king.
Indeed, whoever felt a desire to go with the king, he too went through the sky.
Thus the assembly becomes twelve yojanas in length and breadth. Therein, not even a single person has a mangled or broken body, nor is there anyone with soiled clothes;

for the Wheel-turning Monarch is surrounded by purity. Indeed, the assembly of a Wheel-turning Monarch, moving through the air like that of the Vidyādharas, resembles a multitude of jewels scattered upon a surface of sapphire.
Therefore it is said: "Immediately following [the wheel], the Wheel-turning Monarch proceeds together with his fourfold army.

That Wheel-treasure moves through a region of the sky that is not too high above the tops of the trees, so that those who desire the flowers, fruits, and foliage of the trees are able to grasp them with ease while standing on the ground.
They were able to recognize, “This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief.

Even in their various postures such as standing and so forth, whoever wished to go by which means did so by that very means. Those devoted to crafts such as painting went about while performing their respective tasks;
for just as on the earth, so too all their activities took place in the sky.

They succeed. Thus, having taken the retinue of the wheel-turning monarch, that Wheel-treasure leaves Sineru by its northern side and travels across the ocean to Pubbavideha, which measures eight thousand yojanas.
Therein, it is capable of accommodating a retinue twelve yojanas in depth and thirty-six yojanas in circumference.
The site was easy to access for food and requisites, endowed with shade and water, possessed of a pure and level surface, and delightful;
above it, that Wheel-Treasure remained suspended in the air as if fixed on an axle.

Then, taking that as a sign, the great multitude descended and established their residence there, performing all their duties such as bathing and eating according to their pleasure. Therefore it is said:
“Moreover, monks, in whatever place that wheel-treasure comes to rest,
there the Wheel-turning Monarch takes up residence together with his fourfold army.
When the Wheel-turning Monarch has thus taken up residence, those kings who are there, even upon hearing that “an enemy’s army has arrived,” [do not oppose him].
They do not assemble a military force to become ready for battle.
Immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel-Treasure, there is no being whatsoever who, perceiving him as an enemy, would dare to raise a weapon against the king.
Such is the majestic power of the Wheel-Treasure.
Indeed, by the power of his wheel,
all enemies come under subjection to that king;
thus he is named Arindama, the subduer of foes, the lord of men.
For that very reason, it is called his "wheel.
Therefore, all those kings, having taken gifts appropriate to their own royal splendor and power,
approached that king with bowed heads and performed worship at his feet by means of the consecration of the radiance from the jewels in their own crests.
With such words as “Come, Great King,” they enter into a state of acknowledging his service.
Therefore it was said: “But those, monks, who [live] in the eastern quarter... ‘Instruct us, Great King.
In that context, *svāgataṃ* means a welcome arrival. For when one has arrived, people grieve; when he has departed, they rejoice. When one has arrived...
They rejoice when he arrives and grieve when he departs. You are such a one who rejoices at arrival and grieves at departure; therefore, it is said that your coming is a "welcome arrival.
When this was said, the Wheel-turning Monarch did not say, "Provide me with such-and-such a tribute every year," nor did he seize the wealth of one person to give it to another. Of his own...
However, by means of wisdom appropriate to his status as a Dhamma-king, he examines killing and other such acts, and after teaching the Dhamma in a manner such as,
"Behold, dear ones, this act called killing, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed,
leads to rebirth in hell," he gives the exhortation, "A living being must not be killed," and so forth. By that...
It is said that the Wheel-turning Monarch spoke thus: "No living being is to be killed... [and so on] ...and eat only what you have been given.
But do all people accept this advice of the king? Even among the followers of the Buddha, not all accept it;
how much less would they accept it from a king? Therefore, those who are wise and discerning accept it, while all the mere subordinates follow along.
Therefore, he said, "But those, monks... and so forth.

Then, once that Wheel-Treasure had given such counsel to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha and the morning meal had been taken, it rose into the air by the power of the Wheel-Turning Monarch and plunged into the eastern ocean. And as it plunged further and further into it,
In that manner, having smelled the fragrance of the medicine, the water of the great ocean,
as it descended with the spreading of its waves stilled like a king of serpents who has withdrawn his hood, entered for the distance of a *yojana* and stood within the sea like a wall of beryl.
And at that very moment, on the surface of the great ocean, as if desiring to behold the glory of the King’s merit—
Various scattered gems come from here and there and fill that region.
Then, seeing the surface of the great ocean filled with those various gems, the royal assembly takes them as they please in their laps and so forth;
but when the assembly has taken the gems as they desire, the Wheel-treasure turns back. And as it is turning back—
The assembly was at the front, the king in the middle, and the wheel-treasure at the rear. That ocean water,
as if enticed by the splendor of the wheel-treasure and unable to endure separation from it, approached continuously,
striking against the circumference of its rim.

257. Thus, having conquered Pubbavideha as far as the eastern ocean, the Wheel-turning Monarch, desiring to conquer Jambudīpa as far as the southern ocean, proceeds toward the southern ocean by the path indicated by the Wheel-treasure.
Therefore it was said: "Then, monks, that Wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean..."
"Having crossed over, it flows toward the southern direction. As for the manner of its flowing while thus proceeding— the way it establishes its encampment,
its advance against rival kings, its issuing of instructions to them, its plunging into the southern ocean, the subsiding of the ocean waters, and the taking of jewels—
all this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
Having conquered that Jambudīpa measuring ten thousand yojanas, and having crossed back from the southern ocean,
he went by the same method previously described to conquer Aparagoyāna, which measures seven thousand yojanas;
having likewise completely conquered that ocean-bound territory, he crossed back from the western ocean to [the continent] measuring eight thousand yojanas.
Having likewise gone to conquer Uttarakuru and having similarly conquered it as far as its ocean boundary, he returns from the northern ocean as well.
At this point, the sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans has been attained by the Wheel-turning Monarch.
Having thus achieved victory, and for the purpose of displaying the glory and prosperity of his own kingdom, he and his retinue leap up into the heights of the sky.
Beholding the four great continents— surrounded by five hundred and five hundred minor islands like four lotus ponds amidst a variegated forest of blooming red,
blue, and white lotuses— the wheel-treasure returns in due order to its own royal capital by the very path indicated by the wheel-treasure itself.
Then, that wheel-treasure stands as if adorning the gate of the inner palace.
When that Wheel-Treasure was thus established, there was no need for torches or lamps within the royal palace;
the radiance of the Wheel-Treasure alone dispelled the darkness of night. And for those who desired darkness at night, there was indeed darkness for them.
Therefore it is said: "Having plunged into the southern ocean... [and so on]... such as this."
"The Wheel-Treasure appears.
258. Now, when the Wheel-Treasure has thus appeared for that Cakkavatti, his ministers [prepare] the place for the ordinary auspicious state-elephant.
Having had a section of ground made clean and having had it smeared with fragrant scents such as yellow sandalwood, he prepared it like a celestial mansion:
strewn below with variegated-colored fragrant flowers, and above adorned with a canopy decorated with lovely flower-garlands interspersed with golden stars;
then he said, "O King, consider the arrival of such a jewel among elephants!"
So they say. Having given a great alms-offering according to the method previously described, he sits down having undertaken the precepts and reflecting upon that excellence of merit.

Then, impelled by the power of his merit, and desiring to experience that special honor, [the elephant] comes from either the Chaddanta or Uposatha lineage, his pure white body adorned with feet, neck, and face as radiant as the orb of the rising sun.
The noble elephant, with its seven points of support and its well-proportioned limbs and joints,
with a beautiful trunk like a blooming red lotus, possessing supernormal power like a yogi capable of traveling through the air,
and with its flanks colored as if by powdered emerald, stood firm in that place like a mountain of silver; it was the youngest of all those coming from the Chaddanta lineage.
He comes as the eldest of all from the family of the Uposatha elephant. However, in the text, he appears simply as "Uposatha, the king of elephants.
He appears only to those wheel-turning monarchs who have fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turner and are reflecting according to the method described in the Sutta, and not to others.
Having himself come to the place of the ordinary auspicious elephant and having removed that auspicious elephant, [he takes his place].
It stands there. Therefore it was said: "Furthermore, monks...
[omitted] ...the king of elephants. Now, having seen that elephant-treasure thus manifested, the elephant-keepers and others, joyful and delighted, went with haste and announced it to the king.
The king, arriving in great haste and seeing it, with a mind full of confidence, [thought]: "Excellent!"
"O elephant, if you would but submit to training! Thinking thus, he extended his hand.
Then, like a domestic cow’s calf, the elephant lowered its ears and, displaying a state of gentleness, approached the king;
the king desired to mount it. Thereupon, his attendants, perceiving his intention, [prepared] that jewel of an elephant.
Having adorned it with a golden banner and golden ornaments and covered it with a net of gold, they bring it forward.
Without even letting the king sit upon it, he ascends by means of a ladder made of the seven precious gems, his mind intent on traveling through the air.
At the mere arising of that thought, the royal elephant, like a royal swan, leaps into the blue expanse of the sky, which is darkened by the radiating net of light from sapphires.
Then, in the very manner described for the tour of the wheel, the entire royal assembly follows.

Thus, the king together with his retinue, having traversed the whole earth even before breakfast, returns to the capital city. Such is the great power of the elephant-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch.
Therefore it was said: "Having seen this, such an elephant-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch... and so forth.
The Description of the Elephant Treasure:
When the elephant treasure has thus appeared, the retinue of the wheel-turning monarch has the natural auspicious site for the elephant prepared with a clean, level surface and adorned;
then, just as before, they arouse enthusiasm in the king for the purpose of anticipating its arrival.

Thus, having performed acts of giving and honored [the recipients] in the manner previously described, and having undertaken the moral precepts, he sat upon the palace terrace and recollected his success in merit.
Then, impelled by the power of that merit, there appeared from the Sindhu breed a horse named Kākaṇṭha, whose appearance rivaled a mass of white autumn clouds entwined with streaks of lightning;
it had red hooves and a red beak, and its body was a dense, pure, and glossy mass resembling a cluster of moonbeams.
Because he was endowed with black hair like an *indanīla* gem and possessed a black-colored head, he was "Black-Headed" (*Kāḷasīsa*).
Because he was endowed with hair that was soft, round, and smooth, reaching down to his waist, as if well-trimmed and resembling *muñja* grass, he was "Muñja-Haired" (*Muñjakesa*).
A horse-king named Valāhaka, who travels through the air, would come and alight at that place. All the rest [is as before].
This should be understood in the same manner as described for the elephant-treasure. With reference to such a horse-treasure, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "And again, furthermore.
The Description of the Jewel-Treasure:
Now, when the horse-treasure has appeared in this way, it measures four cubits in height, and its circumference is equal to the hub of a cart-wheel.
Adorned with two golden lotuses at both ends, from which emerge two extremely pure strings of pearls reaching to the tips of the buds,

and surrounded by eighty-four thousand gems, it comes forth like a jewel from Mount Vepulla, rivaling the splendor of the full moon encircled by a host of stars. As it thus approaches, within its lattice of pearls...
Setting aside the space reached by a succession of bamboo poles sixty cubits in length, when it has been raised up, its radiance pervades an area of one *yojana* in every direction during the night;
by this light, that entire space becomes as if filled with daylight at the time of sunrise.
Consequently, farmers engage in plowing, merchants open their shops, and various craftsmen attend to their respective trades.
They employ it, thinking it is still day. Therefore it was said: "Furthermore, monks... the jewel-treasure appears.

Now, for the Wheel-turning Monarch who has thus obtained the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure (*itthiratana*) is the cause of a particular excellence of sensual pleasure. **Commentary on the Woman-Treasure**
It appears. Either they bring the chief queen from the Madda royal family for him, or she comes of her own accord from Uttarakuru through the power of his merit.

As for his remaining prosperity, it has been described in the very Pāḷi in the passage beginning: "Furthermore, monks, the woman-treasure (itthiratana) appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch, beautiful and lovely to behold," and so forth.

In this context, she is "beautiful" (*abhirūpā*) because her form possesses an excellence in its complete configuration. She is "pleasing to behold" (*dassanīyā*) because, when seen, she delights the eyes;
therefore, one should look upon her even while setting aside other distracting activities. She is "graceful" (*pāsādikā*) because, when seen, she gladdens the mind through the influence of joy.
"Supreme" (*paramāya*) means that she is the most excellent due to her capacity to inspire such confidence. "By reason of the beauty of her complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatāya*)—
"By beauty of complexion. "Endowed with" means possessed of. She is handsome because she is neither too tall nor too short;
she is beautiful to behold because she is neither too thin nor too stout; she is pleasing because she is neither too dark nor too pale.
She is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion because she has surpassed human beauty but has not yet reached divine beauty. For the radiance of human complexion—
It does not issue forth outside, nor does it issue forth too far beyond the reach of the devas;
however, the radiance of her body illuminates an area measuring twelve cubits.
Regarding its length and other qualities, the first pair [of terms] refers to the perfection of height, while the second pair refers to the perfection of circumference.
Physical excellence is described by the third pair [of verses]. Alternatively, by these six [verses], the absence of physical defect is shown;
and by the phrase "surpassing human beauty," physical perfection is described.
"Like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of kapok" refers to [cotton] that has been split a hundred times and placed in clarified butter (*sappimaṇḍa*).
The touch of his body is like that of a tuft of cotton or a tuft of seven-fold split kapok. "Cool" refers to the time when it is cool for the king;

"warm" refers to the time when it is warm for the king. "Sandalwood fragrance" means that at all times, the scent of fresh, well-pounded yellow sandalwood blended with the four ingredients wafts from his body.
"Lotus fragrance" refers to the scent issuing from his mouth at times of laughing and speaking.
At that moment, an exceedingly fragrant scent wafted forth, like that of a blue lotus in full bloom.
Now, in order to demonstrate conduct befitting her physical excellence—which was endowed with perfection of form, touch, and fragrance—the text says, "But as for her," and so forth.
Therein, having seen the king, she rose from the seat where she was sitting; [she was] like one consumed by fire...
She rises first, as it were, [before him], thus she is "one who rises early" (*pubbuṭṭhāyinī*).
Having performed such duties as fanning that king with a palm-leaf fan while he is seated, she lies down or sits down afterwards, thus she is "one who lies down afterwards" (*pacchānipātinī*).

She responds to his requests, saying, "What shall I do, O Lord? thus she is "one who responds to what is to be done" (*kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī*). She conducts herself and acts only in a manner pleasing to the king, thus...
"She behaves agreeably" (*manāpacārinī*). She speaks only what is pleasing to the king, thus she is "one who speaks pleasantly" (*piyavādinī*).
Now, to show that her conduct is due solely to purity of heart and not to deceit, he said, "But as for her...
and so forth. In this context, "she does not transgress" means she does not act in excess; she does not even mentally long for another man.

This has been stated. In that regard, those qualities mentioned at the beginning of her description, such as "beautiful," and those mentioned at the end, such as "rising early," are merely her natural qualities.

However, those qualities such as "surpassing human beauty" and so forth arise through the power of past kamma, having been produced from the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) based on the merit of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti).

[These qualities] are to be understood. Alternatively, [the woman’s] beauty and other attributes become fully perfected in every aspect starting from the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana).
Therefore, he said: "Such a Woman-Treasure (itthiratana) manifests.
Commentary on the Householder-Treasure (gahapatiratana):

Furthermore, for the sake of enabling the Wheel-turning Monarch, to whom the Treasure of the Woman has thus appeared, to carry out his financial duties and affairs as he pleases, the Treasure of the Householder appears.
By nature possessed of great wealth and born into a family of great wealth, he is a merchant householder who increases the King’s hoards of riches.
Moreover, through the power of the Wheel-treasure, he possesses a divine eye born of the ripening of kamma.
It becomes manifest, by means of which he sees a treasure within a league beneath the surface of the earth.
Having seen that prosperity, his heart filled with joy, he goes and entertains the king with wealth and accomplishes all his financial requirements.
Therefore it was said: "Furthermore, monks... such a householder-treasure appears."
The Description of the Counsellor-Treasure:

Now, when the Wheel-turning Monarch has thus manifested the Householder-treasure, the Counsellor-treasure appears, capable of managing all his duties. He is the king’s eldest son; by nature he is wise.
He was learned and wise; however, by relying on the power of the king’s merit, the power of his own karma caused the knowledge of others’ minds (*paracittañāṇa*) to arise within him.

By means of this, he was able to discern the mental dispositions of the royal assembly extending twelve *yojanas*, and thus became capable of distinguishing between what was beneficial and what was harmful for the king.
Seeing that power of his own, the king too was delighted at heart.
He invites [the people] by instructing them in all their duties. Therefore it was said: "Furthermore... the Jewel of the Counsellor appears.
In that context, "to place those who should be placed" means to appoint them to their respective positions. 259.
The passage beginning with "Samavepākiniyā" has already been explained above.
260. "By a lucky catch" means by a winning throw. "A great mass of wealth" refers to two or three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] all at once.
"The entire, complete ground of the wise" means that a wise person, having fulfilled the three types of good conduct, is reborn in heaven;
then, returning to the human world, he is reborn endowed with excellence of lineage, physical form, and wealth.
Established therein, having fulfilled the three types of good conduct, one is reborn again in heaven;
this is the entire, complete stage of the wise. The rest is clear everywhere.
(From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*)
The commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta is finished.
10. The commentary on the Devadūta Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Devadūta Sutta. Therein, the passage beginning with "two kinds of houses" has already been explained in detail in the Assapura Sutta.

262. Regarding the phrase "reborn in hell," the Blessed One concludes his teaching from hell in some instances by means of the world of the devas, and in others he concludes from the world of the devas by means of hell.
If he wishes to speak in detail about the excellence of the heavenly realms, he speaks of the suffering of hell only briefly;
likewise, he speaks of the suffering of the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the excellence of the human world [briefly].
He speaks of it partially, elaborating only upon the excellence of heaven.

If he wishes to speak by elaborating upon the suffering of hell, he speaks partially of the excellence in the worlds of the devas and humans, and of the suffering in the animal realm and the sphere of ghosts, while elaborating only upon the suffering of hell. In this sutta, he wishes to elaborate upon the suffering of hell.
Therefore, beginning from the world of the devas, he concludes the teaching with hell.
Having spoken briefly of the excellences of the worlds of devas and humans, as well as the sufferings of the animal realm and the sphere of ghosts, he says, "Monks, those wardens of hell...
and so forth, in order to explain the sufferings of hell in detail.
In this regard, some elders say: "There are no such things as hell-guardians; rather, it is karma itself that acts as the agent, like a mechanical puppet.

This view of theirs has already been refuted in the Abhidhamma by means of such arguments as: "Are there hell-guardians in hell? Yes. And are there those who act as agents? For just as there are those who carry out judicial punishments in the human world, [so too in the hells].
In the same way, there are wardens of hell in hell. Regarding the phrase "of King Yama": he is the king of the *peta*s known as Yamarāja.
At one time, he experiences the splendors of divine celestial mansions, such as the divine wishing-tree, divine parks, and divine dancers;
at another time, he experiences the ripening of kamma. He is a righteous king. Moreover, he is not alone; rather, at the four gates—
There are four people [who speak thus]. He says this with reference to the absence of any divine messenger sent to him from his own presence whom he does not see.
Then Yama, knowing that "this man does not perceive the meaning of what has been said," and wishing to make him perceive it, spoke the words beginning with "Ambho! (O friend!).

“Subject to birth” means having the nature of birth; it means one is not yet liberated from birth, thinking, “Birth indeed exists within me. The same method applies to the subsequent phrases such as “subject to aging,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “having first questioned the divine messenger”: here, the young boy speaks thus according to the facts:
“See, sirs, I too have hands and feet just like yours; however, I am in my own urine and excrement...”
"I am fallen into mire; though I try to rise by my own nature, I cannot bathe.
I am defiled in body; I am not even able to say, 'Bathe me,' for I have been born as such because I am not exempt from birth.
It is not only I who am thus; you too are certainly not exempt from birth. For just as it has come to me, so will birth come to you as well."
"Therefore, before she arrives, perform what is auspicious. Thus he became known as the "Divine Messenger" (*devadūta*);
however, the meaning of the word is exactly as stated in the *Maghadeva Sutta*.
Regarding the second divine messenger, here too the being who has grown old says this according to the actual sense: "Behold..."
"Friends, I too was once young like you, endowed with strength in my thighs, strength in my arms, and swiftness;
those perfections of strength and swiftness have now vanished from me. Although my hands and feet still exist, they no longer perform the functions of hands and feet.
I have become such as this because I am not exempt from old age. But it is not only I; you too are certainly not exempt from old age. For just as it is with me, so it is with you."
“Old age will come to you as well; therefore, before it arrives, perform what is wholesome. Thus he became known as the “Messenger of the Gods.
Regarding the third “Messenger of the Gods,” here too the sick person speaks in a figurative sense: “See, sirs!
I too was once free from disease like you, but now I am struck down by illness in my own urine and excrement.”
"I am fallen into distress; I am not even able to rise up. Although my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the functions of hands and feet.
I have become such as this because I am not exempt from illness. It is not only I who am thus; you too are certainly not exempt from illness.
