For just as it has happened to me, so will illness come to you. Therefore, while it has not yet arrived, it is good [to prepare]."
"Act [as messengers]! Thus he became known as the "Divine Messenger" (*devadūta*).
Regarding the fourth [section], the "Divine Messengers": here, they should be understood either as "those who carry out the execution" (*kammakāraṇā*) or as "executioners" (*kammakāraṇikā*).
In that regard, on the side of those who carry out the execution, thirty-two such executioners speak as follows in terms of their actual meaning:
They say: "When we are reborn, we are not reborn in trees or stones; we are reborn in the bodies of those like you.
Therefore, while we have not yet been reborn, perform what is wholesome. For this reason, they are called "divine messengers" (*devadūta*).
Those who carry out judicial punishments also speak in this sense: "We are carrying out thirty-two types of judicial punishments..."

“We do not [commit such acts] against trees and the like; we commit them only against beings such as yourselves. Therefore, since we have not previously inflicted punishment upon you, may you now perform what is wholesome.
For this reason, they too became known as "divine messengers" (devadūta).
Regarding the fifth divine messenger: here, the deceased being speaks thus in substance—“Behold!”...
"O friend, I have been cast away in the charnel ground and have reached the state of a bloated corpse and so forth;
I have become like this because I am not yet released from death. It is not only I who am thus; you too are certainly not released from death.
For just as it has happened to me, so will death come to you as well; therefore, before its arrival, perform what is wholesome."
There, one named Devadūta was born.
Now, who receives this "Investigation of the Divine Messengers" (devadūtānuyoga) and who does not? First, he by whom much evil has been committed goes and is reborn in hell itself.
However, he by whom only a small amount of evil karma has been committed receives it.
For just as they do exactly what must be done with a thief caught with the stolen goods, yet they do not pass judgment;
but once he has been apprehended after an investigation, they bring him before the court of justice, and he receives his judgment—such is the case here.
For those who have committed minor evil deeds remember [the deed] by their own nature, and they remember it even when being reminded.
In that regard, one named Dīghajayantadamiḷa remembered by his own natural disposition. It is said that this Damiḷa had worshipped the Ākāsacetiya at the Sumanagirivihāra with a red cloth.
Then, having been reborn in the vicinity of the Ussada hell, upon merely hearing the sound of the flames of fire, he remembered the cloth he had worshipped;
he went and was reborn in heaven. Another [story concerns] a young bhikkhu who was his son...
While giving a plain cotton cloth, he placed it at the Buddha’s feet; at the time of his death, he took as a sign the sound "paṭapaṭā.
He was reborn in the Ussada hell, but by means of the sound of the cloth, he recollected that garment and was reborn in heaven.
Thus, indeed, by recollecting a wholesome deed through one's own natural disposition, one is reborn in heaven.
But when they do not remember by their own nature, he questions them regarding the five divine messengers (*devadūta*).

Among them, one remembers by means of the first divine messenger, another by the second and so forth. However, for one who does not remember even by all five, King Yama himself causes him to remember.
It is said that a certain minister, having worshipped the Great Cetiya with a jar of jasmine flowers, gave the merit thereof to Yama. Regarding him—
Because of an unwholesome deed, he was reborn in hell and they led him into the presence of Yama.
While the five divine messengers were unable to find any wholesome merit in him, Yama himself looked on; seeing him, he reminded him:
"Did you not offer worship at the Great Cetiya with a jar of jasmine flowers and give me a portion of that merit? At that moment, he remembered it and went to the world of the gods. Yama—
But even though he looked for himself and did not see [it], he remained silent, thinking: "This being will experience what is called great suffering.
267. "In the Great Niraya" means in the Avīci Great Niraya. What, then, is its measurement?
It is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. The iron ground and the iron roof, as well as each of the walls, are nine times nine yojanas [in thickness].
A flame arises from the eastern wall, reaches the western wall, pierces through it, and travels a hundred leagues beyond.

The same applies to the other directions as well. Thus, in terms of length and breadth up to the boundary of the net, it measures three hundred and eighteen leagues; in circumference, however, it is nine hundred and fifty-four leagues.
But including the surrounding elevations, it measures ten thousand yojanas.
Regarding the phrase "it rises to the same height," the meaning here is that once a foot has been set down, it is impossible to lift it firmly again.
Furthermore, the sense in this context is: it burns from the bottom upwards, and it flames from the top downwards.
Thus, it is perceived as burning at the time of entering, and exactly the same at the time of emerging; therefore, it is said thus.
"Possessed of much excellence" means having reached many hundreds and thousands of years.
But why is this hell designated as *Avīci*? "Interval" (*vīci*) is called a gap; and in that [hell], there is none.
There is no interval between the flames of fire, sentient beings, or suffering; therefore, it has come to be designated as "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted).

For from its eastern wall, flames arise and, intermingling, travel a hundred yojanas, pierce the western wall, and go another hundred yojanas beyond. The same method applies to the remaining directions as well.
Devadatta was reborn in the midst of these six nets; his physical body measured one hundred yojanas.
Both his feet were embedded in the iron ground up to the ankles; both his hands were embedded in the iron walls up to the wrists;
his head was embedded in the iron roof up to the level of his eyebrows; and from below, a single iron spike [pierced him].
Having entered, it pierced through the body; having entered the roof, the spear emerged from the eastern wall, pierced through the heart, and entered the western wall;
the spear emerged from the northern wall, pierced through the ribs, and entered the southern wall.
Because he had struck the Tathāgata while he was motionless, the spear remained motionless as it burned.
He was born such because his karma was similar [to that of others there]. Thus, because the flames are without interval, it is called Avīci (the Uninterrupted).
Within its area of one hundred yojanas, however, beings are packed without interval like rice flour ground in a mortar and filled back in;
one cannot say, "In this place there is a being," or "In this place there is none," whether they are moving or standing still.
There is no space between those who are sitting or lying down; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they do not obstruct one another.
Thus, because there is no interval between beings, it is called *Avīci*.
Furthermore, at the door of the body, six types of consciousness accompanied by equanimity arise, and one accompanied by suffering. Thus...

Just as when six drops of honey are placed on the tip of the tongue and a single drop of molten copper is added, only that [drop of copper] is perceived because of its overwhelming power, while the others become negligible;

so too, here, due to the overwhelming power of burning, there is only uninterrupted suffering, while the others are negligible. Thus, it is called *Avīci* (the Uninterrupted) because of the continuity of suffering.
269. "Mahanta" means measuring one hundred yojanas. "He falls there" means that one foot lands in the Great Hell (Mahāniraya) and the other falls into the Feces Hell (Gūthaniraya).

"Sūcimukha" means having mouths like needles; they are as large as the necks of elephants or as large as a boat carrying a single *doṇa* measure. "Kukkulaniraya" is likewise one hundred yojanas in extent, filled with glowing embers the size of gabled houses—a hell of burning ashes—wherein those who fall are caught on the bottom surface like wooden pestles, stones, or shards thrown onto a heap of chaff.
"They impale" means they impale them by striking them with iron rods. At the time of being impaled, those thorns point downward; at the time of being removed, they point upward.
"Shaken by the wind" means moved by the wind consisting of karma. "They cut even the hands" means they cut them as if pounding meat upon a wooden board.
If one stands up and flees, an iron wall rises up and encircles him.
Below, a razor-edge arises.
The river of alkaline water is called Vetaraṇī, a river of copper-colored iron. There, the lotus leaves are made of iron and have coarse thorns;
below are razor-edges, and on both banks are rattan creepers and *kuśa* grass. There, it is painful and intense.
There he is buffeted from above and below by the harsh wind; he is cut upon lotus leaves,
pierced by thorns in the gravel that is shaped like a crossroads, split by razor-edged blades, scraped by *kuśa* grass on both banks,
dragged by rattan creepers, and sliced by sharp spears.
270. Regarding "with that heated iron hook": when he says, "I am hungry," they bring a large iron pan filled with iron balls and approach him.
Recognizing them as iron balls, he touches them with his teeth.
Then they pry open his mouth with that heated iron hook and, having brought molten copper from a large iron cauldron, pour the molten copper [into his mouth] with streams of red-hot metal.

They act in this very way. "Again in the Great Hell" means that starting from the fivefold binding up to the drinking of molten copper, and starting again from the drinking of molten copper, they subject them to the fivefold binding and so forth once more before casting them into the Great Hell.
Therein, some are released by the fivefold binding alone; some by the second; some by the third; and some by the drinking of molten copper.
He is released; however, as long as his karma is not yet exhausted, they cast him back again into the Great Hell.
A certain young bhikkhu, grasping this sutta, said: "Venerable sir, they cast back into the Great Hell even a being who has experienced such suffering!
[The Buddha replied: "Yes, friend, as long as the karma is not exhausted, it happens thus again and again."
“They are practicing. “Venerable sir, let the recitation wait; please speak only on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna),” he said.
Having had the meditation subject explained, he returned after becoming a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and then took up the recitation.
There is no counting those others in this same place who, having set aside the recitation, attained arahantship. This Sutta is never absent from all the Buddhas.
271. “Having approached a lowly body” means having entered into a lowly body. “In clinging” refers to the grasping of craving and views.
“In the origin of birth and death” refers to that which serves as the cause for both birth and death. “Without clinging” means not grasping by means of the four kinds of clinging.
“In the destruction of birth and death” means they are liberated in *nibbāna*, which is designated as the destruction of birth and death.

"Extinguished in this very life" means they are extinguished through the extinction of all defilements within this very selfhood (*attabhāva*) in the present world. "They have transcended all suffering" means they have indeed gone beyond all suffering.
The commentary on the *Devadūta Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is hereby completed.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Chapter on Analysis (Vibhaṅgavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on One Fortunate Night (Bhaddekarattasutta).

272. "Thus have I heard" is the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, "of one fortunate night" (*bhaddekarattassa*) means of one fortunate night because of being endowed with the practice of insight (*vipassanā*). "Summary" (*uddesa*) refers to the matrix (*mātikā*). "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*) refers to the detailed exposition.
"The past" (*atīta*) refers to the five past aggregates. "One should not pursue" (*nānvāgameyya*) means one should not follow after them by way of craving and views.

"One should not long for" (*nappaṭikaṅkhe*) means one should not yearn for them by way of craving and views. "That which is past" (*yadatītaṃ*) is the statement of the reason here; because that which is past... [is gone].
That which has been abandoned, ceased, and come to an end—one should not pursue that again.
And because that which is future has not yet been reached, is unborn, and unarisen, one should not long for that either.
"There and there" means: whatever phenomenon has arisen in this or that very place, right there and then...
One who contemplates with the seven contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), contemplates either in the forest and so forth, or right there where they are.
The phrase "unshakable" (asaṃhīra) and "unperturbed" (asaṃkuppa) is stated for the purpose of showing insight and the subsequent insight (vipassanā-paṭivipassanā).
For insight is "unshakable" and "unperturbed" because it is not shaken nor perturbed by lust and the other defilements; one should cultivate that.

It means he would increase it and discern it. Alternatively, Nibbāna is "unshakable" (*asaṃhīra*) and "unwavering" (*asaṃkuppa*) because it is not shaken or disturbed by lust and the other defilements. A wise monk who knows this should cultivate it;
the meaning is that he should cause it to grow by repeatedly entering various attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which take that as their object.

Furthermore, for the purpose of cultivating that [virtue], one should apply oneself with diligence (*ātappa*)—so called because it involves the heating and scorching of the defilements—with the thought:
"Today itself the task must be undertaken. Who knows if death will come tomorrow?
Who knows whether there will be life tomorrow or death? "Today itself I shall give a gift, or I shall guard my virtue, or I shall practice some other [meritorious deed]."

Or rather, it shows that one should apply energy in this way: thinking, "I shall do it today," without giving rise to the thought, "There is still time for delay; I will do it tomorrow or the day after.
By the phrase "by the great army" (*mahāsenena*), it refers to his army consisting of many causes of death, such as fire, poison, weapons, and so forth; by means of that great army.
To such a Death as Mahāsena, one might say: "Wait for just a few days while I perform my own necessary duties, such as making offerings to the Buddha.
This may take the form of seeking friendship, or it may take the form of offering a bribe, saying:
"Take this hundred or this thousand [coins] and wait for a few days," or [thinking]: "By means of this..."
"There is no such thing as a compact consisting of a mass of strength, thinking, 'I shall ward it off with a mass of strength.
For 'compact' (saṅgara) is a name for friendship, courtesy, conscientiousness, the granting of favors, and a mass of strength; therefore, this meaning was stated.
'Untiring' means not lazy, one who is industrious. Because he has practiced in this way, he is auspicious for a single night; thus he is called Bhaddekaratta."

Thus, regarding that person who has practiced in this way, the Buddha, the Sage, declares him to be "one blessed with a single night" because of his tranquility in the face of lust and other defilements.

Regarding the phrases "of such a form" and so forth, it means that even though he was dark-skinned, he possessed a complexion like that of a sapphire; thus, it is by way of his beautiful appearance alone [that he is described].
"I was such-and-such in form. By way of wholesome pleasant and joyful feeling, "I was such-and-such in feeling.
By way of the perception and so forth associated with that [feeling], "I was such-and-such in perception, such-and-such in volitional formations, and such-and-such in consciousness" in the past time.

In this context, "he brings delight to them" means he brings craving for those [aggregates] such as form, and causes it to continue. However, by way of inferior form and so forth, he does not conceive: "I was such-and-such in form... pe... I was such-and-such in consciousness."
“He does not bring about delight” means that he does not cause craving or the views associated with craving to proceed.

In such passages as “one might be of such a form,” etc., it should be understood that the bringing about of delight consists precisely in the proceeding of craving and views by way of forms and so forth that are agreeable to him.
And as for the question, “But how, monks, is one carried away by present states?”—this refers to the present... [text fragment]
"Whoever discerns the Dhamma here and there as unshakable and immovable"— this was stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the summary.
Although one might here have said, "And how, monks, does one not discern a presently arisen state," and so forth, nevertheless,
because "unshakable" and "immovable" refer to insight (vipassanā), therefore [the following applies] to that:
Having thus raised the summary headings (mātikā) to demonstrate both non-existence and existence, the detailed exposition is stated.
In that context, "is drawn away" means that due to the absence of insight (vipassanā), one is dragged along by craving and views.
"Is not drawn away" means that due to the presence of insight, one is not dragged along by craving and views. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is completed. 2.
The commentary on the *Ānanda-bhaddekaratta-sutta*.

276. “Thus have I heard” refers to the *Ānanda-Bhaddakāratta-sutta*. Therein, “emerged from seclusion” means emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). “Who now, monks?”—though [the Buddha] already knew, he asked for the purpose of initiating the discourse.

278. “Excellent, excellent!”—thus he gave his approval to the Elder. “It is well indeed of you”—this was said in praise of the teaching because it had been delivered with perfectly rounded words and phrases and was utterly pure.
The rest is clear everywhere. Thus ends the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya in the *Papañcasūdanī*.
The commentary on the Ānanda-Bhaddekaratta Sutta is finished.
3. The commentary on the Mahākaccāna-Bhaddekaratta Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahākaccāna-Bhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, "at Tapodārāma" means at the Hot Water Park.

In the monastery that had thus acquired its name from the lake; for it is said that beneath Mount Vebhāra there was a nāga-abode belonging to the Bhūmaṭṭhaka nāgas, five hundred yojanas in extent, resembling the world of the gods, provided with jeweled floors, monasteries, and groves.
There, in the place where the nāgas sported, was a great lake of water, and from that flowed the river named Tapodā.
It flows as boiling hot water. But why has it become such? It is said that surrounding Rājagaha there is a great world of hungry ghosts (*petaloka*);
this Tapodā flows between two great hell-pots of molten iron (*mahālohakumbhiniraya*), and for that reason it flows boiling hot. And this has been said: "Monks, wherever this Tapodā flows..."
“Bhikkhus, the Tapodā River has clear water, cool water, pleasant water, white water, and it has beautiful landing-places; it is delightful and abounds in fish and turtles.
And lotuses as large as cartwheels bloom there. Moreover, bhikkhus, this Tapodā flows from between two great hells;
that is why this Tapodā flows hot. Now, in the place directly in front of this monastery—
From that, a great pool of water was formed; after the name of that [pool], this monastery is called Tapodārāma.
280. Regarding "Samiddhi": it is said that the physical form (*attabhāva*) of that elder was prosperous, handsome, and pleasing;

therefore, he became known by the very name Samiddhi. "The beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyaka*) means the beginning of the holy life of the Path, which consists of the preliminary practice.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat; this should be expanded in detail according to the method stated in the *Madhupiṇḍika Sutta*. 282.
Regarding the passage "Thus, for me, the eye," it is said that in this sutta the Blessed One established the matrix (*mātikā*) by way of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
The Elder, too, [noted] that in these three suttas—the two preceding ones and the fourth following—it was by way of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) that [the Blessed One taught].
Having grasped the underlying method, thinking, "The matrix (mātikā) and its analysis (vibhaṅga) have already been established;
however, here the matrix is set forth specifically for the purpose of analyzing by way of the twelve sense-bases (dvādasāyatana)," the Elder spoke thus.

But because this Elder, having grasped this method, has committed a grave error—showing a footstep where there is no path, or making a footprint in the sky—the Blessed One, with reference to this very sutta, said:

—“This is the foremost, monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who analyze in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief, namely Mahākaccāna”—thus he placed him in the position of preeminence.

Herein, “the eye” refers to the sensitivity of the eye (*cakkhupasāda*). “Forms” refers to forms produced by the four causes. In this same manner, the remaining sense bases (*āyatana*) are also to be understood.
“Consciousness” means craving-consciousness. “He delights in that” means he delights in both that eye and that form by way of craving and views.
“He pursues it” means he follows after it with craving and views.

Regarding the passage, “Thus was my mind in the past; thus were the phenomena,” here “mind” refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), and “phenomena” refers to the objects of the three planes of existence.

283. "He makes a resolution" means he establishes [it] by way of aspiration (*paṭṭhanā*). "By reason of the resolution" means by reason of the establishment of the aspiration. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Mahākaccāna-bhaddekaratta-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Lomasakaṅgiya-Bhaddekaratta Sutta* 286.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Lomasakaṅgiya-Bhaddekaratta Sutta*. Regarding that, as for "Lomasakaṅgiya":
it is said that this was the Elder Aṅgati by name; however, because there was a slight appearance of hair on his body, he became well known as "Lomasakaṅgiya. [He was like] sandalwood...
"Devaputta" means that, it is said, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, this person was a wealthy and very affluent lay follower (upāsaka) named Candana.
Having honored the Three Jewels with the four requisites, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

thus, by his former name, he came to be known as "Candana Devaputta. "On the Paṇḍukambala stone" means on a stone slab like red wool (rattakambala). It is said that because of its resemblance to red wool...
Its color is like a heap of *jayasumana* flowers; therefore, it is called the "Yellow Blanket Rock" (*Paṇḍukambalasilā*).

But when did the Blessed One dwell there? Seven years after attaining enlightenment, on the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷhī in Sāvatthī, having performed the Twin Miracle in the midst of an assembly twelve *yojanas* wide, he descended and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree.
Having sat down and delivered a teaching on the Dhamma that rescued the great multitude from the great abyss, the Buddhas—
because they do not dwell on the path of men after performing a miracle— therefore, while that very people were still watching him take his steps,
entered the rain-retreat upon the yellow-sandstone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; it was there he dwelt at that time.
There, while residing there, the Blessed One— surrounded by deities who had for the most part gathered from ten thousand world-systems—
having made his mother a bodily witness, was teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka;

and for those deities who were unable to penetrate the discourse on the analysis of the material and immaterial, which is profound, subtle, struck with the three characteristics, and difficult to understand, [he taught].
In order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency, he recited the summary and the detailed exposition of the *Bhaddekaratta* Sutta from time to time.
While learning it there, this son of the gods learned these verses together with their detailed exposition;
however, because the state of a deva is characterized by negligence, he was overwhelmed by celestial objects of sense and gradually forgot the prose discourse, retaining only the verses.
Therefore he said: “In this way, monk, I remember the *Bhaddekaratta* verses. Regarding the phrases “Learn them, however,” and so forth:
one who sits in silence and listens is said to “learn”; one who recites them aloud is said to “master”; one who teaches them to others is said to “retain” them. The rest here is self-evident.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Lomasakaṅgiya-Bhaddekaratta Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta 289.
“Thus have I heard” introduces the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta. Regarding the word *subho*: it is said that he was indeed handsome to behold.
He was handsome; because of the beauty of his limbs, they gave him the name Subha.
They addressed him as "Māṇava" during his youth, and even in his old age he continued to be addressed by that same term.
He was called "Todeyyaputta" because he was the son of the brahmin Todeyya, the chaplain to King Pasenadi. It is said that there was a village named Tudigāma not far from Sāvatthī.
He had a name, and because of his preeminence, he became known as Todeyya. However, he was immensely wealthy, possessing a fortune of seven hundred and seventy million, yet he was extremely miserly;
thinking, "There is no such thing as an inexhaustible supply of wealth for one who gives," he gave nothing to anyone. And this has been said:
“Having seen the exhaustion of collyrium, the accumulation of anthills, and the gathering of honey, a wise man should dwell at home.
Thus he taught the lesson of non-giving itself. To the Perfectly Enlightened One while residing at Dhuravihāra, [he offered] even as much as a single bowl of conjey.
Or, having failed to give even a single spoonful of food out of greed for wealth, he died and was reborn as a dog in that very same house.
Subha loved that dog exceedingly; he fed it with the very food he himself ate and would carry it up to lie upon his own excellent couch.
Then one day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world...
Looking around and seeing that dog, [the Blessed One thought]: "The brahmin Todeyya, out of greed for wealth, has been reborn as a dog in his own house.
Today, when I go to Subha’s house and see me, the dog will bark;
then I shall speak a single word to him, and he, thinking 'The ascetic Gotama knows me,' will go to the hearth."
"He will lie down. On that account, Subha, there will be a private conversation between him and me;
having heard the Dhamma, he will establish himself in the refuges. But the dog, having died, will be reborn in hell.
Having thus understood the young man’s state of being established in the refuges, the Blessed One, on that day, [performed] the care of his body...
Having done so, he entered the village alone; when the young brahmin had departed, the Blessed One entered that house for alms.
Seeing the Blessed One, the dog went up to him while making a "bhukkāra" sound. Then the Blessed One said this to him:
"Todeyya, formerly you were reborn as a dog because you treated me with contempt, saying 'Sir! Sir!', and now it is the same."
“Having made the sound ‘bhuk,’ you will go to Avīci. When the dog heard this, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama knows me,” he became remorseful;
lowering his neck, he lay down in the ashes within the hearth. People tried to lift him up and place him on the bed, but they were unable to do so.
Subha came and asked, “By whom has this dog been removed from the bed?”
He said: "People have said that [my father] was not reborn as anything at all," and they reported that occurrence to him. Having heard this, the young man became angry, thinking:
"My father has been reborn in the Brahma-world; there is no dog named Todeyya. Yet the ascetic Gotama treats my father like a dog; whatever comes to his mouth, he speaks.
Thus, wishing to refute the Blessed One with a falsehood, he—
Having gone to the monastery, he asked about that matter.
The Blessed One, having told him exactly the same thing, spoke for the sake of not deceiving him: "But, young man, is there any wealth left unmentioned by your father?
"There is, Master Gotama; there is a golden necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], worth a hundred thousand."
"A pair of golden sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces], and a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand *kahāpaṇas*.
Go, feed that dog with rice porridge mixed with little water, place him upon the bed, and question him when he has fallen into a slight sleep;
he will tell you everything. Then you will know: 'This is my father. The young man thought: "If..."
"It will surely come true; I shall obtain the wealth. If not, I will rebuke the ascetic Gotama with a lie.
Delighted for both these reasons, he went and did exactly that. The dog, thinking, "I am recognized by him," wept and made the sound "hum hum";
it then went to the place where the treasure was buried, dug at the earth with its paw, and gave a signal. The young brahmin—
Having taken the wealth, he thought: "The interval between rebirths, so subtle and usually concealed from existence, is made manifest even to the ascetic Gotama;
surely this man is omniscient. With a mind full of confidence toward the Blessed One, he prepared fourteen questions.
It is said that he was a student of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*); therefore, it occurred to him: "Taking this gift of the Dhamma, [I shall approach] the ascetic..."
Thinking, “I shall ask Gotama a question,” he approached the Blessed One for a second time.
When he asked his question, the Blessed One, answering it all at once, said: “Kammassakā...,” and so forth.
In this context, those for whom karma is their own property, their own possession, are “kammassakā. Those who are the heirs of karma are “kammadāyādā.”
Kamma is their inheritance; this is the meaning of "kamma-bhaṇḍaka. Kamma is their womb, their cause; thus they are "kamma-yoni. Kamma is their kinsman;
thus they are "kamma-bandhū," meaning their relatives are kamma. Kamma is their refuge, their support; thus they are "kammapaṭisaraṇā.
Regarding the phrase "namely, by way of inferiority and excellence": "You become inferior... [and so forth].
"You are lowly, you are short-lived, you are long-lived... [and so on] ...you are dull-witted, you are wise"—this is the differentiation according to inferiority and excellence.
No one else does this; the meaning is that karma alone thus differentiates beings.
The young man did not understand the meaning of what was said; having bound his mouth with a thick cloth strip, [he was led away].
It was as if something sweet had been placed before him. It is said that he was supported by pride and considered himself wise;

he saw no one as his equal. Then, thinking, "Let this pride not arise—the thought that 'the ascetic Gotama says only what I already know'"—in order to shatter his pride, the Blessed One resolved, "I shall speak in such a way that it is difficult to penetrate from the very beginning."
Thinking, “Then he will entreat me, saying, ‘Venerable Gotama, I do not know;

please explain this to me by making it clear in detail,’ and I shall speak when thus entreated, and in this way it will be meaningful for him,” he spoke after making [the matter] difficult to penetrate.
Now, revealing his own state of non-penetration, he said, “Indeed, I do not...,” and so forth.
"290. 'By the complete' means by that which is fulfilled. 'By the undertaken' means by that which is grasped and adhered to.
'Young man, this practice leads to a short life, namely, the taking of life'—this action of taking life is the practice that leads to a short life. But how does it bring about a short life?
For there are four kinds of kamma: the obstructive (*upapīḷaka*), the interruptive (*upacchedaka*), the productive (*janaka*), [and the supportive]."
Regarding "supporting" (*upatthambhaka*): A deed produced by a powerful kamma comes as a "tormentor" (*upapīḷaka*) during the course of existence and says this in effect:
"If I had known earlier, I would not have allowed you to be born here;
I would have caused you to be reborn in the four states of misery. Very well, you may be born anywhere; as for me, I shall perform the tormenting kamma."
“Having crushed that [fruit], I shall turn it into sapless juice and dregs. From that time forth, he treats it in such a manner.
What does he do? He brings danger near and destroys his wealth.
In this regard, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, there is neither enjoyment nor happiness for the mother.
There is distress arising for his parents; thus he brings about misfortune.
Furthermore, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, the household wealth perishes through kings and others like salt falling into water;
cows that yield pots of milk no longer give milk; and gentle oxen become fierce, one-eyed, or hunchbacked.
Disease breaks out in the cattle pens; slaves and others do not obey one's word; the sown crop does not grow;
what is brought into the house perishes in the house, and what is taken into the forest perishes in the forest; gradually, even mere food and clothing become difficult to obtain;
there is no protection for the womb; at the time of birth, the mother’s breast-milk ceases; and the child, receiving no care—
When [the life-force] is oppressed, it becomes sapless, juiceless, and dregs; this is called "oppressive karma" (*upapīḷaka-kamma*).
However, for one born with a long lifespan due to a long-life-producing karma (*dīghāyuka-kamma*), an interruptive karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) arrives and cuts off that lifespan.
Just as if a man were to shoot an arrow after having made a target eight cubits away, and another person were to strike it with a club immediately after it was released from the bow—
Having struck it, one would cause it to fall right there; in the same way, the obstructive kamma cuts off the lifespan of one reborn through long-lived kamma.
What does it do? It causes one to enter a forest of thieves, or to descend into the waters of predatory fish, or leads one to some other place of danger.
This is called obstructive kamma (*upacchedaka-kamma*); its name is also "injurious" (*upaghātaka*).

Kamma that produces rebirth-linking is called "productive kamma" (janaka-kamma). Kamma that provides support by bringing about the attainment of wealth and so forth for one born into a family with little wealth and so on is called "supportive kamma" (upatthambhaka-kamma).
Among these four types, the first two are exclusively unwholesome; productive kamma may be either wholesome or unwholesome;
supportive kamma is exclusively wholesome. In this context, the kamma of taking life, through its function as "interruptive kamma," leads to a short lifespan.
Wholesome kamma performed by one who takes life is not exalted; it is unable to produce a rebirth with a long lifespan.

Thus, the taking of life leads to a short lifespan. Either it determines the rebirth-linking itself to be short-lived, or through the volition of formal resolve one is reborn in hell, while through the preceding and succeeding volitions, one becomes short-lived according to the method already stated.

“O student, this practice leads to long life. Here, even a minor deed performed in a previous existence—namely, the act of abstaining from taking life—comes into being during the present course of existence and speaks thus in terms of its actual meaning:
“If I had known earlier, I would not have allowed you to be reborn here; I would have caused you to be reborn in the world of the gods. Let it be!”
"Wherever you may be reborn, I shall provide for you a supporting pillar known as 'supporting karma' (upatthambhakakamma)," he says, and thus provides that support.
What does it do? It eliminates dangers and generates wealth.
In this regard, from the moment the child is conceived in the mother’s womb, there is only happiness and satisfaction for the parents.
...it comes to pass. Whatever dangers there may be from humans or non-humans by their very nature, they all depart. In this way, he destroys danger.
Furthermore, from the time the child was conceived in his mother’s womb, there was no limit to the wealth in the house;
jars of treasure entered, filling the house from front to back as it expanded. His parents—
The wealth deposited by others also comes into their possession. Cows yield much milk, oxen are of a gentle disposition, and crops flourish in the place of sowing.
Or, regarding wealth given for interest or on loan, they bring it themselves and repay it without being urged; servants and the like become easy to speak to, and the works...
They do not decline. From the moment of conception, the boy receives protection; female physicians are always present.

If born into a householder family, he attains the status of a merchant chief (*seṭṭhi*); if born into the families of ministers and so forth, he attains the status of a general (*senāpati*) and other such positions.
Thus he acquires wealth. Being free from danger and possessing wealth, he lives for a long time. Such is the kamma of abstaining from taking life.
It conduces to long life.
Or, when one who abstains from taking life performs other sublime wholesome deeds, they are capable of producing a rebirth with a long lifespan;
thus, it also conduces to long life. Or, having determined the rebirth-linking itself, it results in a long life.
One performs [the action]. Either through the volition of formal determination (*sanniṭṭhāna-cetanā*), one is reborn in the world of the gods;
or through the preceding and subsequent volitions, in the manner already stated, one becomes long-lived. By this method, the meaning should be understood in the answers to all questions.
For even acts such as those of harming (*viheṭhana-kamma*) and so forth, when they come into operation, are like those described above in their actual sense, by way of oppression (*upapīḷana*).
By causing a lack of enjoyment, by the arising of disease and so forth when one fails to receive care,
by the lack of excellence in wholesome deeds performed by those who cause harm and the like, by the very process of rebirth-linking from the outset,

or by the sequence of preceding and succeeding volitions according to the method already stated, [kamma] produces much affliction and other such results; and just as non-killing does, so too non-harming and other such virtues produce little affliction and other such results.

293. Here, however, "one who is envious" (*issā-mana*) means one whose mind is associated with envy. "He becomes corrupt" (*upadussati*) means he becomes corrupt while reviling by means of envy itself.
"He binds envy" (*issaṃ bandhati*) means that, like one binding a sheaf of barley, he establishes it as if having bound it so that it does not perish.
"One of little influence" (*appesakkha*) means one with a small retinue; like an arrow shot at night, he is not perceived, like a hand that has been used [and discarded].
Having sat down, one does not even obtain water to drink. 294.
"He is not a giver" means he is not a giver due to the influence of stinginess (*macchariya*). "By that karma" means by that karma of stinginess.
295. "One worthy of salutation" refers to the Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), who are deserving of respectful greeting.
The same principle applies to rising from one’s seat and so forth. However, in this answer to the question, the obstructive and supportive kamma should not be taken into account.
For it is impossible to make oneself of low birth or high birth during the course of existence;

rather, having determined the rebirth-linking itself, kamma that leads to low birth causes one to be reborn in a low family, and kamma that leads to high birth causes one to be reborn in a high family.
296. "One who does not inquire" means that here, by not inquiring, one is not reborn in hell.
However, one who does not inquire does not know: "This should be done; this should not be done. Not knowing, he fails to do what should be done and does what should not be done.
Because of that, he is reborn in hell, while the other is reborn in heaven. Thus, young man... [as before] ...namely this.
"By way of inferiority and superiority"—thus the Teacher brought the teaching to its proper conclusion. The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*, is finished.
It is also called the *Subhasutta*.
6. Commentary on the Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta. In that context, "vain" (*mogha*) means empty and fruitless; "true" (*sacca*)...
It is thus. Furthermore, this was not heard by him directly; however, in the Upāli Sutta, it was said by the Blessed One:
"I declare mental action to be more blameworthy than bodily action or verbal action for the performance of evil karma and the occurrence of evil karma.
This statement was well known among the sectarians.

[The Elder] says this, referring to that [attainment] which has arisen; he speaks with reference to the discussion on the cessation of perception (*abhisaññānirodha*) that arose in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*: "How indeed, sir, does the cessation of perception come about?"—referring to the fact that "that attainment exists.
"He does not experience anything" means he does not experience even a single feeling. "And yet it exists," the Elder [says] regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
He permits [the action] with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). "To be protected" means it must be guarded by freeing one from blame.
"Intentional" (*sañcetanika*) means that which possesses volition (*sañcetana*); the meaning is: having performed intentional karma accompanied by a motive.
The Elder said this because he perceived: "The wanderer is asking specifically with reference to unwholesome [karma]."
"Even as for seeing, monks," said the Blessed One, "I see even a mere sesame seed, a conditioned formation, with my fleshly eye within a space of a league all around, even in the fourfold darkness;
and this wanderer lives not far off, within a distance of only a *gāvuta*.
Why then did the Blessed One speak thus? [The answer is: He spoke thus with reference to the sight of their meeting.

299. *Udāyī* refers to Lāludāyī. *Taṃ dukkhasmiṃ* means that all of it is indeed suffering. Thus, with reference to this suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*), the suffering of defilements (*kilesadukkha*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), he asks: "If it were spoken by the Blessed One. 300. *Ummaṅgaṃ* means a puzzle or a riddle.
*Ummujjamāno* means emerging or raising one's head. *Ayoniso ummujjissati* means he will emerge without the proper method; he will raise his head in an improper way.
And although the Blessed One knew this, he did not [reveal it] by means of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) nor by means of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*).
He did not know it through his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), but rather he understood it by means of [Udāyī’s] intention alone.
For when one speaks, one’s intention is easily discerned: one who wishes to speak stiffens his neck, moves his jaw, his mouth quivers, and he is unable to remain still.
Seeing that manner of his, the Blessed One [knew]: "This Udāyī is unable to remain still..."
He looked [into the matter] and knew: "He will speak only that which is not true. "Right from the beginning" means right at the very start. "Three feelings":
by the one asking, "What does he feel?", having thus determined, "I am asking about the three feelings," it is the three feelings that are asked about.
"To be felt as pleasant" means being a condition for pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
And here, the four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by joy arising from sense-sphere wholesome states,
together with the volitions of the three lower jhānas mentioned below— thus, because they produce pleasant feeling during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence,

it is called "kamma to be experienced as pleasure. Furthermore, in this context, sense-sphere kamma produces pleasure exclusively at the moment of rebirth-linking, whereas during the course of existence...
Even that which has a desirable or neutral object is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Unwholesome volition is called "kamma to be experienced as pain" because it produces only pain during both the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
This produces pain exclusively when occurring at the door of the body, but elsewhere it may be neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Furthermore, that feeling is reckoned as suffering precisely because it arises only in relation to undesirable, desirable, and neutral objects. However,

the four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by equanimity arising from wholesome sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) states, and the volition of the fourth jhāna arising from wholesome fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) states—
thus, by generating the third type of feeling during rebirth-linking and the course of existence— it is "to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhavedaniya*).

This refers to *kamma*. Herein, sense-sphere *kamma* produces exclusively neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*adukkhamasukha*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), but during the course of existence (*pavatta*), it may also produce pleasure when encountering a desirable object.
Furthermore, *kamma* to be experienced as pleasure functions both by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence;
likewise for that to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure. However, *kamma* to be experienced as pain functions only by way of the course of existence.
Furthermore, by way of this [verse], everything is appropriate solely from the perspective of its occurrence.
Regarding this, the Elder Bhagava was indicated as a point of reference by the Tathāgata for the purpose of explaining the *Mahākammavibhaṅga*;
having requested the Tathāgata and thinking, "I shall make the knowledge of the *Mahākammavibhaṅga* clear to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," he [proceeded] with skill in the connection [of the discourse].
Thus he spoke. Therein, "The Great Exposition of Kamma" (*Mahākammavibhaṅga*) means the great analysis of kamma. "Which four... [and so on]...

"Here, Ānanda, a certain person... [and so on]... is reborn in hell"—this is not the exposition of the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma; rather, it is the setting forth of the matrix (*mātikā*) for the sake of the exposition of the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma.
301. "In this case, Ānanda, a certain ascetic... This is a separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhi*). For the Blessed One undertook this for the purpose of explaining:
"Ascetics and brahmins possessing the divine eye, having made this their object and having obtained this condition, acquire this vision.
In that context, the five terms beginning with "ardor" (*ātappa*) are synonyms for energy (*vīriya*) alone. "Concentration of mind" (*cetosamādhi*)...
The concentration of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhusamādhi*). "He sees" means that looking [with the thought], "Where has that being been reborn?", he sees.
"Those who otherwise" refers to those who think, "Because of having fulfilled the ten courses of wholesome action, one is reborn in hell";
he says their knowledge is false. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. "Known" means made manifest.
"By power of view" means by the power of views. "By misapprehension" means by the misapprehension of views. "Having adhered, he speaks" means having resolved upon and grasped [the view], he speaks.
"In this regard, Ānanda," [this] is not yet the vessel for the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma; rather, it is merely the laying down of the headings (*mātikā*).
Here, however, regarding the words of these possessors of the divine eye, [it is determined that] so much is permitted and so much is not permitted.
This has been shown. Therein, "among them" means among those four recluses and brahmins. "This belongs to him" means this statement belongs to him.

"In another way" means by another manner. Thus, regarding the doctrines of these recluses and brahmins, it should be understood that in two instances permission is granted and in three instances it is not;
in this way, everywhere permission and non-permission are to be known.

303. Having thus shown both the permission and the prohibition regarding the words of those possessing the divine eye, he now spoke the passage beginning with "In this case, Ānanda, as for that person," while analyzing the knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma.
"Or else it was done by him previously" means that it was done prior to what was seen being performed by this one possessing the divine eye.
For one is reborn in hell because of what was done previously, and one is also reborn because of what was done later—at the time of death.
Or else, it is produced even by wrong view such as: "Khaṇḍa is supreme, Siva is supreme, the Grandfather is supreme, or the world is created by Īśvara and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*): for that [kamma] which is to be experienced in the present life, the result occurs in this very life;
for that which is to be experienced upon rebirth, it occurs after having been reborn; and for that which is to be experienced in subsequent lives, it occurs later.
In another way, he experiences its result.
Thus, this ascetic or brahmin saw one mass of kamma and one mass of result;
whereas the Perfectly Enlightened One saw three masses of kamma and two masses of result that were not seen by him. Furthermore, regarding what was seen and what was not seen by him:
And he saw four classes of kamma and three classes of result.

This knowledge of knowing these seven points is called the Tathāgata’s Great Analysis of Kamma Knowledge (*Mahākammavibhaṅga-ñāṇa*). In the second instance, nothing was seen by means of the divine eye;
rather, the Tathāgata saw three classes of kamma and two classes of result. This knowledge of knowing these five individual points [is also the Mahākammavibhaṅga-ñāṇa].
This is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the great analysis of kamma. The same method applies to the other two instances as well.
"Incapable" (*abhabba*) means unwholesome kamma that is devoid of actualization. "Appearing as incapable" (*abhabbābhāsa*) means it appears as incapable;
the sense is that it overcomes or obstructs [other kamma]. For when much unwholesome kamma has been accumulated, powerful kamma [overcomes] weak kamma.
To obstruct the result of [a previous] kamma and create an opportunity for one's own result—this is both impossible and appears as impossible.

However, when wholesome kamma has been accumulated and unwholesome kamma is committed immediately thereafter, that unwholesome kamma obstructs the result of the wholesome kamma and creates an opportunity for its own result;
this is impossible yet appears as possible. Even when much wholesome kamma has been accumulated...
Strong kamma obstructs the ripening of weak kamma and makes room for its own ripening;

this is "capable" (bhabba) and "appearing capable" (bhabbābhāsa). However, when wholesome kamma has been performed immediately after unwholesome kamma has been accumulated, it obstructs the ripening of that unwholesome kamma and makes room for its own ripening; this is "capable" but "appearing incapable" (abhabbābhāsa).

Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood by way of its mode of presentation (*upaṭṭhānākāra*). For this is what is meant: it "appears" (*ābhāsati*) as impossible, it "presents itself" (*upaṭṭhāti*) as impossible;

thus it is "an appearance of the impossible" (*abhabbābhāsa*). In that regard, four types of persons have been stated by way of the method beginning with, "This person who here takes life," and so forth.
Among them, the action of the first person is "impossible" and "an appearance of the impossible," because it is unwholesome (*akusala*).
For the first [person], because he has been reborn in hell, it appears as unwholesome (akusala), being the cause for his rebirth there.
For the second, the kamma is incapable yet appears as capable;
for while it is incapable due to its unwholesomeness, it appears as wholesome (kusala), being the cause for the rebirth of other sectarians in heaven.
The same method applies to the other two types of kamma as well. The remainder is clear throughout.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
7. Commentary on the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta 304.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta. In this context, “to be known” means they are to be understood by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
“Mental explorations” (*manopavicāra*) refers to applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); for it is the mind that gives rise to applied thought which is here called “mind.”
"Intended" means they are the mental explorations of the mind; thus, they are "mental explorations" (*manopavicāra*).

"Seven steps" refers to the steps of beings who depend upon either the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) or its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*). For herein, there are eighteen steps of the cycle and eighteen steps of cessation;
these too are to be understood by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). "Of trainers of horses" refers to those who teach the practice of training horses and so forth.
The meaning is "those who are to be tamed and the tamers. The remainder will be clarified in the *Vibhaṅga* itself. "This is the enumeration" refers to the laying down of the matrix (*mātikā*). 305.
The eye-base and so forth have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. As for "eye-consciousness," there are two types of eye-consciousness: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant.
This same method applies to the remaining sensitive-matter consciousnesses as well. Setting aside these ten, the remainder—
Here, "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa) is meant.
"Eye-contact" (cakkhusamphassa) is contact in the eye; this is a designation for the contact associated with eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the others as well.
"Having seen a form with the eye" means having seen a form with eye-consciousness. This same method applies everywhere. "Conducive to joy" (somanassaṭṭhāniya).

It is that which serves as the cause by way of being the object of mental joy (*somanassa*). "It ranges over" (*upavicarati*) means it ranges over by way of the occurrence of sustained application (*vicāra*) therein;

thus, according to this method, the eighteen mental rangings (*manopavicāra*)—consisting of initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) along with their associated factors—are to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "six rangings of mental joy," here they are called "rangings" because they range together with mental joy.
The investigation of mental joy (*somanassūpavicāra*). The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. 306.
"Based on the household life" (*gehasita*) means dependent upon the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "Based on renunciation" (*nekkhammasita*) means dependent upon insight (*vipassanā*).

"Desirable things" (*iṭṭhāna*) refers to those sought after. "Pleasant things" (*kantāna*) refers to those desired. "Delightful things" (*manoramāna*): they are called delightful because the mind finds delight (*ramati*) in them.
“Of those delightful things”: connected with worldly bait (*lokāmisa*), meaning connected with craving (*taṇhā*). “Past”: that which was already obtained. [Objection:
“Let joy arise in relation to the present for now; but how does it arise regarding the past? [Response: Even regarding the past, for one who recollects:
“Just as I experience a desirable object now, so too did I experience it in the past.”
Strong gladness arises.
"Impermanence" refers to the aspect of impermanence (*aniccākāra*).

"Change, fading away, and cessation" means change through the relinquishing of its natural state, fading away through its disappearance, and cessation through its stopping. "By right wisdom" means by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). This...

It is called "joy based on renunciation" (*nekkhammasita-somanassa*). This refers to the joy that arises when one is seated having established insight (*vipassanā*), looking at the dissolution of formations (*saṅkhāra*)—just as a king might look upon his own royal splendor—and while keen and heroic insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) regarding those formations is flowing. For this has also been said: [The verse follows: “Just as a king, having ascended to the top of his palace, looks down upon the multitude of people, so too does the wise man, having ascended to the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world with his divine eye. And it is further said: “Just as a man standing on the ground might look down upon those standing on the ground, so too does the wise man, having ascended to the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world with his divine eye. And it is further said: “Just as a man standing on a mountain peak might look down upon those standing on the ground, so too does the wise man, having ascended to the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world with his divine eye. And it is further said: “Just as a man standing on the bank of a river might look down upon those wading in the water, so too does the wise man, having ascended to the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world with his divine eye. And it is further said: “Just as a man standing on dry land might look down upon those standing in the water, so too does the wise man, having ascended to the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world with his divine eye. And it is further said: “Just as a man standing on the bank of a river
“For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is at peace,
there is a superhuman delight as he clearly discerns the Dhamma.
To whatever extent he comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates,”
"One who understands the deathless attains rapture and gladness.

"These" refers to these six kinds of joy based on renunciation that arise in one sitting after having established insight—by way of impermanence and so forth—into desirable objects that have come into the range of the six sense doors.
307. As for "the past": let there arise grief in one who, having aspired to the present, does not obtain it; but regarding the past...

How does it arise? Even regarding the past, for one who recollects, "Just as I do not obtain a desired object now after longing for it, so too in the past I did not obtain it after longing for it," powerful mental distress arises.
Regarding "the unsurpassed liberations": the unsurpassed liberation is Arahantship; it refers to one who has established an aspiration for Arahantship.
Meaning: "The sphere" (āyatana) refers to the sphere of arahantship (*arahattāyatana*). "Establishing a longing" (*pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato*) means to one who is setting forth an aspiration (*patthana*).
This [sorrow] arises for one who sets forth that aspiration; thus, because it is rooted in aspiration, it is said, "establishing a longing.
These six states of mental distress based on renunciation (*nekkhammasita*) are these very [sorrows] that arise at the six doors toward desirable objects.

For one who, having set their heart on Arahatship when it has come within reach, is unable to exert themselves by establishing insight (vipassanā) through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth for its attainment,
and who grieves, thinking, "I have not been able to reach Arahatship during this fortnight,
this month, or even this year"— just like the Venerable Mahāsīva Thera, a dweller in a forest retreat near a village, whose tears flowed in streams— [this is the case].
The arisen states of dejection should be understood as the six types of dejection based on renunciation (*nekkhammasita*).

The detailed explanation of the basis for this, however, has been set forth in the *Sakkapañhavaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Questions of Sakka) within the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*; one who desires it should take it from there.

308. Regarding the phrase "equanimity arises": here, equanimity refers to equanimity of ignorance (*aññāṇupekhā*). "Of one who has not conquered the obstacle" refers to the obstacle of the defilements (*kilesodhi*).

Because he stands having conquered [the defilements], one whose taints are exhausted is called a "conqueror of the flood" (*oghajina*); therefore, the meaning is "one whose taints are not yet exhausted. Regarding the term "conqueror of ripening" (*vipākajina*):

here too, because he stands having conquered future ripening, only one whose taints are exhausted is called a "conqueror of ripening"; therefore, the meaning is "of one whose taints are indeed not yet exhausted.
"One who does not see the danger" (*anādīnavadassāvī*) means one who does not perceive danger or calamity. These are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.

When desirable objects have thus come into range at these six doors, this equanimity that has arisen—clinging and adhering to forms and so forth, like flies stuck to a lump of sugar—should be understood as the "sixfold house-based equanimity" (*cha gehasitā upekkhā*).
"It does not transcend form" means it does not go beyond form; it does not remain there by way of attachment. These...
Regarding the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation: when desirable or other objects have entered the range of the six doors,

one should understand that these six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation are associated with the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in one who feels no lust for the desirable, feels no hatred toward the undesirable, and feels neither delusion nor confusion in the face of the indifferent.

309. Regarding the phrase "there, depending on this, abandon that" within those thirty-six sets of seven points, the meaning is: "depending on eighteen, abandon eighteen. For this very reason, he said: "In this regard, monks, those six things based on renunciation," and so forth.
"Depending on" (*nissāya*) and "having come to" (*āgamma*) mean depending and having come to by way of their occurrence. In this way, there is the transcendence of these [fetters].
Thus, by the occurrence of those states based on renunciation, those based on the household life are said to have been transcended.

Having thus caused the similar to abandon the similar through similarity itself, he now says, "In this regard, monks, as for those six kinds of joy based on renunciation," and so forth, causing the weak to abandon the strong. Thus, by means of the joys based on renunciation...
By causing the grief based on renunciation and the joy based on renunciation to be abandoned by means of equanimity based on renunciation, the abandoning of the weak by the strong is described.
Standing here, however, the discussion of equanimity should be understood: for among the eight attainments, the first and so forth...
For four bhikkhus who have begun insight meditation by taking the three jhānas and pure formations as their basis, their preliminary insight is accompanied either by joy or by equanimity;
however, the insight leading to emergence is accompanied only by joy. For those who have begun insight meditation by taking the fourth jhāna and so forth as their basis...
The five kinds of preliminary insight are exactly as before. However, that which leads to emergence is accompanied by equanimity.

It is with reference to this that it was said: “Whatever six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation there are, relying on them and coming to them, abandon whatever six kinds of joy based on renunciation there are. And not only for one who practices in this way...

For a bhikkhu, this is merely a distinction of feeling within insight (*vipassanā*); however, in the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), there is also a distinction among the factors of jhāna, the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the path-factors (*maggaṅga*).
What, then, determines this distinction? Some elders say that it is the jhāna serving as the basis for insight that determines it;
some say it is the aggregates (*khandha*) that have become the object (*ārammaṇa*) of insight; and some say it is the individual’s inclination (*puggalajjhāsaya*).

They say that it "determines" [the object]. In their doctrine as well, it should be understood that this same insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*) in the prior stage is what determines it.
Furthermore, the detailed discussion on this point has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-niddesa*).
310. "Diversity" (*nānatta*) means various, many, and of manifold kinds. "Based on diversity" (*nānattasita*) means dependent on diverse objects. "Unity" (*ekatta*)...
"Single": it is "supported by unity" because it is supported by a single object. But what is this equanimity (*upekkhā*)? First, below, "equanimity as non-knowing" was mentioned;
above, he will speak of "six-factored equanimity"; here, two types of equanimity are included: equanimity of serenity (*samatha-upekkhā*) and equanimity of insight (*vipassanā-upekkhā*).

In that regard, since the equanimity toward visible forms is one thing and the equanimity toward sounds and so forth is another—for the equanimity that exists toward visible forms does not exist toward sounds and so forth—[the former] is distinct [from the latter].
It exists. Equanimity toward forms takes only form as its object, not sounds and so forth.

Furthermore, there is one kind of equanimity—the equanimity of serenity (*samatha-upekkhā*)—which arises having taken the earth-kasiṇa as its object, and another which takes the water-kasiṇa and so on.
Therefore, in order to analyze this diversity and that which depends upon diversity, he said: "There is, bhikkhus, equanimity toward forms," and so forth.

But because there are not two or three [identical] bases of infinite space or bases of infinite consciousness and so forth, he spoke thus—"There is, bhikkhus, equanimity dependent on the base of infinite space," and so on—in order to analyze unity as being based on unity.

Therein, equanimity toward the base of infinite space is "dependent on the base of infinite space" by way of association with that base; it is [dependent] upon the aggregates of the base of infinite space.

For one who is practicing insight, insight-equanimity is dependent on the base of infinite space by way of its object. The same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well. Regarding the phrase "abandon that":

here, through the equanimity of the formless-sphere attainment, one causes the abandonment of the equanimity of the fine-material-sphere attainment; and through the equanimity of formless-sphere insight, one abandons the equanimity of fine-material-sphere insight.
Regarding the term "non-identification" (*atammayatā*): here, "identification" (*tammayatā*) means craving; it is the insight leading to emergence that results from the exhaustion of that craving.

It is called "not being made of that" (*atammayata*). "Abandon that" means that here, by means of insight leading to emergence, one causes the abandoning of both the equanimity of the formless-sphere attainments and the equanimity of insight. 311.

"Those who are noble" (*yadariyo*) refers to those whom the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, cultivates in the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). In that regard, there are three points...
One who establishes mindfulness should be understood as one who cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "They do not wish to hear" means they do not desire to listen with faith.
"They do not understand" means they do not apply their minds for the sake of knowing.
"Having bypassed" means having transgressed. "The Teacher’s instruction" means they do not consider the Teacher’s advice to be something to be received or fulfilled. And "not pleased in mind."
"Not pleased. And here, one should not understand "he is dissatisfied" as being due to grief based on worldly attachments;

rather, this is said because there is an absence of the cause for mental satisfaction among those who have not entered the path. "Untainted" means untainted by the outflow of aversion (*paṭigha-avassava*).
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means endowed with both mindfulness and knowledge. "Equanimous" [refers to] the sixfold equanimity.
"Equanimous. Regarding "satisfied," even here the meaning should not be understood as being "elated" by way of the joy associated with household life;
rather, this is said because there is an absence of any cause for dissatisfaction among those practicing the path. "Untainted" means untainted by the outflow of passion (*rāga*).
"Tamed" means subdued. "He runs toward one direction alone" means that running without turning back, he heads toward only a single direction.
It runs, but having turned back, it is able to run toward another direction.
"It runs through the eight directions" means that while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, without turning the body, one runs through the eight directions simultaneously by way of liberation;
that is, having sat facing either the east or any other direction such as the south, one [attains] the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti).
The meaning is that he indeed attains [it]. The remainder is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*, is finished.
8. Commentary on the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta 313.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the *Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta*.

In this context, “exposition and analysis” (*uddesavibhaṅga*) means both the summary (*uddesa*) and the detailed exposition (*vibhaṅga*), that is, the matrix (*mātikā*) and its analytical explanation. “One should examine” means one should weigh, test, scrutinize, and define [the matter].
"Externally" means with respect to external objects. "Undistracted and unscattered": that which stands upon an object by way of attachment is called distracted and scattered;
he spoke thus in order to preclude that. "Not stuck internally": not stuck within the internal range of experience by way of attachment.
"Without clinging, one should not tremble": without grasping or seizing it...

One should not be anxious about consciousness. Just as consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, nor fixed internally, and thus, through non-clinging, one does not become anxious—in this way, a bhikkhu should investigate; this is what is meant.
"The origin and arising of the suffering of birth, aging, and death" refers to birth, aging, and death, as well as the remainder of suffering.
The meaning is that there is no rebirth. 316.
"One who follows after the sign of form" means one who recollects and pursues the sign of form; thus, one is "one who follows after the sign of form. 318.

"In this way, friend, it is not fixed internally" means it is not fixed by way of attachment (*nikanti*). For that which does not stand still by way of attachment does not partake of decline; rather, it partakes of distinction (*visesa*) alone.
320. "Agitation due to clinging" (*anupādā-paritassanā*): In the Khandhaka section, the Teacher said, "Monks, I will teach you agitation due to clinging and non-agitation due to non-clinging.
Having thus taken up [the topic], he explained that agitation occurs when there is grasping, and non-agitation occurs when there is no grasping.
The Great Elder (Mahāthera), however, demonstrated this by treating "non-agitation due to non-clinging" as being identical to "agitation due to clinging."
He spoke thus: "But how is this agitation without clinging (anupādā-paritassanā)? Because of the absence of anything to be clung to.

For if there were any formation (saṅkhāra) suitable to be grasped as permanent, stable, self, or belonging to a self, then this agitation would indeed be 'agitation due to clinging. But since no such formation exists that can be clung to..."
Since there is no [self], form and the other aggregates—though grasped—are in fact ungrasped according to the method beginning with "form is self.
Thus, although this anxiety due to views is identical to anxiety due to grasping, it should be understood that in actual meaning it is simply called "anxiety due to non-grasping.
"It becomes otherwise" means it changes, perishes by abandoning its natural state; thus, "following the transformation of form" refers to [the thought]: "My..."
In such ways as "form has changed" or "what was mine is no longer mine," kamma-consciousness follows upon the breaking up of form.
Born of following upon change means born from a consciousness that has change as its object, due to its following upon change.
"Agitation and the arising of states" refers to the agitation of craving and—

And from the arising of unwholesome states. "They remain having seized the mind" means they remain having seized, grasped, and exhausted the wholesome mind. "With anxiety" means with anxiety due to fear and with anxiety due to craving.
"With distress" means with affliction, accompanied by suffering. "With longing" means with attachment, with affection. Thus, friend, through non-clinging...

“There is agitation” means that, just as for one who takes up an empty casket under the perception that it is a jewel-casket and later falls into distress when it is lost, there is agitation because he did not take hold [of it] beforehand. (321) “And he does not undergo change following the change of form”:
for one whose taints are destroyed, there is no kamma-consciousness at all; therefore, there is no undergoing of change following the disintegration of form. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Uddesavibhaṅga-sutta* of the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima-nikāya*, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the *Araṇavibhaṅga-sutta*.
323. “Thus have I heard” refers to the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, “neither exalt nor disparage” means one should neither elevate nor debase any person by way of worldly attachment.
“Teach only the Dhamma” means one should speak only of the true nature of things.
“The determination of happiness” means happiness as it has been determined. “Speaking behind one’s back” means dispraise in the absence of the person; this is malicious speech.
Meaning: “Not exhausted in one’s presence” means that one should not speak words that are exhausted, crowded, or defiled even in one’s presence.

“One should not insist” means that one should not speak by fixating upon or grasping [a position]. “Conventional designation” refers to worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*) and worldly description (*lokapaṇṇatti*).
“One should not overstep” means one should not transgress it.

324. "Happy with the rebirth-linking of sense-sphere existence" means one who is happy by means of the pleasure associated with sense-sphere existence through that very rebirth-linking of sense-sphere existence.

"Accompanied by suffering" means accompanied by both the suffering of karmic result (*vipāka-dukkha*) and the suffering of defilement (*saṃkilesa-dukkha*). "With affliction" means afflicted precisely by the affliction of karmic results and the affliction of defilements;
likewise for "with fever. "Wrong practice" means a practice that is not according to reality, an unwholesome practice.

326. “In this way he disparages some” means that he disparages certain individuals by way of their attachment to the household life. The same method applies to exalting them as well. “The fetter of existence” (bhava-saṃyojana) is the bond of existence; this is a name for craving (taṇhā).

It is said that the Elder Subhūti was established in this list of foremost disciples (etadagga) on account of this tetrad. For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, the exalting and disparaging of individuals is observed, as it is with the Elder Sāriputta and others; such is the case for the Elder Subhūti.

However, in his teaching of the Dhamma, there is no such thing as saying, "This person has not practiced correctly and has not attained success," or "This one is virtuous, endowed with qualities, modest, pleasant, and perfect in conduct.
Rather, through his teaching of the Dhamma, only this is made known: "This is the wrong path; this is the right path. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples..."
“Among the monks who dwell in freedom from conflict (*araṇavihārī*), this one is Subhūti,” he said. 329. “One who knows the right time”:

Without speaking when the time has not yet arrived or when it has already passed, but rather having recognized the appropriate and fitting time—thinking, “Now, when it is being spoken, the great multitude will grasp it”—one should speak dispraise even behind someone’s back. This same principle applies even regarding the exhaustion of one's reputation (*khīṇavāda*).

330. “Is struck down” (*upahaññati*) means he is harmed. “Even his voice is struck down” means even his sound is broken. “He becomes distressed” (*āturīyati*) means he becomes afflicted, fallen into illness, and beset by disease. “Not fluent” (*avissaṭṭha*) means it is not fluent or unobstructed.
331. *Tadeva* means that very same vessel. *Abhinivissa voharati* (speaking while adhering [to a false notion]):
having gone to a country where people perceive it as a bowl, and upon hearing, "Bring the bowl! Wash the bowl!", the blind, foolish worldling adheres to the idea, "This is not a bowl;
this is a dish; speak thus," and so he speaks. This should be applied to all the following phrases. *Atisāro* means excessive running.

332. In whatever way one speaks without misapprehending—just as in our own country it is said, "he is dropping the vessel," whereas these people say, "he is dropping the bowl"—from that time on, setting aside the local usage, he speaks of the bowl simply as a "bowl" without misapprehending.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
