333. Now, while establishing the classification by way of boundaries (*mariyādabhājanīya*), he said, "In this regard, monks," and so forth.

Therein, "with conflict" (*saraṇo*) means having passion (*saraja*) and being defiled (*sakileso*). "Without conflict" (*araṇo*) means without passion (*arajo*) and free from defilement (*nikkileso*). Furthermore, as for the Elder Subhūti, monks—this elder has attained the foremost position in two respects:
"Among those who dwell without conflict, Subhūti is the foremost; among those worthy of offerings, Subhūti is the foremost."
It is said that the Dhammasenāpati purifies the site, while the Elder Subhūti purifies the offering.

For indeed, when the Dhammasenāpati goes for alms, he stands at the door of a house and, having delimited the preceding period until the alms are brought, enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
emerging from cessation, he receives the gift to be given. And the Elder Subhūti...
In that very way, he enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*), and having emerged from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, he accepts the gift to be given.
"Is it possible to do this? "Yes, it is possible; nor is it surprising that disciples who have attained great direct knowledge (*mahābhiññā*) should act in this manner.
For even in this island of Tambapaṇṇi, during the time of the ancient kings, the Elder Piṅgala-Buddharakkhita..."
He dwelt depending on a village named Uttaragāma. There were seven hundred families there;
not even a single door of a household was such that the Elder did not enter into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) at it. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta: 342.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta. In this context, *cārika* means a journey of hurried travel. If...
"Bhaggava, they are not a burden to you if there is nothing heavy or unpleasant for you.
If he grants permission," [the Buddha said]. It is said that this thought occurred to Bhaggava: "Those who have gone forth have various inclinations;
one delights in a group, while another delights in solitude. If he is one who delights in solitude, he might say, 'Friend, do not enter; the hall has been taken by me.'"
He will say: "If this person is intent on having it for himself alone, he will say, 'Friend, go out; the hall has been obtained by me.
If that were so, I would indeed become the instigator of a dispute between the two of them. What is given is simply given;
what is done is simply done. Therefore, he spoke thus.
"A son of good family" means both one who is a son of good family by birth and one who is a son of good family by conduct. "Has come to dwell" means he has arrived at a dwelling.
From where did he come? From the city of Takkasilā. Herein is the sequential account:
it is said that while King Bimbisāra was ruling in the city of Rājagaha in the Middle Country, King Pukkusāti ruled in the frontier city of Takkasilā. Then, having taken goods from Takkasilā...
Merchants arrived at Rājagaha bringing gifts and saw the king. When they had paid homage and stood before him, the king asked, "Where do you dwell?

They replied, "Your Majesty, we dwell in Takṣaśilā. Then the king, having inquired about the security, abundance of food, and other conditions in their country, as well as the state of their city, asked, "Who is your king? "He is named Pukkusāti," they said.
"Is he righteous, O King? "Yes, Your Majesty, he is righteous. He wins over the people with the four bases of sympathy;
standing in the place of a mother and father to the world, he gladdens the people like a child lying on his lap. "In what stage of life does he abide?
Then they explained his age to him. He was born of the same age as Bimbisāra. Then the king said to them:
“Dear ones, your king is righteous and of the same age as I; you might be able to make your king my friend.

“We can, Your Majesty,” they replied. The king released their customs duties, had houses built for them, and said, “Go, sell your goods, and when it is time to depart, come and see me before you leave. They did so.
When it was time to depart, they saw the king. He said to them, "Go, and in my name ask your king repeatedly after his health, and say, 'The king desires friendship with you.
Having assented, saying "Very well," they went, put away their goods, and after eating breakfast, approached the king.
They paid homage. The king asked, "Tell me, where have you been for all these days that you were not seen?
They reported the entire matter to him. The king was delighted and said, "Excellent, dear ones! By depending on you, I have gained a friendly king in the Middle Country.
Later, merchants living in Rājagaha also went to Takkasilā.
When Pukkusāti returned with those gifts, the king asked, "From where have you come?
Upon hearing, "From Rājagaha," he said, "You have come from the city of my friend. "Yes, Your Majesty," they replied.
Having inquired after his health, saying, "Is my friend well?", he continued, "From this day forward, whatever comes from the city of my friend—whether by caravan on foot or by caravan by cart—"

"Whether merchants come from abroad or from elsewhere, from the moment they enter my territory, let them be provided with lodging houses, let the royal storehouse supply them with provisions, let them be exempted from customs duties, and let no harm whatsoever befall them.
Thus he caused a drum to be beaten. King Bimbisāra likewise caused a drum to be beaten in his own city.
Then Bimbisāra sent a letter to Pukkusāti, saying: "Jewels such as gems and pearls arise in border regions;
whatever jewel arises in my friend’s kingdom that is worth seeing or hearing of, let him not be stingy with it.
Pukkusāti also [sent a reply]: "The Middle Country is indeed a great realm..."
"Let my friend not be stingy regarding such a jewel that may arise there," he said, and sent a messenger with this message.
As time passed and they traveled on, though they did not see one another, their friendship remained firm.
While they were thus living according to their agreement, the first gift-offering arrived for Pukkusāti.
It is said that the king obtained eight priceless five-colored blankets. Thinking, "These blankets are exceedingly beautiful;

I shall send them to my friend," he had eight sturdy caskets made the size of lac-balls, placed the blankets inside them, sealed them with lac, wrapped them in white cloth, put them into baskets, and covered them with cloth.
Having wrapped it up and sealed it with the royal seal, he dispatched his ministers with the message, "Give this to my companion.
He also gave this instruction: "This gift is to be presented in the middle of the city by one surrounded by ministers and others. They went and gave it to Bimbisāra.
Having heard the message, he had the drum beaten to assemble the ministers and others, and then, surrounded by his ministers and the rest, stood in the middle of the city.
Seated upon an excellent couch while a white parasol was being held over him, he broke the seal, removed the cloth,
opened the casket, and released the contents within; seeing the balls of lac, he thought, "My friend Pukkusāti,
thinking 'my friend is a money-lender,' has likely sent this gift," and taking one of the balls, he—
Rolling it in his hand and weighing it, he realized that there was a bundle of cloth inside.
Then, striking it against the leg of his couch, the lac immediately fell away. He opened the casket with his fingernail and saw a precious woolen blanket (*kambalaratana*) within;
he had the others opened as well, and they were all woolen blankets. He then had them spread out, and they were perfect in color.

They were sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width. When the great multitude saw them, they snapped their fingers and waved their garments, saying, "Our king has sent such a gift even without having seen his friend Pukkusāti;
it is indeed fitting to make such a person one's friend," and they were filled with joy. The king [examined] each one...
He had the blankets appraised; they were all found to be priceless. Among them, he sent four to the Perfectly Enlightened One and kept four for his own home.
Then he thought: "When sending later, it is fitting to send something superior to the gift already sent first.
My friend has sent me a priceless gift; what indeed should I send?"
"But is there no jewel in Rājagaha superior to that? "No, there is not, O King of great merit;
nevertheless, from the time he became a stream-enterer, there has been no other jewel capable of producing such joy for him except for the Three Jewels.
He began to search for a jewel—thinking, "A jewel is indeed something possessed of consciousness..."
The "insentient" is of two kinds. Therein, the insentient consists of gold, silver, and so forth; the sentient consists of that which is bound with sense-faculties.

The insentient serves as an adornment and so on for the sentient alone; thus, between these two types of treasure, the sentient is superior. The sentient is also of two kinds: animal treasure and human treasure.
In that regard, the animal treasure consists of the elephant and horse treasures; these too arise solely for the purpose of human enjoyment.
Thus, among these two [categories], the human treasure is the most excellent. The human treasure is also twofold: the woman-treasure and the man-treasure.
Among those, even the woman-treasure that arises for a wheel-turning monarch is for the enjoyment of the man alone.
Thus, even among these two, the jewel of a person alone is the most excellent.
And the jewel of a person is twofold: the jewel of a householder and the jewel of one who has gone forth from the household life.

Among those, even among the jewels of householders, a universal monarch (cakravartin) today pays homage with the fivefold prostration to a novice monk who has just gone forth; thus, between these two as well—
The jewel of the homeless life alone is the best. The jewel of the homeless life is also twofold:
the jewel of those in training (sekha) and the jewel of those beyond training (asekha). Among these, even a hundred thousand of those in training do not equal a single portion of one beyond training;
thus, of these two as well, the jewel of those beyond training alone is the best. That too is twofold: the Buddha-jewel and the disciple-jewel. Among these, even a hundred thousand...
The jewel of the disciples does not reach even a fraction of the jewel of the Buddha; thus, between these two, the jewel of the Buddha alone is supreme.
The jewel of the Buddha is also twofold: the jewel of the *paccekabuddha* and the jewel of the omniscient Buddha (*sabbaññubuddha*).

Among these, even a hundred thousand *paccekabuddhas* do not reach a fraction of the omniscient Buddha; thus, between these two as well, it is the jewel of the omniscient Buddha alone [that is supreme].
It is supreme. For in this world with its devas, there is no jewel equal to the Jewel of the Buddha.
Therefore, thinking, "I shall send an incomparable jewel to my companion," he asked the inhabitants of Takṣaśilā:
"Sirs, are these Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—to be found in your country? And the report, O Great King, was as follows:
“For that long there was nothing there; but from where did this sight come?

Delighted, the king thought, “It would be well, my dear, if for the sake of winning over the people I could send the Fully Enlightened One to the dwelling place of my friend. But Buddhas [do not go] to outlying regions.
They do not rise at dawn; therefore, it is not possible for the Teacher to go. It might be possible to send the great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

However, even though I have heard that the Elders are dwelling in the border regions, it is more appropriate for me to send men and command them to come into my presence to attend upon me; therefore, it is not possible for the Elders to go either.
"However, in whatever manner the Teacher and the Great Disciples departed when they were sent forth by the Dispensation, in that same manner shall I send forth the Dispensation.
Having thus reflected, he had a golden plate made—four cubits in length and a span in width, neither too thin nor too thick—and thought, "Today I shall inscribe the letters upon it. At dawn...
Having bathed his head, undertaken the observances of the Uposatha, and finished his breakfast, he removed his perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Taking a golden casket containing vermilion, he ascended the palace, closing the doors starting from below.
Opening the lion-window facing the eastern direction, he sat upon the terrace of the sky and, writing characters upon a golden tablet, said: "Here..."

“A Tathāgata has arisen in the world—an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Thus, the qualities of the Buddha have first been written down in part. Then:
“Having thus fulfilled the ten perfections and passed away from the Tusita heaven, he took rebirth in the mother’s womb.”
He grasped it; thus was there the opening of the world. While dwelling in his mother’s womb, such-and-such occurred;
while dwelling in the midst of the household, such-and-such occurred. Thus he went forth on the Great Renunciation and thus undertook the Great Struggle.
Having performed the practice of austerities, he ascended the Great Seat of Enlightenment and, sitting upon the Invincible Throne, attained omniscient knowledge.
He penetrated it; as he was penetrating the knowledge of omniscience, this revelation of the world occurred to him:
"In the world with its devas, there is no other such jewel as this.
Whatever wealth there may be here or in the hereafter,"
Whatever exquisite jewel exists in the celestial realms,
there is nothing equal to the Tathāgata;
this too is the exquisite jewel in the Buddha.

“By this truth, may there be well-being!”—Having thus written [the praise] in part regarding the qualities of the Buddha, he then extols the second jewel, the Dhamma: “The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One...
it is to be personally realized by the wise. “The four foundations of mindfulness... the Noble [Eightfold Path]...”
“The Eightfold Path. Having written down a portion of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, [he wrote]:
“The pure [Dhamma] which the Best of Buddhas praised...”
They call the immediate concentration the supreme;
there exists nothing equal to that concentration.
This too is a sublime treasure among the Dhamma.
“By this truth, may there be well-being!
Having thus inscribed the qualities of the Dhamma in part, he praises the third jewel, the Saṅgha, saying: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way...
[and so on] ...it is a field of merit for the world. “Noble sons indeed [listen to] the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma...”

Having heard this, they go forth and renounce the world; some renounce after abandoning the white parasol [of royalty], some the position of viceroy, and some the positions of commander-in-chief and so forth.

Having gone forth, they fulfill this practice—having briefly written down the Cūḷasīla, Majjhimasīla, Mahāsīla, and so on—they [practice] the restraint of the six doors and mindfulness with clear comprehension.
I have written in brief about contentment with the four requisites, the ninefold lodgings, the preliminary work for abandoning the hindrances, the jhānas and direct knowledges,
and the thirty-eight meditation subjects up to the destruction of the taints; however, having written the sixteenfold meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing in detail,
[it is shown that] "the Teacher’s Saṅgha of disciples is endowed with such qualities as these."
Those eight hundred persons who have been praised consist of these four pairs;
they are the disciples of the Sugata worthy of offerings.
"Gifts given to these yield great fruit;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha.
By this truth, may there be well-being!"
Having thus written of the qualities of the Saṅgha in part, and having written: "The Blessed One’s teaching is well-expounded and leads to liberation;

if my friend is able, let him go forth from home into homelessness," he folded the golden plate, wrapped it in fine woolen cloth, placed it inside a casket made of the finest materials, and that casket [he placed] in one made of gold, and that [in another] made of gold...
In a silver casket he placed a silver one; in a jeweled one, a jeweled one; in a coral one, a coral one; in a ruby one, a ruby one;
in a masāragalla stone one, a masāragalla stone one; in a crystal one, a crystal one; in an ivory one, an ivory one;
in a casket made of all kinds of gems, a casket made of all kinds of gems; and in a casket made of kilañja grass, he placed a small box made of kilañja grass.

Again, having carried the wooden casket (*sārakaraṇḍaka*)—which was a golden casket—in the same manner as before, he placed the casket made of all kinds of gems (*sabbaratanamaya*) inside a casket made of *kilañja* grass.

Then, having carried the *kilañja* grass casket in the same manner as previously described, he placed it inside a chest made of all kinds of gems; and having placed that chest outside [of another], he covered it with cloth.
Having wrapped it up and sealed it with the royal seal, he commanded his ministers: "Decorate the road at the place where my commands are issued;
let the road be eight cubits wide, but let only the space of four cubits be cleared away;
in the center, prepare a space of four cubits with royal splendor. Then, having decorated the auspicious elephant, he—
Having prepared a palanquin above, raised a white parasol, and caused the city streets to be sprinkled and swept,
adorned with hoisted flags and banners, and beautifully decorated with plantain trees, full water-pots, perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth,
he dispatched swift messengers to the intermediate officials, instructing them: "Let each person perform such worship in their own district," while he himself, adorned with all his ornaments...

Having adorned himself and surrounded by a body of troops accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, he went as far as the boundary of his own territory and sent a message through the minister, saying:
"Dear sir, my friend Pukkusāti should accept this gift;
let him not receive it amidst the women of the harem, but rather ascend to the palace and accept it there."
Having thus given these instructions, [the King] prostrated with the fivefold salutation, thinking, "The Teacher is going to the border country," and turned back.
The officials of the interior likewise prepared the road according to that same procedure and brought offerings.
Pukkusāti also, starting from his own royal boundary, prepared the road according to that same procedure and [reached] the city.
Having removed his ornaments, he went out to meet the gift. As the gift reached Takkasilā, it arrived on the Uposatha day;
the minister who had gone to fetch the gift took it and delivered the message the king had sent.
Upon hearing this, the king deliberated on what should be done for those who had come with the gift, and taking the gift himself, he ascended the palace.
Thinking, "Let no one enter here," he had the door guarded;

then, opening the window-lattice, he placed the gift upon a high seat and sat himself on a low seat. Breaking the seal and removing the outer cloth, he began unrolling it from the palm-leaf basket in successive layers.
Seeing a casket made of precious material, he thought: "This is not of small value."
"There will be another jewel; surely a jewel worthy of being heard has appeared in the Middle Country.
Then, having opened that casket, broken the royal seal, and drawn aside the fine woolen cloth from both sides, he saw a golden tablet.
So, having spread it out, he began to read from the beginning, saying: "How delightful indeed are these letters—equal at the head, equal at the edges, and perfectly square!

As he read the qualities of the Buddha, "Herein the Tathāgata has arisen in the world," a powerful joy arose within him, and the ninety-nine thousand pores of his body stood with their hairs bristling. His own...
He did not know whether [the teacher] was standing or sitting. Then, thinking, "Even in hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons it would be difficult to hear this teaching;
yet now, by depending on this companion, I am able to hear it," a powerful joy arose within him even more intensely.
Being unable to recite further, he sat down until the surge of that joy subsided, and then continued: "Well-expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One..."
He began with the qualities of the Dhamma, saying, "The Dhamma. There too, it was exactly the same for him.
Then, having sat down until the surge of rapture had subsided, he proceeded to begin with the qualities of the Saṅgha, saying, "Well-practiced. There too, it was exactly the same for him.
Finally, having recited the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) to its very end, he attained the fourfold and fivefold jhānas.
He spent his time solely in the bliss of *jhāna*. No one else was permitted to see him; only his junior attendant (*cūḷupaṭṭhāka*) would enter.
In this way, he passed about half a month.
The citizens gathered in the royal courtyard and raised a clamor, saying, "From the day the gift was accepted..."
“There is no display of military strength nor any theatrical performance; there is no rendering of legal judgments.
The king intends to show the gift sent by his ally to whomever he wishes. Kings, indeed, strive to seize a kingdom for themselves even by deceiving someone with a gift.
What, then, is our king doing? At this, the king raised a shout of acclamation.
Having heard this, he thought, "Shall I uphold the kingdom, or shall I uphold the Teacher? Then it occurred to him:
"The personhood produced by a kingdom cannot be reckoned even by an accountant or a chief minister; I shall uphold the Teacher’s dispensation.
Taking the sword placed upon his bed, cutting off his hair, and opening the lion-window, he said: "Take this..."
"Rule the kingdom! he said, and threw his mass of hair together with the crest-jewel into the midst of the assembly.
The great multitude, lifting it up, cried out all at once: "O King, there have never been kings like you who receive such a gift from a friend!
Even the king’s beard and mustache were only two finger-breadths long; indeed, they say it was as if he had already gone forth into homelessness.
Then, having sent his junior attendant and had two saffron robes and an earthen bowl brought from the marketplace,
he thought, "My going-forth is for the sake of those who are Arhats in the world. Addressing himself to the Teacher,
he put on one saffron robe as an undergarment and the other as an upper robe, placed the bowl upon the left shoulder, took up a walking staff, and [thought], "He shines..."
"Is it indeed for me to go forth, or not? Having paced back and forth several times on the great terrace, he thought, "Going forth suits me," and opening the door, he descended from the palace.

As he was descending, however, the dancers and others stationed at the three gates did not even recognize him, thinking, "A solitary Buddha (paccekabuddha) has come to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma to our king."

They thought thus. But having ascended to the upper terrace and seen the places where the king had stood and sat, they realized, "The king has gone," and they cried out all at once, like the people on a ship sinking in the middle of the ocean.
As soon as the noble youth had stepped onto the ground, eighteen armies and all the city-dwellers and military forces surrounded him, raising a great cry.
They cried out. The ministers also said this to him: "Your Majesty, the kings of the Middle Country are full of guile;
having sent a message, they will find out whether the Jewel of the Buddha has appeared in the world or not, and then they will come.
Turn back, Your Majesty! [He replied: "I have faith in my friend; there is no possibility of double-dealing from his part toward me."
“There is none; you may stay,” he said. They followed him nonetheless.
The noble son drew a line with a walking stick and asked, “To whom does this kingdom belong? “To you, O Lord,” they replied.
“Whoever crosses this line shall be punished by royal decree. [This was spoken] by the Bodhisatta in the Mahājanaka Jātaka.
Unable to bear the separation, Queen Sīvalī turned back and departed. The great multitude followed along the path she had taken.
However, the multitude was unable to part with that letter; placing it upon their heads, they cried out as they turned back.
The noble youth [thought]: "In the place where I have gone, [I left] my tooth-stick or mouth-water..."
Thinking, "He will give it," he departed without taking even a single servant.
It occurred to him, "My Teacher went forth all alone after making the Great Renunciation," and so he went alone.
Thinking, "I am ashamed before my Teacher"—and thinking, "It is said that my Teacher, having gone forth, did not mount a vehicle"—he did not take even a single-layered sandal.
He did not mount [the vehicle], nor did he carry an umbrella of leaves. The great multitude, having climbed up trees, walls, watchtowers, and so forth, looked on, saying, "This king of ours is going.
The noble son thought, "It is a long way to go;
it is not possible for one person to traverse the path alone," and followed a certain caravan leader. Because of his delicate nature, the noble son...
As he walks upon the earth, blisters arise on the soles of his feet and burst open, and painful sensations arise.
When the caravan leader has pitched camp and is seated, a son of good family steps off the road and sits at the foot of a tree.
At that place where he sits, there is no one to perform massage for his feet or massage for his back.

The son of good family, having attained the fourth *jhāna* of mindfulness of breathing and having suppressed the distress, fatigue, and fever of the journey, passes the time in the delight of *jhāna*.
When dawn has risen on the following day, he attends to his physical needs and again follows the caravan leader. At the time of the morning meal—
Taking the bowl of the noble son, they placed hard and soft food into it and gave it to him.

That food was sometimes with unhusked grains, sometimes moist, sometimes with an equal amount of sugar, and sometimes slightly under-salted or over-salted; yet the noble son, having reflected upon the place from which he had entered, partook of it as if it were the Deathless (amata).
Following this method, he traveled one hundred and ninety-two leagues. [He arrived at] the gateway of the Jeta Grove monastery.
However, even though he was traveling nearby, he did not ask, "Where does the Teacher dwell?

Why? Because of his reverence for the Teacher and because of the message sent by the king. For the king had sent the message thinking that the Teacher had arisen in Rājagaha, as if the Tathāgata had appeared right there; therefore, without asking him, [he traveled] forty-five yojanas.
He had passed beyond the road. Having reached Rājagaha at the time of sunset, he asked, "Where does the Teacher dwell?
"From where have you come, venerable sir? "From up north. "The Teacher says that on the road you have come from, at a distance of forty-five yojanas from here, there is a place called Sāvatthī;
He dwells there. The noble youth thought: "Now is not the right time; it is not possible to go."
“Having stayed right here today, I shall go to the presence of the Teacher tomorrow.
Then he asked, “Where do those who have gone forth and arrived at an improper time stay? “In this potter’s workshop, venerable sir,” he replied.
Thereupon, having requested permission from that potter, he entered it for the sake of lodging and sat down.
On that very day, as the Blessed One surveyed the world at dawn, he saw Pukkusāti and thought:
"This son of good family, having read only the message sent by his friend, has renounced a great kingdom extending over more than three hundred leagues and gone forth for my sake;
he has already traveled two hundred leagues minus eight to reach Rājagaha."
If I do not go, he will die a helpless death after staying for only one night without having realized the three fruits of recluseship;
but if I go, he will realize the three fruits of recluseship.
It was solely for the sake of gathering people together that I fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kappas.
“[He] has fulfilled [his duty]; I shall show him favor. Having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, surrounded by the community of monks, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī.
After the meal, returning from the alms round, he entered the Fragrant Chamber and, having calmed his bodily fatigue and exhaustion for a short while, thought:
“This son of good family, out of reverence for me, has performed what is difficult to do...”

Having abandoned his kingdom, which extended for more than a hundred yojanas, and without taking even a single servant who might have provided him with water for rinsing his mouth, he departed all alone.
Without having taken leave of anyone among Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and the others, he himself took his own bowl and robes and went forth by himself.
And as he went, he neither leaped into the air nor [touched] the earth.

He summarized: “This clansman has gone forth out of shame for me, not sitting in even a single vehicle—be it elephant, horse, chariot, golden palanquin, or the like—and not even putting on a single-layered sandal, nor taking up even a leaf-parasol;
therefore, it is fitting that I too should go on foot. Having thought thus, he proceeded on foot.
Thus, concealing this splendor of a Buddha— namely, the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—
he traveled in the guise of a certain bhikkhu like the full moon shrouded by clouds;
and in the time of a single afternoon meal, having traversed forty-five yojanas, he arrived at the hour of sunset before the sons of noble family.
As soon as he had entered, he reached that potter’s workshop. With reference to him it was said:

“At that time, Pukkusāti by name, a clansman who had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith for the sake of the Blessed One, had already arrived and taken up residence in that potter’s workshop.”

Having gone thus, however, the Blessed One—without entering the potter’s hall by force, thinking, “I am the Fully Enlightened One,” but remaining at the door while asking the noble son for permission—said, “If those bhikkhus...,” and so forth. “Urunda” means secluded and unconfined.
“May the venerable one dwell at ease” means in whichever posture of conduct he finds comfort.
"May the Venerable One dwell at his ease," he said, granting him permission.

For what noble son, having renounced a kingdom of more than one hundred and fifty leagues and gone forth into homelessness, would begrudge another fellow practitioner a potter's shed that had been discarded and fallen into ruin?
Yet some foolish men, having gone forth in this Teaching, are overcome by such things as stinginess regarding their dwelling place.
In their own dwelling places, they strive to prevent others from living there, thinking, "This is my hut;

this is my courtyard. The Lord of the World, though exceedingly delicate, sat down—having abandoned his perfumed chamber which resembled a celestial palace—in a place like a rubbish heap, strewn here and there with ashes, broken vessels, grass, leaves, and the filth of chickens, pigs, and the like.
Having spread a grass mat in the potter’s workshop and arranged his rag-robe (paṃsukūlacīvara),
he sat down as if entering and sitting within a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) resembling a celestial palace,
perfumed with divine scents. Thus, the Blessed One was born into the unbroken lineage of Mahā-Sammata, and though he was a son of noble family, he grew up in the womb of a Kṣatriya.

The Blessed One was endowed with the great resolve, and the noble son was also endowed with the great resolve. The Blessed One had renounced his kingdom and gone forth, and the noble son had done likewise.
The Blessed One was golden-hued, and the noble son was also golden-hued. The Blessed One was an attainer of meditative absorptions, and the noble son was also an attainer of meditative absorptions.
Thus, both were Kṣatriyas, both were endowed with the great resolve, both were renunciants who had left their kingdoms, and both were golden-hued.
Both of them, golden-hued and attainers of meditative absorption, entered the potter’s workshop and sat down;
thus the potter’s workshop shone exceedingly with them. This should be illustrated by the example of a cave into which two lions have entered.
Regarding those two, the Blessed One said: "I am delicate, most delicate; with a single meal after the midday meal, [I traveled] forty-five yojanas..."
The noble son, however—without even giving rise to the thought, "I have come from nine thousand two hundred yojanas;
let me lie down for a moment to dispel the fatigue of the road"—remained seated and entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
The other, likewise, without giving rise to the thought, "I have come from nine thousand two hundred yojanas; let me lie down for a moment to dispel the fatigue of the road," remained seated.
He attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Then the Blessed One, for much of the night," and so forth.
But surely the Blessed One had come thinking, "I will teach the Dhamma to this clansman"; why then did he not teach it?
Because the clansman’s weariness from the journey toward the path had not yet subsided; he would not have been able to receive the teaching of the Dhamma. So long as that...
He did not teach [the Dhamma], thinking, "May it be stilled. Others say: "Rājagaha is crowded with people and not secluded from ten kinds of sounds;
that noise subsides after only one and a half watches of the night, and he did not teach while staying there.
That is not the reason, for the Blessed One has the power to still even a sound as vast as the Brahma-world by his own majesty.
He was able [to teach], yet he did not preach because he was waiting for the subsiding of the fatigue from the journey.
"There, for much of the night" means for about one and a half watches. "This thought occurred to him":

having emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), the Blessed One—like opening a jeweled lion-window in a golden palace—beheld those [beings] adorned with the fivefold clarity (*pañcapasāda*).

He opened his eyes and looked; then, seeing the noble son sitting like a golden statue—immovable and unflinching like a firmly driven wooden pillar, free from fidgeting with the hands, fidgeting with the feet, or shaking of the head—he thought:
"He is indeed inspiring" (*pāsādiko*), and so forth. In this context, *pāsādika* means "bringing about confidence. It is a gerundive (future passive participle) used as a neuter noun.
Now, he conducts himself with a graceful deportment. The meaning here is that he conducts himself in such a way that his deportment becomes graceful as he conducts himself.
For among the four modes of deportment, three do not shine;
for when a bhikkhu is walking, his hands shake, his feet shake, and his head shakes; and when he is standing, his body [shakes].
He becomes rigid; even his posture while lying down is unpleasant.

However, after the meal, having swept the day-quarters, spread out a piece of leather, and washed his hands and feet, the posture of one who has folded his legs in the fourfold cross-legged position (pallaṅka) shines forth.
And this clansman, having folded his legs in the cross-legged position, [attains] the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna).
Having sat down after eating, the Blessed One, inspired by his very deportment, reflected: "He is indeed inspiring.
Why did he ask, "What if I were to question him"? Does the Blessed One not know that he has gone forth for his own sake?
No, he does not not know; however, without being asked, the discourse does not become established, and if the discourse is not established...
He asked in order to establish a discussion, thinking, "How can a conversation arise?
And as for the phrase "and having seen, you would know": everyone knows that this is the Buddha when the Tathāgata shines with the glory of a Buddha.
Such knowledge is not extraordinary; however, [he spoke thus] concealing the Buddha’s glory and appearing in the guise of a certain alms-collector.
While walking, he becomes difficult to recognize. Thus, Venerable Pukkusāti, by saying “one might not know him,” he speaks of his very nature;
for even though he was sitting in a single potter’s shed, they did not know him.

“This thought occurred to him” means that it occurred to him after he had recognized the state of the subsiding of the fatigue from the journey. “‘So be it, friend,’ said the noble youth” refers to his companion.
Having read merely the message sent, he renounced his kingdom and went forth, thinking: "I shall be able to hear the sweet teaching of the Dhamma from the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
Having gone forth and traveling for such a long distance, he did not find anyone who would even utter the words, "I shall teach the Dhamma to you, monk";
yet [the Buddha] said, "I shall teach the Dhamma to you, monk."
What has been spoken will he not listen to with diligence? For this person is like a thirsty hog and like a thirsty elephant;
therefore, pledging himself to listen with diligence, he said, "So be it, friend.
343. "These six elements," said the Blessed One, without first explaining the preliminary practice for a clansman, [spoke] from the very beginning.
He has begun to explain precisely the characteristic of insight (vipassanālakkhaṇa), which is absolute emptiness (accantasuññatā) and serves as the proximate cause for Arahatship.
For one whose preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā) is not yet purified, [the Teacher first explains] restraint in virtue (sīlasaṃvara), guarding the doors of the sense faculties,
moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga), the seven true qualities (saddhamma), and the four meditative absorptions (jhāna).

He explains this preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*). However, for one in whom this is purified, he does not explain that [preliminary practice], but rather explains only insight (*vipassanā*), which is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for Arahantship. And for this clansman, the preliminary practice is purified;
for indeed, having been taught the Dispensation (*sāsana*), while remaining in the excellent palace itself, he attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*).
He had produced [a vehicle] that served as a means of transport for him when he was traveling ninety-nine leagues;

his novice morality was also complete. Therefore, without explaining the preliminary practice, [the Teacher] began to explain to him the characteristic of insight—absolute emptiness—which is the proximate cause for Arahantship.
In this context, "consisting of six elements" means that while the elements exist, the person does not exist.

For the Blessed One shows the non-existent by means of the existent in some instances, the existent by means of the non-existent in others, the existent by means of the existent in others, and the non-existent by means of the non-existent in others;
this should be elaborated in full according to the method stated regarding "all taints. Here—
However, he spoke thus while demonstrating the non-existent by means of the existent.

For if the Blessed One had set aside the designation "person" and, having merely said "elements," caused the mind to fix upon them, the clansman might have become doubtful, fallen into confusion, and would not have been able to receive the teaching. Therefore, the Tathāgata [proceeded] step by step.

Having abandoned the conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*) of "man," [the Buddha] spoke thus like a teacher skilled in various dialects who teaches a craft through whatever language is appropriate, saying: "Whether called 'being' (*satta*), 'man' (*purisa*), or 'person' (*puggala*), these are merely designations;

in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as a 'being. Having established the mind upon the mere elements (*dhātu*), I shall cause you to penetrate the three fruits. This was said in the *Anaṅgaṇa-sutta*.
In this context, "one who has six elements" means *cha-dhāturo*. This is what is meant: that which you perceive as a "person" consists of six elements;

herein, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), no person exists, for "person" is merely a conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti-matta*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
Regarding the phrase "having four foundations" (*catur-adhiṭṭhāno*): here, "foundation" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is said to mean a "basis" (*patiṭṭhā*); thus, it means "having four bases."
The meaning is this: this person, the bhikkhu, consists of six elements, six bases of contact, and eighteen mental explorations;

turning away from just these, and grasping Arahantship which is the supreme accomplishment, he grasps it by being established in these four points—thus it is called "the four foundations" (*caturadhiṭṭhāna*). "Established where" means established in those foundations.
“Or conceit does not arise” means that either conceiving or pride does not arise. “The sage is called ‘peaceful’” means that the sage whose taints are destroyed is called “calmed” and “extinguished.

“One should not neglect wisdom” means that from the very beginning, for the sake of penetrating the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship, one should not neglect the wisdom of concentration and insight. “One should guard truth” means...
For the sake of realizing Nibbāna, the ultimate truth, one should from the very beginning guard the truth of speech.
One should cultivate generosity means that for the sake of abandoning all defilements by means of the path of Arahatship, one should from the very beginning cultivate the abandonment of defilements.

"He should train only in peace" means that for the sake of the subsiding of all defilements by means of the path of Arahatship, one should from the very beginning [cultivate] the subsiding of defilements.
One should train. Thus, these foundations of serenity, insight, and wisdom have been taught as preliminary supports for the purpose of attaining the foundations of wisdom and so forth. 345.

"Sphere of contact" (*phassāyatana*) means the source (*āyatana*) of contact; that is, its origin. The "foundation of wisdom" and so forth should be understood by way of the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship and the other qualities mentioned previously.
348. Now, according to the order in which the matrix (mātikā) was laid down, one might have expected it to be stated: "Wherein conceptual proliferation (maññassa) does not proceed.
However, once Arahantship has been attained, there is no further need for such tasks as "one should not neglect wisdom" and so forth.
Thus, although the Blessed One has placed the matrix out of its sequential order, he analyzes the exposition (vibhaṅga) in accordance with the nature of the Dhamma itself.
He said, "One should not neglect wisdom," and so forth. In this regard, who neglects wisdom and who does not?

First, one who has gone forth in this dispensation but maintains his livelihood through the twenty-one kinds of improper search, such as medical practice and the like, and is unable to establish a state of mind appropriate for the going-forth—this person is said to neglect wisdom. As for the one who...
But one who has gone forth in the Dispensation, established in virtue, mastered the word of the Buddha, undertaken a suitable ascetic practice (dhutaṅga),
taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to his own preference, and relying on a secluded lodging, performs the preliminary work for the kasiṇas,
attains meditative absorption, and then develops insight, thinking "Arahatship this very day," and wanders about— this is wisdom.
"Not being negligent" means this. However, in this sutta, this diligence through wisdom is stated by way of the meditation subject on the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*).
As for what ought to be said regarding the meditation subject on the elements here, that has already been explained below in the *Hatthipadopama-sutta* and others.
354. Furthermore, "only consciousness remains"—this too is a separate connection (*anusandhi*) here. From below...

For while the meditation subject consisting of form has already been explained, this teaching is now commenced in order to demonstrate the meditation subject consisting of the formless by way of feeling;

or alternatively, it was begun so as to show that very consciousness which acts as the agent of kamma for this bhikkhu through the insight to be arrived at regarding the earth element and so forth, by analyzing it according to the consciousness element.
In that context, as for "it remains": for what purpose does it remain? It remains for the purpose of the Teacher’s discourse and for the purpose of the noble son’s penetration.
"Pure" means free from defilement. "Bright" means luminous.
"He also cognizes pleasure" means that when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling. The same applies to the other two phrases.
This is the method. However, if this discussion of feeling had not been explained below, it would have been appropriate to explain it here;
but since it has already been explained in the *Satipaṭṭhāna*, it should be understood according to the method explained there.
The phrase "to be experienced as pleasant," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of showing the arising and passing away by way of conditions. Therein, "to be experienced as pleasant" means:
It is that which has become a condition for pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

"Only equanimity remains"—for at this point, it is just as if a skilled master jeweler, having pierced a piece of leather with a diamond needle and repeatedly dropping [beads] upon it, were to have his pupil take each one as it fell and thread it onto a string.

Just as one making a network of pearls or strings of pearls makes them repeatedly, so too this clansman, by attending again and again to the meditation subject given by the Blessed One after he had spoken and spoken, made it proficient;
thus both his material meditation subject and his immaterial meditation subject became proficient. Then the Blessed One said: "After that, only equanimity will remain."
But for what purpose does it remain? It remains for the purpose of the Teacher’s discourse. Some say it is for the purpose of the noble son’s penetration;

that should not be accepted. For while the noble son was standing on the terrace of his palace reading the message to his friend, he had already produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, which served as a vehicle for him as he traveled along this much of the path.
He accomplishes it. It remains only for the purpose of the Teacher’s discourse.
For at this point, the Teacher spoke in praise of the fine-material-sphere jhāna for the clansman. This is what is meant: "Bhikkhu, this fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna is familiar to you.
The passage beginning with "purified" is a description of the praises of that very equanimity. "One should tie up a torch" means a pan of burning coals.
One would prepare it. "One would kindle it" means: having placed charcoal there and applied fire, one would fan it with a bellows to make the fire blaze.
"One would throw it into the mouth of a furnace" means: having spread out the coals, one would place it on top of the coals, or one would throw it into the heated [furnace].
"Drawn out" means: its defects have been removed. "With impurities removed" means: with dross eliminated. "In the same way" means: just so.
Just as that gold serves for whatever kind of ornament one desires, even so he praised this equanimity of the fourth jhāna,
saying that it serves for whatever purpose one wishes among these: insight, direct knowledge, cessation,
or the transition to existence (bhavokkantī).
But why did the Blessed One, in this case, speak in praise rather than in dispraise of this fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere for the purpose of exhausting attachment?
For a clansman’s obsession with attachment toward the fourth jhāna is powerful.
If he were to speak in dispraise, [the thought would arise]: "For me, having gone forth and come from nine thousand two hundred yojanas..."

The fourth jhāna accomplished the function of a vehicle; "I have come along this entire path through the bliss of jhāna and the delight of jhāna, yet he speaks dispraise of such a sublime state—is he speaking knowingly or unknowingly?"—thus a clansman might fall into doubt and confusion.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke in its praise.
361. "Tadanudhammaṃ" (in accordance with that): here, the immaterial-sphere jhāna is called "dhamma"; because it follows that, the fine-material-sphere jhāna is said to be "anudhamma.
Alternatively, the resultant jhāna is "dhamma," and the wholesome jhāna is "anudhamma. "Tadupādāya" means by taking up or grasping that.
"Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ" (for a long period of time) refers to twenty thousand aeons; for this is stated by way of the resultant [state].
The same method applies even beyond this.
Having thus described the praise of the formless-sphere jhāna in four sections, he now spoke the passage beginning with "He understands thus" in order to show its disadvantage.
In that context, regarding the phrase "this is conditioned": although twenty thousand eons [are the lifespan] here, it is still conditioned.
There is life, but this is conditioned, constructed, and produced by effort; it is made by one who acts.
It is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, temporary, subject to falling away, disintegration, and destruction;
it is followed by birth, permeated by aging, struck down by death, established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become a non-refuge.
The same method applies to the base of infinite consciousness and the others as well.
Now, taking up the teaching by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship, he said: "He does not even form that," and so forth.
For just as a skilled physician, seeing the effects of poison, causes vomiting, removes the poison from its place, and then administers an antidote;
Just as one might drop poison onto the ground without allowing it to touch either the shoulder or the head,
even so the Blessed One spoke in praise of the formless-sphere jhānas to the clansman. Having heard this,
the clansman exhausted his attachment to the fine-material-sphere jhānas and established his aspiration for the formless-sphere jhānas.
The Blessed One, knowing that, addressed that bhikkhu who had not yet attained or acquired [these states]:
"There exists this so-called attainment in the base of infinite space and so forth. For their lifespan in the first Brahma-world is twenty thousand eons;
in the second, forty; in the third, sixty; and in the fourth, eighty-four thousand eons. Yet that is impermanent, unstable, and non-eternal."
It is temporary, subject to falling away, disintegration, and destruction; it is followed by birth, permeated by aging, and struck down by death;
it is established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become a non-refuge;
and even after experiencing prosperity therein for so long, one performs the passing away of an ordinary person and falls once more into the four states of misery.
"All this must be abandoned"—by this single phrase, he described all that danger as "this is conditioned.
Upon hearing this, the son of good family exhausted his attachment to the formless-sphere jhānas.

The Blessed One, knowing that his attachment to the fine-material and formless spheres had been exhausted, spoke the words beginning with "He does not construct that" while reaching the pinnacle of Arahantship for him.
Or again, suppose a certain great warrior, having gratified a king, were to receive an excellent village yielding a hundred thousand [measures] of revenue;
then, the king, remembering his prowess and thinking, "This warrior is of great power, yet he has received but little," might say, "My son, this village is not suitable for you;
take another yielding four hundred thousand [measures] of revenue," and would give it to him.
Saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," he would dismiss him and seize the other village. Before the messenger had even arrived, the king would summon him and say, "What use have you for that place?
A plague of snake-bites breaks out there. However, in such-and-such a location there is a great city;
raise the royal parasol there and rule over it. He would do accordingly.
In this context, the Perfectly Enlightened One is to be seen as the king; the noble son Pukkusāti as the great warrior;
the first village obtained as the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna);

and the time when he was told, "Relinquish that [first] village and take the other," as the relinquishing of attachment to the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing and the subsequent teaching on the formless attainments (āruppa). [This occurred] before he had even reached that [other] village.
It is like the time when [the king] summoned him and said, "What use have you for that? A disease caused by wind and snakes arises there.
There is a city in such-and-such a place; go there, raise the royal parasol, and rule the kingdom.

In the same way, by describing the danger through such statements as "this is conditioned in the formless realm," he causes the aspiration to turn away from those attainments even before they are reached, and takes up the teaching culminating in Arahatship above them.
In this context, "he does not form" means he does not project or heap up. "He does not intend" means he does not conceptualize.
"For existence or non-existence" refers to growth or decline; it should also be applied in terms of eternalism and annihilationism.
"He does not cling to anything in the world" means that among the things in the world, such as forms and so forth, he does not grasp even a single dharma with craving. He does not...

"He clings. "He understands: 'There is no further state of being such,'" said the Blessed One; standing within the domain of his own Buddhahood, he reached the pinnacle of the teaching at the level of Arahantship.
But the son of good family, according to his own specific supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), penetrated the three fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
It is just as if a king, eating various delicacies from a golden vessel, were to eat according to his own measure.
Just as when a prince is sitting on his father’s lap and shows attachment to a ball of food, one might offer that ball to him;
the prince would take a mouthful only according to the size of his own mouth, while the king would either eat the remainder himself or place it back in the bowl—
so too the Dhamma-king, the Tathāgata, grasps the pinnacle of Arahatship according to his own measure.
He gave a teaching, and by means of his own natural aptitude, the son of good family penetrated the three fruits of recluseship.

Previously, however, while he was being told such talk on absolute emptiness—struck by the three characteristics—as "the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-bases," he had neither doubt nor perplexity, nor even [the thought]: "Is it really thus? Thus indeed was it taught to me by my teacher."
It is said that there was indeed no sluggishness or hesitation [in his mind].
Furthermore, it is said that in certain places Buddhas wander in disguise; thus, there arose doubt as to whether this one might be a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, and uncertainty arose.
However, once he had realized the fruit of Non-Returner (anāgāmiphala), he reached the conclusion: "This one is my Teacher."

"If that is so, why did he not confess his transgression? "Because there was no opportunity. For the Blessed One would have continued the teaching exactly according to the schedule he had set forth, delivering it without interruption as if pouring down the sky-river (the Ganges).

"He" refers to the Arahant. "Not clung to": he understands that it is not fit to be grasped by swallowing it up and making it one's own conclusion. "Not rejoiced in": he understands that it is not fit to be rejoiced in by way of craving or views.
364. "One who is disjoined experiences that": for if, with reference to pleasant feeling, there were a latent tendency to lust in him;

with reference to painful feeling, a latent tendency to aversion; and with reference to the other [neutral feeling], a latent tendency to ignorance were to arise, then he would indeed experience while being conjoined.
But because they do not arise, one who is disjoined experiences that—being escaped from and liberated. "Ending with the body" means...
"Ending with the body": the meaning is that it arises as long as the body functions and does not arise thereafter.

The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "Not being delighted in, they will become cool": because there is no further indulgence of the defilements (*kilesa*) within the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*), having ceased to be delighted in them, they will cease right here within these same twelve sense-bases. The defilements...
For even though they have ceased by coming to Nibbāna, it is said that they have ceased where there is no [further existence].
This meaning should be illustrated by the question regarding the origin: “Where this craving, while ceasing, comes to cease. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Having come to Nibbāna, though they have become cooled, here indeed they will become fully cooled. But are not the feelings here...

[These] have been described as such, not as defilements (*kilesa*). Even those things that are felt become cooled precisely because they are devoid of defilement. Otherwise, it would be well said that there is no such thing as their "cooling" at all. 365.
Regarding the phrase "Just so," here is the application of the simile: Just as a certain man [might approach] an oil lamp...
Just as when the oil is exhausted while a lamp is burning, one pours more oil in, or when the wick is exhausted, one inserts a new wick, so that the flame of the lamp remains uninterrupted;

even so, an ordinary person (puthujjana), remaining in a single existence, performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds, and by means of those, he is reborn both in the happy realms and in the states of misery. Thus, there is no interruption in the continuity of feelings.
Just as one who is dissatisfied with a flame of a lamp might hide nearby, thinking, "By means of this man,
the lamp-flame will not be extinguished," and then cut off that man's head— so too, through the failure to supply the wick and the oil,

the lamp-flame goes out for lack of nutriment; even so, the practitioner, being dissatisfied with the wick, [cuts it off] by means of the path of Arahantship, [abandoning] the wholesome and unwholesome.
He utterly cuts them off; because they have been cut off, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, no further feelings arise after the breakup of the body.
Therefore—because the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship is superior to the wisdom of concentration and insight at the beginning—therefore.
"Endowed with this" means endowed with this supreme foundation of the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. In the destruction of all suffering...
"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge on the path of Arahantship; however, in this sutta, the knowledge pertaining to the fruit of Arahantship is intended.
For this very reason it was said: "That liberation of his is established in truth and is unshakable.
Here, "liberation" means the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, and "truth" means Nibbāna, the ultimate truth.

Thus, it is called "unshakeable" (akuppa) by virtue of making the unshakeable its object. "False" (musā) means what is contrary to reality. "Of a false nature" (mosadhamma) means having the characteristic of perishing.
"That truth" (taṃ saccaṃ) means that which is not contrary to reality, the true nature. "Of a non-false nature" (amosadhamma) means having the characteristic of not perishing.

"Therefore" (tasmā) means because, from the beginning, by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), through verbal truth, [one transcends] the truths of suffering (dukkha-sacca) and its origin (samudaya-sacca).
And the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) is indeed Nibbāna alone, which is more excellent; therefore, "endowed with this" means endowed with this supreme foundation of the ultimate truth.
367. "In the past" refers to the time when he was an ordinary person (puthujjana).
"Bases exist" refers to the base of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the base of defilements (kilesūpadhi), and the base of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi).
"The substrata consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure" refers to these substrata. "Fully undertaken and taken up" means they are completely grasped and held as the highest goal.

"Therefore" means because the relinquishing of defilements through serenity and insight at the outset, and the relinquishing of defilements through the path of stream-entry and so forth, are surpassed by the relinquishing of defilements through the path of arahantship itself; therefore. "Endowed with this" [means...].
He is endowed with this supreme foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna).

Regarding the terms "animosity" (āghāta) and so forth: animosity is so called by way of causing resentment; malice (byāpāda) by way of being corrupted; and corruption (sampadosa) by way of becoming defiled.
Thus, by these three terms, the unwholesome root of hatred (dosā-akusalamūla) alone is expressed. Therefore—because, from the beginning, by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)—

Because of the subsiding of defilements—that is, because the subsiding of defilements through the path of stream-entry and so forth is surpassed by the subsiding of defilements through the path of Arahantship alone—it is said:
"Thus endowed. By this, he is endowed with the supreme foundation of peace.
369. "This is a conceiving": this applies to all three types—conceiving by way of craving, conceiving by way of conceit, and conceiving by way of views.
Regarding the phrase "this I am" (*ayamahamasmīti*), here only that which is designated by craving (*taṇhāmaññita*) is intended as "this I.

In the terms "disease" (*roga*) and so forth: it is a disease in the sense of being an affliction; a boil in the sense of being an internal corruption; and a dart in the sense of having entered within. "The sage is called 'peaceful'" (*muni santo vuccatīti*):
the sage whose taints are exhausted is called peaceful and extinguished (*nibbuto*). "Abiding where" (*yattha ṭhitaṃ*): abiding in whatever place. "In brief" (*saṅkhittena*): [refers to] the Buddhas.
It is said that all the Buddha’s teachings are indeed concise; there is no such thing as an extensive teaching, and even the discussion on the *Samantapaṭṭhāna* is concise.

Thus, the Blessed One brought his teaching to its natural conclusion. Among the four types of persons beginning with the "one who knows by what is condensed" (*ugghāṭitaññū*), the noble son Pukkusāti is one who knows by what is elaborated (*vipañcitaññū*); thus, by way of the "one who knows by what is elaborated," the Blessed One—
He spoke this *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta*.
"Venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not complete. Why is it that a clansman’s supernaturally produced bowl and robes do not appear?
Because in the past he did not give the eight requisites. For a clansman must have given gifts and made the aspiration.
It should not be said that "it was not given. However, alms-bowls and robes produced through supernormal power (*iddhi*) arise only for those in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*);
since this person was to receive a new rebirth-linking (*punapaṭisandhika*), they did not arise for him. Furthermore, why did the Blessed One not ordain him after having sought him out himself?
Because there was no opportunity. The life-span of the noble youth was exhausted; he was a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) destined for the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*).
Mahābrahmā was as if he had come and sat down in the potter’s hall; therefore, he himself did not search for them.
He set out to seek his bowl and robes—at what time did he set out? At the rising of the dawn.
It is said that the conclusion of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, the rising of the dawn, and the emission of rays occurred at one and the same moment. The Blessed One...
It is said that as soon as he had finished his teaching, he emitted six-colored rays of light;

the entire potter’s dwelling became a single blaze of light. The six-colored rays, spreading out in dense networks and clusters, streamed forth and made all the directions appear as if covered with golden cloths and as if illuminated by the profusion of various colored flowers and gems.
The Blessed One [said], "O inhabitants of the city..."
"May they see me," he resolved. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the city-dwellers announced to one another, "The Teacher has indeed arrived;
he is sitting in the potter's workshop. They then informed the king.
The king came, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked, "Venerable sir, at what time did you arrive? "Yesterday..."
"O Great King, it was at the time of sunset. "By what deed, Blessed One?

"Your friend King Pukkusāti, having heard the message sent by you, went forth into homelessness and, while coming toward me, passed beyond Sāvatthī and traveled forty-five yojanas until he entered this potter’s shed."
He sat down. I approached him for the purpose of winning him over and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma; the son of good family realized the three fruits, Great King.
"Where is he now, venerable sir? "He has gone, Great King, having requested full ordination, to search for a bowl and robes because his bowl and robes were incomplete.
The king went in the direction in which the son of good family had gone.
The Blessed One also, having come through the air, appeared right there in the Fragrant Chamber of the Jeta Grove.
The noble son, while searching for his bowl and robes, went neither to King Bimbisāra nor to the land-trading merchants of Takkasilā.
For it occurred to him thus: "It would not be fitting for me to go here and there like a cock, seeking only what is pleasant and unpleasant."
"Having searched [the vicinity], it is appropriate to seek out a robe and bowl; avoiding large cities, we shall seek them at water-crossings, cemeteries, rubbish heaps, and in side-streets.
Thus he began to search for scraps of cloth among the heaps of refuse in the side-streets.
"He deprived him of life": while he was looking at a scrap of cloth on that heap of refuse, young calves, being agitated, [attacked him].
A cow ran up, pierced him with her horn, and killed him. Emaciated by hunger, the noble son reached the end of his life while still in the air and fell down.
He was like a golden statue placed face-down in a heap of refuse;
having passed away, he was reborn in the Aviha Brahma-world, and as soon as he was reborn, he attained Arahantship. In the Aviha Brahma-world...
It is said that as soon as they were reborn, seven persons attained arahantship. For this has been said:
“Seven bhikkhus have been reborn in the Aviha realm, liberated, with lust and hatred utterly destroyed, having crossed over the attachment to the world.”
And who were those who crossed the mire, the realm of death so difficult to cross?
Who, having abandoned the human body, attained union with the divine?
Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—these were the three.
"Bhaddiya and Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi and Siṅgi— having abandoned their human bodies, they have attained divine union.
King Bimbisāra also thought, "My friend, having merely read the message sent by me, has abandoned the sovereignty that came into his hands..."
"He has come such a long distance; this son of good family has performed a difficult task. We shall honor him with the honors due to one who has gone forth.
Saying, "Search for my companion," he sent messengers here and there. Those sent found him fallen in a place of refuse;
having seen him, they returned and reported it to the king. The king went and saw the son of good family, and said: "Indeed, sir..."
"We were able to pay honor to our companion, but now our companion has become destitute.

Having lamented thus, they had the noble youth carried on a litter and placed in a suitable location. Since they did not know how to perform the honors due to one who was not yet ordained, they summoned bathers, barbers, and others;
they bathed the noble youth's head and dressed him in clean garments.

Having had him adorned with royal attire and placed upon a golden litter, they carried him out from the city while performing worship with all kinds of musical instruments, perfumes, garlands, and the like.

Having caused a great funeral pyre to be prepared with abundant fragrant wood and performed the funeral rites for the body of the noble youth, he took the relics and established a cetiya. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Dhātuvibhaṅga-sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 11.
The commentary on the Saccavibhaṅga-sutta.
371. “Thus have I heard” refers to the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, “proclaiming” means:
“This is the noble truth of suffering,” and so on, up to “this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
Furthermore, in this context, “making known” (paññāpanā) means the establishing of the truth of suffering and the other truths; for just as one who sets down a seat establishes the seat.
"It is called 'making known' (paññapeti). Establishing (paṭṭhapanā) means making known (paññāpanā). Unveiling (vivaraṇā) means making manifest (vivaṭakaraṇā).
Analysis (vibhajanā) means the act of dividing (vibhāgakiriyā). Clarifying (uttānīkammaṃ) means making evident (pākaṭabhāvakaraṇaṃ).
Supporting (anuggāhakā) means supporting by means of both kinds of gathering: gathering through material gifts and gathering through the Dhamma. Producing (janetā)" means...
The "giver-birth" is the mother. "One who nurtures" means one who nourishes. This illustrates that Moggallāna was like a foster-mother.

For the birth-giving mother, having carried the child in her womb for nine or ten months while avoiding salt, sour liquids, and the like, delivers him from her womb and entrusts him to a foster-mother.
That woman, having nourished the child with milk, butter, and other such things—

As it grows, it spreads about as it pleases; even so, Sāriputta, while gathering together those who had gone forth—whether in his own presence or in that of others—by means of the two methods of attraction, tending to the sick, and engaging them in the subject of meditation, he recognized their attainment of stream-entry.
From the time they rose above the fears of the states of misery, [he thought]: "Now, by their own individual effort..."
Having become indifferent toward those who will be reborn in the higher paths, he exhorts others who are newly ordained.

Mahāmoggallāna likewise, having gathered those ordained in his own presence or in the presence of others and engaged them in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), does not fall into indifference even toward those who have attained the three lower fruits. Why? Because it occurred to him thus: [as it was said]...
The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, just as even a tiny amount of excrement is foul-smelling... even a tiny amount of urine...

saliva... pus... or blood is foul-smelling, even so, bhikkhus, I do not praise even a tiny amount of existence, not even for as long as a finger-snap. Therefore, until they reach arahantship, [they remain].
Thus, without falling into indifference toward them, he attains *arahantship* while they themselves have not yet reached it. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, just as the progenitor is Sāriputta; just as the one who brings up what has been born is Moggallāna.
Bhikkhus, Sāriputta trains others in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), while Moggallāna [trains them] in the supreme goal. “He is capable” means he is able.
"Knowledge regarding suffering" refers to the knowledge of hearing, of comprehension, and of penetration; likewise for the origin of suffering.
Regarding the cessation of suffering, it is appropriate to understand it as the knowledge of hearing and of penetration; likewise for the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

In the case of the thought of renunciation and so forth, it arises either by way of being the opposite of sensual desire, or by way of having emerged from sensual desire, or as it arises in one who is comprehending sensual desire.

The "resolve of renunciation" (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) arises either as one who effects the striking down of the state of sensual desire and the pacification of sensual desire, or as one who has arisen in seclusion from sensual desire.

The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. All of these are obtained in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), but at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), they are obtained in a single state of consciousness.
For in that [moment], there is obtained only a single resolve that eradicates the volition of wrong resolve (micchā-saṅkappa-cetanā).

They are not obtained as distinct entities. Right speech and the others, though occurring in various minds during the preliminary stage, are obtained in a single mind at the moment of the Path in the manner already described.
This is the summary here; however, the detailed discussion of the Truths has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* and in the *Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta*.
The commentary on the *Saccavibhaṅgasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished. 12.
The commentary on the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta*.
376. Thus have I heard: this is the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī":
*Gotamī* is her clan name (*gotta*). On the day of her naming, however, brahmins who had received honors, seeing the perfection of her marks, said:
"If she obtains a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*). If she [obtains] a son..."
"He will obtain [a son], and he will become a wheel-turning monarch; in either case, his offspring will be very great," they prophesied.
Therefore, they gave her the name Mahāpajāpatī. Here, however, she is called Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī by combining her name with her clan.
"New" means unwashed. "Woven by herself" does not mean woven by her own hand alone.
On one occasion, however, surrounded by a group of kinswomen, she came to the weavers’ workshop, took hold of the end of a shuttle, and demonstrated the manner of weaving.
It was with reference to this that it was said [in the text].
But when did the thought arise in Gotamī to give a pair of robes to the Blessed One? After he had attained full enlightenment.
At the time of his first visit upon arriving at Kapilavatthu, King Suddhodana took the Teacher—who had entered for alms—and led him into his own residence.
Then, beholding the Blessed One’s physical splendor, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī thought, “How truly radiant is the personhood of my son! Thereupon, a powerful surge of joy arose within her.
Then he thought: “For twenty-nine years my son lived in the midst of the household, and during that time I gave him nothing more than even a single mocaka fruit;
now, however, I shall give him a robe. “In this royal palace there are many garments of great value, yet they do not please me; with my own hands—”
"What indeed would satisfy me? I shall give it after making it with my own hands," he thought, and resolved thus.
Then, having had cotton brought from the market, he pounded it with his own hands, carded it, and spun fine thread.
Having had a hall built right within his own residence, he summoned craftsmen and provided them with his own personal food, snacks, and meals.
Having given [the money], she had it spent; and from time to time, accompanied by a group of kinsmen, she went and took the weaving looms.

When the work was finished, she paid great honor to the craftsmen, placed a pair of garments in a perfumed box, and having them take leave of her, she informed the king, saying, "I shall go taking a robe for my son. The king [prepared] the road.
Having had the streets swept clean, water-jars filled, and banners and flags raised,
they prepared the road from the gate of Rājagaha’s palace to the Nigrodha Monastery and strewed it with flowers. Mahāpajāpatī, too,
having adorned herself with all her ornaments and surrounded by a group of kinswomen, placed the casket upon her head and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone there, she said, "Venerable sir, here is a pair of new cloths for me," and so forth.
When he said a second time, "Give them to the Saṅgha, Gotamī," she replied, "Venerable sir,
I am able to give cloth robes from my storehouse of cloth even to a hundred monks, a thousand monks, or even a hundred thousand monks."
"But this, venerable sir, was personally spun and personally woven by me for the sake of the Blessed One;
may the Blessed One accept it from me," she said, making her request. Thus she begged up to three times, and the Blessed One likewise refused each time.
Why, then, did the Blessed One cause what was being given to him to be given to the community of monks? Out of compassion for his mother.

It occurred to him: "Three volitions regarding her have arisen—volition directed toward me, volition directed toward her, and volition directed toward another. Let three volitions also arise regarding the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
thus, these six volitions will together conduce to her welfare and happiness for a long time. But the sophist said: "What is given to the Saṅgha..."
“‘It is of great fruit’—therefore it was said thus. He should be asked: “Do you say that what is given to the Saṅgha is more fruitful than what is given to the Teacher?
[If he says: “Yes, I say so,” [then reply: “Bring a sutta [to prove it]. [The Buddha said: “Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha;
when you have given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored. But is this the only meaning of that sutta?

Is there a reason for this? Yes, it is precisely this. If that is so, then from the statements, "Therefore, Ānanda, give a cake to the scavengers" and "Therefore, Kaccāna, give molasses to the scavengers," what has been given to the scavengers would be even more fruitful.
For in this way too, one could say, "The Teacher causes [others] to give what is being given to himself. This applies even to kings, royal ministers, and others.
