They cause their own received gifts to be given to elephant-keepers and others; these [latter] might even become greater than kings and such.
Therefore, do not take it thus:
"Neither in this world nor in the next..."
"There exists no one equal or even superior to the Buddha,
whom they call the foremost among those worthy of offerings,
for those seeking merit who desire abundant fruit."

For according to the Teacher’s own word, there is no one more worthy of offerings than the Teacher himself. It was with this in mind—that these six volitions of hers would, by being unified, lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time—that he refused her up to three times and then had the gift bestowed upon the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, he spoke thus so that future generations might develop reverence for the Saṅgha.
He thought: "I shall not remain for long; however, my teaching will be established within the community of monks. Future..."
Having refused it up to three times with the words, "May the people generate respect for the Saṅgha," he had it given to the Saṅgha.
For when this is so, future generations, thinking—"The Teacher gave even what was being offered to himself to the Saṅgha;
the Saṅgha is indeed worthy of offerings"—will develop respect for the Saṅgha and consider that the four requisites should be given to it. The Saṅgha, by means of the four...
"Without being exhausted by the conditions, he will master the word of the Buddha and practice the duty of a recluse;

thus my teaching will endure for five thousand years. This should also be understood from the words, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept [it]," for there is no one more worthy of offerings than the Teacher. Indeed, for the Elder Ānanda...
Mahāpajāpatī harbored resentment or enmity. The Elder did not wish that her offering should fail to be of great fruit.
For the Elder was wise, learned, and had attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training;
seeing that what is given to the Teacher is of great fruit, he requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it," in order that she might receive its merit.
Again, the caviller says: "From the statement, 'If you give [the gift] to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored,' it follows that the Teacher is included within the Saṅgha.
He should be asked: "Do you know how many refuges there are, and how many kinds of verified confidence?
If he knows, he will say, "Three. Then he should be told: "According to your own tenet, because the Teacher is included within the Saṅgha..."

There would be only two [categories]. This being the case, even the going-forth and the full ordination authorized thus—"Monks, I allow going-forth and full ordination by means of these three goings for refuge"—would not be valid. Consequently, you are neither one who has gone forth nor a householder.
Furthermore, while the Perfectly Enlightened One was seated in the Fragrant Chamber, the monks were performing the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā...

They also perform formal acts of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*); since these would be invalid if the Teacher were included within the Saṅgha, yet they are not so, therefore it cannot be said that "the Teacher is included within the Saṅgha. 377.
*Āpādikā* means one who causes growth; when your hands and feet are unable to perform the functions of hands and feet, [she provides] the hands...
"And having increased [them] in both feet" means she was their caregiver. "She nourished them" means she nourished you by bathing, feeding, and giving you drink two or three times a day.
Regarding the phrase "she gave him breast milk": it is said that Prince Nanda was but a few days old when the Bodhisatta was born;
when he was born, Mahāpajāpatī gave her own son to the nurses and herself [gave milk] to the Bodhisatta.
While performing her duties as a nurse, she suckled him with her own breast; it was with reference to this that the Elder spoke thus.

Having thus described Mahāpajāpatī’s great helpfulness, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with “Venerable sir, having come to the Blessed One,” etc., in order to demonstrate the Tathāgata’s great helpfulness.
In that context, “having come to the Blessed One, venerable sir” means depending upon and relying on the Blessed One.
378. Then the Blessed One, expressing his appreciation for the two kinds of assistance with particular emphasis, said, "It is so," and so forth.
In that context, "when, Ānanda, one person comes upon another" means when a pupil-person comes upon a teacher-person.
"Of this person, by this person, Ānanda" means of this teacher-person, by this pupil-person.
"I say it is not easy to repay" means I say that a reciprocal service is not easily performed.

"Salutation" refers to the act of saluting upon seeing a teacher during such acts as bowing down; or, in whichever direction the teacher resides, one goes while performing the postures facing him, or sits having saluted, or lies down having saluted.
Furthermore, upon seeing the teacher from afar, rising up and going forward to meet him is called "rising up.
Moreover, upon seeing the teacher, one pays homage by raising the hands in *añjali* and placing them upon the head;
or one pays homage while facing the direction in which he dwells; likewise, whether walking, standing, or sitting, one maintains the *añjali*.
"Having taken it up, he pays homage indeed"—this is called the act of joining the palms (*añjalikamma*).
Performing a fitting service, however, is called the act of respectful conduct (*sāmīcikamma*). When giving robes and so forth, one does not give just anything;
rather, one gives what is of great value—whether worth a hundred, five hundred, or even a thousand [coins]. The same principle applies to alms-food and other requisites. What need is there for more?

Even if one were to fill the space between the world-systems with the four superior requisites and offer them by seizing the peak of Mount Sineru, one would still not be able to perform an action worthy of the Teacher.
Why, then, does he begin with the words "These fourteen"? This discourse is concerned with the personal offering (*pāṭipuggalika-dakṣiṇā*).
[The discourse] has arisen. The Elder Ānanda also urged [the donor] specifically toward a personal offering (*pāṭipuggalika-dakkhiṇā*), saying, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept it.

He began this teaching in order to show that an offering given on fourteen specific occasions is called a "personal" one. "This is the first" means that this offering is first both by way of its qualities and by way of its seniority.

For this is the first, the foremost, the eldest; there is no measure for this offering. The second and third are also supreme offerings indeed, while the remaining ones do not reach the state of being supreme offerings.
"One who is free from passion for sensual pleasures among outsiders" refers to one who holds the doctrine of karma and the doctrine of action, possessing mundane fivefold super-knowledge.
"A virtuous worldling" refers to one who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-sīlavā*).
One is called a person of good character and nature who, being honest and free from deceit,

earns his livelihood by lawful and equitable means such as agriculture or trade without oppressing others. Regarding "the bad character of worldlings," those called worldlings of bad character are fishermen, fishers, and the like,
who earn their livelihood by oppressing others.

Now, defining the ripening of a gift given to an individual, he said, "In this regard, Ānanda," and so forth. Therein, the phrase "to one who has gone to the animal realm" does not include what is given for the sake of nourishing [a pet] on account of its qualities or its usefulness. Nor is included what is given merely as a mouthful or half a mouthful. However, that which is given to dogs, pigs, chickens, crows, and the like— [The remainder of the passage continues: ...is included. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no fruit for one who gives to such beings; rather, the fruit is small because the recipient is small. For example, when a person gives a single grain of rice to a crow, they do not obtain the fruit of giving a whole cartload of rice. But when one gives even a single grain of rice to a *patisambhidā*-attainer, one obtains the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cartloads of rice. Therefore, it is said: "It is not the case that there is no fruit for one who gives to such beings. And it is not the case that there is no fruit for one who gives to those who have gone to the animal realm; rather, the fruit is small because the recipient is small. Thus, it is said: "But when one gives even a single grain of rice to a *patisambhidā*-attainer... and so on. This is the meaning. It is not the case that there is no fruit for one who gives to those who have gone to the animal realm; rather, the fruit is small because the recipient is small. Therefore, it is said: "But when one gives even a single grain of rice to a *patisambhidā*-attainer... and so on. This is the meaning. It is not the case that there is no fruit for one who gives to those who have gone to the animal realm; rather, the fruit is small because the recipient is small. This was said with reference to giving as much as one desires to anyone who has arrived, anticipating the fruit [of that gift].
"Giving to an animal" means this. "A hundredfold virtues" means a hundred benefits. "To be anticipated" means to be desired.
This is what is meant: this offering [yields] a hundred years of life, a hundred of beauty, a hundred of happiness, and a hundred of strength.
The "stream of inspired eloquence" (paṭibhānasota) bestows five hundred benefits: it grants a lifespan of one hundred existences, and it grants beauty, happiness, strength, and inspired eloquence;
it makes one free from fear. Even when "one hundred existences" (bhavasata) is mentioned, this is the very same meaning.
By this method, the principle is to be applied everywhere.

Regarding the phrase "one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry": even a lay follower who has gone for refuge at its minimum limit is said to be "practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. A gift given to such a person is incalculable and immeasurable.
For one established in the five precepts, it is even more fruitful than that; for one established in the ten precepts, it is even more so.
Beyond that is the level of one who has gone forth as a novice; beyond that, the level of an ordained bhikkhu; beyond that, the level of one who is ordained and perfect in his duties;
beyond that, the level of one who possesses insight; beyond that, the level of one who has begun insight;
but at the ultimate limit, one who possesses the path is said to be "practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry."
A gift given to such a person yields even greater fruit than that.
But can one give a gift to one who possesses the Path (maggasamaṅgin)? Yes, one can.

For when one who has begun insight meditation enters a village for alms, taking his bowl and robes, if one stands at the door of his house and, taking the bowl from his hand, offers solid and soft food—
They place it [in his bowl]. At that moment, the bhikkhu emerges from the path; this gift is said to be given to one who possesses the path (*maggasamaṅgin*).
Alternatively, he may be sitting in the assembly hall, and people go and place hard and soft food in his bowl;
at that moment, he emerges from the path—this gift, too, is given to one who possesses the path.

Or alternatively, while he is sitting in his monastery or in the assembly hall, lay devotees take his bowl, go to their own homes, and place hard and soft food inside it; at that very moment, he emerges upon the path.
This gift is also said to be given to one who possesses the path. In this regard, just as water flows into a pipe, [the result] follows for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
The incalculability of a gift given to one who has entered the path should be understood.

Just as the water in various great rivers and in the great ocean is incalculable, so too should the incalculability of a gift given to stream-enterers and others be understood by way of its superior quality.

Furthermore, it should be understood by way of the immeasurability of the soil of the great earth, beginning from a mere speck of dust on a spot the size of a chariot wheel up to the soil of the entire great earth.
This meaning should be illustrated.
Why, then, was it begun with the words, "These seven indeed"? For it was said: "Give to the Saṅgha, Gotamī;
when given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored. In that context, a gift given in these seven places is [considered as given] to the Saṅgha.
He began this teaching in order to demonstrate that [the gift] is indeed "given. In this context, "in the presence of the Buddha and the two-fold Saṅgha" means:
on one side is the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, on the other side is the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and the Teacher is seated in the middle;
this is what is called "in the presence of the Buddha and the two-fold Saṅgha. Regarding the phrase "this is the first": there is no gift whatsoever equal in measure to this offering.
Furthermore, the second offering and others do not equal this supreme offering.
But is it possible to give a gift to both Saṅghas with the Buddha at their head once the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?
It is possible. How so? By placing an image together with the relics upon a seat in the presence of both Saṅghas, and [placing] a support...
Setting aside the water for the merit-offering (*dakkhiṇodaka*), one should first give everything to the Teacher and then give it to both Saṅghas;
in this way, it is said that a gift has been given to both Saṅghas with the Buddha at their head. In that regard, what should be done with what was given to the Teacher?
It should be given to whichever monk is devoted to the Teacher and is perfect in his duties (*vatta*).
It should be given. For what belongs to a father passes to his son; it is also permissible to give it to the Saṅgha of monks.
Furthermore, taking ghee and oil, lamps should be lit; taking a cloth, banners should be raised.
"To the Saṅgha of monks" refers to the great Saṅgha of monks which is not delimited. The same method applies to the Saṅgha of nuns as well.

"Those who have merely attained the lineage" (*gotrabhū*) means those who experience only the state of lineage; the meaning is "monks in name only. "With saffron robes around their necks" (*kāsāvakaṇṭhā*) means those whose necks are adorned with saffron robes.
It is said that they will wander about having tied a single piece of saffron cloth either on their hand or around their neck.
However, their household duties—such as farming, trade, and so forth—will remain exactly as they were before, while their wives and children will continue to frequent the doors of their homes.
Regarding the phrase "they give a gift intended for the Saṅgha among those who are immoral," it does not mean "the Saṅgha of the immoral.

For there is no such thing as an "immoral Saṅgha. Rather, it is immoral lay followers who, among those [monks] who are immoral, give a gift while saying, "We give this to the Saṅgha," intending it for the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha.
Thus, even a sacrificial gift (dakkhiṇā) given by the Blessed One to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha...
It is said that they are "incalculable by way of their qualities. It is also said that even an offering given to the Sangha with a yellow robe around the neck is incalculable by way of its qualities.
For an offering directed toward the Sangha belongs to one who is able to show reverence toward the Sangha;
yet, showing reverence toward the Sangha is difficult to accomplish.
For if someone, having prepared a gift with the thought, "I shall give an offering to the Saṅgha," goes to a monastery and says,

"Venerable sirs, please assign one elder on behalf of the Saṅgha," and then, having received a novice from the Saṅgha, falls into a change of heart, thinking, "I have obtained a novice," his offering does not go to the Saṅgha. [The same applies if he intends for] a great elder...
Even for one who, having obtained [a monk], gives rise to joy thinking, "I have obtained a great elder," it does not occur at all. However, for one who— having obtained anyone from the Saṅgha,
whether a novice or one fully ordained, a youth or an elder, a fool or a wise man— being free from doubt,
is able to show honor to the Saṅgha by thinking, "I give this to the Saṅgha," for him...
It is said that a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha is called "gone to the Saṅgha. It appears that those living beyond the great ocean act in this way.

For there, a certain householder who was the owner of a monastery, thinking, "I shall give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha," requested from the Saṅgha, saying, "Please designate one [monk]," and asked, "Give me one. He obtained an immoral monk, cleared away the seating area, and...
Having prepared a seat, fastened a canopy above it, and honored it with perfumes, incense, and flowers, he washed his feet, anointed them with oil, and,
as if performing an act of prostration toward the Buddha, gave the gift to the Saṅgha with deep reverence. Later, after the meal,
that monk went to the man’s house door and said, "Give me a hoe for the purpose of maintaining the monastery."
The lay follower arrived and, while still seated, kicked the spade with his foot and gave it back, saying, "Take it.
People said to him, "It was impossible for you to have shown such honor to him this early in the morning; now there is not even a trace of courtesy left—what is this?
The lay follower replied, "Venerable sirs, that was an act of respect toward the Saṅgha, not toward him."
"But who purifies the offering given to the Saṅgha with yellow robes around their necks? "The eighty great elders, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, purify it.
Furthermore, although those elders have long since attained final Nibbāna, starting from them down to those existing today who are free from taints (khīṇāsava), they indeed purify it.
"But in no way, Ānanda, is there any distinction regarding an offering made to the Saṅgha:

'There is the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha,' 'there is the Saṅgha now,' and 'there will be the Saṅgha with yellow robes in the future. The Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is not to be equated with the Saṅgha now;
nor is the Saṅgha now to be equated with the Saṅgha with yellow robes in the future."
It should not be brought forward. It must be spoken of at that very moment.

For a worldling-monk (puthujjana-samaṇa) who has been designated from the Saṅgha is an individual stream-enterer (sotāpanna); indeed, for one capable of showing reverence toward the Saṅgha, a gift given to a worldling-monk bears greater fruit.
This applies likewise to an individual once-returner (sakadāgāmī) and so forth who has been designated [from the Saṅgha].

The same principle applies here. For one who is able to show respect toward the Saṅgha, a gift given even to an immoral person from whom it has been specifically designated after being offered to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is indeed more fruitful.

As for what was said, "Great King, a gift given to the virtuous is very fruitful, but not so to the immoral," that was stated setting aside this specific principle. "Ānanda, there are these four... [and so forth].
This should be understood in this tetrad as "purifications of the offering.
381. "It is purified by the giver" means it is purified by way of its great fruit; the meaning is that it becomes of great fruit.
"One of beautiful nature" means one of pure nature, not one of evil nature. And herein, the Great King Vessantara is an example of being purified by the giver.
This should be told. For he caused the earth to quake after giving his children to the brahmin Jūjaka.
Regarding the statement "it is purified through the recipient," the story of the fisherman living at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River should be told.
It is said that after giving alms-food three times to the Elder Dīghasoma while lying on his deathbed, [he thought], "To the noble one..."
"The almsfood given by me to the Elder Dīghasoma is being taken away," he said.
Regarding the phrase "not even as a donor," the hunter living in Vaḍḍhamāna should be mentioned here.

It is said that when he was giving an offering to the departed spirits (petadakkhiṇa), he gave it three times to one who was immoral; on the third occasion, [the spirit thought], "A non-human being, an immoral one, is plundering me."
Viravi said: "When it was given to one virtuous bhikkhu and brought back, it reached him at that very moment.
Regarding the phrase "it is purified by the giver," here the story of the peerless gift (*asadisadāna*) should be told.
Regarding the phrase "that offering is purified by the giver," it is just as when a skillful farmer [improves] even a field that lacks essence.

Having obtained [the field] at the proper time, having ploughed it, having removed the soil, and having established seeds of high quality, one who does not fall into negligence in guarding it day and night obtains a greater harvest than from another’s field of high quality;
even so, the virtuous person attains a great fruit even when giving to one who is immoral. By this method, purification should be understood in all instances.

Regarding the phrase "one free from lust giving to those free from lust": here, "one free from lust" refers to a non-returner (*anāgāmī*); however, an *arahant* is one who is exclusively free from lust.
Therefore, a gift given by an *arahant* to an *arahant* is indeed the foremost. Why? Because of the absence of attachment to existence (*bhavālaya*) and the longing for existence (*bhavapatthanā*).

[Objection: But does one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) not have faith in the fruit of giving? [Response: Those who have faith in the fruit of giving are not like one whose taints are destroyed.
...they exist. However, an action performed by one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome because of his freedom from desire and lust;
it stands in the category of the functional (kiriya). For this very reason, they say that his gift is supreme.
But was it the Buddha who gave what was so fruitful for the Elder Sāriputta, or was it the Elder Sāriputta?
"Given to the Perfectly Enlightened One. They say that what was given by the Perfectly Enlightened One to the Elder Sāriputta yields great fruit.
For there is no one other than the Perfectly Enlightened One capable of knowing the ripening of a gift.
Indeed, for one who is able to give with the fourfold perfection, the gift yields its result in that very same lifetime. In this regard:
Perfection (*sampadā*): (1) the arising of the gift through the Dhamma and in accordance with justice, without oppressing others;

(2) the greatness of the volition by way of prior intention and so forth; (3) the excellence of qualities by way of the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*); and (4) the perfection of the object by way of having emerged from cessation on that very day.
From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta is finished.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Chapter on the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatanavagga).
1. Commentary on the *Anāthapiṇḍikovādasutta* 383.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Anāthapiṇḍikovādasutta*. In this context, "gravely ill" means being extremely sick and having reached the bed of death.
"Addressed" means that, it is said, as long as the householder’s feet were still able to walk outside, during that time—on that day—[he spoke].
He attended upon the Buddha one, two, or three times, and his attendance was unbroken.

As much as his attendance upon the Teacher had been, so too was his attendance upon the Great Elders. Today, because his ability to travel on foot had ceased, he had retired to his bed due to illness;
desiring to send a message, he addressed a certain man. "He approached him" means...
Having taken leave of the Blessed One, she approached at the time of sunset.
"Receding" means they shrink back; they become thin. "Advancing" means they increase, spread out, and become powerful.
"Advancement is perceived for them, not recession" refers to that moment when the death-bed sensation arises.
It was like a fire blazing in a high wind; as long as the heat was not exhausted, it could not be extinguished even by great effort, but once the heat was spent, it was extinguished.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta thought: "This pain of the Great Merchant is terminal; it cannot be [relieved]."
“The rest of the talk is useless; I shall speak a discourse on the Dhamma to him. Then, while speaking that discourse to him, he said, “Therefore, in this regard,” and so forth.

Therein, “therefore” means: because there is no one capable of warding off the death-pain that has arisen when grasping the eye with the three types of grasping; therefore, “I shall not cling to the eye.”
"I shall not grasp the eye by means of the three graspings. And there shall be no consciousness dependent on my eye; nor shall even the consciousness dependent on the eye exist for me.
'Not form'—previously, the form of the sense bases was spoken of, but here, speaking of all form pertaining to the realms of sense-desire and existence (*kāmabhava*), he says thus."
386. "Neither this world" means: "I shall not cling to a dwelling place or to food and clothing.

This is stated for the purpose of being undisturbed regarding the requisite conditions. "Nor the other world": here, with the exception of the human world, all remaining worlds are called "the other world.
This refers to [the thought]: "Having been reborn in such-and-such a deva-world, I shall exist in such-and-such a place; this..."
This was spoken for the purpose of abandoning such anxiety as, "I shall eat this, I shall consume this, I shall wear this, I shall clothe myself in this.
Having thus liberated [the mind] by means of these three graspings— thinking, "I shall not cling even to that, nor shall my consciousness be dependent upon it"—
the Elder brought his teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
“387. ‘Olīyasi’ means: seeing your own prosperity, you cling; you adhere to sense-objects.
Thus the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, “Even this householder, though so faithful and confident, fears the fear of death—who else would not fear it?
gave him firm exhortation and spoke thus. And such as this [prosperity] is not mine...

Regarding the phrase "a discourse on the Dhamma heard before": this lay follower says, "I have never heard such a discourse on the Dhamma even from the presence of the Teacher," thinking, "Does the Teacher not speak such subtle and profound talk?
He does not fail to speak it. For in this way [he has not heard it], because the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six classes of consciousness, the six...

Having shown the six bodies of contact, the six bodies of feeling, the six elements, the five aggregates, the four formless states, and both this world and the next, and having included them within Arahantship by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, he spoke words never heard before; therefore, he speaks thus.
Furthermore, this lay follower is devoted to giving and delights in giving; when going into the presence of the Buddhas, he does not go with empty hands.
He had never been there before. When going before the meal, he would go taking rice-gruel, hard food, and so forth; after the meal, he would go taking ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth.
When these were unavailable, he would have sand brought and scatter it over the Gandhakuṭi courtyard.
Having given alms and observed the precepts, he returned home. This lay follower was surely of the same spiritual lineage as the Bodhisattvas; therefore, the Blessed One—
For twenty-four years, he spoke almost exclusively on the subject of giving to the lay follower, saying:
“Lay follower, this so-called ‘giving’ is the path traveled by the Bodhisattvas; it is also the path traveled by me.

For four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand additional aeons, I gave gifts. You are following the very same path that I have traveled. [The Venerable] Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, and others...
Even the great disciples, when those who had come into their presence, would speak only of the discourse on giving. For this very reason he said:
"Householder, such a discourse on the Dhamma does not occur to white-robed householders. This is what is meant:
householder, for householders there is a strong [attachment] toward fields, lands, gold, silver, female and male slaves, children, wives, and so forth.
“Ālaya” means intense obsession with craving; for them, the discourse—“herein no attachment should be made, no craving should be made”—neither occurs to the mind nor is pleasing.
He approached the Blessed One: why did he approach? It is said that as soon as he was reborn in the Tusita heaven...
Seeing his own person shining like a mass of gold thirty *gāvutas* in size, as well as the splendor of his park, celestial mansion, and other riches, he reflected:
"This prosperity of mine is great; what deed did I perform on the path of men?
Looking back, he saw his service to the Three Jewels and thought: "This state of being a deva is a ground for negligence."
"Indeed, while I am rejoicing in this prosperity, there might even be a lapse of mindfulness;
well then, let me go and speak in praise of my Jetavana, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Noble Path, and the Elder Sāriputta, and having returned from there, I shall enjoy this prosperity.
He did exactly so. To show that, [the text says] "Then..."
"Anāthapiṇḍika," and so forth, was said.
Therein, "frequented by the assembly of seers" means frequented by the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).

Having thus described the excellence of Jetavana with the first verse, he now spoke the words beginning with "action and knowledge" while describing the excellence of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). Therein:
"Kamma" is the volition of the path. "Vijjā" is the wisdom of the path. "Dhamma" is the factor of concentration.
"Sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamaṃ" shows that for one established in virtue, life is supreme. Alternatively, "vijjā" refers to right view and intention;
"dhamma" refers to right effort, mindfulness, and concentration; "sīla" refers to right speech, action, and livelihood; and "jīvitamuttamaṃ" [refers] to this...
The life of one established in virtue is indeed supreme. "By this mortals are purified" means that by this Eightfold Path, sentient beings are cleansed.
"Therefore" means because they are purified by the Path and not by lineage or wealth; therefore, "one should wisely investigate the Dhamma."
One should investigate the states conducive to concentration by means of skillful means (*upāya*).

"In this way one is purified therein" means that one is purified in that Noble Path. Alternatively, "one should wisely investigate the states" means that one should investigate the states of the five aggregates by means of skillful means.
"In this way one is purified therein" means that one is purified in those four Truths.
Now, speaking in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he said, "Sāriputta indeed," and so forth. In this context, "Sāriputta indeed" is an emphatic expression;
it means that among those [disciples] possessing wisdom and the other [faculties], Sāriputta alone is superior. "By means of tranquility" refers to the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Gone to the further shore" means having reached Nibbāna. Any bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna may be considered at most equal to him, but not superior.
He says that there is indeed someone superior to the Elder. The remainder is clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
2. Commentary on the Channovāda Sutta 389.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Channovāda Sutta. Therein, "Channa" refers to the elder of that name, not the elder who had gone forth at the time of the Great Renunciation.
"From seclusion" means from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Inquiries after his illness" refers to nursing the sick.

This is described as the praise of the Buddha; therefore, he spoke thus. "The weapon" (*sattha*) refers to the weapon that takes away life. "I do not desire" (*nāvakaṅkhāmi*) means I do not wish for it.
"Without reproach" (*anupavajja*) means without rebirth and without reconnection [to a new existence].
"This is mine," and so forth, are stated by way of the grasping of craving, conceit, and views. "Having seen cessation" (*nirodhaṃ disvā*) means having seen its exhaustion and passing away.
"Having understood: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,' I contemplate it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
(393) "Therefore"—meaning because he says, "I am drawing the knife because I am unable to endure the final moment of death"—therefore.
"The venerable worldling": by this he indicates, "Pay attention to this as well. "Constantly" means at all times.
"Of one who is dependent" means of one who is dependent on craving and views. "Shaken" means it is agitated. "Tranquility" refers to tranquility of body and mind;

the meaning is that there is what is called tranquility of the defilements. "Inclination" is inclination toward craving. "When inclination is absent" means when there is no attachment, longing, or obsession for the sake of existence.
"There is no coming or going" means there is no so-called "coming" by way of rebirth-linking, nor any "going" by way of death.
There is no name. "Passing away and reappearing" means passing away by way of decease (*cavana*) and reappearing by way of rebirth (*upapajjana*).
"Neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two" means it does not exist in this world, nor in the world beyond, nor in both places.

"This alone is the end of suffering" means that this indeed is the end of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) and the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa-dukkha*); this is its limit, its boundary, its state of final enclosure.

This indeed is the meaning here. As for those who, taking the statement "not between the two," assert the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their rebuttal has already been stated above.
394. "He drew a weapon" means he drew a life-taking weapon; he severed the windpipe. Then, in that...
In that very moment, the fear of death overcame him and the sign of his future rebirth appeared. Realizing his own status as a worldling (*puthujjana*), he was moved with spiritual urgency;

establishing insight (*vipassanā*) and comprehending conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), he attained *arahantship* and, becoming one whose head is level [with the enlightened], passed into final *nibbāna*.
Although this state of being blameless in the presence [of others] was declared while the Elder was still a worldling...
There was a declaration; however, because of that declaration, his final nibbāna occurred without obstacle.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke, taking that very declaration as his basis. "Families of reproach" means families that should be visited.
By this, the Elder [meant]: "Venerable sir, while such male attendants and female attendants exist, that bhikkhu..."
"Will you attain final Nibbāna within your own dispensation? he asked. Then the Blessed One, illustrating his lack of social attachment to families, said to him, "These, Sāriputta," and so forth.
It is said that at this point, the Elder’s state of non-association with families became manifest.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Channovāda Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 3.
The commentary on the Puṇṇovāda Sutta.
395. Thus have I heard: this is the Puṇṇovāda Sutta. Therein, "seclusion" means solitude. "That" refers to both that eye and the visible form.
"With the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering" means that through the convergence of delight—which is craving—there is the convergence of the suffering of the five aggregates.
Thus, at the six sense doors, there is suffering and its origin; by way of these two truths, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown.
Having brought it to its conclusion, he showed it. In the second method, by means of the two truths—cessation and the path—he brought the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) to its conclusion and showed it.
And with the words, “And you, Puṇṇa,” there is a separate connection (*anusandhi*).

Thus, having first included the teaching concerning the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and the turning away from it within the stage of Arahantship, [the Teacher] now intends to make the Elder Puṇṇa roar the lion’s roar on seven points.
And with the words "And by this you...
and so forth, he speaks. (396) "Fierce" means wicked and sinful. "Harsh" means cruel. "Will revile" means they will revile [him] by means of the ten bases of abuse.
"Will insult" means: "What kind of ascetic are you? We shall do this and that to you."
They will threaten him. "It will be thus for me in this matter" means: "In this case, such will be my fate.
"With a staff" means with a four-cubit staff or a small mallet. "With a weapon" means with a single-edged blade or the like.
"They seek out a weapon-taker" means they seek out a weapon that would take away life. This was said by the Elder regarding the third *pārājika* offense.
This was said with reference to the monks' search for a weapon after they had heard a discourse on foulness and were loathing their own bodies.
Regarding the phrase "by means of self-taming and tranquility" (*damūpasamena*):

here, "taming" (*dama*) is a name for the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth. For in the passage, "Tamed by truth, endowed with self-taming, having reached the end of knowledge, he has lived the holy life," it is the restraint of the sense faculties that is called "taming."
It has been said: "If truth, self-control, and generosity exist, is there anything found here superior to patience? In this context, wisdom is called "self-control.
In the passage, "By giving, by self-control, by restraint, and by speaking the truth," the Uposatha observance is called "self-control.
However, in this sutta, it should be understood that patience is "self-control. "Tranquility" (upasama) is a synonym for that very same thing.

397. Now, as for the Venerable Puṇṇa: who was this Puṇṇa, and why did he wish to go there? He was indeed a resident of Sunāparanta; however, having perceived that Sāvatthī was an unsuitable place for his dwelling, he wished to go there.
Herein is the account of the sequence of events: it is said that in a certain merchant village in the kingdom of Sunāparanta there were these two brothers.
Of them, sometimes the elder would take five hundred carts and, having gone to the countryside, would bring back goods; sometimes...

The youngest brother. On this occasion, however, having left the youngest at home, the eldest brother took five hundred carts and, wandering on a journey through the countryside, eventually reached Sāvatthī.
Having halted the caravan not far from the Jeta Grove, he ate his morning meal and, surrounded by his attendants, sat down in a comfortable spot.
At that time, the residents of Sāvatthī, having finished their morning meal and resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha,

with their upper robes purified and carrying perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, went out through the southern gate toward the Jetavana— leaning, inclining, and tending toward the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Seeing them, he asked, "Where are these people going?"
He questioned a certain man: "Noble sir, do you not know that the jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha have appeared in the world?
It is for this reason that these great crowds are going into the presence of the Teacher to hear the discourse on the Dhamma.
At the mere word "Buddha," it pierced through his skin and hide, and remained fixed, reaching right down to his bone marrow. Then, surrounded by his own retinue...
Having gone to the monastery together with that assembly, he stood at the edge of the gathering while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma in a sweet voice;
having heard the Dhamma, he conceived the desire for the going-forth.

Then, when the Tathāgata perceived the proper time and had dismissed the assembly, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, invited him for the following day’s meal, and on the second day prepared a pavilion.
Having had seats prepared and having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he partook of his morning meal, undertook the observance-day precepts, and summoned the treasurer.
After explaining everything—stating how much merchandise had been sold and how much had not—he said: "This property belongs to my younger brother."
Having surrendered everything with the words, "I give it all," he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and became devoted to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, as he applied his mind to the meditation subject, it did not manifest before him. Thereupon, he thought:
"This country is unsuitable for me; what if I were to take my meditation subject from the Teacher and return to my own place?"

“I shall go. Then, having wandered for alms in the morning and having emerged from seclusion in the evening, he approached the Blessed One, requested a meditation subject, uttered seven lion-roars, and departed.
Thus it is said: “Then the Venerable Puṇṇa… dwelt.”
But where did he dwell? He dwelt in four places. First, having entered the kingdom of Sunāparanta and reached the mountain named Ajjuhatthapabbata, he entered the village of merchants for alms.
Then his younger brother, recognizing him, gave him alms and, having made a promise that he should not go elsewhere but stay right there, had him reside in that very place.

From there, he went to the monastery named Samuddagirivihāra. There was a walking path (*caṅkama*) constructed there by carving it out of iron-stone (*ayakanta-pāsāṇa*), which no one at all was able to walk upon.

When the waves of the ocean came there and struck the iron-stones, they produced a great sound. The Elder [thought]: "This is a comfortable dwelling for those who are attending to their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)."
Saying, "Let it be so," he resolved that the ocean become silent.
From there, he went to the place called Mātulagiri. There, a great multitude of birds had gathered, and their noise was continuous day and night;
thinking this place was not conducive to comfort, the Elder went from there to the monastery called Makulakārāmavihāra.
This place was not too far from the merchant village, nor too near; it was accessible for coming and going, secluded, and free from noise.
The Elder, considering this spot to be comfortable, had night-quarters, day-quarters, and walking-paths constructed there and entered upon the rains retreat.
Thus he dwelt in four locations.
Then one day, during that very same rainy season, five hundred merchants loaded their goods onto a ship, intending to go to the other side of the ocean.

On the day they were boarding the ship, the Elder’s younger brother, having fed the Elder and received the precepts from him, paid his respects and departed, saying: "Venerable sir, the great ocean is indeed immeasurable."
"May you attend to us without any hindrance," he said, and then boarded the ship.
The ship, traveling with supreme speed, reached a certain island. Thinking, "We shall take our morning meal," the men disembarked on the island.
There was nothing else on that island; it consisted solely of a sandalwood forest.
Then one man, having struck the tree with an axe and recognized that it was red sandalwood, said:
"Sirs, we are going to the other sea for the sake of profit, but there is no profit greater than this;
a single block of wood even four finger-breadths thick is worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold. Let us take away as much merchandise as can be carried and fill our ship with this sandalwood. They—
They did so. The non-human beings dwelling in the Sandalwood Grove became angry and thought, "These men have destroyed our sandalwood grove;
we shall have them killed. Then they said, "If they are killed right here, the entire grove will become a single heap of corpses;
therefore, we shall sink their ship in the middle of the ocean. Thereupon, they boarded their ship.
Just a moment after he had departed, those non-human beings raised up a storm and manifested terrifying forms themselves.
Terrified, the people each paid homage to their own respective deities.
The Elder’s younger brother, the householder Cūḷapuṇṇa, stood paying homage to the Elder, thinking, "May my brother be my refuge."
The Elder, it is said, at that very moment directed his attention and, perceiving their impending calamity, leapt into the air and stood before them.
When the non-human beings saw the Elder, they departed, thinking, "Venerable Puṇṇa the Elder is coming," and the storm subsided.
The Elder comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid," and asked, "Where do you wish to go? "Venerable Sir," they replied.
“Let us go to our own place,” they said. The Elder stepped onto the boat’s stern and resolved, “May it go to the place desired by these people.
The merchants, having reached their own place, informed their wives and children of what had occurred, saying, “Come, let us go for refuge to the Elder.
Then five hundred of them, together with five hundred women of their own households, [went] to the three...
Having established themselves in the refuges, they declared themselves lay disciples (*upāsaka*).
Then, having unloaded the goods from the ship and set aside one portion for the Elder, they said, "Venerable sir, this is your portion.
The Elder replied, "I have no need for a separate portion; however, has the Teacher been seen by you? "He has not been seen before."
"Venerable sir," they replied. "In that case, build a circular pavilion for the Teacher; in this way you shall see the Teacher.
"Very well, venerable sir," they said, and with that portion and their own portions, they began to construct the circular pavilion.
It is said that from the time it was commenced, the Teacher made use of it. The guardian deities [perceived] a radiance at night.

Having seen this, they formed the perception that "there are deities of great power. When the lay disciples had completed the construction of the assembly hall and the lodgings for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and had prepared the requisites for the offering, they informed the Elder: "Venerable sir, we have performed our duty;
please invite the Teacher. At the time of evening, the Elder [went] to Sāvatthī by means of his supernormal power.
Having arrived, he requested the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, the inhabitants of the merchant village wish to see you; please have compassion for them.
The Blessed One consented. The Elder, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, returned to his own place.
The Blessed One then addressed the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, tomorrow we shall go for alms in the merchant village of Sunāparanta."

“Give a voting ticket (*salāka*) to four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus. The Elder replied, “Very well, venerable sir,” and after announcing the matter to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he said, “Let the bhikkhus who travel through the air take the voting tickets.

On that day, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna took the first voting ticket. Meanwhile, the inhabitants of the village of Vāṇija, thinking, “The Teacher will surely arrive tomorrow,” gathered in the middle of the village.

Having constructed a pavilion, they prepared the hall for almsgiving. The Blessed One, having attended to his body early in the morning, entered the Fragrant Chamber and sat down, having entered into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). Sakka’s stone seat of yellow silk became warm.
Wondering, "What is this?", he reflected and, seeing that the Teacher was going to Sunāparanta, addressed Vissakamma: "Dear son..."

“Today the Blessed One will go for alms as far as three hundred yojanas; therefore, construct five hundred gabled houses and place them ready for his departure at the gateway of the Jeta Grove. He did exactly so.
The gabled house for the Blessed One had four openings, those for the two chief disciples had two openings each, and the remaining ones had one opening each.
The Teacher emerged from the fragrant chamber and entered the foremost gabled hall among the series of halls that had been set out in order.
Beginning with the two chief disciples, the four hundred and ninety-nine monks also went into the hall and sat down.
There was one empty gabled hall remaining, and all five hundred gabled halls rose up into the air.
When the Teacher reached the mountain named Saccabandha, he placed his gabled pavilion in the air.
On that mountain lived a false-views ascetic named Saccabandha, who, having attained the pinnacle of gain and fame, resided there while instilling wrong views in the great multitude.
Yet, within him, like a lamp inside a jar, the underlying potential for Arahatship burned brightly.
Seeing him, [the monk] thought, "I shall teach him the Dhamma," and having gone there, he taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the ascetic attained Arahatship;

the higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to him by way of the Path itself. Having become an "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come, monk!), wearing robes and bowl produced through supernormal power, he entered the gabled house.
The Blessed One, together with five hundred bhikkhus who were staying in the gabled houses, went to the village of Vaṇijagāma;

having made the gabled houses invisible, he entered Vaṇijagāma. The merchants, having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, led the Teacher to the Makula Monastery. The Teacher entered the circular pavilion. The great multitude...

While the Teacher was allaying his fatigue from the meal, the man had his morning meal, undertook the factors of the Uposatha, and taking abundant perfumes and flowers, returned to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. The Teacher taught the Dhamma;
the release of the great multitude from their bonds occurred, and there was a great clamor regarding the Buddha.
The Teacher remained right there for several days for the sake of gathering the great multitude, but he took up residence for the dawn-watch in the Great Fragrant Chamber itself.

Having stayed there for several days and walked for alms in the merchant village, he dismissed the Elder Puṇṇa, saying, "You stay right here," and proceeded to the bank of the river named Nammadā that lies between. There, the Nammadā Nāga King—
Having gone out to meet the Teacher and led him into the Nāga abode, he paid honor to the Three Jewels.
After the Teacher had preached the Dhamma to him, he departed from the Nāga abode. He requested, "Venerable Sir, grant me something to attend upon.
The Blessed One showed him the Footprint Shrine on the bank of the Nammada River; it remains covered whenever the waves come in.
When he had passed away, his funeral rites were performed with great honor. The Teacher, departing from there, went to Mount Saccabandha and said to Saccabandha:
"By you, the great multitude has been led down the path to the states of misery;
therefore, remaining right here, cause them to abandon their false views and establish them on the path to Nibbāna. He, in turn, requested that he be allowed to attend upon the Teacher.
The Teacher displayed his footprint-relic as if carving an impression upon a moist lump of clay on a solid rock surface, and from there he went back to Jetavana.
It was with reference to this matter that it was said: "In that very same rainy season," and so forth.
"He attained final Nibbāna" means he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. For seven days, the great multitude [honored] the Elder.
Having performed the funeral rites for the body, having gathered much fragrant wood, and having cremated the body, he took the relics and erected a stupa.
"A number of bhikkhus" refers to the bhikkhus who were present at the elder’s cremation. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Puṇṇovāda Sutta is finished.
4. The commentary on the Nandakovāda Sutta:
"Thus have I heard... Regarding this, at that time the Blessed One [was staying with] Mahāpajāpatī...

Having requested the community of bhikkhunīs to depart and having assembled the community of bhikkhus, he placed the burden upon the Saṅgha by saying, "Let the elder bhikkhus exhort the bhikkhunīs in turn. It is with reference to this that it was said. In that context, "in turn" means by rotation.
"He does not wish [to do so]" means that when his own turn arrives, he either goes to a distant village or engages in needlework and such activities.

Having begun, he had him say, "This is indeed his conceptual proliferation (papañca). However, the Blessed One gave this instruction by way of a method specifically for the sake of the Elder Nandaka. Why?

Because when these bhikkhunīs see the Elder, their minds become one-pointed and they gain confidence; therefore, they are desirous of receiving his exhortation and desirous of hearing his discourse on the Dhamma.
Therefore, the Blessed One gave the instruction by turn, thinking, "When Nandaka’s turn arrives, he will give the exhortation and deliver a discourse on the Dhamma.
However, the Elder did not take his turn; why was that?
It is said that those bhikkhunīs had formerly been members of the harem when the Elder was ruling over Jambudīpa. The Elder, by means of his knowledge of past lives—

Knowing that reason, he thought: "Seeing me seated in the midst of this community of bhikkhunīs, expounding the Dhamma by bringing forth similes and reasons, another bhikkhu who has attained the knowledge of past lives might observe this circumstance and say:
'Venerable Nandaka does not release his harem even until today; this venerable one shines indeed.'"
"Or rather, one might think he should be said to be 'surrounded by a retinue. Seeing this point, the Elder did not take his turn.
And knowing that for these bhikkhunīs, a teaching from the Elder himself would be more suitable, the Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Nandaka.
To explain how those bhikkhunīs previously knew of his status as a member of the harem, this is the background story:
It is said that formerly in Bārāṇasī, a thousand people consisting of five hundred male slaves and five hundred female slaves lived together in one place, performing their work collectively.
At that time, this Elder Nandaka was the senior male slave, and Gotamī was the senior female slave.
She was the attendant upon the feet of the eldest slave; she was wise and capable. She would coordinate even a thousand laborers as they performed meritorious deeds.
Then, at the time of the entry into the rains retreat, five Paccekabuddhas descended from Mount Nandamūlaka to Isipatana.
Having wandered for alms in the city, they went back to Isipatana itself and said: "In the hut for the rains retreat..."
“Let us request manual labor for our benefit. Having put on their robes, they entered the city in the evening and stood at the gate of the merchant’s house.

The eldest female slave, taking a water-jar, was going to the watering-place when she saw the Paccekabuddhas entering the city. When the merchant heard the reason for their arrival, he said, “For us...”
“There is no space; let them go,” he said.
Then, as they were departing from the city, the eldest female slave saw them entering while carrying a water-pot;
she set down the pot, paid homage, bowed low, covered her face, and said: “The noble lady has only just entered the city and already departed; what indeed—”
He asked, “What is it? “We have come to request manual labor for the hut for the rainy-season retreat,” they replied. “Was it obtained, venerable sir? “It was not obtained, lay follower.
“But can this hut only be built by the wealthy, or can it also be built by the poor?
“It can be done by anyone. “Very well, venerable sir, we shall build it. Please accept alms from me tomorrow.”
Having invited them and led them to the water, she took a jar again and returned, standing on the path to the bathing place.
She said to the female slaves who had arrived, "Stay right here," and when they had all gathered, she asked:
"Sisters, will you always perform the work of another’s slave, or do you wish to be freed from the state of slavery? "We wish to be freed this very day, noble lady."
"If it is so, since I have invited five Paccekabuddhas for tomorrow's meal who received no manual labor, please give them a day’s work for yourselves," he said.
They agreed, saying "Very well," and when their husbands returned from the forest in the evening, they informed them.
The husbands agreed and gathered at the door of the eldest slave's house.
Then the eldest female slave, on the following day, explained the benefits, saying, "Sirs, give manual labor for the Paccekabuddhas.
She even coaxed those who were unwilling to do so with earnest exhortation and made them agree.
On the next day, after she had given food to the Paccekabuddhas, she gave instructions to all the sons of the slaves. They immediately entered the forest and gathered building materials.
Having gathered them together by the hundreds, they constructed individual huts, each with its own surrounding walkways and other facilities;

having set out beds, stools, drinking water, and vessels for food, they obtained the consent of the Paccekabuddhas to dwell there for three months and established a system of taking turns to provide alms.
On whichever day one was unable to provide for his turn, his eldest female slave would bring the provisions from her own home.
She gave them. Having thus tended [the fields] for three months, the senior female slave had each male slave provide a single garment.
There were five hundred coarse garments. Having exchanged them, she made three robes (*tricīvara*) for the five *paccekabuddhas* and gave them to them.
The *paccekabuddhas* departed for wherever was convenient. That thousand of men on foot also became virtuous together.
Having done so, upon the dissolution of his body, he was reborn in the world of the devas.
Those five hundred women were from time to time in the houses of those five hundred men, and from time to time they were all in the house of the eldest son of the slave alone.
Then, at one time, the eldest son of the slave passed away from the world of the devas and was reborn in a royal family.
Furthermore, those five hundred celestial maidens were reborn in families of great wealth and entered his household when he was established in his kingdom.
Wandering through the cycle of existence in this manner, they were reborn in noble kṣatriya families in the city of Koliya and the city of Devadaha at the time of our Blessed One.
The Elder Nandaka also went forth and attained Arahatship. Our eldest slave-girl’s daughter reached maturity and was established in the position of chief queen to King Suddhodana;
the other daughters likewise entered the households of various princes.
Their husbands, five hundred royal princes, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse during the "Water-Bag Quarrel" and went forth into homelessness. As for the princesses—

To cause them to become weary of the world, they sent a message to the Blessed One. When they were thus weary, the Blessed One led them to Kuṇāla Lake, established them in the fruit of stream-entry, and on the day of the Great Assembly, established them in Arahatship.
Those five hundred princesses also went forth under Mahāpajāpatī. This venerable Nandaka [taught] those bhikkhunīs up to that point.
In this way, this matter is to be illustrated.
"The royal park" (*rājakārāma*) is a monastery built by Pasenadi in the southern direction of the city, at a site similar to the Thūpārāma.
"Well-seen with right wisdom" (*sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ*) means seen according to its true nature through the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) by way of cause and reason.
401. *Tajjaṃ tajjan* means "of that same nature, of that same nature. In terms of meaning, however, it is said that those various feelings arise in dependence upon their respective conditions.
402. *Pagevassa chāyā* means that the shadow produced in dependence on the roots and so forth is impermanent even earlier [than the tree itself].
413. *Anupahacca* means "without having struck. In that context, one makes the flesh into a mass and attaches the skin to it.
"It damages the body of flesh" means: by binding the skin repeatedly and causing it to adhere to the flesh, one damages the body of flesh.
Without doing so [in that manner], "the flesh smeared over the sinews" refers specifically to the flesh that adheres and is spread over all the skin.
"The fetter and bond of internal defilements" is said with reference to all internal defilements whatsoever.
414. But why did he say, "These seven indeed"? For that wisdom which was described as cutting off defilements is not able to cut them by its own inherent nature alone.

Just as an axe does not cut what is to be cut by its own inherent nature, but cuts it only by depending on the appropriate effort of a person, so too [wisdom] cannot [function] without the six [factors].
Wisdom is able to cut off the defilements by means of the factors of enlightenment; therefore, he spoke thus. "For this reason" (*tena hi*) means:

because you have demonstrated the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six groups of consciousness, the simile of the island, the simile of the tree, and the simile of the oxen, and have brought the teaching to its conclusion through the destruction of the taints by means of the seven factors of enlightenment—for that reason.
“You yourself should exhort those bhikkhunīs with that very same exhortation.

415. “She is a stream-enterer”: she who is the last among them in terms of her qualities is a stream-enterer; the others, however, are once-returners, non-returners, and those whose taints are destroyed.
If this is so, how is it that they are said to have their intentions fulfilled? It is because of the fulfillment of their aspirations. For whichever [bhikkhunī]...

For it occurred to that bhikkhunī: "When indeed, while listening to the Venerable Nandaka’s teaching of the Dhamma, might I realize the fruit of stream-entry on this very seat? And she realized the fruit of stream-entry.
For whichever [bhikkhunī] had thought, "The fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship," she realized arahantship.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "They were both glad and fulfilled in their purpose.
The commentary on the *Nandakovāda Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is hereby concluded.
5. Commentary on the *Rāhulovāda Sutta* 416.

"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*. In that context, "states conducive to the ripening of liberation" (*vimuttiparipācanīya*) means those which bring about the ripening of liberation; thus they are called "conducive to the ripening of liberation.
"States" (*dhammā*) refers to fifteen states. These [are enumerated] by way of being the causes for the purification of the faculty of faith and the others.
It should be understood. For this has been said:

"By avoiding persons lacking faith, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons endowed with faith, and by reflecting upon discourses that inspire confidence—in these three ways the faculty of faith is purified. By [avoiding] persons who are indolent..."
By avoiding persons of slack energy, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who have aroused energy, and by reviewing the right exertions—
through these three modes, the faculty of energy is purified. By avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, by serving, associating with,
and attending upon persons of established mindfulness, and by reviewing the foundations of mindfulness— through these three modes, the faculty of mindfulness [is purified].

It is purified. By avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who are concentrated, and by reviewing the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and liberations (vimokkha), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified through these three modes.
By avoiding persons who lack wisdom, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons possessed of wisdom, and [by reflecting on] the practice of profound knowledge...
"For one who reflects, the faculty of wisdom becomes purified through these three aspects. Thus, for one who avoids these five types of persons, cultivates, frequents,
and attends upon these [other] five types of persons, and reflects upon these five aggregates of discourses,
these five faculties become purified through these fifteen modes."
Furthermore, there are fifteen states that ripen liberation: the five faculties beginning with faith;

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandonment, and the perception of dispassion—these five perceptions conducive to penetration;
and the five qualities beginning with spiritual friendship as taught to the Elder Meghiya. At what time, then?
"It occurred to the Blessed One" refers to when he was surveying the world at the time of dawn.

"Of many thousands of deities" refers specifically to those very deities who had made their aspiration together with the Venerable Rāhula while he was making his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during the time of the Nāga King Pālita.
Among them, some were earth-dwelling deities, some were sky-dwelling deities, some were born in the realm of the Four Great Kings, some in the world of the gods, and some in the Brahma-world.
On this day, however, they all assembled together in one place, namely, in the Andhavana grove.
Regarding the term "Dhammacakkhu" (the Eye of Dhamma), in the Upāli-ovāda and Dīghanakha Suttas, it is stated that the first path is called the Dhammacakkhu.
In the *Brahmāyu-sutta*, there are three fruits; in this sutta, it should be understood that there are four paths and four fruits known as the "Dhamma-eye.
For therein, some deities became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), non-returners (*anāgāmī*), and those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Furthermore, there is no limit to the number of these deities by way of calculation. The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Rāhulovāda Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 6.
Commentary on the Cha-chakka Sutta.

420. Thus have I heard: this is the Chachakka Sutta. Therein, "beautiful in the beginning" means I shall teach having made it beautiful, auspicious, and faultless at the outset. The same method applies to the middle and the end as well.
Thus the Blessed One praised the Noble Lineage with nine [stanzas], the Great Foundation of Mindfulness with seven, and the Great Horse-Race [Sutta] with exactly seven verses. This...
However, he praised the Sutta with nine terms.
"To be known" means they are to be understood by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). By the mind-base (*manāyatana*), only the consciousness of the three planes is spoken of;
by the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), external phenomena of the three planes are meant; and by the mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), [all are included] except for two.

The five types of sensory consciousness and the remaining twenty-two kinds of mundane resultant consciousness [constitute the "remainder"]. Contact and feeling are associated only with the aforementioned resultant consciousnesses.
"Craving" refers to the craving that arises at the moment of the impulsion (javana) conditioned by resultant feeling. 422.
"The eye is self" is a separate transition. This is for the purpose of demonstrating the non-self nature of the two truths explained previously.
This teaching has been commenced. In this context, "he does not re-arise" (na upapajjati) is not appropriate [as a literal negation]. "He passes away" (veti) means he departs, ceases.
"But this, monks,"—this is a separate connection (anusandhi).
For this teaching was commenced to show the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) by way of three graspings (gāha), and the origin of suffering (dukkha-samudaya) by way of two truths.
They say that this is also intended to show the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). In such passages as "This is mine," it should be understood as the grasping of craving, conceit, and views.
"He regards" means he sees by way of those three types of grasping.
Having thus shown the round of existence, [the text now proceeds] by way of the opposites of those three graspings, namely: cessation and the path.
Or, in order to show the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) by way of two truths, he said, "But this," and so forth.
"This is not mine," and so forth, are statements negating craving and the rest. "He contemplates" means he sees it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Having thus shown the turning away, he now says "The eye," etc., in order to show the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) again by way of the three underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
He said, "Bhikkhus," and so forth. Therein, "rejoices" and so on are stated by way of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*).
"Underlies" means it remains unabandoned. "Of suffering" refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) and the suffering of the defilements (*kilesa-dukkha*).
Having thus explained the round of existence by way of these three underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), he now explains the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*) by way of their rejection.
Showing this again, he said, "Furthermore, the eye... and so forth. "Having abandoned ignorance" means having abandoned the ignorance that is the root of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Having produced true knowledge" means having produced the knowledge of the path of Arhatship.
"It is possible" means that by this very method of discourse, the teaching, by way of both the round of existence and its unraveling, has reached its conclusion.
Having brought [the meaning] together again and showing it by summarizing that very point, he said: "Seeing thus, monks," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of about sixty monks," this is not surprising: that sixty monks attained arahantship while the Tathāgata himself was teaching.
For even when the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) was speaking this Sutta, sixty monks attained arahantship.
They attained it even while Mahāmoggallāna was speaking, and they attained it even while the eighty great elders were speaking;
this too is not surprising, for those disciples had attained the great higher knowledges (*mahābhiññā*).
Later, however, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the elder named Māleyyadeva [recited] this discourse at the lower Lohapāsāda.
He preached it. At that time as well, sixty bhikkhus attained arahantship. And just as he had done at the Lohapāsāda, the Elder preached this sutta at the Mahāmaṇḍapa as well.
Departing from the Mahāvihāra, he went to Cetiyapabbata, and there too he preached it.
Thence he went to the Sākiyavaṃsa Vihāra, the Kūṭāli Vihāra, Antarasobbha, Muttaṅgaṇa, Vātakapabbata, and Pācinaghara.
In Lokantare, he preached the Dīghavāpiya Sutta on the surface of the Nomaṇḍala lake. In those places as well, sixty monks in each attained *arahantship*.
Having departed from there, the Elder went to Cittalapabbata. At that time, in the Cittalapabbata monastery, there was a Great Elder of more than sixty years' standing;
in the lotus pond, there was a secluded spot known as the Kuruvaka Ford.
There was an elder who had gone down into the water thinking, "I shall bathe there. The deity-elder went up to him and said, "Venerable sir, I shall wash you.
The elder, through mere courtesy, thought, "They say there is one named Māleyyadeva;
this must be he," and knowing this, he said, "Are you Deva? "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "Friend, I have been a lay follower for sixty years..."
No one was even permitted to touch his body with their hand; however, [the king] said, "Please bathe him," and having stepped out, sat down on the bank.
The elder performed all the preliminary services, such as massaging his hands and feet, and bathed the great elder. That day happened to be a day for hearing the Dhamma.
Then the great elder said, "Your Majesty, it is fitting that you give us the gift of the Dhamma. The elder replied, "Very well."
"Venerable Sir," they replied. When the sun had set, they announced the recitation of the Dhamma.
Sixty great elders, each of whom was already over sixty years of age, went for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. At the conclusion of his formal recitation, the Elder Deva began this Sutta;
and at the conclusion of the Sutta, the sixty great elders attained Arahatship. Then [they went] to the Tissamahāvihāra.
Having gone there, he taught, and sixty elders were present there as well. Then he went to the Nāgamahāvihāra in the village of Kāḷakaccha and taught there;
sixty elders were present there as well. Then, having gone to Kalyāṇī, he taught on the fourteenth day in the lower palace;
sixty elders were present there as well. On the Uposatha day, he taught in the upper palace; sixty elders were present there as well.
Thus, while the Elder Devatthera was preaching this sutta, sixty people attained arahantship at each of the sixty locations.
However, while the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga was preaching this sutta at the Ambila-Kāḷaka Vihāra, the human assembly extended for a *gāvuta* and the divine assembly for a *yojana*.
At the conclusion of the sutta, one thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship.
Among the gods, however, there was only one worldling (puthujjana) here and there.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Chachakka Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
7. Commentary on the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta 428.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta. In this context, *mahāsaḷāyatanika* means a discourse on the Dhamma that illuminates the six great sense-bases (*āyatana*).
429. “Not knowing” means not knowing by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). “They go to accumulation” means they go to growth.
The meaning is: "they attain mastery. "Bodily" refers to the distress of the five sense doors. "Mental" refers to the distress of the mind door.
The same method applies to "torment" and so forth. 430.
"Bodily pleasure" is pleasure of the five sense doors. "Mental pleasure" is pleasure of the mind door. And here, by means of the five-door javana...
There is neither entering nor emerging; it exists merely as something that has arisen. Everything occurs by way of the mind-door.
And this powerful insight, which serves as the condition for emergence from the path, also occurs solely by way of the mind-door.
"One who has become such" means one who possesses mental pleasure associated with a wholesome state of consciousness. "But previously indeed for him... [the rest follows].
For that bhikkhu, the vocal action, the mental action, and the livelihood are called "previously purified," meaning they have been completely pure from the very beginning.
However, the five factors consisting of right view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration are called the "factors that must be practiced at all times.
Thus, the supramundane path consists of either eight factors or seven factors.
The caviller, however, taking this very passage from the Sutta—“Whatever view one has of things as they really are”—claims that “the supramundane path is five-factored.
He is to be refuted by the immediately following statement: “In this way, this noble eightfold path reaches fulfillment through development.
Furthermore, he should be convinced as follows: “The supramundane path...”

There is no such thing as a "five-factored" [path] per se; rather, these five factors, which are the causes for performing [the path] everywhere, fulfill their function by way of abstinence at the moment of the Path.
For among the abstentions described as "abstinence from the four types of verbal misconduct," one abandons wrong speech and develops right speech.
When one thus develops right speech, these five factors do not exist apart from it.

They fulfill [the path] together with that very abstinence. The same method applies to right action and right livelihood as well. Thus, from the beginning, verbal actions and the rest must be entirely pure.
However, since these five factors fulfill [the path] by way of abstinence (*virati*), there is no such thing as a "five-factored path. This is also stated in the Subhadda Sutta: "In whatever..."
"Subhadda, in this Dhamma and Vinaya, there is the Noble Eightfold Path. Furthermore, in many hundreds of other suttas, it is the eightfold path alone that is taught.
As for the "four foundations of mindfulness," these are the four foundations of mindfulness associated with the path. The same applies to the right efforts and so forth.

The same method applies here. "Coupled together" (*yuganandhā*) means simultaneous coupling in a single moment; otherwise, there would be attainment in one moment and insight in another, thus they would be of different moments.
However, in the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), they are simultaneous.
"True knowledge and liberation" (*vijjā ca vimutti ca*) refers to the true knowledge of the path of Arahantship and the liberation that is its fruit. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 8.
The commentary on the Nagaravindeyya Sutta.

435. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ*: thus was it heard by me; this is the Nagara-vindeyya Sutta. Therein, "they move on even and uneven ground" means that at times they move on even ground, and at times on uneven ground. "Even conduct is also the cause" means that indeed, even conduct is the reason for this.
437. "What are the modes? means what are the causes? "What are the sequences? means what are the subsequent realizations?

But why did he say, "there is nothing there," when in the forest there are indeed the five strands of sensual pleasure—forms and so forth—which are exceedingly delightful by way of green grass, campaka groves, and the like?
"Is it? "No, it is not. But this was not said with reference to the forest grove; rather, it was said with reference to the forms of women and so forth.
For those things remain having completely seized the mind of a man. As it has been said:
"Monks, I do not see even a single form that remains having completely seized the mind of a man as much as this [form of a woman]."
“Monks, it is the form of a woman. Monks, the form of a woman stands obsessing the mind of a man.
This should be expanded in full. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Nagaravindeyya Sutta* is finished.
9. The commentary on the *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta*. Therein, "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means from the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
