"Serene" (*vippasannāni*) is said with reference to the physical basis (*okāsa*). For when one has emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), the physical basis established by the five sense-faculties (*pasāda*) becomes serene, and the complexion of the skin is purified. Therefore, he spoke thus.

"By dwelling in emptiness" (*suññatavihārena*) means by dwelling in the attainment of the fruition of emptiness. "The dwelling of the Great Man" (*mahāpurisavihāra*) refers to [the state] of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Tathāgatas, and the Great Disciples.

This is the dwelling place of the Great Beings. Regarding the passage beginning with "By whichever path I [went]," from the monastery up to the threshold pillar (*indakhīla*) of the village is called the "entered path" (*paviṭṭhamagga*);
from entering the village, walking through the sequence of houses, until exiting by the city gate, this is called the "path to be traversed" (*caritabbapadesa*);
and from outside the threshold pillar back to the monastery, this is the "returned path" (*paṭikkantamagga*).
"Or repulsion in the mind": this refers to whether or not there exists any kind of defilement that strikes against the mind.
"Training day and night": by one who trains throughout both the day and the night.
Regarding the passage beginning "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?", the reflection of one bhikkhu is different from that of various other bhikkhus.

"Reviewing is diversity. How so? A certain bhikkhu, having returned from his almsround after the meal and put away his bowl and robes, sits in a secluded place and reviews: "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?
Knowing that they have not been abandoned, he exerts energy and, by means of the path of non-returning, eradicates the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Immediately after the path comes the fruit, and immediately after the fruit comes the path; emerging from that, one who reviews understands: "They have been abandoned.
This same method applies to the hindrances and so forth. However, it is by means of the path of Arahantship that their abandoning and so on occur;
thus, there is a variety of reviewing for a single bhikkhu. Among these various types of reviewing, another bhikkhu...
One reflects on one [thing], another on one; thus there is a variety of reflections among various bhikkhus.
The rest is clear throughout.
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdani*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Indriyabhāvanāsutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Indriyabhāvanāsutta. Therein, "at Gajaṅgalā" means in a town of that name.
"Suveḷuvana" means a great forest thicket covered with a certain species of bamboo called suveḷu; he dwells there.

"He does not see a form with the eye, he does not hear a sound with the ear" is said with the intention of teaching that a form should not be seen with the eye and a sound should not be heard with the ear.

"Otherwise, there would be no discipline for the Noble One"—by this statement, the Blessed One established a foundation for the purpose of explaining the peerless development of the faculties within his own teaching.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, "The Teacher has shown the foundation; come now, let me cause a discourse on the development of the faculties to be delivered to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in this assembly," made a request to the Teacher regarding this.
The Blessed One said, beginning with “Bhagavā...”. Then, while explaining the development of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*) to him, the Blessed One said, beginning with “Then, Ānanda...”.
454. Likewise, as for this so-called equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), it is peaceful, it is sublime;
the meaning is that it is not tormenting. Thus, this bhikkhu, even regarding a visible object at the eye-door—whether the object is desirable and pleasing, or undesirable...
Regarding the unpleasant, and regarding neutral objects as well as pleasant and unpleasant ones, one does not allow the mind to become attached, repelled, or deluded;
rather, having encompassed them, one establishes insight into neutrality. "One with eyes" means one whose eyes are possessed of purified vision.
For one afflicted by eye disease, the upward opening and closing of the eyes is not possible; therefore, such a person is not included.
456. “Slightly bent” means standing having risen up like a chariot-pole. 461.

Regarding the phrases “perceiving the repulsive in the repulsive,” and so forth: one dwells perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive either by suffusing it with loving-kindness (*mettā*) or by resolving it according to the elements (*dhātu*).
One dwells perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive by suffusing it with the foul (*asubha*) or by resolving it as impermanent (*anicca*).
Or he dwells perceiving the repulsive. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Having avoided both of these, what does one who wishes to dwell in equanimity do? When desirable and undesirable objects come into range, he is neither glad nor sad.
For this has been said: "How does one dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive? Toward an undesirable object, he pervades it with loving-kindness (*mettā*)."
Or he brings it to mind by way of its elements; thus one dwells perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive?
One applies the meditation on the foul (*asubha*) to a desirable object, or one brings it to mind as impermanent;
thus one dwells perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive?
How does he dwell? Toward both an undesirable and a desirable object, he either pervades it with loving-kindness (*mettā*) or resolves it by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
Thus, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive. How does he dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the non-repulsive and the repulsive?
Toward both a desirable and an undesirable object, he pervades it with the perception of foulness (*asubha*).
Or he brings it to mind as impermanent; thus he dwells perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive.
How does he dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the unrepulsive?
Here, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad; he dwells equanimous...
“He dwells mindful and clearly comprehending… [and so on] … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad;
he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Thus, avoiding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.”
And among these three methods: in the first method, what is agreeable, disagreeable, and both agreeable-and-disagreeable—whether defiled or undefiled—is applicable.
In the second method, the defiled is applicable; in the third method, both the defiled and the undefiled are applicable.
Again it is said: "In the first [method], the defiled is applicable; in the second, both the defiled and the undefiled; in the third..."
“Only the absence of defilement is appropriate. The remainder is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Indriyabhāvanā-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The Commentary on the Latter Fifty [Discourses] is finished.
And this [work], because it was begun with the words, "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the exposition of the root of all phenomena," is good in the beginning;
It is "good in the middle" because of the statement in the middle: "Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla";
and it is "good in the end" because of the statement at the conclusion: "The Noble One with developed faculties.
Thus the Majjhima Nikāya is called "the Great Insight," being good in these three ways.
Thus it is completed by way of description.
And at this point— the concluding discourse:
It was requested by the wise elder, the venerable Buddhamitta,
who formerly lived together with me in the city of Mayūradūta.
[This is the commentary] on the *Paravādavidhaṃsana*, the most excellent work of the *Majjhimanikāya*.
I have begun to compose this sub-commentary (*maṭṭhakathā*) on the *Papañcasūdanī*.
For this work has been completed by extracting the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*),
covering one hundred and seven recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) of the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Since the *Visuddhimagga* also consists of fifty-nine recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) because it was composed for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of the scriptures, this commentary,
together with it, according to the method of counting verses, is as follows:
It should be understood that there are one hundred and sixty-six recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).
This [work], measuring one hundred and sixty-six [sections] by way of recitation sections,
elucidates the *Samaya* (the Vinaya) for those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra.
By me, who has composed this work taking the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā* as my guide,
whatever wisdom has been accumulated thereby, may the world always be happy.
[This was written] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as moral conduct, right behavior, integrity, and gentleness.
To the Great Poet, the foremost of debaters who speaks with words that are appropriate, excellent, sweet, noble, and radiant—words flowing forth from the bliss produced by perfection of expression;

who is endowed with the analytical discernment of wisdom capable of penetrating and immersing himself in his own tradition and the traditions of others; who possesses unimpeded power of knowledge within the Teacher’s Dispensation, including the Tipiṭaka scriptures together with their commentaries;
who is adorned with the various qualities such as the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and surrounded by the four analytical insights (*catuppaṭisambhidā*).
This is the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya entitled the *Papañcasūdanī*, composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa—

so called by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsī Elders, who were lamps of the Elder tradition and possessed wisdom firmly established in the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), and whose wisdom was vast and pure.
May he remain in the world for as long as there are seekers of the way across the world,
showing to sons of noble family the method for the purification of views—
even the mere name "Buddha" belongs to that pure-minded Tathāgata.
"In the world, for the World-Chief, the Great Seer,
there is activity. Thus ends in every respect the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.
